title: Proposition 13.28.11
text: Proposition 13.28.11 . 03E01F83CA7A For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$, 2C63A2647FAC 13.28.12 \begin{equation}  \inf _{a\in \mathcal A_+(Y,\theta )}d_\theta (u,a) =d_\theta (u,P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I})=\tau (u). \end{equation} On ordinary models, $p\mapsto P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ is a $1$-Lipschitz retraction onto the ideal models, and $P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ is the unique ideal model nearest to $p$. There are $a_ j\in \mathcal A_+(Y,\theta )$ with $d_\theta (u,a_ j)\to 0$ if and only if $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. Proof. The ideal envelope of $u$ is $q_{D_ u}$, by lemma 20.3.20 . For any positive atomic measure $E$ of mass at most $A$, the nonatomic measure $\sigma _ u$ and the signed atomic measure $D_ u-E$ are mutually singular. Thus ( 13.28.5 ) gives 57E1FB41A4EB 13.28.13 \begin{equation}  d_\theta (u,q_ E)=\tau (u)+\| D_ u-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Among ideal models, the minimum is attained exactly at $E=D_ u$. Since the analytic models of positive mass are dense among the ideal models (corollary 13.28.7 ), this gives ( 13.28.12 ). Taking the atomic part does not increase total variation, which proves the Lipschitz assertion. Finally, lemma 13.28.1 shows that $P_\theta [u]=p_{\mu _ u}$ equals $q_{D_ u}=p_{D_ u}$ if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$, that is, $\tau (u)=0$. $\square$

title: Example 13.28.14
text: Example 13.28.14 . 730582377A86 There is an ordinary model $p$ on $Y$ with zero mass whose multiplier ideals $\mathcal I(tp)$ are trivial for every $t>0$. It satisfies \[  P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}=0,\qquad \inf _{a\in \mathcal A_+(Y,\theta )}d_\theta (p,a)=A.  \] Proof. Choose a compact real interval inside a coordinate disk. Construct a binary Cantor set $K$ in it: at level $k$ there are $2^ k$ pairwise disjoint intervals of length $r_ k=\exp (-4^{k+1})$, each containing its two children of level $k+1$, and $K$ is the intersection of the unions over all levels. Let $\sigma $ be the probability measure on $K$ assigning mass $2^{-k}$ to each interval of level $k$. It has no atoms. Put $u(x)=A\int _ YG(x,y)\, \mathrm{d}\sigma (y)$, so that $T_ u=A\sigma $. On the chosen compact coordinate disk, $G(x,y)\leq \log |x-y|^2+C$ for a fixed constant $C$. For $x\in K$, integrating over the interval of level $k$ containing $x$, and using $G\leq 0$ elsewhere, gives \[  u(x)\leq A2^{-k}(2\log r_ k+C)\longrightarrow -\infty .  \] Thus $u=-\infty $ on $K$, while $u$ is smooth off $K$, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=-\theta $ there. Hence $K$ is polar, $\mu _ u=A\sigma $ and $U(u)=0$. By lemma 13.28.1 , $p=P_\theta [u]$ has the same polar curvature. Since this measure already has mass $A$, we get $T_ p=T_ u$, and therefore $p=u-\sup _ Yu$. The Lelong numbers of $p$ vanish because $\sigma $ has no atoms, so all its multiplier ideals are trivial and its ideal envelope is zero. Finally $\tau (p)=A$, which gives the distance by ( 13.28.12 ). $\square$

title: 13.28.15 The ordinary-type topology on a curve
search_title: The ordinary-type topology on a curve
text: We now compare the polar metric with the topology on ordinary singularity types introduced in section 18.8 . That topology also uses the ordinary envelope, but it measures the total variation only of the atomic part of the curvature. On ideal models the atomic part is the whole polar measure, so the two topologies agree there. On arbitrary ordinary models, diffuse polar mass can concentrate without being detected by the atomic total variation. We keep $Y$, $\theta $, $A$ and the decomposition $\mu _ u=D_ u+\sigma _ u$, and we use $\eta =\theta /A$ for $L^1$ norms. Let $\mathfrak S(Y,\theta )=\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )/{\sim }$ be the space of ordinary singularity types, and write $[u]$ for the class of $u$. Recall from proposition 18.8.4 that $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ is the uniform topology on $\mathfrak S(Y,\theta )$ generated by the $L^1$ distances between ordinary envelopes and between ideal envelopes, by the total variation of divisorial Lelong numbers on each fixed modification, and by the controlled ideal relations $\mathcal U(t,a)$ of ( 18.8.3 ). For ordinary classes put D1D81F67E5DB 13.28.16 \begin{equation}  d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta ([u],[v]) =\| P_\theta [u]-P_\theta [v]\| _{L^1(\eta )} +\| D_ u-D_ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Theorem 13.28.17 . 1BAAC809D02C The finite pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ induces $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ on $\mathfrak S(Y,\theta )$. For $0\leq s\leq A$, the classes of ideal models \[  \mathcal C_ s=\{ [q_ D]:D\text{ positive atomic},\  D(Y)\leq s\}   \] form a complete metric space both for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ and for the distance $\| D-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}$ between $[q_ D]$ and $[q_ E]$, and these two metrics induce the same topology. The space $\mathcal C_ s$ is not totally bounded if $s>0$, and $\mathcal C_0=\{ [0]\} $. Proof. A smooth compact modification of a smooth curve is an isomorphism, and the divisor weight of a point is one. Hence the divisorial distance in proposition 18.8.4 is exactly the atomic total variation, and the two summands of ( 13.28.16 ) are among the coordinates defining $\tau _{\theta ,0}$. Conversely, suppose that a net $[u_ j]$ converges to $[u]$ for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $. The ideal envelope of $u$ is $q_{D_ u}$, by lemma 20.3.20 . Convergence of the atomic parts in total variation implies $L^1$ convergence of these envelopes, by theorem 13.28.4 , theorem 13.28.8 . These results also apply to nets: the map $D\mapsto q_ D$ goes between metric spaces, so sequential continuity is equivalent to continuity. It remains to check the controlled ideal relations. At a point $x$ with local coordinate $z$, the multiplier ideals on the curve are \[  \mathcal I(tu)_ x=(z^{\lfloor tD_ u(\{ x\} )\rfloor }).  \] This follows from theorem 5.37.3 , lemma 5.37.1 : on a smooth curve the Lelong number at $x$ determines the ideal, and the logarithmic germ with that Lelong number has the displayed ideal. Write $D_ j=D_{u_ j}$ and $D=D_ u$, and fix $t>0$ and $a>1$. The set $F=\{ x:D(\{ x\} )\geq 1/(2t)\} $ is finite. At its points, $aD_ j(\{ x\} )\geq D(\{ x\} )$ and $aD(\{ x\} )\geq D_ j(\{ x\} )$ eventually. Outside $F$, the bound \[  \sup _ x|D_ j(\{ x\} )-D(\{ x\} )|\leq \| D_ j-D\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow 0  \] makes both $\mathcal I(tu)_ x$ and $\mathcal I(tu_ j)_ x$ unit ideals for large $j$. Hence both inclusions in ( 18.8.3 ) hold eventually at every point. This proves that $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ induces $\tau _{\theta ,0}$. The map $D\mapsto q_ D$ is injective, so $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ is a metric on $\mathcal C_ s$. The positive atomic measures of mass at most $s$ are closed in total variation: a limit is positive, satisfies the mass bound, and is carried by the countable union of the sets of atoms of the sequence. Completeness of the space of finite signed measures therefore gives completeness for total variation. A $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal C_ s$ is Cauchy in total variation; its limit is again atomic, and theorem 13.28.8 gives convergence of the envelope coordinate. This proves completeness for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ as well as the equality of the two topologies. If $s>0$, fix $0<b\leq s$ and infinitely many distinct points $x_ j$. The measures $b\delta _{x_ j}$ have pairwise total-variation distance $2b$, so $\mathcal C_ s$ is not totally bounded for either metric. For $s=0$ only the zero measure remains. $\square$ By lemma 20.3.20 , for $0\leq \delta \leq A$ the set $\mathcal C_{A-\delta }$ consists exactly of the classes of ideal models of mass at least $\delta $. The whole set $\mathcal C_ A$, including the models of zero mass, is complete. Its subset of positive mass is incomplete: for a point $x$, the measures $D_ j=A(1-1/j)\delta _ x$ form a Cauchy sequence whose limit $A\delta _ x$ has zero mass. For general ordinary classes, the corresponding statement concerns a pseudometric. Put \[  \mathcal G_{\theta ,\delta } =\left\{ [u]:P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I},\quad \int _ Y\mathrm{MA}_\theta (P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I})\geq \delta \right\} .  \] For $0\leq \delta \leq A$ this set is complete for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $, since every class $[u]$ in it is at distance zero from $[q_{D_ u}]\in \mathcal C_{A-\delta }$; limits need not be unique as ordinary classes. The set is not totally bounded when $\delta <A$. At $\delta =A$ the pseudometric vanishes identically on it, although it contains distinct classes by proposition 18.10.1 . The union of these sets over all $\delta >0$ is incomplete, by the same one-atom sequence.

title: 13.28.18 Concentration of diffuse polar curvature
text: The atomic total variation cannot be omitted from theorem 13.28.17 . On $\mathbb P^1$ with its Fubini–Study form $\theta $ of area one, fix a rational $0<\tau <1$ and take the atomic probability measures $\nu _ j$ and the ideal models $r_ j=P_\theta [(1-\tau )q_ j]_{\mathcal I}$ of proposition 18.6.6 , choosing the rational approximations so that the largest atom of $\nu _ j$ tends to zero. The ordinary and ideal envelopes of $r_ j$ both tend to zero in $L^1$, and for each $t>0$ and $a>1$, the pair $([r_ j],[0])$ eventually lies in $\mathcal U(t,a)$. The currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r_ j$ converge weakly to $\theta $. Nevertheless, \[  d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta ([r_ j],[0]) \geq \| D_{r_ j}\| _{\mathrm{TV}}=1-\tau >0.  \] Thus these weaker conditions do not imply convergence for $\tau _{\theta ,0}$, even at a fixed positive mass. The opposite difficulty concerns diffuse polar mass: the pseudometric controls the ordinary envelope in $L^1$, but not the total variation of the diffuse measure itself. Proposition 13.28.19 . 4651CC70BDA5 For the Fubini–Study form $\theta $ of area one on $\mathbb P^1$, the space $(\mathfrak S(\mathbb P^1,\theta ),d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta )$ is incomplete. In fact, there is a $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence without limit consisting of ordinary models of one fixed positive non-pluripolar mass, all with trivial multiplier ideals. Proof. Choose a nonatomic polar probability measure $\sigma $ with compact support in an affine chart, using the Cantor construction in example 13.28.14 . Fix $0<c<1$ and a point $x$ in that chart. Translating and shrinking the support towards $x$ gives nonatomic polar probability measures $\sigma _ j$ supported in disks about $x$ with radii tending to zero. Let $p_ j=p_{c\sigma _ j}$ be the ordinary models of lemma 13.28.1 . Their polar measures are $c\sigma _ j$, their masses are $1-c$, and $D_{p_ j}=0$. Hence their Lelong numbers vanish, their multiplier ideals are trivial, and their ideal envelopes are zero. We claim that $p_ j\to q_{c\delta _ x}$ in $L^1$. Write $q_ y=q_{c\delta _ y}$. Rotations of $\mathbb P^1$ preserving $\theta $ and sending $x$ to $y$ can be chosen to depend continuously on $y$ near $x$. They transport $q_ x$ to $q_ y$, so continuity of translations in $L^1$ gives $q_ y\to q_ x$ in $L^1$ as $y\to x$. Set \[  w_ j=\int _{\mathbb P^1}q_ y\, \mathrm d\sigma _ j(y).  \] The common $L^1$ bound for normalized potentials makes this integral well defined. The function $w_ j$ is nonpositive, its curvature current dominates $c\sigma _ j$, and $w_ j\to q_ x$ in $L^1$. By ( 13.28.3 ), $p_ j$ is the upper envelope of all $v\leq 0$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq c\sigma _ j$, so $w_ j\leq p_ j$. By normalized compactness, every subsequence of $p_ j$ has a further subsequence converging in $L^1$ to some $v\leq 0$. The inequalities $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_ j\geq c\sigma _ j$ pass to the limit and give $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq c\delta _ x$. Since $q_ x=p_{c\delta _ x}$, the same envelope description gives $v\leq q_ x$. The lower bound $w_ j\leq p_ j$ gives $v\geq q_ x$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. This identifies every cluster point and proves the claim. Since $P_\theta [p_ j]=p_ j$ and $D_{p_ j}=0$, the classes $[p_ j]$ form a $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence. A limit $[v]$ would satisfy $D_ v=0$ and $P_\theta [v]=q_ x$. This is impossible: the ordinary envelope preserves all multiplier ideals and hence all atoms, whereas $q_ x$ has an atom of mass $c$ at $x$. The sequence therefore has no limit in $\mathfrak S(\mathbb P^1,\theta )$. $\square$ On ordinary models, $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ and the topology of the polar metric $d_\theta $ are also different. Choose the Cantor support of $\sigma $ inside a positive real interval in the affine coordinate $z$, away from zero. The rotations $R_ j(z)=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\varepsilon _ j}z$, with $0<\varepsilon _ j\to 0$, move this support off itself. Put $p=p_{c\sigma }$ and $\widetilde p_ j=p\circ R_ j^{-1}$. By rotation invariance of the envelope, the $\widetilde p_ j$ are ordinary models with polar measures $c(R_ j)_*\sigma $, which have no atoms. Continuity of rotations in $L^1$ yields $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta ([\widetilde p_ j],[p])\to 0$, whereas the polar measures have disjoint supports, so $d_\theta (\widetilde p_ j,p)=2c$ by theorem 13.28.4 . Conversely, polar total variation controls both terms of ( 13.28.16 ), by theorem 13.28.8 . Thus $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ is strictly weaker than the polar metric topology on ordinary models, although the two agree on ideal models. The failure of continuity under smooth gauge changes with a fixed zero obstacle (proposition 18.11.2 ) gives a further difference: the polar metric is invariant under such changes, by section 13.29 .

title: 13.28.20 Convergence for all obstacles
text: We keep the compact curve $Y$ and its positive form $\theta $ of area $A$. The topology $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ of 18.12 is generated by the topologies $\tau _{\theta ,F}$ for all smooth obstacles $F$, in which the ordinary and ideal envelopes below $F$ replace those below zero. On a curve the envelopes below $F$ are still determined by the polar measure, and their ideal counterparts by its atomic part. This gives a description of $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ by a single pseudometric and allows a comparison with polar total variation. Choose, as in proposition 18.12.1 , a countable family $\{ F_ k\} _{k\geq 1}\subset C^\infty (Y,\mathbb R)$ that is dense for the uniform norm, with $F_1=0$. Write $d_{O,F}$ and $d_{I,F}$ for the $L^1$ distances between the ordinary envelopes $P_{\theta ,F}[\cdot ]$ and between the ideal envelopes $P_{\theta ,F}[\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$, which define $\tau _{\theta ,F}$ (section 18.8 ), and put 0B5C0EA6F405 13.28.21 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta ([u],[v]) & =\| D_ u-D_ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\\ & \quad +\sum _{k=1}^\infty 2^{-k}\bigl (\min \{ 1,d_{O,F_ k}([u],[v])\} \\ & \qquad \qquad +\min \{ 1,d_{I,F_ k}([u],[v])\} \bigr ). \end{split} \end{equation} Proposition 13.28.22 . E7DAF71126F6 The pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ induces the uniformity of $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $. Two classes have distance zero if and only if they have the same polar curvature. The closure of the analytic classes is $\{ [u]:\mu _ u=D_ u\} =\mathcal G_\theta $, where $\mathcal G_\theta =\{ [u]:P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\} $ as in ( 18.9.2 ). On each set $\mathcal C_ s$, $0\leq s\leq A$, the pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ is a complete metric inducing the topology of total variation of the atomic measures. On ordinary models, polar total variation implies convergence for $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $. Proof. Step 1: envelopes below an obstacle. For any smooth $F$, translating the competitors by $F$ gives \[  P_{\theta ,F}[u]-F=P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[u-F],  \] and likewise for the ideal envelope. The background $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F$ on the right is a smooth real form of area $A$, though it need not be positive. We claim that these two envelopes are the models of $\mu _ u$ and of $D_ u$, respectively, in that background, in the sense of proposition 13.29.1 . Set $\mu =\mu _ u$ and let $w_\mu $ be its Green potential, and put $r=P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[w_\mu -F]$. By the gauge bounds of proposition 18.5.1 , $r+F$ differs from $P_\theta [w_\mu ]=p_\mu \sim w_\mu $ by a bounded function, so $r\sim w_\mu -F$. Hence $r=P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[r]$ is an ordinary model, and its polar measure is $\mu $. Moreover $u-F\preceq r$, and both have mass $A-\mu (Y)$. If this mass is positive, corollary 13.19.8 , applied in the big background $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F$, shows that $P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[u-F]=r$. If it is zero, the curvature measures of $u-F$ and $w_\mu -F$ both equal $\mu $, so these functions differ by a constant, and again $P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[u-F]=r$. The assertion for the ideal envelope follows in the same way from ideal projection and the classification of atomic models. It also follows that the envelope $P_{\theta ,F}[u]$ is the upper envelope of all $v\leq F$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \mu $. Step 2: the uniformity. By proposition 13.29.1 , polar total variation gives $L^1$ convergence of these models for every fixed $F$. The same assertion for atomic measures gives continuity of every ideal-envelope coordinate with respect to the total variation of the atomic parts. The controlled ideal relations are also implied, uniformly, by atomic total variation: for fixed $t>0$ and $a>1$, the bound $\| D-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}<(a-1)/(at)$ guarantees both inclusions in ( 18.8.3 ), by the formula for multiplier ideals on a curve. Indeed, if $tE(\{ x\} )\geq 1$, the bound gives $aD(\{ x\} )>E(\{ x\} )$; otherwise the target ideal is the unit ideal. Interchange $D$ and $E$ for the other inclusion. Each divisorial coordinate is the atomic total variation. Therefore the envelope terms in the series, together with the atomic term, generate exactly the uniformity of $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $: finitely many coordinates control the sum up to its uniformly small tail, and the sum controls each fixed coordinate. Step 3: zero distance and analytic closure. By Step 1 with $F=0$, distance zero forces equal polar measures; the classification at every obstacle proves the converse. The same classification shows that the ordinary and ideal envelopes agree at every $F$ if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$. Hence theorem 18.12.3 identifies the closure of the analytic classes. Step 4: the sets $\mathcal C_ s$. For a $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal C_ s$, the atomic measures converge in total variation to a measure of mass at most $s$, which is again atomic. The convergence of models in Step 2 gives convergence of every obstacle coordinate, and the summable tail then gives convergence for $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $. Conversely, convergence for $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ implies convergence of the atomic parts, because of the first summand. This proves completeness and the equality of topologies on $\mathcal C_ s$. Finally, polar total variation controls the atomic part and all ordinary-envelope coordinates, which proves the last assertion. $\square$ On a curve, membership in the relative envelope class of the ideal envelope has the same polar criterion, including for ideal envelopes of zero mass. Corollary 13.28.23 . 017BC9CAC896 For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ put $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. The following are equivalent: \[  \begin{gathered} u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q),\qquad \mu _ u=D_ u,\\ P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I},\\ P_{\theta ,F}[u]=P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \quad \text{for every smooth real }F. \end{gathered}  \] This also holds when $D_ u(Y)=A$, that is, when $q$ has zero mass. Proof. The classifications of ordinary and ideal models in lemma 13.28.1 , lemma 20.3.20 show that $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$. Step 1 of the proof of proposition 13.28.22 shows that this is equivalent to equality of the envelopes at every smooth obstacle. Membership of $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q)$ implies the latter by proposition 18.12.2 . Conversely, assume that $\mu _ u=D_ u$. By lemma 20.3.20 , $\mu _ q=D_ u$. Ordinary equivalence preserves polar curvature by corollary 5.27.15 , so every potential equivalent to $q$ has non-pluripolar mass $A-D_ u(Y)$, by Stokes' theorem. Hence \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q)=A-D_ u(Y).  \] If $D_ u(Y)<A$, then $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, and proposition 13.24.2 puts $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q)$. If $D_ u(Y)=A$, the positive curvature measures $T_ u$ and $T_ q$ both dominate $D_ u$ and both have total mass $A$. Hence $T_ u=T_ q=D_ u$. The distribution $u-q$ is harmonic, and therefore constant on the compact connected curve. Thus $u=q+C$ for a constant $C$, and proposition 16.28.62 gives $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q)$ also in this case. $\square$ Proposition 13.28.24 . 4805035AEC54 For the Fubini–Study form $\theta $ of area one on $\mathbb P^1$, the pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ is incomplete on $\mathfrak S(\mathbb P^1,\theta )$: some Cauchy sequence of ordinary models of one fixed positive mass with trivial multiplier ideals has no limit. On ordinary models, its topology is strictly weaker than that of polar total variation and strictly stronger than $\tau _{\theta ,0}$. Proof. Use the diffuse polar probability measures $\sigma _ j$ concentrating at a point $x$ and the models $p_ j=p_{c\sigma _ j}$ from the proof of proposition 13.28.19 , with $0<c<1$. Fix a smooth obstacle $F$ and put $q_{y,F}=P_{\theta ,F}[q_{c\delta _ y}]$. Rotations preserving $\theta $ and sending $x$ to $y$ can be chosen to depend continuously on $y$ near $x$; they transport the obstacle $F$ to its composition with the rotation. Since envelopes below two obstacles differ by at most the uniform distance between the obstacles, continuity of rotations in $L^1$ gives $q_{y,F}\to q_{x,F}$ in $L^1$ as $y\to x$. The uniform $L^1$ bound near $x$ makes the average $w_{j,F}=\int q_{y,F}\, \mathrm d\sigma _ j(y)$ well defined. It lies below $F$, its curvature current dominates $c\sigma _ j$, and it converges to $q_{x,F}$ in $L^1$. The description of envelopes below obstacles in Step 1 of the proof of proposition 13.28.22 gives $w_{j,F}\leq P_{\theta ,F}[p_ j]\leq F$. These bounds and normalized compactness give $L^1$ precompactness. Every cluster point of the envelopes has curvature at least $c\delta _ x$, so it is at most $q_{x,F}$, and the lower bound gives the reverse inequality. Hence $P_{\theta ,F}[p_ j]\to q_{x,F}$ for every $F$. The ideal envelopes of the $p_ j$ below $F$ all equal $P_\theta (F)$, since their multiplier ideals are trivial, and their atomic parts vanish. Thus $[p_ j]$ is a $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence. Since $F_1=0$, a limit would also be a $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-limit, which proposition 13.28.19 excludes. For the strict comparison with polar total variation, use the rotated diffuse models $\widetilde p_ j=p\circ R_ j^{-1}$ from the end of 13.28.15 . For every smooth $F$, \[  P_{\theta ,F}[\widetilde p_ j] =P_{\theta ,F\circ R_ j}[p]\circ R_ j^{-1}.  \] The same obstacle bound and the $L^1$ continuity of rotations give convergence to $P_{\theta ,F}[p]$. All atomic parts vanish, so $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta ([\widetilde p_ j],[p])\to 0$, whereas the polar total-variation distance remains $2c$. Proposition 13.28.22 gives the implication in the other direction. Finally, the sequence in proposition 18.11.2 converges for the zero obstacle but not for some smooth obstacle. By Step 1 of the proof of proposition 13.28.22 , replacing its members by their ordinary models does not change any obstacle envelope, so $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ is strictly stronger than $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ already on ordinary models. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.28.22
text: Proposition 13.28.22 . E7DAF71126F6 The pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ induces the uniformity of $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $. Two classes have distance zero if and only if they have the same polar curvature. The closure of the analytic classes is $\{ [u]:\mu _ u=D_ u\} =\mathcal G_\theta $, where $\mathcal G_\theta =\{ [u]:P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\} $ as in ( 18.9.2 ). On each set $\mathcal C_ s$, $0\leq s\leq A$, the pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ is a complete metric inducing the topology of total variation of the atomic measures. On ordinary models, polar total variation implies convergence for $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $. Proof. Step 1: envelopes below an obstacle. For any smooth $F$, translating the competitors by $F$ gives \[  P_{\theta ,F}[u]-F=P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[u-F],  \] and likewise for the ideal envelope. The background $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F$ on the right is a smooth real form of area $A$, though it need not be positive. We claim that these two envelopes are the models of $\mu _ u$ and of $D_ u$, respectively, in that background, in the sense of proposition 13.29.1 . Set $\mu =\mu _ u$ and let $w_\mu $ be its Green potential, and put $r=P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[w_\mu -F]$. By the gauge bounds of proposition 18.5.1 , $r+F$ differs from $P_\theta [w_\mu ]=p_\mu \sim w_\mu $ by a bounded function, so $r\sim w_\mu -F$. Hence $r=P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[r]$ is an ordinary model, and its polar measure is $\mu $. Moreover $u-F\preceq r$, and both have mass $A-\mu (Y)$. If this mass is positive, corollary 13.19.8 , applied in the big background $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F$, shows that $P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[u-F]=r$. If it is zero, the curvature measures of $u-F$ and $w_\mu -F$ both equal $\mu $, so these functions differ by a constant, and again $P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[u-F]=r$. The assertion for the ideal envelope follows in the same way from ideal projection and the classification of atomic models. It also follows that the envelope $P_{\theta ,F}[u]$ is the upper envelope of all $v\leq F$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \mu $. Step 2: the uniformity. By proposition 13.29.1 , polar total variation gives $L^1$ convergence of these models for every fixed $F$. The same assertion for atomic measures gives continuity of every ideal-envelope coordinate with respect to the total variation of the atomic parts. The controlled ideal relations are also implied, uniformly, by atomic total variation: for fixed $t>0$ and $a>1$, the bound $\| D-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}<(a-1)/(at)$ guarantees both inclusions in ( 18.8.3 ), by the formula for multiplier ideals on a curve. Indeed, if $tE(\{ x\} )\geq 1$, the bound gives $aD(\{ x\} )>E(\{ x\} )$; otherwise the target ideal is the unit ideal. Interchange $D$ and $E$ for the other inclusion. Each divisorial coordinate is the atomic total variation. Therefore the envelope terms in the series, together with the atomic term, generate exactly the uniformity of $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $: finitely many coordinates control the sum up to its uniformly small tail, and the sum controls each fixed coordinate. Step 3: zero distance and analytic closure. By Step 1 with $F=0$, distance zero forces equal polar measures; the classification at every obstacle proves the converse. The same classification shows that the ordinary and ideal envelopes agree at every $F$ if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$. Hence theorem 18.12.3 identifies the closure of the analytic classes. Step 4: the sets $\mathcal C_ s$. For a $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal C_ s$, the atomic measures converge in total variation to a measure of mass at most $s$, which is again atomic. The convergence of models in Step 2 gives convergence of every obstacle coordinate, and the summable tail then gives convergence for $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $. Conversely, convergence for $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ implies convergence of the atomic parts, because of the first summand. This proves completeness and the equality of topologies on $\mathcal C_ s$. Finally, polar total variation controls the atomic part and all ordinary-envelope coordinates, which proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: Corollary 13.28.23
text: Corollary 13.28.23 . 017BC9CAC896 For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ put $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. The following are equivalent: \[  \begin{gathered} u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q),\qquad \mu _ u=D_ u,\\ P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I},\\ P_{\theta ,F}[u]=P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \quad \text{for every smooth real }F. \end{gathered}  \] This also holds when $D_ u(Y)=A$, that is, when $q$ has zero mass. Proof. The classifications of ordinary and ideal models in lemma 13.28.1 , lemma 20.3.20 show that $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$. Step 1 of the proof of proposition 13.28.22 shows that this is equivalent to equality of the envelopes at every smooth obstacle. Membership of $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q)$ implies the latter by proposition 18.12.2 . Conversely, assume that $\mu _ u=D_ u$. By lemma 20.3.20 , $\mu _ q=D_ u$. Ordinary equivalence preserves polar curvature by corollary 5.27.15 , so every potential equivalent to $q$ has non-pluripolar mass $A-D_ u(Y)$, by Stokes' theorem. Hence \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q)=A-D_ u(Y).  \] If $D_ u(Y)<A$, then $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, and proposition 13.24.2 puts $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q)$. If $D_ u(Y)=A$, the positive curvature measures $T_ u$ and $T_ q$ both dominate $D_ u$ and both have total mass $A$. Hence $T_ u=T_ q=D_ u$. The distribution $u-q$ is harmonic, and therefore constant on the compact connected curve. Thus $u=q+C$ for a constant $C$, and proposition 16.28.62 gives $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q)$ also in this case. $\square$

title: 13.29 Background changes on curves
Proposition 13.29.1
text: Proposition 13.29.1 . C9C98321BEFC Polar curvature identifies $\mathcal M(\sigma )$ with the set of polar measures of mass at most $A_\sigma $. Write $p_\sigma (\mu )$ for the model with polar measure $\mu $. Then \[  U_\sigma (p_\sigma (\mu ))=A_\sigma -\mu (Y),\qquad d_\sigma (p_\sigma (\mu ),p_\sigma (\nu ))=\| \mu -\nu \| _{\mathrm{TV}},  \] and ideal projection corresponds to taking the atomic part. The space $(\mathcal M(\sigma ),d_\sigma )$ is complete and geodesic, and convergence for $d_\sigma $ implies convergence in $L^1$ and in capacity. If $A_\sigma =0$, its only member is the smooth potential $u_\sigma $ of lemma 5.29.22 . Proof. Suppose first that $A=A_\sigma >0$, and write $\sigma =A\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,A\eta )$, the inequalities for ordinary envelopes in proposition 18.5.1 give \[  P_{A\eta }[v]+\min _ Yh \leq P_\sigma [v-h]+h \leq P_{A\eta }[v]+\max _ Yh.  \] For a model $p$ in background $A\eta $, the potential $q=P_\sigma [p-h]$ therefore satisfies $q+h\sim p$, and since the envelope depends only on the ordinary type, $P_\sigma [q]=P_\sigma [p-h]=q$. Conversely, for $q\in \mathcal M(\sigma )$, the same bounds with $v=q+h$ show that $P_{A\eta }[q+h]\sim q+h$, and taking the envelope back recovers $q$. Thus $p\mapsto P_\sigma [p-h]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal M(A\eta )$ onto $\mathcal M(\sigma )$. Smooth gauge changes preserve curvature currents, and ordinary equivalence preserves their polar parts by corollary 5.27.15 . Consequently the bijection preserves polar curvature. It also preserves singularity volumes, and subtracting the same smooth function commutes with maxima. The classification and the distance formula of lemma 13.28.1 , theorem 13.28.4 , applied to the positive form $A\eta $, now give the first assertions. The same gauge bounds for ideal envelopes show that the transported ideal projections are ordinarily equivalent. Both are ordinary models by corollary 18.4.4 , and ordinary models of the same type are equal. Thus the bijection commutes with ideal projection, which still takes the atomic part. Completeness and the geodesics follow from the identification with polar measures, as in corollary 13.28.7 . For convergence to a model of positive mass, note that $\sigma $ is big because $\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(-h)=A\eta >0$, and that the convergence of the polar masses gives a common positive lower-volume bound; then apply proposition 13.22.4 , theorem 13.23.3 . For a limit of zero mass, the current estimate ( 13.28.9 ) follows from the same polar decomposition as before. Normalized compactness and the uniqueness of harmonic functions give $L^1$ convergence, and lemma 5.27.11 on a finite cover gives convergence in capacity. If $A_\sigma =0$, lemma 5.29.22 leaves only $u_\sigma $ after normalization. Its curvature current vanishes, and both envelope operations fix it. All assertions reduce to statements about the zero measure and the one-point metric space. $\square$

title: Corollary 13.29.2
text: Corollary 13.29.2 . 02F73F083FCE For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\sigma )$ put \[  q=P_\sigma [u]_{\mathcal I},\qquad \mu _ u=\mathbf1_{\{ u=-\infty \} }(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u),\qquad D_ u=\sum _{y\in Y}\nu (u,y)\delta _ y.  \] The following are equivalent: \[  \begin{gathered} u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\sigma ,q),\qquad \mu _ u=D_ u,\\ P_\sigma [u]=P_\sigma [u]_{\mathcal I},\\ P_{\sigma ,F}[u]=P_{\sigma ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \quad \text{for every smooth real }F. \end{gathered}  \] If $A_\sigma =0$, all four conditions hold for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\sigma )$. Proof. Suppose first that $A=A_\sigma >0$, and write $\sigma =A\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. Put $v=u+h$ and $q_+=P_{A\eta }[v]_{\mathcal I}$. The gauge change preserves the curvature current and its pole set, hence both $\mu _ u$ and $D_ u$. By proposition 18.5.1 , $q+h\sim q_+$. The gauge invariance of the relative envelope class and its invariance under equivalent references (proposition 16.28.62 ) give \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\sigma ,q) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad v\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,A\eta ,q_+).  \] By corollary 13.28.23 , this is equivalent to $\mu _ u=D_ u$. The gauge bounds for the ordinary and ideal envelopes, corollary 5.27.15 and the classifications in the positive background $A\eta $ identify the polar curvatures of $P_\sigma [u]$ and $P_\sigma [u]_{\mathcal I}$ with $\mu _ u$ and $D_ u$, respectively. Both envelopes are ordinary models, the ideal one by corollary 18.4.4 . The classification of models in proposition 13.29.1 therefore shows that they are equal if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$. For a smooth real $F$, the bijection $a\mapsto a+h$ between competitors gives \[  P_{\sigma ,F}[u]+h=P_{A\eta ,F+h}[v],  \] and the same identity for the ideal envelopes. Indeed, this bijection preserves the obstacle bound, the ordinary order and multiplier-ideal equivalence, and addition of $h$ commutes with upper regularization. Since $F\mapsto F+h$ is a bijection of the smooth obstacles, corollary 13.28.23 gives the remaining equivalence. If $A_\sigma =0$, lemma 5.29.22 gives $u=-h+c$ for a constant $c$, and the curvature current of $u$ vanishes. Thus $\mu _ u=D_ u=0$. All potentials in this background are smooth and ordinarily equivalent, so their ordinary and ideal competitor families below every obstacle coincide, and they are nonempty after a constant translation. The reference $q$ is ordinarily equivalent to $u$, and proposition 16.28.62 gives $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\sigma ,q)$. $\square$

title: Theorem 13.29.3
text: Theorem 13.29.3 . 151BAA2FA1AB Let $\theta _0,\theta _1$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms on $Y$ with positive areas $A_ i=A_{\theta _ i}$, and put $\lambda =A_1/A_0$. The map \[  F_{10}:\mathcal M(\theta _0)\longrightarrow \mathcal M(\theta _1), \qquad F_{10}(p_{\theta _0}(\mu ))=p_{\theta _1}(\lambda \mu ),  \] is a bijection and satisfies 7ADEC26E190A 13.29.4 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  d_{\theta _1}(F_{10}(p),F_{10}(q))& =\lambda d_{\theta _0}(p,q),\\  U_{\theta _1}(F_{10}(p))& =\lambda U_{\theta _0}(p),\\  P_{\theta _1}[F_{10}(p)]_{\mathcal I} & =F_{10}(P_{\theta _0}[p]_{\mathcal I}). \end{split} \end{equation} For a third smooth background $\theta _2$ of positive area, the same construction gives $F_{21}F_{10}=F_{20}$. Proof. Multiplication by $\lambda $ is a bijection from the polar measures of mass at most $A_0$ onto those of mass at most $A_1$. By proposition 13.29.1 , it gives the asserted bijection, and the distances satisfy \[  \| \lambda \mu -\lambda \nu \| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\lambda \| \mu -\nu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}.  \] The volume identity follows from $A_1-\lambda \mu (Y)=\lambda (A_0-\mu (Y))$. Taking the atomic part commutes with multiplication by $\lambda $, which gives the ideal-envelope identity. The area ratios multiply, proving the composition rule. $\square$

title: Equation 13.29.4
text: 7ADEC26E190A 13.29.4 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  d_{\theta _1}(F_{10}(p),F_{10}(q))& =\lambda d_{\theta _0}(p,q),\\  U_{\theta _1}(F_{10}(p))& =\lambda U_{\theta _0}(p),\\  P_{\theta _1}[F_{10}(p)]_{\mathcal I} & =F_{10}(P_{\theta _0}[p]_{\mathcal I}). \end{split} \end{equation}

title: Proposition 13.29.5
text: Proposition 13.29.5 . D21EE85B9F1F Choose a smooth real $h$ with $\theta _1=\lambda \theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. For $p\in \mathcal M(\theta _0)$ and $q=F_{10}(p)$, C555907478C9 13.29.6 \begin{equation}  \begin{gathered} q=P_{\theta _1}[\lambda p-h],\\ \lambda p+\min _ Yh\leq q+h\leq \lambda p+\max _ Yh. \end{gathered} \end{equation} If $U_{\theta _0}(p)=0$, then \[  q=\lambda p-h-\sup _ Y(\lambda p-h).  \] Proof. The form $\theta _1-\lambda \theta _0$ has integral zero, so the scalar Poisson equation gives $h$, as in lemma 5.29.22 . Write $p=p_{\theta _0}(\mu )$. Scaling the competitors in the ordinary envelope shows that $\lambda p$ is an ordinary model for $\lambda \theta _0$. The gauge construction in the proof of proposition 13.29.1 therefore makes $P_{\theta _1}[\lambda p-h]$ an ordinary model in background $\theta _1$. The curvature current of $\lambda p-h$ in this background is $\lambda (\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p)$, so its polar measure is $\lambda \mu $. The construction preserves this measure, which gives the first identity in ( 13.29.6 ). The function $\lambda p-h+\min _ Yh$ is a competitor for $q$, which gives the lower bound. If $v\leq 0$ is any competitor for $q$, then $v+h-\max _ Yh$ is $\lambda \theta _0$-plurisubharmonic, nonpositive and more singular than $\lambda p$, so it is at most $\lambda p$. Taking the upper envelope gives the upper bound. These inequalities hold also at the poles, and off the common pole set they imply $|q-\lambda p|\leq \operatorname {osc}_ Yh$. At zero mass, the polar measures exhaust the curvature currents of both $p$ and $q$. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q-\lambda p+h)=0$, and the uniqueness of harmonic functions together with the normalization $\sup _ Yq=0$ gives the last formula. $\square$

title: 13.30 A complete space over varying curve backgrounds

section: 13.30 A complete space over varying curve backgrounds
text:
The polar description also compares models in different backgrounds. Using the background as an additional coordinate gives a complete space that includes the zero-area boundary. The singularity coordinate still records the diffuse polar curvature, and taking its atomic part still gives the nearest ideal model. We keep the compact connected curve $Y$ and the smooth positive form $\eta $ of area one. Let \[  \mathcal B(Y)=\{ \sigma \in C^\infty (Y,\Lambda ^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}): A_\sigma =	extstyle \int _ Y\sigma \geq 0\}   \] be the set of admissible backgrounds. Choose $C^ k$ norms on smooth forms, defined by a fixed smooth metric on $Y$, and put 8E9F949AEF0D 13.30.1  egin{equation}  b(\sigma ,	au )=\sum _{k=0}^\infty 2^{-k-1} \min \{ 1,\| \sigma -	au \| _{C^ k}\} . \end{equation} This is a complete metric for the $C^\infty $ topology on $\mathcal B(Y)$. Indeed, a $b$-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in every $C^ k$ norm; the limits agree and define a smooth form, whose area is nonnegative by $C^0$ convergence. Conversely, convergence in every $C^ k$ norm gives convergence for $b$: a finite part of the sum becomes small, and the tail is uniformly small. Let $\mathcal M(\sigma )$ be the space of ordinary models of proposition 13.29.1 , and define \[  \mathscr M(Y)=\{ (\sigma ,p):\sigma \in \mathcal B(Y), p\in \mathcal M(\sigma )\} .  \] For such a pair write $\mu _ p^\sigma =\mathbf1_{\{ p=-\infty \} }(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p)$, and set 685F813E23E8 13.30.2  egin{equation}  D((\sigma ,p),(	au ,q)) =b(\sigma ,	au )+\| \mu _ p^\sigma -\mu _ q^	au \| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Let $\mathscr I(Y)\subset \mathscr M(Y)$ consist of the pairs $(\sigma ,p)$ with $P_\sigma [p]_{\mathcal I}=p$, and let $\mathscr A_+(Y)$ consist of the pairs $(\sigma ,p)$ for which $p$ has analytic singularities and positive non-pluripolar mass in background $\sigma $. For a finite measure $\mu $ on $Y$, write $\mu =\mu ^{\mathrm{at}}+\mu ^{\mathrm{na}}$ for its decomposition into an atomic and a nonatomic part. Theorem 13.30.3 . C5551396F93B The metric space $(\mathscr M(Y),D)$ is complete. Its restriction to each fixed-background fiber is the polar metric $d_\sigma $. The map \[  R(\sigma ,p)=(\sigma ,P_\sigma [p]_{\mathcal I})  \] is a $1$-Lipschitz retraction onto the closed subspace $\mathscr I(Y)$, and $R(\sigma ,p)$ is the unique ideal pair nearest to $(\sigma ,p)$. Moreover, 34DDD9664A6D 13.30.4  egin{equation}  \overline{\mathscr A_+(Y)}^{\, D}=\mathscr I(Y),\qquad \operatorname {dist}_ D((\sigma ,p),\mathscr I(Y)) =(\mu _ p^\sigma )^{\mathrm{na}}(Y). \end{equation} If $(\sigma _ j,p_ j)	o (\sigma ,p)$ for $D$, then $p_ j	o p$ in $L^1(Y,\eta )$ and in capacity for $\eta $, including when $A_\sigma =0$. Proof. By proposition 13.29.1 , polar curvature identifies $\mathscr M(Y)$ with the set of pairs $(\sigma ,\mu )$ in which $\sigma \in \mathcal B(Y)$ and $\mu $ is a polar measure of mass at most $A_\sigma $. In these coordinates, ( 13.30.2 ) is the restriction of the product metric $b+\| \cdot \| _{\mathrm{TV}}$, so it separates pairs and restricts to $d_\sigma $ on every fiber. Suppose that $(\sigma _ j,\mu _ j)$ is a Cauchy sequence. Completeness of $b$ gives $\sigma _ j	o \sigma $ in the $C^\infty $ topology, and completeness of the space of finite signed measures gives $\mu _ j	o \mu $ in total variation. The limit $\mu $ is positive and satisfies $\mu (Y)\leq A_\sigma $. Choose polar sets $E_ j$ carrying the $\mu _ j$. Their union $E$ is polar, and \[  \mu (Y\setminus E)\leq \| \mu -\mu _ j\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $\mu $ is a polar measure and defines a model in background $\sigma $. title: 15.37 Relative equations under positive lower mass
search_title: Relative equations under positive lower mass
section: 15.37 Relative equations under positive lower mass
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, with a smooth semipositive big real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ and a model reference $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Given a nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $, we seek solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $, $\lambda >0$, and of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu $, $c>0$, relative to a prescribed model reference. The main difficulty is to keep the singularity condition when approximating $\mu $: a bounded difference from the reference may be lost in the limit. We assume that the reference $\varphi $ satisfies ( 16.28.67 ): $\varphi $ is an envelope fixed point, $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $ in the sense of definition 5.40.4 , and $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )\not\equiv -\infty $ for some $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. Throughout this chapter, unless explicitly stated otherwise, we assume that $\theta $ has positive lower mass: E4532A30340F 15.37.1 \begin{equation}  v_-(\theta )>0. \end{equation} Here $v_-(\theta )=\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (0)$ is the infimum of $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$ over all bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$; see definition 13.14.14 and the discussion following definition 16.28.58 . The bounded mass property is not assumed. Approximating $\mu $ by measures with $L^ p$ densities gives solutions of the ordinary singularity type of $\varphi $ by theorem 15.12.1 , but the constants in their bounds $|u-\varphi |\leq C$ need not remain uniform, so a limit can leave this type. What survives the limit is membership in the relative envelope class of definition 16.28.61 : stretching the potential away from $\varphi $ by any finite factor still leaves an envelope that is not identically $-\infty $. Positive lower mass of $\theta $ prevents these stretched envelopes from collapsing. On disjoint contact sets, one finite measure controls the rooftop envelopes of arbitrarily many potentials. Consequently, a sequence of potentials whose measures are dominated by a fixed finite measure has, after extraction, a common lower envelope in the relative class. This envelope keeps limits in the class and controls the measures of deep sublevel sets, so convergence in capacity passes to the Monge–Ampère measures themselves. When the dominating measures are bounded Monge–Ampère measures that vary with the potentials, exponential comparison provides the common envelope instead. For a positive exponent the solution is unique. At exponent zero the scalar is unique, but the normalized potential need not be: on projective manifolds with nonclosed Hermitian backgrounds, the same smooth measure can have several smooth normalized solutions (corollary 15.37.34 ). Since bounded mass is not assumed, members of the relative class may have infinite extended mass; the envelope constructions of subsection 16.28.66 remain available for them. The solutions constructed below have finite mass because the right-hand sides of their equations are finite. Fix $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ with $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )\not\equiv -\infty $, and write \[  \mathcal E_\varphi =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ), \qquad \mathcal E_0=\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,0), \qquad \mu _ u=\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u).  \] Here $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\psi )$ denotes the relative envelope class of a reference $\psi $ (definition 16.28.61 ), and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta $ is the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 13.14.3 , a positive measure whose total mass may be infinite. As in definition 16.7.1 , $u\preceq v$ means $u\leq v+C$ for a constant $C$, and $u\sim v$ means $u\preceq v\preceq u$. For $u,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $b\geq 1$, we use the stretching envelopes $Q_ b(u,w)=P_\theta (bu-(b-1)w)$ introduced before definition 16.28.61 , and the rooftop envelopes $P_\theta (u_1,\ldots ,u_ N)=P_\theta (\min _ iu_ i)$. Fix also a Hermitian form $\omega \geq \theta $ for capacity and a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ for $L^1$ convergence. For $a\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, proposition 16.28.65 gives $P_\theta [a]=P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $. Since $a-\sup _ Xa$ is one of the competitors defining $P_\theta [a]$, it follows that C37817AD17BA 15.37.2 \begin{equation}  a-\sup _ Xa\leq P_\theta [a]=\varphi . \end{equation}

text: For a positive exponent, the right-hand side $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $ changes when $u$ is translated, and this fixes the additive constant. At exponent zero, translation leaves the equation unchanged; instead, a positive scalar in front of the prescribed measure is needed to match its mass. Theorem 15.37.4 . C568B2958DB9 Let $\mu $ be a nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure on $X$. Then: For every $\lambda >0$ there is a unique $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ with $\mu _ u=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $. There are $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and a unique $c>0$ with $\mu _ u=c\mu $. The theorem is proved in subsection 15.37.30 . The case of the reference zero, which has minimal singularities because $\theta \geq 0$, is treated first in theorem 15.37.28 ; its solutions then serve as comparison potentials for the reference $\varphi $. For general measures the theorem asserts membership in $\mathcal E_\varphi $, not a bounded difference from $\varphi $.

text: The domination principle compares a potential $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ with a potential $v$ whose measure is larger on $\{ u<v\} $. We first treat the case in which $\mu _ u$ is finite. Stretching $u$ away from $\max (u,v)$ produces envelopes whose measures are bounded, by contact support, by the fixed measure $\mu _ u$; the small tails of this finite measure then exclude collapse. By theorem 16.28.70 and ( 15.37.1 ), the uniform lower mass bound is \[  \mu _ a(X)\geq \kappa :=(1-\varepsilon )^ n v_-(\theta )>0 \qquad (a\in \mathcal E_\varphi ).  \] Theorem 15.37.6 . 5023B8CBC940 Let $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ have finite $\mu _ u$, and let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $v\preceq \varphi $. If, for some $0\leq c<1$, \[  \mu _ u\leq c\mu _ v\quad \hbox{on }\{ u<v\} ,  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. It suffices to prove $u\geq w$ for $w=\max (u,v)$. Upward stability (proposition 16.28.62 ) gives $w\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, and locality gives $\mu _ u\leq c\mu _ w$ on $\{ u<w\} $. For $b>1$ put $q_ b=Q_ b(u,w)$, which belongs to $\mathcal E_\varphi $ by lemma 16.28.63 . It satisfies $q_ b\leq u$, and by contact support its measure is carried by \[  D_ b=\{ b^{-1}q_ b+(1-b^{-1})w=u\} .  \] On $D_ b$ the potential $b^{-1}q_ b+(1-b^{-1})w$ touches $u$ from below, so positivity of mixed products and ordered contact give \[  b^{-n}\mu _{q_ b}+(1-b^{-1})^ n\mu _ w\leq \mu _ u.  \] Choose $b$ so large that $(1-b^{-1})^ n>c$. Comparing this inequality with $\mu _ u\leq c\mu _ w$ on $D_ b\cap \{ u<w\} $ forces both $\mu _ w$ and $\mu _{q_ b}$ to vanish there. Since $\mu _ w(X)$ may be infinite, this subtraction is first carried out on common finite truncation levels of the potentials, where all measures are finite; exhausting the complements of the pole sets then gives the assertion for the extended measures. It follows that $\mu _{q_ b}$ is carried by $D_ b\cap \{ u=w\} \subseteq \{ q_ b=u\} $. Since $q_ b\leq u$, ordered contact applied once more gives F1593AD00D2B 15.37.7 \begin{equation}  \mu _{q_ b}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ q_ b=u\} }\mu _ u, \end{equation} with coefficient one, independent of $b$. As $b\to \infty $ through the integers, the potentials $q_ b$ decrease, because the obstacles $bu-(b-1)w=u-(b-1)(w-u)$ do. Suppose that they decreased to $-\infty $ identically. Then theorem 5.25.2 would give $M_ b:=\sup _ Xq_ b\to -\infty $, and ( 15.37.7 ) would imply \[  \kappa \leq \int _ X\mu _{q_ b} \leq \mu _ u(\{ u\leq M_ b\} )\longrightarrow 0,  \] because $\mu _ u$ is finite and does not charge the pole set of $u$. This is impossible, so the decreasing limit $q$ is not identically $-\infty $. Now fix $a>0$. Since neither $q$ nor $u$ is identically $-\infty $, their pole sets have zero smooth volume, and hence so does $\{ u<w-a\} $. Thus $u\geq w$ almost everywhere, and then everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . In particular $u\geq v$. $\square$

text:

u .  \] Proof. Start with an arbitrary subsequence. By lemma 15.37.13 , a further subsequence has a common lower envelope $h\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, and $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $. u \longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus proposition 15.37.17 gives convergence in capacity along this subsequence. For the measures themselves, the common lower bound gives \[  \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j\leq -T\} ) \leq

title: 15.37.20 Moving bounded carrier measures
section: 15.37 Relative equations under positive lower mass
text: In the approximation scheme of subsection 15.37.30 , the measures of the approximating solutions are dominated by Monge–Ampère measures of uniformly bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials $\psi _ j$, which vary with $j$. For a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potential $\psi $, write $\omega _\psi =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $. A single dominating measure is then unavailable, but an exponential domination $\mu _{u_ j}\leq A\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}\omega _{\psi _ j}^ n$ still provides a common lower envelope. A smaller-background potential and a strict big potential give comparison functions whose constants are uniform in $j$. If every $u_ j$ has the ordinary singularity type of $\varphi $, smaller-background comparison gives the same construction even when $v_-(\theta )=0$. Convergence of the potentials $\psi _ j$ in capacity then identifies the limiting equation. Proposition 15.37.21 . 69ED083168C9 Fix $A,\lambda >0$, $C\in \mathbb R$ and $L\geq 0$. For $j\geq 1$, suppose that $u_ j\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, $u_ j\leq \varphi +C$, and D519538AEA33 15.37.22 \begin{equation}  \mu _{u_ j}\leq A \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}\omega _{\psi _ j}^ n, \qquad \psi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega ),\qquad \| \psi _ j\| _\infty \leq L. \end{equation} Assume either $v_-(\theta )>0$ or $u_ j\sim \varphi $ for every $j$. Then \[  h=P_\theta \left(\inf _ j u_ j\right)\in \mathcal E_\varphi .  \] No convergence of $\psi _ j$ or $u_ j$ is assumed, and in the second alternative the constants in $u_ j\sim \varphi $ need not be uniform in $j$. Proof. Translate all $u_ j$ by one constant so that $u_ j\leq \varphi \leq 0$; this changes $A$ by a fixed factor. Translate each $\psi _ j$ so that it takes values in $[-2L,0]$; this does not change its measure. Set $q=P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ and choose $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $a>0$ such that \[  q\leq \varphi , \qquad \rho \leq 0,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq a\omega .  \] Here $q\not\equiv -\infty $ by the model condition, and $\rho $ exists because $\theta $ is big. Fix $0<\delta <(1-\varepsilon )a$. For a fixed real $b\geq 1$, put $r_{j,b}=Q_ b(u_ j,\varphi )$. The stretching lemma puts it in $\mathcal E_\varphi $, and $r_{j,b}\leq u_ j\leq 0$. Contact support and positivity imply \[  \mu _{r_{j,b}} \leq b^ n\mathbf1_{D_{j,b}}\mu _{u_ j}, \qquad D_{j,b}=\{ b^{-1}r_{j,b}+(1-b^{-1})\varphi =u_ j\} .  \] On this contact set, $\varphi \leq 0$ gives $u_ j\leq r_{j,b}/b$. Thus ( 15.37.22 ) yields 53CEBC73788B 15.37.23 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda r_{j,b}/b}\mu _{r_{j,b}} \leq b^ n A\omega _{\psi _ j}^ n, \end{equation} where the weights are evaluated off the pluripolar pole sets. Choose $C_ b\geq 0$ so large that \[  \delta ^ n\exp (\lambda C_ b/b)\geq b^ n A,  \] and define \[  s_{j,b}=q+(1-\varepsilon )\rho +\delta \psi _ j-C_ b.  \] This is a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, since \[  \begin{split}  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s_{j,b} & = (\varepsilon \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q) +(1-\varepsilon )(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho ) +\delta \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j\\ & \geq \delta \omega _{\psi _ j}. \end{split}  \] Consequently $\mu _{s_{j,b}}\geq \delta ^ n\omega _{\psi _ j}^ n$: this inequality holds away from the poles by the local positive product inequality, and then globally because the bounded reference measure does not charge pluripolar sets. Also $s_{j,b}\leq -C_ b$ and $s_{j,b}\preceq \varphi $. Together with ( 15.37.23 ), we conclude \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda s_{j,b}/b}\mu _{s_{j,b}} \geq b^ n A\omega _{\psi _ j}^ n \geq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda r_{j,b}/b}\mu _{r_{j,b}}.  \] If $v_-(\theta )>0$, apply corollary 15.37.11 with first potential $r_{j,b}$ and second potential $s_{j,b}$. It gives $r_{j,b}\geq s_{j,b}$. In the second alternative, $r_{j,b}\sim \varphi $: if $u_ j\geq \varphi -K_ j$, the potential $\varphi -bK_ j$ is a competitor for $r_{j,b}$. Hence the smaller-background envelope $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(r_{j,b})$ is not identically $-\infty $, and $s_{j,b}\preceq r_{j,b}$. Therefore corollary 15.2.3 also gives $r_{j,b}\geq s_{j,b}$, without a lower-mass hypothesis. Since $\psi _ j\geq -2L$, we now have a lower bound independent of $j$: \[  H_ b=q+(1-\varepsilon )\rho -2\delta L-C_ b \leq r_{j,b}.  \] The potential $H_ b$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $. By the definition of $r_{j,b}$, therefore, \[  b^{-1}H_ b+(1-b^{-1})\varphi \leq u_ j \quad \hbox{for every }j.  \] For $b=1$ this shows that the infimum envelope $h$ is not identically $-\infty $. For general $b$, the left side is a competitor for $h$, so it lies below $h$; it is thus a competitor in the defining condition of the relative class for $b$. Since $h\leq \varphi $, we obtain $h\in \mathcal E_\varphi $. Undoing the common translation finishes the proof. $\square$ Corollary 15.37.24 . D3170E7413EC Under the hypotheses of proposition 15.37.21 , if $u_ j\to u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ in $L^1(X)$, then $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $. Proof. The common envelope gives $h\leq u_ j\leq \varphi +C$. Along an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence, lemma 5.24.3 gives $h\leq u\leq \varphi +C$, and upward stability gives the conclusion. $\square$

title: 15.37.25 Convergence with a common envelope
section: 15.37 Relative equations under positive lower mass

title: 15.37.31 Normalization at exponent zero
section: 15.37 Relative equations under positive lower mass
text: In this section the background is a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$ with $v_-(h)>0$, and the reference is zero; thus $\theta =h$ and $\varphi =0$ in the notation of the chapter, and $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ is the minimal envelope class. Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero. Recall from ( 15.28.1 ) that the subsolution threshold $b_ h(f)$ is the limit of the normalizing constants of the truncations $\min (f,k)$; by theorem 15.28.4 , it is the largest $a\geq 0$ for which some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$. We show that $b_ h(f)$ is exactly the scalar of the normalized equation in the minimal envelope class: scalar comparison bounds every subsolution coefficient by this scalar. Dominated continuity also identifies the equation satisfied by every limit of normalized greatest exponential solutions; whether these limits coincide is a question about the potentials. Corollary 15.37.32 . 74BE83BA167D Let $h$ be a Hermitian form on $X$ with $v_-(h)>0$, and let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero. There is $v\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v)=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The number $b_ h(f)>0$ is the unique positive scalar for which this equation has a solution in that envelope class. For $\lambda >0$, let $u_\lambda $ be the greatest solution of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V$ from theorem 15.35.2 , and set $v_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda $. Each $u_\lambda $ belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$. If $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$ and $v_{\lambda _ j}\to v$ in $L^1$, then the convergence holds in capacity, and $v$ belongs to the same envelope class and satisfies the equation above. Proof. By theorem 15.37.28 , applied with $\theta =h$, there are $c>0$ and $w\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. If $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w) \leq \frac ca\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s).  \] Every $h$-plurisubharmonic $s$ satisfies $s\preceq 0$, so the scalar assertion of corollary 15.37.11 , with reference zero, gives $c/a\geq 1$. Taking the maximum over all subsolution coefficients $a$, theorem 15.28.4 yields $b_ h(f)\leq c$. The reverse inequality holds because $w$ itself is a subsolution with coefficient $c$. The same argument identifies the scalar of every solution in this envelope class with $b_ h(f)$. For $\lambda >0$, theorem 15.37.28 also gives a solution $s_\lambda $ of the exponential equation in the envelope class. Since $s_\lambda $ is in particular a subsolution, the greatest-solution property gives $s_\lambda \leq u_\lambda $. Upward stability (proposition 16.28.62 ) places $u_\lambda $ and its translate $v_\lambda $ in that class. Write $c_\lambda =\exp (\lambda \sup _ Xu_\lambda )$. The corollary identifies the equation of every such limit; the examples below show that this equation alone need not determine the normalized potential.

title: 15.37.33 Nonuniqueness in the minimal envelope class

section: 15.37 Relative equations under positive lower mass
text:
In this subsection the manifold and the background are no longer fixed. The examples of 14.29.1 are smooth solutions on projective manifolds with nonclosed Hermitian backgrounds. Comparison with a Kähler form shows that these backgrounds have both positive lower mass and bounded mass, and smooth potentials belong to the minimal envelope class. Thus even both mass bounds together allow several normalized solutions with the same scalar. Corollary 15.37.34 . 13248E1C4143 In every complex dimension $n\geq 3$, there are a projective manifold $X$ of dimension $n$, a smooth nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$, and a nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure $
u $ on $X$ such that \[  0<v_-(\omega )\leq v_+(\omega )<+\infty ,  \] but the equation \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)=c
u , \qquad u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0), \qquad \sup _ Xu=0,  \] has at least two smooth solutions. The only positive constant for which it has a solution is $c=1$. Relative to a Kähler volume form on $X$, the measure $
u $ has a real analytic density, positive off two connected smooth real hypersurfaces and vanishing quadratically along them. Proof. Use the form and the two potentials of 14.29.1 . Since the manifold is projective, lemma 19.9.12 gives bounded mass. Fix a Kähler form $\Omega $ on $X$ and choose $\varepsilon >0$ with $\varepsilon \Omega \leq \omega $. Lower-volume monotonicity, theorem 13.17.1 , applied to the zero potential in both backgrounds, gives \[  v_-(\omega )\geq v_-(\varepsilon \Omega ) =\varepsilon ^ n\int _ X\Omega ^ n>0.  \] Here the potentials of the same ordinary type as zero are exactly the bounded ones, so these lower volumes are the infima defining $v_-$. The two smooth potentials belong to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0)$ by proposition 16.28.62 , and their extended measures are the ordinary top powers. Their common measure $
u $ is finite and does not charge pluripolar sets. The construction gives $c=1$, and corollary 15.37.11 shows that no other positive scalar is possible. The density and its zero set were computed in 14.29.1 . $\square$

title: 10.31 Big backgrounds under bounded mass
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, let $\theta $ be a smooth big real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, not necessarily closed or semipositive, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. As in section 15.37 , we solve the equations $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $, $\lambda >0$, and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu $, $c>0$, for an arbitrary nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $, with $u$ in the relative class of $\varphi $. We replace the smaller-background model condition used there by upper and positive lower mass bounds. Throughout this chapter we make two standing assumptions. First, $X$ has the bounded mass property of definition 13.14.14 : $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $ for one, and hence every, Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$ (proposition 13.14.15 ). Second, $\varphi $ satisfies ( 13.20.5 ): it is an ordinary model, $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $ (definition 5.40.4 ), and its lower singularity volume is positive. Recall from definition 16.28.58 that the lower and upper volumes $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ are the infimum and the supremum of $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$ over all $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\sim u$. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ for capacity and a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$. The two assumptions give the two bounds needed for approximation: every member of the relative class of $\varphi $ has Monge–Ampère mass at least $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )>0$ and at most $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )<\infty $. With these bounds, first moments relative to a reference prevent collapse and keep limits in the relative class, while higher moments control convergence against a smoothed measure. This first gives solutions in the class of the potential $V_\theta $ with minimal singularities. To pass to the reference $\varphi $, we project a solution in the relative class of $V_\theta $ onto the relative class of $\varphi $. The projection keeps only part of the exponentially weighted measure, but weighted addition can fill any remaining deficit; maximizing the weighted mass therefore gives the required equation. The same contact estimates keep limits in the relative class when the model reference varies in the volume comparison of section 13.22 . For general finite non-pluripolar data the solutions lie in the relative full-mass class; for $L^ p$ densities, a stronger moment estimate shows that they differ from $\varphi $ by a bounded function. A positive exponent determines the solution uniquely; at exponent zero only the scalar is unique. For $a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, write \[  \mathcal E_\varphi =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ), \qquad \theta _ a=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a,\qquad \mu _ a=\mathrm{MA}_\theta (a).  \] Here $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$ is the relative full-mass class of definition 13.18.4 , consisting of the $u\preceq \varphi $ with $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )$; $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$ is the relative envelope class of definition 16.28.61 ; and the two classes coincide by theorem 13.18.5 . As in definition 16.7.1 , $u\preceq v$ means $u\leq v+C$ for a constant $C$, and $u\sim v$ means $u\preceq v\preceq u$. The measure $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (a)$ is the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 13.14.3 ; it is finite by proposition 13.14.16 . Put \[  \ell =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )>0, \qquad M=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )<\infty .  \] By theorem 13.18.5 , every $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ satisfies A6F2ACEED83F 10.31.1 \begin{equation}  \ell \leq \mu _ u(X)\leq M. \end{equation} We use the stretching envelopes $Q_ b(u,w)=P_\theta (bu-(b-1)w)$ introduced before definition 16.28.61 , the rooftop envelopes $P_\theta (u_1,\ldots ,u_ N)=P_\theta (\min _ iu_ i)$, and $V_\theta =P_\theta (0)$ (section 5.40 ). For $a\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, proposition 16.28.65 gives $P_\theta [a]=\varphi $, and hence, as in ( 15.37.2 ), \[  a-\sup _ Xa\leq \varphi .  \] We refer to this inequality as the envelope identity. Finally, zero domination refers to theorem 13.19.1 with coefficient zero: if $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, $v\preceq \varphi $ and $\mu _ u(\{ u<v\} )=0$, then $u\geq v$.

title: 10.31.2 Equations for finite measures
text: A positive exponent determines a unique solution in the relative class. At exponent zero, the equation determines its positive scalar, but normalized potentials may still differ, as in corollary 15.37.34 . Theorem 10.31.3 . 2568C6F1B2F7 For every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $ on $X$: There are $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and a unique $c>0$ such that $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu $. For each $\lambda >0$ there is a unique $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ such that $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $. If $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for some $p>1$, the solutions in both parts may be taken with $u\sim \varphi $. Part (1) is theorem 10.31.45 , part (2) is theorem 10.31.44 , and the assertion for $L^ p$ densities is corollary 10.31.56 . The standing assumptions also give $v_-(\omega )>0$. Indeed, choose $C>0$ with $\theta \leq C\omega $. Since $\varphi \preceq 0$, theorem 13.17.1 gives \[  0<\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi ) \leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{C\omega }(0) =C^ n v_-(\omega ).  \]

title: 10.31.7 Relative moments
text:
For $w\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and $u\leq w$, the relative first moment $\int _ X(w-u)\, \mu _ u$ measures how far $u$ lies below $w$, weighted by the measure of $u$. A uniform bound on these moments prevents a sequence from collapsing and keeps its limits in $\mathcal E_\varphi $. The proof compares rooftop masses with the fixed measure of a potential of the same type as $w$ whose mass is close to the upper volume $M$. For a real number $t$, write $t_+=\max (t,0)$. Proposition 10.31.8 . 56A4FC216C27 Fix $w\in \mathcal E_\varphi $. Suppose $u_ j\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, $u_ j\leq w$, and \[  K:=\sup _ j\int _ X(w-u_ j)\, \mu _{u_ j}<+\infty .  \] Then $\sup _ Xu_ j$ is bounded below. If $u_ j	o u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ in $L^1(X)$, then $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $. The same conclusions hold if $u_ j\leq w$ is replaced by a common upper bound $u_ j\leq \varphi +C$ and the integral is replaced by $\int _ X(w-u_ j)_+\, \mu _{u_ j}$. Proof. We first treat the case $u_ j\leq w$. Since $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (w)=M$, we may choose $w'\sim w$ with $\mu _{w'}(X)>M-\ell /2$. Translate $w'$ so that $w'\leq w$, and put $p_ j=P_	heta (u_ j,w')$. These rooftops belong to $\mathcal E_\varphi $. Contact support and ordered contact imply C1417B0EF5E7 10.31.9  egin{equation}  \int _ X(w'-p_ j)\, \mu _{p_ j} \leq \int _ X(w-u_ j)\, \mu _{u_ j}\leq K. \end{equation} Indeed, the integrand vanishes on the contact part $\{ p_ j=w'\} $, and on the remaining contact part $p_ j=u_ j<w'\leq w$. We shall use the following estimate for maxima. If $a\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, $a\leq w'$, and $t>0$, then 525AD3E9DFE4 10.31.10  egin{equation}  \mu _ a(\{ a>w'-t\} ) \leq \mu _{w'}(\{ a>w'-t\} )+M-\mu _{w'}(X). \end{equation} To see this, put $m=\max (a,w'-t)$. It has the ordinary singularity type of $w'$, so $\mu _ m(X)\leq M$. On $\{ a>w'-t\} $, locality gives $\mu _ m=\mu _ a$. On the complementary set, where $m=w'-t$, ordered contact gives $\mu _ m\geq \mu _{w'}$. Integrating over the two sets proves ( 10.31.10 ). Suppose that a subsequence had $\sup _ Xu_ j	o -\infty $; then also $\sup _ Xp_ j	o -\infty $. Splitting the mass of $p_ j$ at the level $w'-s$, $s>0$, and using ( 10.31.9 ) and ( 10.31.10 ), we obtain \[  \ell \leq \mu _{p_ j}(X) \leq  rac Ks+\mu _{w'}(\{ p_ j>w'-s\} )+M-\mu _{w'}(X).  \] For fixed $s$, the middle term tends to zero as $j	o \infty $, since $w'$ is finite off a pluripolar set and $\mu _{w'}$ is finite and non-pluripolar. Letting $j	o \infty $ and then $s	o \infty $ gives $\ell \leq M-\mu _{w'}(X)<\ell /2$, a contradiction. This proves the first assertion. Now suppose $u_ j	o u$ in $L^1$. Then $u\leq w\preceq \varphi $. Fix $b>1$ and suppose that $Q_ b(u,w)\equiv -\infty $. Since $w-w'$ is bounded, translating competitors by a constant shows that $Q_ b(u,w')\equiv -\infty $ as well. Keep the same $p_ j$ and set \[  h_ j=Q_ b(p_ j,w')\in \mathcal E_\varphi .  \] We claim that $\sup _ Xh_ j	o -\infty $. Otherwise, since $h_ j\leq p_ j\leq w'$, theorem 5.25.2 would give a subsequence converging in $L^1$ to some $h
ot\equiv -\infty $. title: Lemma 10.31.14
text: Lemma 10.31.14 . E0503BA0806A Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u\sim V$ and $u\leq V$. Let $\chi :\mathbb R_{\leq 0}\to \mathbb R_{\leq 0}$ be increasing and concave, with $\chi (0)=0$ and $\chi '\geq 1$, and assume that $\chi $ is $C^{1,1}$ on compact intervals. Set \[  b=V+\chi (u-V),\qquad p=P_\theta (b),  \] where the obstacle $b$ is defined off the pole set of $V$ and is set equal to $-\infty $ on that set. Then $p\sim V$ and \[  \mu _ p\leq \mathbf1_{\{ p=b\} }\chi '(u-V)^ n\mu _ u.  \] The measures and contact sets in this inequality may be restricted to the complement of the pole set of any fixed strict analytic barrier for $\theta $, that is, of any $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities such that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq a\omega $ for some $a>0$. Proof. The difference $u-V$ is bounded, so $V-C\leq b\leq u\leq V$ for some constant $C$. Hence $p\sim V$. The obstacle is quasi-continuous: away from sets of arbitrarily small capacity, $u$ and $V$ are finite and continuous, and their difference has a fixed bounded range. The general contact theorem theorem 15.8.6 therefore applies. Choose a strict analytic barrier $\rho $ and translate it so that $\rho \leq V$; put $\Omega =X\setminus \{ \rho =-\infty \} $. On this open set $u$, $V$ and $p$ are locally bounded. Let $\tau =\chi ^{-1}$; then $\tau $ is convex and $0<\tau '\leq 1$. By lemma 5.28.13 , the function \[  w=V+\tau (p-V)  \] is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $ and satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)\geq \tau '(p-V)^ n\mu _ p.  \] Since $p\leq w\leq V$ on $\Omega $, the removability lemma lemma 5.24.7 extends $w$ across the analytic set $X\setminus \Omega $, preserving its smooth lower curvature bound. The inequality $p\leq b$ implies $w\leq u$, with equality on $D=\{ p=b\} $. Ordered contact gives \[  \mathbf1_ D\tau '(p-V)^ n\mu _ p \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mu _ u.  \] On $D$ the derivative $\tau '(p-V)$ equals $1/\chi '(u-V)$. Together with contact support for $p$, this proves the claim on $\Omega $. The analytic set $X\setminus \Omega $ is not charged by the non-pluripolar measures involved. $\square$

A bounded carrier representation reduces an arbitrary finite non-pluripolar measure to increasing bounded densities, whose solutions have measures dominated by one fixed finite measure; theorem 10.31.5 then passes to the limit. Theorem 10.31.22 . AC1DBB01A890 For every finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $ with $\mu (X)>0$, the following assertions hold. For every $\lambda >0$ there is a unique $u\in \mathcal E_ V$ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu .  \] There are $v\in \mathcal E_ V$ with $\sup _ Xv=0$ and a unique scalar $c>0$ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_	heta (v)=c\mu .  \] Proof. First suppose that $\mu $ is a probability measure with $A_	heta (\mu )<\infty $, and let $\mu _ j$ be its smooth probability approximations. The theorems for the minimal ordinary type, theorem 15.16.2 , theorem 15.16.7 , apply to their smooth, nonzero densities. For the normalized equation, they give $v_ j\sim V$ with $\sup _ Xv_ j=0$ and $\mu _{v_ j}=c_ j\mu _ j$. Since $\mu _ j$ is a probability measure, the mass bounds $\ell _ V\leq \mu _{v_ j}(X)\leq M_ V$ give $\ell _ V\leq c_ j\leq M_ V$. After extraction, $c_ j	o c>0$ and $v_ j	o v$ in $L^1(X)$. The preceding proposition applies, so $v\in \mathcal E_ V$ and $\mu _{v_ j}ightharpoonup \mu _ v$. The right-hand sides converge weakly to $c\mu $, which proves the equation. For the positive-exponent equation, take $u_ j\sim V$ satisfying $\mu _{u_ j}=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}\mu _ j$, and write $a_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$ and $v_ j=u_ j-a_ j$. The mass bounds and Jensen's inequality give \[  \ell _ V\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda a_ j},\qquad M_ V\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda a_ j}\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_ j}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ j \geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda a_ j-\lambda A_	heta (\mu _ j)},  \] and $\sup _ jA_	heta (\mu _ j)<\infty $ by lemma 5.44.12 . Thus $a_ j$ is bounded above and below. After extraction, $a_ j	o a$, $v_ j	o v$ in $L^1(X)$, and $\mu _{v_ j}\leq C\mu _ j$. The preceding proposition gives $v\in \mathcal E_ V$, convergence in $L^1(\mu )$ and weak convergence of the Monge–Ampère measures. Set $u=v+a$. By the smoothing lemma, the right-hand sides converge weakly to $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $. This proves the equation, and $u\in \mathcal E_ V$. The same conclusions hold for every nonzero finite measure whose normalization to a probability measure has finite $A_	heta $, since scaling the measure only changes the positive scalar, or translates the solution of the exponential equation by a constant. The fixed-dominator theorem theorem 10.31.5 gives $v\in \mathcal E_ V$ and weak convergence to $\mu _ v$. Since $c_ k\mu _ k	o c\mu $ in total variation, $\mu _ v=c\mu $. For the positive-exponent equation, let $u_ k\in \mathcal E_ V$ solve $\mu _{u_ k}=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ k}\mu _ k$. To pass from the minimal class to the reference $\varphi $, we project a solution $z\in \mathcal E_ V$ onto $\mathcal E_\varphi $. The small stretches of lemma 13.20.1 first show that the rooftop $P_	heta (\varphi ,z)$ is not identically $-\infty $ and has the full upper volume of $\varphi $. Contact support then bounds the measure of the projection by the measure of $z$ on the set where the two coincide. The argument uses only that the reference of $z$ lies above $\varphi $, so we formulate it for an arbitrary ordinary model above $\varphi $; this will also allow the reference to vary. For $b>1$ sufficiently close to one, lemma 13.20.1 gives \[  h_ b=Q_ b(\varphi ,\eta )\leq \varphi ,  \] which is not identically $-\infty $. Set $a=1-b^{-1}$. The potential \[  k_ a=a z_{1/a}+(1-a)h_ b  \] lies below both $\varphi $ and $z$. text:
We now let the reference vary. Recall from definition 13.22.1 the comparison \[  d_	heta (u,v)=2\, \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\max (u,v)) -\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u)-\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (v)  \] and, for $\delta >0$, the set $\mathcal M_\delta (	heta )$ of ordinary models $u=P_	heta [u]$ with $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u)\geq \delta $. For models $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ in this comparison, theorem 13.23.3 provides increasing lower models whose upper volumes approach that of $\varphi $. Projecting finite families of potentials onto these lower models makes their rooftops comparable. To keep the limit in the relative class of $\varphi $, domination of the measures is needed only where the potentials lie below one fixed member of that class; domination on all of $X$ gives, in addition, convergence in capacity and convergence of the measures. Theorem 10.31.30 . 558CBE100687 Let $\varphi _ j,\varphi \in \mathcal M_\delta (	heta )$ for some $\delta >0$, with $d_	heta (\varphi _ j,\varphi )	o 0$. Suppose $u_ j\in \mathcal E_{\varphi _ j}$, $u_ j	o u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ in $L^1(X)$, and $\chi \in \mathcal E_\varphi $. If one finite non-pluripolar measure $

u +\mu _\chi $. Using lemma 5.44.2 , extract a subsequence along which $u_ j	o u$ almost everywhere for smooth volume and \[  I_ j:=\int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{u_ j}-\mathrm{e}^ u|\, \mathrm{d}\Lambda \leq 2^{-j}.  \] Apply theorem 13.23.3 to extract further, keeping these estimates, and obtain increasing models $w_ j\leq \varphi _ j,\varphi $ with lower volume at least $\delta /2$ and $d_	heta (w_ j,\varphi )	o 0$. Moreover $g_ j$ increases with $j$. The finite rooftop of these projections and $g_ j$ lies below $q_{j,N}$. Since $q_{j,N}\leq g_ j$, the finite-rooftop proposition and upward stability give $q_{j,N}\in \mathcal E_{\psi _ j}$, and hence $\mu _{q_{j,N}}(X)\geq \delta /2$. Partition the contact set of $q_{j,N}$ into disjoint pieces, one for each obstacle. On a piece where $q_{j,N}=u_ l$, we have $u_ l\leq g_ j\leq \chi $, so the hypothesis bounds the measure there by $
u $. On the piece where $q_{j,N}=g_ j$, the measure is bounded by $\mu _{g_ j}\leq \mu _\chi $. Consequently $\mu _{q_{j,N}}\leq \Lambda $. Put $F_ j=\min (\mathrm{e}^ u,\mathrm{e}^{g_ j})$. Since $h_ j\leq u\leq \varphi $, monotonicity and ( 10.31.31 ) show that $u$ and $\varphi $ have the same upper volume, and theorem 13.18.5 gives $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $.
