title: 24.11 Equations on singular spaces
text: On a resolution of a singular space, a pulled-back Hermitian form degenerates, and the pulled-back density can vanish or become singular. Existence on the resolution must therefore be combined with an estimate that allows the solution to descend. 9.11 develops potentials, envelopes, ideal equivalence and extended Monge–Ampère measures on reduced irreducible compact unibranch spaces, keeping the original nonclosed background. On projective cones, theorem 9.11.34 , theorem 9.11.43 solve explicit equations, for prescribed angular and radial data, in full ordinary logarithmic classes and in the bounded class of the closed background. The logarithmic construction includes nonclosed deformations that preserve the determinant, and its full solution descends even when the smooth residual is nonconstant on the exceptional fiber. The continuity results discussed in section 25.10 use additional geometric and integrability hypotheses, notably log terminal singularities. On the regular locus of a compact reduced irreducible Hermitian space of dimension at least two there is a conformal Gauduchon metric uniformly comparable to the original metric; see section 25.10 . This existence theorem does not by itself give the nonlinear equations asked for below. In dimension one, theorem 9.11.54 gives a different sufficient condition: the normalization is a torus, the prescribed ordinary type has finitely many logarithmic poles of total weight smaller than the mass of the background, and the measure has a nonnegative $L^ p$ density, $p>1$, with respect to the flat area on the normalization. Convolution with a Green function compensates for the degeneracy of the pulled-back background. The atoms at the poles determine the mass of every potential in the prescribed type and give uniqueness even among solutions that are a priori rough, and the residual descends continuously. The projective cusp of example 9.11.57 has an unbounded density on the curve itself although the data on the normalization are smooth. Every background on a curve is closed, so this construction gives no equation with a nonclosed background in higher dimension. The family of logarithmic densities in theorem 9.11.60 makes the integrability issue precise. Densities on the normalization with local form $C_0|z|^{-2}(\log (1/|z|))^{-\gamma }$ are integrable for $\gamma >1$, but they give a solution in the prescribed ordinary type exactly when $\gamma >2$. For $1<\gamma \leq 2$, the constructed solution keeps all multiplier ideals and the same non-pluripolar mass, but loses the lower bound defining the type. Multiplier-ideal equivalence alone therefore does not give a bounded residual. A criterion for general integrable data remains to be found. Problem 24.11.1 . A63319B4B931 Consider reduced irreducible compact unibranch complex spaces with a Hermitian form, as in 9.11 . Beyond the projective cones of subsection 9.11.27 , determine geometric conditions on such spaces and conditions on the measure that give existence and uniqueness of solutions in specified singularity classes. Identify estimates ensuring finite mass, descent from resolutions and continuity, and describe their behavior under common refinements of resolutions. In the cone examples, the pulled-back density vanishes on the exceptional divisor, and the logarithmic remainder solves an equation in a strictly positive background; the bounded equation for the closed background uses instead an energy that is coercive off that divisor. More general spaces of higher dimension require a replacement for these two controls. The curve construction uses a Green operator on the normalization; a linear construction by traces on a singular space needs further estimates across the singular locus.

title: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
search_title: Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: To solve an equation on a singular complex space, we pass to a resolution and then descend the solution. The pullback background can degenerate along exceptional fibers, and removing a logarithmic pole can leave a residual that does not descend. The examples in this appendix address these two difficulties directly. Except in the local toric calculations of 9.11.10 , 9.11.16 , $X$ denotes a reduced irreducible compact complex space of pure dimension $n\geq 1$ that is unibranch : its germ at every point is irreducible, or equivalently, its normalization is a homeomorphism. We write $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ for the regular and singular loci. Every point of $X$ has a neighborhood that embeds as a closed analytic subset of an open set in some $\mathbb C^ N$. Smooth functions and forms on $X$ are defined through such local embeddings: they are locally restrictions of smooth functions and forms on the ambient open sets. A Hermitian form on $X$ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form that is locally the restriction of a smooth strictly positive ambient $(1,1)$-form. Fix a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. A resolution of $X$ is a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map $\pi :Y\to X$ from a compact complex manifold $Y$; on $Y$ the pullback $\pi ^*\theta $ is an ordinary smooth form, to which the theory of the main text applies. In the last three sections, $X$ is a specific space of this kind. The basic tool is descent through a resolution. The pullback $\pi ^*\theta $ has no component along the fibers of $\pi $, so the maximum principle on the connected compact fibers shows that every $\pi ^*\theta $-plurisubharmonic function on $Y$ is constant on fibers and descends to $X$. This correspondence preserves envelopes and convergence. Exceptional sets carry no non-pluripolar mass, so the extended Monge–Ampère measure defined through a resolution does not depend on the resolution. On a projective cone, a logarithmic pole at the vertex becomes a divisor on the incidence resolution, and removing it leaves a strictly positive residual background. This gives uniqueness in the prescribed ordinary class, including for certain nonclosed backgrounds. The bounded equation on the cone uses closedness and an energy identity. The full logarithmic potential descends even when its smooth residual varies along the contracted divisor. On a curve whose normalization is a torus, a periodic Green function gives a separate construction. It allows the pulled-back background to vanish at singular points, and it treats every potential in a fixed ordinary type with finitely many logarithmic poles. A projective cusp shows that the residual can be continuous even though the density on the curve is unbounded. On products of a cuspidal curve with elliptic curves, a smooth potential repairs the degenerate background of the normalization, and two torsion identities fix the masses of all bounded potentials. For data close to the reference density, a positive solution gives uniqueness in the whole bounded class by a $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ energy comparison, even though the background is nonclosed. We use three facts about unibranch spaces. Resolutions and common smooth refinements of two resolutions exist, and a proper bimeromorphic map to a unibranch space has connected fibers Theorem 9.10.9 , Theorem 9.10.8 (Hironaka's Chow lemma) , Theorem 9.10.5 (Zariski's main theorem) . The Fornaess–Narasimhan criterion identifies plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ as the upper semicontinuous functions that are subharmonic on holomorphic disks Theorem 9.10.13 (Fornaess–Narasimhan) . The ramified disk lift used below is the argument in the proof of Theorem 9.10.14 (Grauert–Remmert) .

title: 9.11.1 Potentials and disk tests
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Since $X$ may be singular, $\theta $-plurisubharmonicity is defined by testing along holomorphic disks. Let $\Delta \subset \mathbb C$ be the unit disk. For a holomorphic map $f:\Delta \to X$, the pullback $f^*\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $\Delta $ and therefore has smooth local potentials. Disk tests thus express the background inequality even when $\theta $ has no local potential on $X$. Definition 9.11.2 . 76A75EB639CB An upper semicontinuous function $u:X\to [-\infty ,+\infty )$, not identically $-\infty $ on any nonempty open subset, is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic if it satisfies the following disk condition. For every holomorphic $f:\Delta \to X$, the function $u\circ f+a$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ wherever $a$ is a smooth local potential for $f^*\theta $. The set of these functions is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Two choices of $a$ differ by a harmonic function, so the condition is independent of that choice. On every disk where $u\circ f\not\equiv -\infty $, it gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ f)+f^*\theta \geq 0$ in the sense of distributions. Lemma 9.11.3 . E7163CA56764 Every member of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is locally the sum of a plurisubharmonic function on $X$ and a smooth function. If $X$ is smooth, this definition agrees with definition 5.22.1 . Proof. In a local embedding, choose an ambient smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function $r$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r\geq \theta $ on a smaller neighborhood. For a disk $f$ and a local potential $a$ of $f^*\theta $, the function $r\circ f-a$ is subharmonic. Hence $(u+r)\circ f$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. The Fornaess–Narasimhan criterion, together with the assumption that $u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any open set, shows that $u+r$ is plurisubharmonic. The smooth case now follows from lemma 5.43.2 . $\square$

section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Lemma 9.11.3 . E7163CA56764 Every member of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is locally the sum of a plurisubharmonic function on $X$ and a smooth function. title: 9.11.4 Descent through a resolution
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a resolution. Near a fiber of $\pi $, the background $\pi ^*\theta $ is dominated by the pullback of a local $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact form, so a local correction makes a $\pi ^*\theta $-plurisubharmonic function plurisubharmonic near the fiber. It is then constant on each compact irreducible component of the fiber, and connectedness of the fiber identifies these constants. Theorem 9.11.5 . F4C06D21AA94 Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a resolution. Pullback $u\mapsto u\circ \pi $ is an order-preserving bijection \[  \pi ^*:\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\longrightarrow \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta ).  \] It preserves suprema of individual functions, boundedness, and ordinary singularity comparisons. Proof. Pullback preserves the disk inequalities. Every nonempty open subset of $Y$ meets the locus where $\pi $ is biholomorphic, so a pullback is not identically $-\infty $ on any nonempty open set. Injectivity follows from surjectivity of $\pi $. For the converse, take $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta )$. Near a fiber, choose the local correction $r$ on $X$ used above. The function $v+r\circ \pi $ is plurisubharmonic on the inverse image of that neighborhood, since \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+r\circ \pi )\geq \pi ^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r-\theta )\geq 0.  \] Its restriction to each compact irreducible component of the fiber is constant, possibly $-\infty $, by the maximum principle on a resolution of that component. Connectedness of the fiber makes these constants equal: intersecting components have the same value, and the finite intersection graph of the components is connected. Since $r\circ \pi $ is constant on the fiber, so is $v$. Thus $v=u\circ \pi $ for a unique function $u$ on $X$. This function is upper semicontinuous: for each real $c$, the closed set $\{ v\geq c\} $ has closed image under the proper map $\pi $, and that image is $\{ u\geq c\} $. If $u$ were identically $-\infty $ on a nonempty open set, the same would hold for $v$ on its inverse image. Hence $u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any nonempty open set. It remains to verify the disk condition for $u$ with the background $\theta $ itself. Let $f:\Delta \to X$ be a holomorphic disk with $u\circ f\not\equiv -\infty $. Near a given point of $\Delta $, take a curve in the fiber product $\Delta \times _ XY$ dominating the disk. Its normalization gives, after shrinking, a finite cover $\rho (t)=t^ k$ and a holomorphic lift $f':\Delta \to Y$ with $\pi \circ f'=f\circ \rho $. Choose a smooth local function $a$ on the original disk with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a=f^*\theta $. The function \[  (u\circ f+a)\circ \rho =v\circ f'+a\circ \rho  \] is subharmonic by lemma 5.43.2 . Subharmonicity descends through $\rho $ by the finite-disk argument following that lemma. Thus $u\circ f+a$ is subharmonic near every point, which proves that pullback is a bijection. Since $\pi $ is surjective, pullback preserves suprema, uniform bounds and inequalities up to additive constants; this proves the remaining assertions. $\square$

Since $\pi $ is surjective, pullback preserves suprema, uniform bounds and inequalities up to additive constants; this proves the remaining assertions. $\square$

title: 9.11.6 Envelopes and normalized compactness
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Fix a resolution $\pi :Y\to X$. The envelopes of section 5.40 and definition 5.40.4 are defined on $X$ by the same formulas: for an obstacle $f:X\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$, $P_\theta (f)$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of all $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\leq f$ pointwise, and $P_\theta [u]$ is defined as in definition 5.40.4 . In the next proposition we assume that the family of these competitors is nonempty and locally uniformly bounded above. The descent bijection identifies the competitors on $X$ and on $Y$; the remaining issue is whether upper semicontinuous regularization commutes with pullback. Proposition 9.11.7 . 622B386B559D For such an obstacle $f:X\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$, the envelope $P_\theta (f)$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and \[  P_{\pi ^*\theta }(f\circ \pi )=P_\theta (f)\circ \pi .  \] The same identity holds for the ordinary envelope $P_\theta [u]$, for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Proof. The preceding theorem identifies the competitor families. Let $s$ be their pointwise supremum on $X$; its pullback is the pointwise supremum upstairs. The regularization of $s\circ \pi $ on $Y$ is $\pi ^*\theta $-plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $, since there is a competitor below it. By the theorem, it descends to a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $q$. Since $q\geq s$ and $q$ is upper semicontinuous, $q\geq s^*$. For the reverse inequality, fix $x\in X$ and $y\in \pi ^{-1}(x)$. For each neighborhood $U$ of $x$, the unregularized supremum upstairs is bounded by $\sup _ U s$ on the open neighborhood $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ of $y$. Therefore $q(x)\leq \sup _ U s$, and taking the infimum over $U$ gives $q(x)\leq s^*(x)$. This proves the identity and shows that $P_\theta (f)=s^*$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. The proof for $P_\theta [u]$ is identical, because pullback preserves the ordinary singularity order together with its constants. $\square$ We give the normalized space $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\sup _ Xu=0\} $ the $L^1$ topology of the pullbacks to $Y$. By theorem 5.25.2 and descent, it is compact. On a fixed resolution, different smooth positive volume forms give equivalent norms. Under a further modification, pullback is continuous by lemma 5.43.19 and bijective by descent, hence a homeomorphism between the normalized compact spaces. Since any two resolutions are dominated by a common one, the topology does not depend on the resolution; the norms on different models are not compared.

title: 9.11.8 Ideal envelopes defined on resolutions
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Multiplier ideals on smooth models give a singularity relation on $X$. Call two potentials $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ resolution-ideal equivalent if $u\circ \pi \sim _{\mathcal I}v\circ \pi $ on one resolution $\pi :Y\to X$ (the ideal type of section 5.33 ), that is, if $\mathcal I(k\, u\circ \pi )=\mathcal I(k\, v\circ \pi )$ for every real $k>0$. By lemma 5.43.24 , applied on a common refinement, this does not depend on the resolution. The ideal projection of theorem 18.4.2 then defines an envelope in this class. Proposition 9.11.9 . C43A6C429C4D For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, there is a unique potential $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}^{\mathrm{res}}$ on $X$ satisfying \[  P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}^{\mathrm{res}}\circ \pi =P_{\pi ^*\theta }[u\circ \pi ]_{\mathcal I}  \] on every resolution $\pi :Y\to X$, where the right-hand side is the multiplier-ideal envelope of definition 18.4.1 on $Y$. It preserves the resolution-ideal class, is idempotent, has supremum zero, and is independent of the resolution. Proof. For a fixed resolution, the right-hand side exists by theorem 18.4.2 and descends by theorem 9.11.5 . Under a further smooth modification, the competitor families of the ideal envelopes correspond by the descent theorem and lemma 5.43.24 , and the regularized suprema commute by the argument of proposition 9.11.7 . Thus two resolutions give the same pullback on a common refinement, and hence the same function on $X$. Idempotence, preservation of the class and the normalization follow from the corresponding assertions on $Y$ and surjectivity of $\pi $. $\square$ An intrinsic restricted ideal trace on a subspace contained in the singular locus would require a regularization compatible with restriction to that subspace; the resolution-ideal envelope provides neither the regularization nor the trace.

text:
The resolution-ideal relation above uses smooth volume forms on smooth models. An integrability ideal on a singular space can instead use a volume form determined by its canonical bundle and a boundary divisor. The following local example shows how this additional weight changes the ideal. In this subsection, replace the compact space fixed above by the affine surface \[  X=\{ z_1z_2=z_3^2\} \subset \mathbb C^3, \qquad E=\{ z_1=z_3=0\} ,\qquad D=	frac 12 E.  \] The finite map \[  \pi :\mathbb C^2\longrightarrow X, \qquad \pi (s,t)=(s^2,t^2,st),  \] identifies $X$ with the quotient by $(s,t)\mapsto (-s,-t)$. It has degree two and is unramified away from the origin. Holomorphic germs at the origin of $X$ correspond to convergent series in $s,t$ containing only monomials $s^ at^ b$ with $a+b$ even. Indeed, every such series has the form $F_0(s^2,t^2)+stF_1(s^2,t^2)$ with $F_0,F_1$ convergent. On $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the canonical two-form \[  \Omega = rac{\mathrm{d}z_1\wedge \mathrm{d}z_3}{z_1} = rac{\mathrm{d}z_3\wedge \mathrm{d}z_2}{z_2}  \] is defined on the respective charts $z_1
eq 0$ and $z_2
eq 0$. These charts cover $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the formulas agree, and $\pi ^*\Omega =2\, \mathrm{d}s\wedge \mathrm{d}t$. The residue form $\Omega $ generates the dualizing sheaf of this hypersurface. Since $\operatorname {div}(z_1)=2E$, the meromorphic fourth tensor power \[   eta = rac{\Omega ^{\otimes 4}}{z_1}  \] generates $\omega _ X^{[4]}(4D)$, the reflexive fourth power of the dualizing sheaf twisted by $4D$. Take the fourth root of its squared absolute value to define the adapted volume $\mathrm{d}V_ D$ on $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$; for zero boundary use the squared absolute value of $\Omega $ and write $\mathrm{d}V_0$. Their pullbacks are 0C6FD486D0E4 9.11.11  egin{equation}  \pi ^*\mathrm{d}V_ D=C_ D|s|^{-1}\, \mathrm{d}A_ s\, \mathrm{d}A_ t, \qquad \pi ^*\mathrm{d}V_0=C_0\, \mathrm{d}A_ s\, \mathrm{d}A_ t, \end{equation} where $\mathrm{d}A$ denotes Euclidean area and $C_ D,C_0>0$ depend only on the convention for absolute values of forms. Replacing a generator by a holomorphic unit multiplies the volume by a positive factor bounded above and below on smaller neighborhoods. For $B\in \{ 0,D\} $ and a plurisubharmonic function $u$ on this $X$, define the adapted-volume integrability ideal by 727AAF0F7AFF 9.11.12  egin{equation}  \mathcal I_ B^{\mathrm{ad}}(u)_ x =\left\{ f\in \mathcal O_{X,x}: \int _{U\cap X_{\mathrm{reg}}}|f|^2\mathrm{e}^{-u}\, \mathrm{d}V_ B<\infty ight\} , \end{equation} where the neighborhood $U$ of $x$ may be chosen for each germ $f$. This uses the weight convention of definition 6.8.5 . It defines a different object from the resolution-ideal class: the volume in ( 9.11.12 ), including its boundary weight, is part of the definition. The polar-coordinate calculation needed here also keeps track of the strict integrability boundary. Lemma 9.11.13 . A56815B99E6B Let $A,B,\alpha , eta ,T>0$. Then \[  \int _ T^\infty \int _ T^\infty \exp  igl (-\alpha p- eta q+\min (Ap,Bq) igr ) \, \mathrm{d}q\, \mathrm{d}p<\infty \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad  rac\alpha A+ rac eta B>1.  \] At equality the integral diverges. Proof. Split the quadrant along $q=Ap/B$. On the part $q\geq Ap/B$, set $p_0=\max \{ T,BT/A\} $. After discarding the strip $T<p<p_0$, integration in $q$ gives \[   rac1 eta \int _{p_0}^\infty \exp \left(-\left[\alpha -A+ rac{ eta A}{B}ight]pight) \, \mathrm{d}p.  \] The discarded strip has finite integral because $ eta >0$. On the other part, integration in $p$ gives the corresponding tail with coefficient $ eta -B+\alpha B/A$; its discarded strip is finite because $\alpha >0$. Both coefficients are positive exactly when $\alpha /A+ eta /B>1$. If that sum equals one, either tail is an integral of a positive constant over a half-line. $\square$ Proposition 9.11.14 . DA5FE7ECD89D The plurisubharmonic function \[  u=\max \{ \sqrt2\log |z_1|^2,\, 2\log |z_2|^2\}   \] on $X$ does not have analytic singularities at the origin. Its adapted-volume ideals are \[  \mathcal I_ D^{\mathrm{ad}}(u)=(z_1,z_3,z_2^2)\mathcal O_ X, \qquad \mathcal I_0^{\mathrm{ad}}(u)=(z_1,z_2,z_3)\mathcal O_ X.  \] In particular, the same potential requires the generator $z_2^2$ in place of $z_2$ when the boundary $D$ is included. Proof. The function is the restriction of a maximum of two plurisubharmonic functions on $\mathbb C^3$. On the axes parametrized by $(z_1,z_2,z_3)=(\zeta ,0,0)$ and $(0,\zeta ,0)$, its logarithmic coefficients are $\sqrt2$ and $2$. An analytic singularity $c\log \sum _ j|f_ j|^2+O(1)$ restricts to a logarithmic coefficient equal to $c$ times an integer on either axis, provided that it is finite off the origin there. The ratio of the two coefficients would therefore be rational, which it is not. Pullback by the finite degree-two map reduces local integrability to the cover. Neighborhoods of the origin contain and are contained in images of sufficiently small bidisks, so it suffices to integrate over a bidisk in $s,t$. The pullback weight is \[  u\circ \pi =\max \{ 2\sqrt2\log |s|^2,\, 4\log |t|^2\} .  \] For $s^ at^ b$, $a,b\geq 0$, set $p=-\log |s|^2$ and $q=-\log |t|^2$. By ( 9.11.11 ), angular integration gives, up to a positive constant, \[  \int _ T^\infty \int _ T^\infty \exp \left(-\left[a+	frac 12ight]p-(b+1)q +\min (2\sqrt2\, p,4q)ight) \, \mathrm{d}q\, \mathrm{d}p  \] for the boundary $D$. Indeed, the measure and the weight on the cover are invariant under separate rotations of $s,t$. Parseval's identity and Tonelli's theorem show that every nonzero coefficient of a weighted-integrable holomorphic series must satisfy its monomial test. Only exponents with $a+b$ even occur. In the first test, the minimal allowed exponents, under addition of nonnegative even-total exponents, are \[  (2,0),\quad (1,1),\quad (0,4).  \] To see this, every term with $a\geq 2$ is divisible by $s^2$, every term with $a=1$ has odd $b\geq 1$ and is divisible by $st$, and a term with $a=0$ has even $b$ and passes the test exactly when $b\geq 4$. Each of the three displayed exponents passes the test. Splitting a convergent invariant series into these three groups and dividing gives convergent invariant coefficient series on a smaller bidisk. They descend to holomorphic germs on $X$, bounded on a smaller neighborhood. Since the three generators are weighted-integrable, every such combination is weighted-integrable. This proves the first ideal at the origin. For the second test, every nonconstant even-total monomial is allowed, with minimal exponents $(2,0),(1,1),(0,2)$, and the same argument gives the second ideal. Away from the origin, $u$ is locally bounded and $X$ is smooth. The only additional volume singularity lies along $E$: with $z_2
eq 0$, $z_3$ is a normal coordinate and $z_1=z_3^2/z_2$, so $\mathrm{d}V_ D$ is a smooth positive factor times $|z_3|^{-1}$ times smooth volume. This is locally integrable. Both ideals therefore equal $\mathcal O_ X$ there, as do the ideals generated by the displayed coordinates, which proves the sheaf identities. $\square$ The calculation depends on the prescribed volume as well as on $u$. It does not change the resolution-ideal equivalence used in proposition 9.11.9 . The next calculation expresses the exponent test for a general full-dimensional affine toric cone.

title: 9.11.16 Adapted monomial tests on affine toric spaces
search_title: Adapted monomial tests on affine toric spaces
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: The quotient calculation expresses integrability as a strict inequality on exponents. On an affine toric space the same inequality comes from the recession of a convex function, while the canonical bundle and boundary supply the translation of the exponent. This also applies to cones with more rays than their dimension. In this subsection let $N$ be a lattice of rank $n\geq 1$, let $M=\operatorname {Hom}(N,\mathbb Z)$, and let $\sigma \subset N_{\mathbb R}$ be a full-dimensional strongly convex rational polyhedral cone. Its dual cone is $\sigma ^\vee =\{ m:\langle m,v\rangle \geq 0\text{ for all }v\in \sigma \} $. The normal affine toric space \[  X_\sigma =\operatorname {Spec}\mathbb C[\sigma ^\vee \cap M]  \] is understood with its analytic structure. Its dense torus $T=\operatorname {Hom}(M,\mathbb C^*)$ has characters $\chi ^ m$, and its unique closed orbit is a vertex $o$. Choose nonzero generators $b_1,\ldots ,b_ s$ of the semigroup $\sigma ^\vee \cap M$; their characters embed $X_\sigma $ as a closed affine subset of $\mathbb C^ s$ and all vanish at $o$. For each ray $\rho $ of $\sigma $, write $v_\rho $ for its primitive lattice generator and $D_\rho $ for the corresponding prime divisor. Fix an effective rational boundary $D=\sum _\rho a_\rho D_\rho $ such that $K_{X_\sigma }+D$ is $\mathbb Q$-Cartier. With $K_{X_\sigma }=-\sum _\rho D_\rho $, this means that there is $w_ D\in M_{\mathbb Q}$ with A72FB1B5D26F 9.11.17 \begin{equation}  \langle w_ D,v_\rho \rangle =1-a_\rho \quad \text{for every }\rho . \end{equation} Take an integer $q>0$ with $qw_ D\in M$. For torus coordinates $t_1,\ldots ,t_ n$ determined by a basis of $M$, the meromorphic tensor \[  B_ D=\chi ^{qw_ D} \left(\frac{\mathrm dt_1}{t_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \frac{\mathrm dt_ n}{t_ n}\right)^{\! \otimes q}  \] generates $\omega _{X_\sigma }^{[q]}(qD)$. Indeed, its order along $D_\rho $ is $-qa_\rho $. The adapted volume $\mathrm dV_ D=|B_ D|^{2/q}$ is independent of this choice for local integrability, as in ( 9.11.11 ). We use the ideal $\mathcal I_ D^{\mathrm{ad}}(u)$ defined by the holomorphic-germ integral in ( 9.11.12 ) on this $X_\sigma $. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function invariant under the compact torus of coordinate rotations. The logarithmic map $\operatorname {Log}:T\to N_{\mathbb R}$ satisfies $\langle m,\operatorname {Log}t\rangle =\log |\chi ^ m(t)|$. There is a finite convex function $g$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ with \[  u(t)=2g(\operatorname {Log}t).  \] To see convexity, pull $u/2$ back by the exponential covering of $T$. It is independent of the imaginary coordinates, so its distributional complex Hessian is the real Hessian of $g$ up to a positive constant. A nontrivial plurisubharmonic function of this form gives a finite convex function. The factor two matches the weight $\mathrm e^{-u}$. For a finite convex function $g$ write \[  (\operatorname {rec}g)(v)= \lim _{t\to \infty }\frac{g(x+tv)-g(x)}t.  \] The convex difference quotients increase to this limit in $\mathbb R\cup \{ +\infty \} $; the limit does not depend on the base point $x$. The latter fact follows by comparing $g(x+tv)$ with convex combinations of $g(t v/(1-\delta ))$ and $g(x/\delta )$, for $0<\delta <1$, and then reversing the translation. Define the Newton set 4B4F6518339A 9.11.18 \begin{equation}  P(u)=\left\{ \ell \in M_{\mathbb R}: \sup _{x\in -\sigma }\bigl (\langle \ell ,x\rangle -g(x)\bigr )<\infty \right\} . \end{equation} Only its interior will enter the integrability test; the set itself need not be closed. Lemma 9.11.19 . 5D5A847F99AC Let $C$ be a closed full-dimensional convex cone in a Euclidean space, let $g$ be finite and convex, and let $\ell $ be a linear form. Then \[  \int _ C\exp \bigl (2\langle \ell ,x\rangle -2g(x)\bigr )\, \mathrm dx<\infty \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \langle \ell ,v\rangle <(\operatorname {rec}g)(v) \quad (v\in C\setminus \{ 0\} ).  \] This condition is also equivalent to $\ell $ being an interior point of $\{ a:\sup _ C(\langle a,x\rangle -g(x))<\infty \} $. The integral has the same finiteness on every translate of $C$. Proof. Set $F=g-\ell $. Suppose its recession is positive on $C\setminus \{ 0\} $. Then $F(x)\geq \gamma |x|-A$ on $C$ for some $\gamma >0$ and $A$. Otherwise there are $x_ j\in C$ with $|x_ j|\to \infty $ and $F(x_ j)/|x_ j|\leq 1/j$. After taking a subsequence, $x_ j/|x_ j|\to v\in C$ with $|v|=1$. For fixed $t>0$, convexity gives \[  F\left(t\frac{x_ j}{|x_ j|}\right) \leq \left(1-\frac t{|x_ j|}\right)F(0) +\frac t{|x_ j|}F(x_ j).  \] Continuity gives $F(tv)\leq F(0)$ for every $t$, contradicting positive recession. A bound on the remaining compact set gives the asserted $A$. Exponential decay proves integrability. The same bound persists when $\ell $ is changed by a sufficiently small linear form, so $\ell $ lies in the stated interior. Conversely, if $(\operatorname {rec}F)(v)\leq 0$ for some nonzero $v\in C$, then $F(tv)\leq F(0)$ for $t\geq 0$. Choose a compact ball $K$ in the interior of $C$. On the half-tube $\{ tv+x/2:t\geq 1,\  x\in K\} $, convexity gives \[  F(tv+x/2)\leq \tfrac 12F(2tv)+\tfrac 12F(x).  \] Thus $\mathrm e^{-2F}$ has a positive lower bound on a set of infinite volume. If instead $\ell $ is in the stated interior, for each nonzero $v\in C$ one may perturb $\ell $ within that interior by a linear form positive on $v$. Dividing its defining upper bound along $tv$ by $t$ gives the strict recession inequality for $\ell $. Finally, translating $C$ replaces $g(x)$ by $g(x+b)$ and multiplies the exponential by a constant; recession is unchanged. $\square$ Theorem 9.11.20 . CD69C52538E4 For $m\in \sigma ^\vee \cap M$, the following are equivalent: \[  \chi ^ m\in \mathcal I_ D^{\mathrm{ad}}(u)_ o, \qquad \chi ^ m\in \Gamma (X_\sigma ,\mathcal I_ D^{\mathrm{ad}}(u)), \qquad m+w_ D\in \operatorname {int}P(u).  \] Equivalently, $\langle m+w_ D,v\rangle <(\operatorname {rec}g)(v)$ for every nonzero $v\in -\sigma $. Proof. On the torus, polar coordinates turn the weighted monomial integral into a positive constant times \[  \int _ Q\exp \bigl (2\langle m+w_ D,x\rangle -2g(x)\bigr )\, \mathrm dx,  \] where $Q$ is the logarithmic image of the domain. The omitted toric divisors have measure zero on the regular locus. A basis of neighborhoods of $o$ is given by $|\chi ^{b_ j}|<\epsilon $ for every $j$, with $0<\epsilon <1$. Their logarithmic domains satisfy 4CC45280AE88 9.11.21 \begin{equation}  -\sigma -b\  \subset  Q_\epsilon =\{ x:\langle b_ j,x\rangle <\log \epsilon \text{ for all }j\}  \  \subset \  -\sigma , \end{equation} for $b\in \operatorname {int}\sigma $ sufficiently far along an interior ray. Indeed, every $\langle b_ j,b\rangle $ is strictly positive, and the $b_ j$ generate the dual cone. The convex-cone lemma gives necessity and sufficiency at $o$, including divergence when a recession inequality is an equality. For a compact subset of $X_\sigma $, the embedding coordinates have absolute value at most some $R>1$. Its logarithmic image is contained in $\{ x:\langle b_ j,x\rangle \leq \log R\} $, which is contained in $b_ R-\sigma $ for a sufficiently large $b_ R\in \operatorname {int}\sigma $. E77092231FA9 Let $\mathfrak a=(\chi ^{a_1},\ldots ,\chi ^{a_ r})$ be a nonzero monomial ideal on $X_\sigma $, with $a_ j\in \sigma ^\vee \cap M$, and let $c>0$ be real. Proof. For a finite sum and $c>0$, its $c$-th power is comparable to the sum of the $c$-th powers of its terms. Thus the integrand is comparable to \[  \sum _ j |\chi ^ m|^2|\chi ^{a_ j}|^{2c}\mathrm e^{-u}\, \mathrm dV_ D.  \] Each term gives the preceding logarithmic integral with exponent $m+w_ D+ca_ j$. For $\lambda >0$ put \[  u_\lambda =\lambda \log (|x|^2+|y|^2+|z|^2+|w|^2).  \] The adapted-volume ideal at the vertex is \[  \mathcal I_0^{\mathrm{ad}}(u_\lambda )_ o =\mathfrak m_ o^{\, \max \{ 0,\lfloor \lambda \rfloor -1\} } \mathcal O_{X,o}.  \] In particular, the constant germ is integrable exactly when $\lambda <2$. Proof. On the torus use $x,y,z$ as characters, so $w=yz/x$. The character lattice is $\mathbb Z^3$, with semigroup generators \[  (1,0,0),\quad (0,1,0),\quad (0,0,1),\quad (-1,1,1).  \] The dual cone has primitive rays $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,1)$, $(1,1,0)$ and $(1,0,1)$. The residue form $\Omega =\mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm dy\wedge \mathrm dz/x$ generates the canonical sheaf of this hypersurface; it equals $yz$ times the logarithmic torus form. Hence $w_0=(0,1,1)$, which pairs to one with each primitive ray. Write $d(m)=m_1+m_2+m_3$. Each semigroup generator has degree one. title: Lemma 9.11.19
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Lemma 9.11.19 . 5D5A847F99AC Let $C$ be a closed full-dimensional convex cone in a Euclidean space, let $g$ be finite and convex, and let $\ell $ be a linear form. Then \[  \int _ C\exp \bigl (2\langle \ell ,x\rangle -2g(x)\bigr )\, \mathrm dx<\infty \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \langle \ell ,v\rangle <(\operatorname {rec}g)(v) \quad (v\in C\setminus \{ 0\} ).  \] This condition is also equivalent to $\ell $ being an interior point of $\{ a:\sup _ C(\langle a,x\rangle -g(x))<\infty \} $. The integral has the same finiteness on every translate of $C$. Proof. Set $F=g-\ell $. Suppose its recession is positive on $C\setminus \{ 0\} $. Then $F(x)\geq \gamma |x|-A$ on $C$ for some $\gamma >0$ and $A$. Otherwise there are $x_ j\in C$ with $|x_ j|\to \infty $ and $F(x_ j)/|x_ j|\leq 1/j$. After taking a subsequence, $x_ j/|x_ j|\to v\in C$ with $|v|=1$. For fixed $t>0$, convexity gives \[  F\left(t\frac{x_ j}{|x_ j|}\right) \leq \left(1-\frac t{|x_ j|}\right)F(0) +\frac t{|x_ j|}F(x_ j).  \] Continuity gives $F(tv)\leq F(0)$ for every $t$, contradicting positive recession. A bound on the remaining compact set gives the asserted $A$. Exponential decay proves integrability. The same bound persists when $\ell $ is changed by a sufficiently small linear form, so $\ell $ lies in the stated interior. Conversely, if $(\operatorname {rec}F)(v)\leq 0$ for some nonzero $v\in C$, then $F(tv)\leq F(0)$ for $t\geq 0$. Choose a compact ball $K$ in the interior of $C$. On the half-tube $\{ tv+x/2:t\geq 1,\  x\in K\} $, convexity gives \[  F(tv+x/2)\leq \tfrac 12F(2tv)+\tfrac 12F(x).  \] Thus $\mathrm e^{-2F}$ has a positive lower bound on a set of infinite volume. If instead $\ell $ is in the stated interior, for each nonzero $v\in C$ one may perturb $\ell $ within that interior by a linear form positive on $v$. Dividing its defining upper bound along $tv$ by $t$ gives the strict recession inequality for $\ell $. Finally, translating $C$ replaces $g(x)$ by $g(x+b)$ and multiplies the exponential by a constant; recession is unchanged. $\square$

title: 9.11.24 Extended measures and finite damping
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Choose a resolution $\pi :Y\to X$. Two resolutions are isomorphic over the complement of a proper analytic subset of $X$, and their extended measures agree there. Since these measures do not charge pluripolar sets, the omitted analytic sets do not affect the comparison, even when the total mass is infinite. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ define 96D4B9F40B0A 9.11.25 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u) =\pi _*\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{Y,\pi ^*\theta }(u\circ \pi ), \end{equation} where $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{Y,\pi ^*\theta }$ is the extended measure of theorem 13.14.3 on $Y$. Theorem 9.11.26 . D12D6E199E87 The right-hand side of ( 9.11.25 ) is the same for every resolution, including resolutions that modify regular points. It is a positive $\sigma $-finite Borel measure, gives zero mass to $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and to locally pluripolar sets, and may have infinite total mass; for bounded $u$ it is finite. Put $r_ n=\max (n-2,0)$. There are finite constants $C$ and, for each $q>r_ n$, $C_ q$, depending only on the fixed background data and, for $C_ q$, on $q$, such that for every nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and every $p>0$, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{pu}\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u) \leq C(1+p^{-1})^{r_ n},\qquad \int _ X(1-u)^{-q}\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u) \leq C_ q.  \] The constants may be obtained on any one fixed resolution. Proof. Given two resolutions, choose a proper analytic subset $S\subset X$ containing $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and the images of both exceptional sets. Each map is an isomorphism over $X\setminus S$, and there the two measures are given by the same bounded local products, followed by truncation and exhaustion. On each resolution, the inverse image of $S$ is a proper analytic subset and has zero extended mass by theorem 13.14.3 . Hence both pushforwards give $S$ zero mass. This proves independence, including for resolutions whose exceptional sets lie over regular points. Positivity follows from positivity on $Y$. On $X\setminus S$ either resolution is a Borel isomorphism, so a countable exhaustion of $Y$ by sets of finite measure pushes forward to one on $X$; adjoining the null set $S$ proves $\sigma $-finiteness. A locally pluripolar subset of $X$ pulls back to a pluripolar set off the exceptional locus, and the exceptional locus itself has zero mass. This gives the asserted vanishing. If $u$ is bounded, its pullback is bounded on the compact manifold $Y$, and local bounded-product estimates give finite total mass. For general nonpositive $u$, apply theorem 13.15.23 on $Y$ to the smooth background $\pi ^*\theta $. Pushforward and the identity $u\circ \pi $ identify the weighted integrals exactly, and the constants come from $\pi ^*\theta $ and a Hermitian metric on $Y$. $\square$ We define convergence in capacity on $X$ as convergence in capacity of the pullbacks to a resolution, using a smooth Hermitian metric there. The local capacity comparison of section 5.29 makes the metric immaterial, and lemma 5.43.20 , applied on a common resolution, makes the choice of resolution immaterial. By theorem 13.15.23 and proper pushforward, both damped measures in the theorem depend weakly continuously on nonpositive potentials for this convergence in capacity. For nonpositive potentials $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ converging in capacity, the undamped measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u_ j)$ converge weakly if, in addition, their total masses are uniformly bounded and their masses on $\{ u_ j<-T\} $ tend to zero uniformly in $j$ as $T\to \infty $. Pullback preserves these mass and sublevel conditions. General equations on singular spaces require estimates for the degeneracy of the pulled-back background and of the density; see 24.11.1 . For the cone geometry below, a radial construction gives solutions in a prescribed logarithmic class and in the bounded class of a closed background.

title: 9.11.27 Equations on projective cones
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text:
The residual construction of section 15.22 has a counterpart on a projective cone, which is a singular space. A logarithmic pole at the vertex becomes a divisor on the incidence resolution, and removing it leaves a positive residual background. The radial equation below determines both the solution and its normalization scalar. Uniqueness among bounded residuals holds because the lifted density is smooth and its positive locus is connected and dense, even though the density vanishes on the exceptional section. Let $B\subset \mathbb P^ N$ be a smooth connected, linearly nondegenerate, projectively normal variety of dimension $n-1$, where $N\geq n\geq 2$. Let $X\subset \mathbb P^{N+1}$ be its projective cone, with vertex $p=[0:\cdots :0:1]$, and let $	heta _0=\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}|_ X$ be the restriction of the Fubini–Study form of $\mathbb P^{N+1}$. Write the ambient homogeneous coordinates as $[Z:W]$, with $Z=(Z_0,\ldots ,Z_ N)$. The incidence resolution $\pi :Y	o X$ is a smooth $\mathbb P^1$-bundle $f:Y	o B$; its section $E=\pi ^{-1}(p)$ is contracted, and $\pi $ is an isomorphism off $E$. These cones are reduced, irreducible, compact and normal, hence unibranch, and their vertices are singular. Indeed, the homogeneous coordinate ring of $B$ is normal by projective normality. Adjoining $W$ preserves normality, and so do the degree-zero projective charts. Algebraic normality passes to the associated analytic space by the algebraic–analytic normality theorem. Smoothness and connectedness of $B$ give irreducibility. In the chart $W=1$, the ideal of the affine cone has no linear terms, by linear nondegeneracy. Its tangent space at the origin therefore has dimension $N+1>n$, so $p$ is singular. The incidence construction is the bundle of lines in $\mathcal O_ B\oplus \mathcal O_ B(-1)$ and has the stated contraction and isomorphism properties. Write \[   egin{gathered} \omega _ B=\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}|_ B,\qquad  eta =\pi ^*	heta _0,\qquad \sigma =f^*\omega _ B,\ d=\int _ B\omega _ B^{n-1},\qquad x= rac{\| Z\| ^2}{\| Z\| ^2+|W|^2}. \end{gathered}  \] The same symbol $x$ denotes its pullback to $Y$. Choose $\Psi \in C^\infty (\mathbb P^ N,\mathbb R)$ with $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi >0$ and $k\in C^\infty ([0,1])$ with $k>0$. Put $\psi =\Psi |_ B$ and define on $Y$ DF6E62BA10C0 9.11.28  egin{equation}   egin{gathered} s= rac{\mathrm{e}^\psi x}{1-x+\mathrm{e}^\psi x},\qquad \ell =\log (1-x+\mathrm{e}^\psi x),\qquad \sigma _\psi =f^*(\omega _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi ),\ B_\psi = eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\ell ,\qquad 
u =k(s)B_\psi ^ n,\qquad \mu =\pi _*
u ,\ I=\int _0^1 k(r)r^{n-1}\, \mathrm{d} r,\qquad M=ndI. \end{gathered} \end{equation} These data prescribe the measure $\mu $ before the equation is solved. The local form and the fiber integral below describe its degeneracy along $E$ and show that its total mass is $M$. Choose a local holomorphic lift $b(z)$ of the embedding of $B$, and write $S(z)=\sum |b_ j(z)|^2$ and $Z=t b(z)$. In these local coordinates $(z,t)$ on $Y$, \[   eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|t|^2S),\qquad \sigma =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log S.  \] On $0<x<1$ put $ho =\log (|t|^2S)$, $ho _\psi =ho +\psi $, $h(r)=\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ r)$ and $\zeta _\psi =\mathrm{d}ho _\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}ho _\psi $. Then $x=h'(ho )$, $s=h'(ho _\psi )$ and $\ell =h(ho _\psi )-h(ho )$. Differentiation gives 4720371980C9 9.11.29  egin{equation}  B_\psi =s\sigma _\psi +s(1-s)\zeta _\psi ,\qquad \sigma _\psi ^ n=0,\qquad \zeta _\psi ^2=0. \end{equation} Near $E$, a local potential of $B_\psi $ is $\log (1+\mathrm{e}^\psi |t|^2S)$; at $t=0$ its Hessian has rank one, in the transverse direction. At the infinity section, with $v=1/t$, a local potential is $\log (\mathrm{e}^\psi S+|v|^2)$; its tangential Hessian is $\sigma _\psi $ and its transverse coefficient is positive. These computations show that $B_\psi $ is smooth and semipositive, and positive off $E$. Since $n\geq 2$, its top power vanishes on $E$. Along a fiber, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}ho _\psi =\mathrm{d}(\arg t)/(2\pi )$ and $\mathrm{d}ho _\psi =\mathrm{d} s/[s(1-s)]$. Base components disappear after wedging with $\sigma _\psi ^{n-1}$, so ( 9.11.29 ) gives \[  f_*
u =nI(\omega _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1}.  \] Since $\omega _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ is closed, Stokes' theorem on $B$ gives $\int _ B(\omega _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1}=d$, hence $
u (Y)=M$. Smooth measures give $E$ zero mass. Therefore $\mu (X)=M$ and $\mu (\{ p\} )=0$. Taking $\psi =0$ and $k=1$ gives $\int _ Y eta ^ n=d$.

title: 9.11.30 Logarithmic poles at the vertex
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces

text: Without a logarithmic pole, the residual background is $\beta $, which degenerates along $E$. The radial construction still gives a bounded solution, and closedness of $\beta $ gives an energy argument for its uniqueness. Theorem 9.11.43 . 4CE6B71B5B25 For the same cone and prescribed measure, there is a unique pair $(c,u)$, with $c>0$ and $u$ a bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$, such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta _0}(u)=c\mu $. Every bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function has mass $d$. Formula ( 9.11.35 ), with $\theta _0$ in place of $\theta _ H$, holds on every resolution and common refinement. Since $R(1)=1$, $Q$ is smooth at $s=1$, and its derivative is also smooth at zero. Put $U=\ell +Q(s)$. It is smooth on $Y$ and equals $Q(0)$ on $E$. On $0<x<1$, a local potential for $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ is $F(\rho _\psi )$, where $F(r)=h(r)+Q(h'(r))$. Differentiation gives $F'=P(s)$ and $F''=c_ bk(s)s^ n(1-s)/P(s)^{n-1}$. Subtracting $K_ b=\sup _ Xu_0$ gives the required solution. Let $w$ be a bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function. Its pullback $g=w\circ \pi $ is bounded and $\beta $-plurisubharmonic. Integrating the bounded expansion and using that $\beta $ is closed gives $\int _ Y(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)^ n=\int _ Y\beta ^ n=d$; this forces the scalar of any solution to be $c_ b=d/M$. The resolution identity follows from theorem 9.11.26 . Now suppose that $w$ solves the equation, and put $q=U-K_ b$, $D=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ and $v=g-q$. text: Theorem 9.11.43 . 4CE6B71B5B25 For the same cone and prescribed measure, there is a unique pair $(c,u)$, with $c>0$ and $u$ a bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$, such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta _0}(u)=c\mu $. The scalar is $c_ b$. The smooth function $\ell +Q(s)$ on $Y$ is constant on $E$ and descends to a continuous function on $X$; its normalization with supremum zero is $u$. If $\Psi =0$ and $k$ is nonconstant, or if $\psi $ is nonconstant, the solution is nonconstant. Proof. Set $P(s)=sR(s)$ with the data in ( 9.11.42 ). Then BB19755D6BE9 9.11.44 \begin{equation}  P(s)^ n=c_ bn\int _0^ s k(r)r^{n-1}\, \mathrm{d} r,\qquad P(0)=0,\qquad P(1)=1. \end{equation} Smoothness and positivity of $R$ follow from its integral formula. Since $R(1)=1$, $Q$ is smooth at $s=1$, and its derivative is also smooth at zero. Put $U=\ell +Q(s)$. It is smooth on $Y$ and equals $Q(0)$ on $E$. On $0<x<1$, a local potential for $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ is $F(\rho _\psi )$, where $F(r)=h(r)+Q(h'(r))$. Differentiation gives $F'=P(s)$ and $F''=c_ bk(s)s^ n(1-s)/P(s)^{n-1}$. title: 9.11.47 The quadric cone
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Let $X=\{ Z_0Z_1=Z_2^2\} \subset \mathbb P^3$. Its base conic is the quadratic Veronese image of $\mathbb P^1$, so $n=d=2$. Its homogeneous coordinate ring $\mathbb C[\xi ^2,\xi \eta ,\eta ^2]$ is the invariant ring of the sign involution acting on the normal polynomial ring $\mathbb C[\xi ,\eta ]$, and is therefore normal; thus the base is projectively normal. In the chart \[  \pi (z,t)=(t,tz^2,tz),\qquad S=1+|z|^2+|z|^4,\qquad L=1+|t|^2S,  \] one has $\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log L$. Differentiation gives \[  \det ((\log L)_{j\bar k})=\frac{|t|^2(SS_{z\bar z}-|S_ z|^2)}{L^3}=\frac{|t|^2(1+4|z|^2+|z|^4)}{L^3}.  \] Writing $\lambda _4$ for Euclidean volume, we obtain 6E82FAF4001B 9.11.48 \begin{equation}  \frac{\beta ^2}{2}=\frac{|t|^2(1+4|z|^2+|z|^4)}{\pi ^2(1+|t|^2(1+|z|^2+|z|^4))^3}\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _4. \end{equation} The transverse vanishing order on $E=\{ t=0\} $ is exactly two. For $\Psi =0$ and $k=1/2$, one has $I=1/4$ and $M=1$, so $\mu _0=\theta _0^2/2$, extended by zero at $p$, is a probability measure. The logarithmic scalar and the solution mass are $c_ a=2(1-a^2)$ for every admissible deformation, including the nonclosed ones. This exact normalization follows from the preservation of the determinant. For $\Psi =0$ and $k(s)=1+s$, one has $I=5/6$, $M=10/3$ and $c_ b=3/5$. Put $R(x)=\sqrt{(3+2x)/5}$ and $r_0=\sqrt{3/5}$. The normalized bounded solution is E97B7922C415 9.11.49 \begin{equation}  u(x)=-2(R(x)-r_0)+2\log \frac{1+R(x)}{1+r_0}. \end{equation} Indeed, $u'=-2/[5(1+R)]=(R-1)/(1-x)$, with a removable singularity at $x=1$. Thus $u=Q(x)-Q(0)$; it is strictly decreasing in $x$, and $u(p)=\sup _ Xu=0$. As a function of $x$ it is smooth on a neighborhood of $[0,1]$, and $x$ is the restriction of a smooth ambient function, so $u$ is the restriction of a smooth ambient function. Its prescribed measure is $\mu _1=(1+x)\theta _0^2$, of mass $10/3$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta _0}(u)=(3/5)\mu _1$, of mass two. Formula ( 9.11.48 ) also shows how the lift of this measure vanishes along $E$. For a real parameter $\epsilon $, the function $\Psi =\epsilon |Z_0|^2/(|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2)$ is smooth on $\mathbb P^2$ and preserves $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi >0$ for sufficiently small $|\epsilon |$. Its restriction to the conic takes the values $\epsilon $ and zero at $[1:0:0]$ and $[0:1:0]$. For small nonzero $\epsilon $, the logarithmic residual is therefore nonconstant on $E$ and does not descend. Deformations supported away from $p$, including nonclosed ones, leave that residual and the full descended solution unchanged.

title: 9.11.50 Logarithmic equations on normalized curves
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text:
On a curve the pulled-back background can be degenerate, but its total mass still determines the equation. A periodic Green function on the normalization compensates for the degeneracy. The normalization also gives direct control of descent, of the atoms at the poles and of continuity. Let $X$ be a connected compact reduced unibranch curve whose normalization is a torus: \[  \pi :E=\mathbb C/\Lambda \longrightarrow X,  \] a finite bijective holomorphic map, where $\Lambda \subset \mathbb C$ is a lattice. It is biholomorphic outside a finite set. Let $h$ be a Hermitian form on $X$ in the sense of the beginning of this appendix. In the flat coordinate $z=x+\mathrm iy$ on $E$, set \[  dA=dx\, dy,\qquad V=\int _ EdA,\qquad  eta _0=dA/V,\qquad  eta =\pi ^*h=b eta _0.  \] Here $b$ is smooth and nonnegative, positive over $X_{m reg}$, and may vanish at the other points. Put $H=\int _ E eta >0$. Every two-form on a curve is closed, and this is essential for the following construction. Lemma 9.11.51 . 99DF4FD89931 There is a real periodic distribution $G$ with mean zero, smooth off zero, such that E623581B83B2 9.11.52  egin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=\delta _0- eta _0,\qquad G(z)=\log |z|^2+	ext{a smooth function near }0. \end{equation} For $r\in L^ p(E, eta _0)$, $p>1$, its convolution satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} igl (G*(r eta _0) igr ) =\left(r-\int _ Er eta _0ight) eta _0.  \] The convolution is bounded and continuous, and it is smooth if $r$ is smooth. Proof. With the normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ fixed in the Conventions, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=(\Delta v)/(4\pi )\, dA$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=\delta _0$, as in lemma 5.37.18 . Cutting off this logarithm in a coordinate disk, with a cutoff equal to one near zero, gives a function $L$ on $E$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L=\delta _0+q eta _0$, where $q$ is smooth and $\int _ Eq eta _0=-1$ by Stokes' theorem. Let $e_\xi $ be the characters of the torus, with $-\Delta e_\xi =\lambda _\xi e_\xi $. The nonconstant characters have $\lambda _\xi >0$, growing quadratically on the dual lattice. Define the correction $S$, of mean zero, by its Fourier coefficients \[  S_\xi = rac{4\pi }{V} rac{(q+1)_\xi }{\lambda _\xi } \quad (\xi 
e 0),\qquad S_0=0,  \] where $(q+1)_\xi $ is the Fourier coefficient of $q+1$. Integration by parts shows that these coefficients decay faster than any power of $\lambda _\xi $. Hence the series and all its derivatives converge uniformly, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=-(q+1) eta _0$. Conjugate symmetry of the coefficients makes $S$ real. Subtracting the mean of $L+S$ from $L+S$ proves ( 9.11.52 ). In particular, $G$ belongs to $L^ r$ for every finite $r$. The convolution uses the group law and the Haar probability $ eta _0$. Write $K=G*(r eta _0)$. Testing against smooth functions and using Fubini's theorem proves its distributional equation. Smooth input gives smooth output by the same Fourier argument. For $p'=p/(p-1)$, Hölder's inequality gives \[   egin{aligned}  \| K\| _\infty & \leq \| G\| _{p'}\| r\| _ p,\  |K(z+s)-K(z)| & \leq \| r\| _ p\| G(\cdot +s)-G\| _{p'}. \end{aligned}  \] Approximating $G$ by smooth functions shows that translation is continuous in $L^{p'}$, and hence that $K$ is continuous. $\square$ Choose finitely many distinct points $q_1,\ldots ,q_ k\in E$ and weights $a_ j>0$, possibly none, with \[   egin{aligned}  A& =\sum _ j a_ j<H,&  M& =H-A,\  \Phi & =G*((H-b) eta _0),&  \Psi & =\Phi +\sum _ j a_ jG(\cdot -q_ j). \end{aligned}  \] The function $\Phi $ is smooth, and 0567315FF18B 9.11.53  egin{equation}   eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi =M eta _0+\sum _ j a_ j\delta _{q_ j}. \end{equation} Thus $\Psi $ is a $ eta $-plurisubharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, whose logarithmic poles are exactly the points $q_ j$, with coefficients $a_ j$ measured on the normalization. The proper bijection $\pi $ is a homeomorphism, so we may define $\psi =\Psi \circ \pi ^{-1}$; its disk inequalities are proved below. The ordinary type of $\psi $ consists of the potentials $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with \[  w\leq \psi +C,\qquad \psi \leq w+C  \] for a finite constant $C$, the inequalities being understood for extended real values. Theorem 9.11.54 . 2489A49CB212 Let $0\leq f\in L^ p(E, eta _0)$ for some finite $p>1$, with $F=\int _ Ef eta _0>0$, and set $
u =\pi _*(f eta _0)$. Every potential in the ordinary type of $\psi $ has extended non-pluripolar mass $M$. In this type there is a unique normalized solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=c
u , \qquad \sup _ Xu=0, \qquad c= rac{H-A}{F}>0.  \] Every member of the type that solves $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(w)=c'
u $ for some constant $c'>0$, with no regularity assumed, has $c'=c$ and differs from the normalized solution by a constant. The solution is continuous with real values off its finite pole set, and continuous at the poles as a map into $\mathbb R\cup \{ -\infty \} $ with the order topology. Its residual relative to $\psi $ extends to a continuous real function on $X$. If there are no poles, the solution itself is continuous with real values everywhere. The type and the equation do not depend on the choice of a resolution or of a common refinement. The measure $
u $ is non-pluripolar. Proof. Set $c=M/F$ and \[  v=G*((cf-M) eta _0),\qquad U=\Psi +v.  \] The lemma gives a bounded continuous $v$ and the positive current 5C30CCD83A1D 9.11.55  egin{equation}   eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U=cf eta _0+\sum _ j a_ j\delta _{q_ j}. \end{equation} In each disk, adding a smooth local primitive of $ eta $ gives a function with positive distributional Laplacian, and hence a subharmonic representative. Continuity off the poles and the explicit logarithmic values identify this representative with $U$ as defined above. The same argument applies to $\Psi $. The supremum $S=\sup _ EU$ is finite, and we put $u=(U-S)\circ \pi ^{-1}$. Every holomorphic disk $g:\Delta 	o X$ lifts holomorphically to $\widetilde g=\pi ^{-1}\circ g$. Indeed, for a nonconstant disk the inverse image of the finite singular set is discrete, and off this set the lift is holomorphic. Since $\pi ^{-1}$ is a homeomorphism, $\widetilde g$ is continuous on the whole disk. Near an omitted point its image therefore stays in a bounded coordinate neighborhood in $E$, and the removable singularity theorem in one variable extends it holomorphically. A constant disk lifts to a constant map, and a nonconstant disk cannot have image in a finite set. Choose a smooth local primitive $\eta $ of $ eta $ near the lifted image, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta = eta $. Then $\eta \circ \widetilde g$ is a primitive of $g^*h$, and \[  u\circ g+\eta \circ \widetilde g=(U-S+\eta )\circ \widetilde g  \] is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. That the composition is subharmonic follows from decreasing smooth local regularizations and the holomorphic chain rule for the Laplacian. Any other primitive on the disk differs by a harmonic function. These are exactly the disk tests of definition 9.11.2 , and the same argument shows that $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. A constant disk at a pole has the permitted restriction $\equiv -\infty $. A nonconstant lift meeting $q_ j$ with order $\ell $ gives the pole coefficient $\ell a_ j$. The homeomorphism $\pi $ gives continuity off the poles. Near a pole, the smooth logarithmic remainder of $\Psi $ and the bounded continuous function $v$ give continuity with extended values. The residual is the descent of $v-S$, including at the poles, so no difference of two infinite values is involved. The solution belongs to the stated ordinary type. For the mass and uniqueness assertions, let $w$ be any member of the type and put $W=w\circ \pi $. Pulling back along coordinate disks of the normalization shows that $W$ is $ eta $-plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $. The two type inequalities make $W$ locally bounded away from $Q=\{ q_ j\} $, and at each pole they give \[  W=a_ j\log |z-q_ j|^2+O(1),  \] with value $-\infty $ at $q_ j$. The positive Radon measure $T_ W= eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W$ has total mass $H$ by Stokes' theorem. Its atom at $q_ j$ has weight exactly $a_ j$. This follows from the planar atom identity of lemma 5.37.18 . Explicitly, choose a smooth local primitive $\eta $ of $ eta $ near $q_ j$, and let $m(r)$ be the circular mean of $W+\eta $ around $q_ j$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(W+\eta )=T_ W$, it satisfies \[  m'(r)= rac{2T_ W(B_ r)}r  \] for almost every $r$, by the divergence theorem and regularization. If $	au =T_ W(\{ q_ j\} )$, integration gives $m(r)/\log r^2	o 	au $, while the bounded logarithmic remainder gives the limit $a_ j$. Hence the non-pluripolar product of $W$, defined in dimension one by truncation, is \[  \langle  eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Wangle =\mathbf1_{E\setminus Q}T_ W.  \] Indeed, on each relatively compact set avoiding $Q$, a sufficiently low truncation equals $W$, and the indicator removes the poles. Its mass is $H-A=M$ for every member of the type. For ( 9.11.55 ), removing the atoms leaves $cf eta _0$. The definition ( 9.11.25 ) gives the asserted equation on $X$. A locally pluripolar set pulls back to a set on which some quasi-subharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, equals $-\infty $; such sets have zero flat area. Hence $
u $ is non-pluripolar. Suppose that $w$ solves the equation with a constant $c'>0$. Comparing total masses gives $c'F=M$, so $c'=c$. Since $\pi $ is a Borel homeomorphism and the atoms are fixed, $T_ W=T_ U$. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(W-U)=0$, where $W-U$ is an integrable function. Every nonconstant Fourier coefficient of $W-U$ vanishes, so the difference is constant almost everywhere. Subharmonic functions are determined by their averages over shrinking disks, so the values of $W$ and $U$ differ by the same constant everywhere, and the same holds on $X$. This includes members of the type with no regularity assumed. Finally, a resolution $ho :Y	o X$ factors through $E$ by the disk-lifting argument. The resulting proper holomorphic map $Y	o E$ has generic degree one. For smooth compact curves, the multiplicities in a fiber sum to the degree, so every fiber is a single point of multiplicity one, and the map is biholomorphic. The same holds for every common refinement, which proves the independence assertion directly. $\square$ The integrability hypothesis on $f$ refers to flat area on $E$. On $X_{m reg}$, the density of $
u $ with respect to $h$ is $(f/b)\circ \pi ^{-1}$; both measures give the finite singular set zero mass. No positive lower bound for $b$ and no bound for the density on $X$ is required.

e 0}}  igl ((z-\lambda )^{-2}-\lambda ^{-2} igr ), \qquad y=x'.  \] The summands are $O(|\lambda |^{-3})$ on compact sets away from the lattice, so the series converges normally. e 0$. Since $y$ is odd, the map $(x,y)$ is injective and immersive away from zero: use $dx$ where $y
e 0$, and $dy=x''dz$ otherwise. The hypothesis $p>1$ in theorem 9.11.54 guarantees that the Green correction is bounded and continuous. For merely integrable densities, the solution can leave the ordinary type. The following family of densities locates the boundary exactly, and it also gives continuous residuals for some densities outside every $L^ p$, $p>1$. We keep the notation $X,E,h, eta , eta _0,H,\Psi ,\psi ,A,M$ of subsection 9.11.50 , with $A<H$. Fix $q\in E$ and a flat coordinate $z$ centered at $q$, and put $r=|z|$ and $t=\log (1/r)$, so that $t>1$ on a small punctured disk around $q$. For $C_0>0$ and $\gamma >1$, choose a positive density $f_\gamma $, smooth away from $q$, which equals \[  f_\gamma =C_0r^{-2}t^{-\gamma }  \] on a sufficiently small punctured disk around $q$, and extend it smoothly and positively to the complement. Set \[  F_\gamma =\int _ Ef_\gamma  eta _0,\qquad c_\gamma =M/F_\gamma ,\qquad 
u _\gamma =\pi _*(f_\gamma  eta _0).  \] The local integral of $f_\gamma $ is finite exactly for $\gamma >1$. For every such $\gamma $, this density lies outside $L^ p(E, eta _0)$ for every $p>1$. Since $f_\gamma  eta _0$ is absolutely continuous on $E$, the measure $
u _\gamma $ is non-pluripolar by the pullback argument in the proof of theorem 9.11.54 . Theorem 9.11.60 . E80960D59FB4 For this family, the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=c
u _\gamma $ with some constant $c>0$ has a solution in the ordinary type of $\psi $ if and only if $\gamma >2$. In that case $c=c_\gamma $, the normalized solution is unique in the whole type, and its residual is continuous but, on the normalization, not Hölder continuous for any positive exponent. For $1<\gamma \leq 2$, there is a solution $u_\gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ of \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u_\gamma ) =c_\gamma 
u _\gamma  \] with non-pluripolar mass $M$, whose pullback to $E$ has the same multiplier ideals as $\Psi $ at every positive weight. It violates the lower inequality $\psi \leq u_\gamma +C$ of the ordinary type, and no solution with any positive constant exists in the ordinary type of $\psi $. Proof. The coefficient below differs from that in ( 10.23.2 ) because here $ eta _0=dA/V$. Define on the punctured coordinate disk 7B4446B6082E 9.11.61  egin{equation}  P_\gamma (t)=  egin{cases}  \displaystyle  rac{4\pi C_0}{V(\gamma -1)(\gamma -2)} t^{2-\gamma },& \gamma 
e 2,\[4pt] \displaystyle - rac{4\pi C_0}{V}\log t,& \gamma =2. \end{cases} \end{equation} Direct differentiation gives \[  P_\gamma ''(t)= rac{4\pi C_0}{V}t^{-\gamma },\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_\gamma =f_\gamma  eta _0  \] off $q$. title: 9.11.63 Nonclosed equations on cuspidal products
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text:
On a cuspidal curve, the pullback of a Hermitian form to the normalization degenerates at the preimage of the cusp, but adding a smooth potential turns it into a positive form. On the products below we perturb the background by a nonclosed form all of whose powers are $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. This fixes the mass of every bounded potential and gives an energy comparison, although the background is not closed. A perturbative solution near a constant-coefficient form then provides a positive solution against which every bounded solution can be compared. Fix $n\geq 2$. For $j=1,\ldots ,n$, let $E_ j=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$ with coordinate $z_ j$, and put $\kappa _ j= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$. Replace a neighborhood of a point $p\in E_1$ by the cusp with normalization $z\mapsto (z^2,z^3)$; equivalently, the holomorphic functions at the marked point are the functions on $E_1$ whose first derivative vanishes there. Denote the resulting compact curve by $C$ and its cusp by $q$. Put \[  X=C	imes E_2	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n,\qquad Y=E_1	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n.  \] The normalization $\pi :Y	o X$ is finite and bijective, hence a homeomorphism, and has generic degree one. The space $X$ is reduced, irreducible and unibranch, and its singular locus is $\{ q\} 	imes E_2	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n$. Choose a Hermitian form $h_ C$ on $C$ which near $q$ is the restriction of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(|x|^2+|y|^2)$, where $(x,y)=(z^2,z^3)$ are the coordinates of the cusp. Its pullback is $\eta =ho \kappa _1$, where $ho $ is smooth, positive off $p$, and B5525E6496F5 9.11.64  egin{equation}  ho =4|z|^2+9|z|^4\quad \hbox{near }p. \end{equation} Write $\lambda >0$ for the average of $ho $ on $E_1$, and set \[  h_0=h_ C+\sum _{j=2}^ n\kappa _ j,\quad H_0=\pi ^*h_0=\eta +\sum _{j=2}^ n\kappa _ j,\quad K_0=\lambda \kappa _1+\sum _{j=2}^ n\kappa _ j,\quad \Omega =K_0^ n.  \] Forms on the factors are pulled back to the products without change of notation. Proposition 9.11.65 . D0F33FF75830 There are a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\alpha $ on $X$, mixing the factors $C$ and $E_2$, and a smooth real function $v_0$ on $Y$ such that, for every sufficiently small nonzero real $\varepsilon $, the Hermitian form $h=h_0+\varepsilon \alpha $ is not closed and \[   egin{gathered} H=\pi ^*h,\qquad k=H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_0=K_0+\varepsilon \pi ^*\alpha \geq 	frac 12K_0,\ \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H^ r)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^ r)=0\quad (r\geq 0). \end{gathered}  \] Moreover $\int _ YH^ n=\int _ Yk^ n=:M>0$. Proof. Choose real smooth functions $A$ on $C$, supported away from $q$, and $B$ on $E_2$. Let \[  \alpha =\partial A\wedge  ar\partial B+ ar\partial A\wedge \partial B =\partial (A ar\partial B)+ ar\partial (A\partial B).  \] The form $\alpha $ is real and satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\alpha =0$. At a point where $\partial A=0$, $\partial  ar\partial A
