e 0$, \[  \partial \alpha =-\partial A\wedge \partial  ar\partial B +\partial  ar\partial A\wedge \partial B
e 0.  \] Thus $\mathrm d\alpha 
e 0$. The form $\alpha $ vanishes near the singular locus. Its operator norm relative to $H_0$ is bounded on its support, and its norm relative to $K_0$ is bounded everywhere. Choose $|\varepsilon |$ so small that both norms, multiplied by $|\varepsilon |$, are less than $1/2$. This proves positivity of $h$ in the ambient sense, semipositivity of $H$, and the inequality $K_0+\varepsilon \pi ^*\alpha \geq 	frac 12K_0$. The equation $\partial _ z\partial _{ ar z}v=\lambda -ho $ on $E_1$, whose right-hand side has mean zero, has a smooth real periodic solution, obtained by dividing its nonzero Fourier coefficients. Its pullback $v_0$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_0=(\lambda -ho )\kappa _1$, which proves the formula for $k$. The forms $H_0$ and $K_0$ are closed. Hence $\mathrm dk$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}k$ come from the complex surface $E_1	imes E_2$, so that $\mathrm dk\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}k=0$ for degree reasons, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}k=0$. The same identities hold for $H$. The Leibniz rule now gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^ r)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H^ r)=0$ for all $r$; this uses both torsion identities, not only pluriclosedness. Expanding $(H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_0)^ n$ and integrating by parts shows that every term containing $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_0$ integrates to zero. Hence the masses agree, and positivity of $k$ makes them positive. $\square$ Fix an integer $s\geq n+3$ before making a further choice of $\varepsilon $. Use the Fourier Sobolev norm $\| w\| _{H^ t}^2=\sum _{m\in \mathbb Z^{2n}}(1+|m|^2)^ t|\widehat w(m)|^2$ on $Y$, and write $H^ t_0$ for the subspace of real functions in $H^ t$ with zero mean with respect to $\Omega $. In the remaining formulas, $\alpha $ denotes its pullback to $Y$. Theorem 9.11.66 . 6EDDAD49D627 For sufficiently small nonzero $\varepsilon $, depending on $n$, $s$ and the fixed forms, there are explicit constants $R,\delta >0$ such that every $g\in H^ s_0$ with $\| g\| _{H^ s}\leq \delta $ admits a unique $w\in H^{s+2}_0$ with $\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}\leq R$ satisfying \[  (k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n=(f_\varepsilon +g)\Omega , \qquad f_\varepsilon = rac{k^ n}{\Omega },\qquad k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 	frac 14K_0.  \] The constants may be chosen as in ( 9.11.67 ). In particular, $w$ is of class $C^2$. Proof. Set $b_1=\lambda $ and $b_ j=1$ for $j\geq 2$. The operator \[  L_0w= rac{nK_0^{n-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w}{\Omega } =\sum _ j b_ j^{-1}\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ j}w  \] has Fourier eigenvalues $\ell (m)=-\pi ^2\sum _ jb_ j^{-1}(m_{2j-1}^2+m_{2j}^2)$. It has an inverse $H^ s_0	o H^{s+2}_0$ of norm \[  A_0=\sup _{m
e 0} rac{1+|m|^2}{|\ell (m)|} \leq  rac{2\max _ jb_ j}{\pi ^2}.  \] Let $L_\varepsilon w=nk^{n-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w/\Omega $. It preserves zero mean because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^{n-1})=0$. Fix $\varepsilon _0\leq 1$ within the positivity range. The finite expansion of $k^{n-1}$ gives \[  L_\varepsilon -L_0=\sum _{j=1}^{n-1}\varepsilon ^ jP_ j, \qquad P_ jw=n inom {n-1}{j}  rac{K_0^{n-1-j}\wedge \alpha ^ j\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w}{\Omega }.  \] Choose bounds $e_ j$ for the norms $\| P_ j\| _{H^{s+2}	o H^ s}$, which are finite since multiplication by smooth coefficients is bounded on $H^ s$, and set $B=\sum _ j\varepsilon _0^{j-1}e_ j$. If $|\varepsilon |\leq \varepsilon _0$ and $|\varepsilon |A_0B\leq 1/2$, the Neumann series gives $\| L_\varepsilon ^{-1}\| \leq A:=2A_0$. The remainder is \[  Q(w)=\sum _{r=2}^ n inom nr rac{k^{n-r}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ r}{\Omega }.  \] For $s>n$, Fourier convolution and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, together with $\sum _ m(1+|m|^2)^{-s}<\infty $, make $H^ s$ an algebra. Multiplication by smooth coefficients and the finite expansion therefore give a constant $C_ Q$ such that, on the unit ball of $H^{s+2}$, \[   egin{aligned}  \| Q(w)\| _{H^ s}& \leq C_ Q\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}^2,\  \| Q(w)-Q(z)\| _{H^ s}& \leq C_ Q(\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}+\| z\| _{H^{s+2}})\| w-z\| _{H^{s+2}}. \end{aligned}  \] Each term of $Q(w)$ has zero integral against $\Omega $: for smooth $w$, its integral is $\int w\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^{n-r})\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^{r-1}=0$, and Sobolev approximation gives the general case. The Sobolev embedding also gives a constant $D$ such that the pointwise operator norm of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ with respect to $K_0$ is at most $D\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}$. Choose E79D47E722CF 9.11.67  egin{equation}  0<R\leq \min \{ 1,(4AC_ Q)^{-1},(4D)^{-1}\} ,\qquad \delta =R/(2A). \end{equation} The equation is equivalent to $L_\varepsilon w+Q(w)=g$. The map $w\mapsto L_\varepsilon ^{-1}(g-Q(w))$ takes the closed ball of radius $R$ in $H^{s+2}_0$ into the ball of radius $3R/4$ and has Lipschitz constant at most $1/2$. Its fixed point gives existence and uniqueness in that ball. Since $k\geq K_0/2$ and the operator norm of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ is at most $1/4$, the form $k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ is at least $K_0/4$. The embedding $H^{s+2}\subset C^2$ follows from $s\geq n+3$. $\square$ The perturbation $g$ may depend on all torus variables. For example, writing $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$, every sufficiently small nonzero multiple of $\prod _ j\cos (2\pi x_ j)+\prod _ j\cos (2\pi y_ j)$ is an admissible perturbation with zero mean. Thus the construction does not force the solution to have separated variables. Lemma 9.11.68 . 7426C6119D9F Every bounded $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,k)$ satisfies $\int _ Y(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=M$. The same holds with $H$ in place of $k$. Proof. The products are the bounded products of proposition 5.28.2 . For $r\geq 1$, the bounded local recursion and Stokes' theorem on the compact manifold $Y$ give \[  \int _ Y k^{n-r}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ r =\int _ YU\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^{n-r})\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^{r-1}=0.  \] Alternatively, one may convolve $U$ on the torus, add a fixed local positive quadratic function, and pass to the limit in the decreasing bounded expansion; every smooth integral vanishes by the same identity. Expanding the top power proves the assertion. The proof for $H$ is identical, since its powers are also $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed and its mass is $M$. $\square$ Proposition 9.11.69 . FEAE8B85485E Let $V$ be a solution $w$ given by theorem 9.11.66 . If a bounded $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,k)$ satisfies $(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^ n$, then $U-V$ is constant. Proof. Convolve $U$, $V$ and $k$ with the same nonnegative radial kernel $\varrho _ j$ on the torus, of radius $r_ j\downarrow 0$, and write \[  U_ j=U*\varrho _ j,\quad V_ j=V*\varrho _ j,\quad k_ j=k*\varrho _ j, \quad A_ j=k_ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j,\quad B_ j=k_ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j.  \] Translations preserve positivity, so $A_ j\geq 0$ and $B_ j\geq  eta K_0$ with $ eta =1/4$. The forms $k_ j$ converge smoothly, and $V_ j$ converges in $C^2$. On lifted coordinate balls, choose a common positive quadratic function $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq k$. Convolution gives $q*\varrho _ j=q+b r_ j^2$ for a fixed $b>0$. The radial averages of the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $U+q$ and $V+q$ decrease as the radii decrease. Hence $U_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ and $V_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ decrease to $U+q$ and $V+q$; the identical constants cancel in the difference. Put $\phi _ j=U_ j-V_ j$ and $T_ j=\sum _{r=0}^{n-1}A_ j^ r\wedge B_ j^{n-1-r}$. The identities $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}k_ j=0$ and $\mathrm dk_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}k_ j=0$ persist under convolution, since the torsion is still pulled back from $E_1	imes E_2$. Differentiating the monomials therefore gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ j=0$. Also $T_ j\geq B_ j^{n-1}\geq  eta ^{n-1}K_0^{n-1}$. Stokes' theorem applied to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\phi _ j^2)$ yields E6758962B60C 9.11.70  egin{equation}  -\int _ Y\phi _ j(A_ j^ n-B_ j^ n) =\int _ Y\mathrm d\phi _ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi _ j\wedge T_ j \geq  eta ^{n-1}\int _ Y\mathrm d\phi _ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi _ j\wedge K_0^{n-1}. \end{equation} Only the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closedness of $T_ j$ is needed here. We treat the four terms on the left separately. Expand $A_ j^ n$ with respect to the local plurisubharmonic potential $U_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ and the smoothly converging coefficient $k_ j-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$. The weighted limit lemma 5.27.2 gives $\int U_ jA_ j^ n	o \int U(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n$. Decreasing convergence and the uniform convergence of $V_ j$ give the corresponding limit for $\int V_ jA_ j^ n$. Since $B_ j^ n$ has uniformly converging continuous densities, bounded pointwise convergence and dominated convergence give the limit of $\int U_ jB_ j^ n$. The term $\int V_ jB_ j^ n$ converges by $C^2$ convergence. A finite partition of unity gives the global statements. Since the two limiting measures are equal, the left-hand side of ( 9.11.70 ) tends to zero. The flat Fourier Poincaré inequality now shows that the $L^2$ norm of $\phi _ j$ minus its average tends to zero. Bounded convergence gives $\phi _ j	o U-V$ in $L^2$, so $U-V$ is constant almost everywhere. Local smooth corrections and the canonical plurisubharmonic representatives extend this equality to every point. $\square$ Theorem 9.11.71 . 127BF0018B1A Let $f\in H^ s(Y)$ be strictly positive and set \[  
u =\pi _*(f\Omega ),\qquad c= rac{M}{\int _ Y f\Omega }.  \] If $\| cf-f_\varepsilon \| _{H^ s}\leq \delta $, there is a unique bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=c
u .  \] The function $u$ is continuous and locally Hölder continuous of exponent $1/3$ in ambient coordinates. The measure $
u $ is non-pluripolar and gives the singular locus zero mass. On the regular locus its density with respect to $h^ n$ is $f/J$, where $J=H^ n/\Omega $; near the cusp this density is $\lambda f/ho $. The equation holds on every resolution and every common smooth refinement. Every bounded solution of an equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u')=c'
u $ with $c'>0$ has $c'=c$. Proof. The function $g=cf-f_\varepsilon $ has zero mean. Let $w$ be the solution given by theorem 9.11.66 . The potential $v_0+w$ is bounded and $H$-plurisubharmonic. Descent through the resolution $\pi $ (theorem 9.11.5 ) gives \[  u=(v_0+w)\circ \pi ^{-1}-\sup _ Y(v_0+w),  \] which satisfies the disk condition with the background $h$ itself. Since the normalization is a homeomorphism, $u$ is continuous. The definition of the extended measure and theorem 9.11.26 give the equation. Any other bounded solution pulls back to a bounded $H$-plurisubharmonic potential. Since $\pi $ is a Borel homeomorphism, equality of the pushforward measures means equality on $Y$. Subtracting $v_0$ and applying proposition 9.11.69 gives uniqueness. The mass identity of lemma 9.11.68 forces the scalar of every bounded solution to be $M/
u (X)=c$. The singular locus pulls back to the divisor $\{ p\} 	imes E_2	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n$, which has zero smooth volume. If a set is locally pluripolar, a local plurisubharmonic function equal to $-\infty $ on it pulls back to a plurisubharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, away from that divisor; its pole set has zero smooth volume. Thus $
u $ is non-pluripolar. On the regular locus, the change of variables formula gives the density $f/J$. Near the cusp $\alpha =0$, so \[  H^ n=n!ho \, \kappa _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \kappa _ n, \qquad \Omega =n!\lambda \, \kappa _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \kappa _ n.  \] The ratio gives the density $\lambda f/ho $; the generic degree of $\pi $ and both factorials have been accounted for. For the Hölder assertion, put $d=z-z'$ and $a=z+z'$. Then \[  z^2-z'^2=da,\qquad z^3-z'^3=d(3a^2+d^2)/4.  \] If $|a|\geq |d|/4$, the first modulus is at least $|d|^2/4$, which controls $|d|^3$ on a bounded chart. Otherwise the second modulus is at least $13|d|^3/64$. Hence $|z-z'|\leq C(|z^2-z'^2|+|z^3-z'^3|)^{1/3}$. The $C^1$ regularity of $v_0+w$ in $z$ and in the other product coordinates gives the asserted ambient estimate. Every resolution $\sigma :Z	o X$ factors through $Y$: in the cusp chart, the quotient $y/x$ is bounded off the exceptional set and extends holomorphically to the smooth source, giving the normalization coordinate. Write $\sigma =\pi \circ \mu $. The map $\mu $ is a proper modification. The bounded pullback products agree off its exceptional locus, and they give this analytic set zero mass by proposition 5.28.2 . Hence their pushforwards agree on all of $Y$. This proves the equation on every resolution, and the same argument applies to further common refinements. The full potential is exactly $u\circ \sigma $, which is constant on every fiber, and surjectivity preserves all ordinary comparisons. $\square$ Existence alone holds for a larger class of data: on the normalization, the positive form $k$ places the equation in the bounded-mass regime of section 10.31 . The smallness condition above is needed for the quantitative regularity and for the positive solution used in the uniqueness comparison. Corollary 9.11.72 . 5F7DB1E779E6 For the same $X$ and $h$, every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p(Y,\Omega )$, $p>1$, admits a bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)= rac{M}{\int _ Yf\Omega }\, \pi _*(f\Omega ).  \] Proof. The torus $Y$ is Kähler, so it has bounded mass by lemma 19.9.12 . Since $k>0$, zero is an ordinary model for $k$: $P_ k[0]=0$. Its lower volume is $M>0$ by lemma 9.11.68 , because the potentials of the same ordinary type as zero are exactly the bounded ones. Hence theorem 10.31.3 , applied on $Y$ with background $k$ and reference zero, gives a bounded $k$-plurisubharmonic solution for the measure $f\Omega $, and its scalar is $M/\int f\Omega $. Adding $v_0$ and using theorem 9.11.5 , theorem 9.11.26 gives the normalized equation on $X$. The datum is non-pluripolar as in theorem 9.11.71 . Neither smallness nor strict positivity of $f$ is needed for this existence statement. $\square$ The spaces $X$ contain no rational curves. Indeed, a holomorphic map $\mathbb P^1	o X$ lifts locally to $Y$ through the cusp normalization, and the local lifts glue by uniqueness. Every flat holomorphic one-form on $Y$ pulls back to zero on $\mathbb P^1$, so the lifted map has zero derivative and is constant. The results of this section depend on this explicit geometry, on the bounded ordinary type and on the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closedness of all powers of the background. Ambient Hölder regularity and uniqueness in the whole bounded class are proved only for data in the small Sobolev neighborhood above. The general problem 24.11.1 , including arbitrary pole types and backgrounds whose powers are not $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, remains open.

Hence $\mathrm dk$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}k$ come from the complex surface $E_1	imes E_2$, so that $\mathrm dk\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}k=0$ for degree reasons, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}k=0$. The Leibniz rule now gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^ r)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H^ r)=0$ for all $r$; this uses both torsion identities, not only pluriclosedness. Expanding $(H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_0)^ n$ and integrating by parts shows that every term containing $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_0$ integrates to zero. Hence the masses agree, and positivity of $k$ makes them positive. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.11.66
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Theorem 9.11.66 . 6EDDAD49D627 For sufficiently small nonzero $\varepsilon $, depending on $n$, $s$ and the fixed forms, there are explicit constants $R,\delta >0$ such that every $g\in H^ s_0$ with $\| g\| _{H^ s}\leq \delta $ admits a unique $w\in H^{s+2}_0$ with $\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}\leq R$ satisfying \[  (k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n=(f_\varepsilon +g)\Omega , \qquad f_\varepsilon =\frac{k^ n}{\Omega },\qquad k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq \tfrac 14K_0.  \] The constants may be chosen as in ( 9.11.67 ). In particular, $w$ is of class $C^2$. Proof. Set $b_1=\lambda $ and $b_ j=1$ for $j\geq 2$. The operator \[  L_0w=\frac{nK_0^{n-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w}{\Omega } =\sum _ j b_ j^{-1}\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ j}w  \] has Fourier eigenvalues $\ell (m)=-\pi ^2\sum _ jb_ j^{-1}(m_{2j-1}^2+m_{2j}^2)$. It has an inverse $H^ s_0\to H^{s+2}_0$ of norm \[  A_0=\sup _{m\ne 0}\frac{1+|m|^2}{|\ell (m)|} \leq \frac{2\max _ jb_ j}{\pi ^2}.  \] Let $L_\varepsilon w=nk^{n-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w/\Omega $. It preserves zero mean because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^{n-1})=0$. Fix $\varepsilon _0\leq 1$ within the positivity range. The finite expansion of $k^{n-1}$ gives \[  L_\varepsilon -L_0=\sum _{j=1}^{n-1}\varepsilon ^ jP_ j, \qquad P_ jw=n\binom {n-1}{j} \frac{K_0^{n-1-j}\wedge \alpha ^ j\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w}{\Omega }.  \] Choose bounds $e_ j$ for the norms $\| P_ j\| _{H^{s+2}\to H^ s}$, which are finite since multiplication by smooth coefficients is bounded on $H^ s$, and set $B=\sum _ j\varepsilon _0^{j-1}e_ j$. If $|\varepsilon |\leq \varepsilon _0$ and $|\varepsilon |A_0B\leq 1/2$, the Neumann series gives $\| L_\varepsilon ^{-1}\| \leq A:=2A_0$. The remainder is \[  Q(w)=\sum _{r=2}^ n\binom nr\frac{k^{n-r}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ r}{\Omega }.  \] For $s>n$, Fourier convolution and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, together with $\sum _ m(1+|m|^2)^{-s}<\infty $, make $H^ s$ an algebra. Multiplication by smooth coefficients and the finite expansion therefore give a constant $C_ Q$ such that, on the unit ball of $H^{s+2}$, \[  \begin{aligned}  \| Q(w)\| _{H^ s}& \leq C_ Q\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}^2,\\  \| Q(w)-Q(z)\| _{H^ s}& \leq C_ Q(\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}+\| z\| _{H^{s+2}})\| w-z\| _{H^{s+2}}. \end{aligned}  \] Each term of $Q(w)$ has zero integral against $\Omega $: for smooth $w$, its integral is $\int w\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^{n-r})\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^{r-1}=0$, and Sobolev approximation gives the general case. The Sobolev embedding also gives a constant $D$ such that the pointwise operator norm of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ with respect to $K_0$ is at most $D\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}$. Choose E79D47E722CF 9.11.67 \begin{equation}  0<R\leq \min \{ 1,(4AC_ Q)^{-1},(4D)^{-1}\} ,\qquad \delta =R/(2A). \end{equation} The equation is equivalent to $L_\varepsilon w+Q(w)=g$. The map $w\mapsto L_\varepsilon ^{-1}(g-Q(w))$ takes the closed ball of radius $R$ in $H^{s+2}_0$ into the ball of radius $3R/4$ and has Lipschitz constant at most $1/2$. Its fixed point gives existence and uniqueness in that ball. Since $k\geq K_0/2$ and the operator norm of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ is at most $1/4$, the form $k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ is at least $K_0/4$. The embedding $H^{s+2}\subset C^2$ follows from $s\geq n+3$. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.11.68
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Lemma 9.11.68 . 7426C6119D9F Every bounded $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,k)$ satisfies $\int _ Y(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=M$. The same holds with $H$ in place of $k$. Proof. The products are the bounded products of proposition 5.28.2 . For $r\geq 1$, the bounded local recursion and Stokes' theorem on the compact manifold $Y$ give \[  \int _ Y k^{n-r}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ r =\int _ YU\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^{n-r})\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^{r-1}=0.  \] Alternatively, one may convolve $U$ on the torus, add a fixed local positive quadratic function, and pass to the limit in the decreasing bounded expansion; every smooth integral vanishes by the same identity. Expanding the top power proves the assertion. The proof for $H$ is identical, since its powers are also $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed and its mass is $M$. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.11.69
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Proposition 9.11.69 . FEAE8B85485E Let $V$ be a solution $w$ given by theorem 9.11.66 . If a bounded $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,k)$ satisfies $(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^ n$, then $U-V$ is constant. Proof. Convolve $U$, $V$ and $k$ with the same nonnegative radial kernel $\varrho _ j$ on the torus, of radius $r_ j\downarrow 0$, and write \[  U_ j=U*\varrho _ j,\quad V_ j=V*\varrho _ j,\quad k_ j=k*\varrho _ j, \quad A_ j=k_ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j,\quad B_ j=k_ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j.  \] Translations preserve positivity, so $A_ j\geq 0$ and $B_ j\geq \beta K_0$ with $\beta =1/4$. The forms $k_ j$ converge smoothly, and $V_ j$ converges in $C^2$. On lifted coordinate balls, choose a common positive quadratic function $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq k$. Convolution gives $q*\varrho _ j=q+b r_ j^2$ for a fixed $b>0$. The radial averages of the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $U+q$ and $V+q$ decrease as the radii decrease. Hence $U_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ and $V_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ decrease to $U+q$ and $V+q$; the identical constants cancel in the difference. Put $\phi _ j=U_ j-V_ j$ and $T_ j=\sum _{r=0}^{n-1}A_ j^ r\wedge B_ j^{n-1-r}$. The identities $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}k_ j=0$ and $\mathrm dk_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}k_ j=0$ persist under convolution, since the torsion is still pulled back from $E_1\times E_2$. Differentiating the monomials therefore gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ j=0$. Also $T_ j\geq B_ j^{n-1}\geq \beta ^{n-1}K_0^{n-1}$. Stokes' theorem applied to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\phi _ j^2)$ yields E6758962B60C 9.11.70 \begin{equation}  -\int _ Y\phi _ j(A_ j^ n-B_ j^ n) =\int _ Y\mathrm d\phi _ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi _ j\wedge T_ j \geq \beta ^{n-1}\int _ Y\mathrm d\phi _ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi _ j\wedge K_0^{n-1}. \end{equation} Only the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closedness of $T_ j$ is needed here. We treat the four terms on the left separately. Expand $A_ j^ n$ with respect to the local plurisubharmonic potential $U_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ and the smoothly converging coefficient $k_ j-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$. The weighted limit lemma 5.27.2 gives $\int U_ jA_ j^ n\to \int U(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n$. Decreasing convergence and the uniform convergence of $V_ j$ give the corresponding limit for $\int V_ jA_ j^ n$. Since $B_ j^ n$ has uniformly converging continuous densities, bounded pointwise convergence and dominated convergence give the limit of $\int U_ jB_ j^ n$. The term $\int V_ jB_ j^ n$ converges by $C^2$ convergence. A finite partition of unity gives the global statements. Since the two limiting measures are equal, the left-hand side of ( 9.11.70 ) tends to zero. The flat Fourier Poincaré inequality now shows that the $L^2$ norm of $\phi _ j$ minus its average tends to zero. Bounded convergence gives $\phi _ j\to U-V$ in $L^2$, so $U-V$ is constant almost everywhere. Local smooth corrections and the canonical plurisubharmonic representatives extend this equality to every point. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.11.71
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text:
Theorem 9.11.71 . 127BF0018B1A Let $f\in H^ s(Y)$ be strictly positive and set \[  
u =\pi _*(f\Omega ),\qquad c= rac{M}{\int _ Y f\Omega }.  \] If $\| cf-f_\varepsilon \| _{H^ s}\leq \delta $, there is a unique bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=c
u .  \] The function $u$ is continuous and locally Hölder continuous of exponent $1/3$ in ambient coordinates. The measure $
u $ is non-pluripolar and gives the singular locus zero mass. On the regular locus its density with respect to $h^ n$ is $f/J$, where $J=H^ n/\Omega $; near the cusp this density is $\lambda f/ho $. The equation holds on every resolution and every common smooth refinement. Every bounded solution of an equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u')=c'
u $ with $c'>0$ has $c'=c$. Proof. The function $g=cf-f_\varepsilon $ has zero mean. Let $w$ be the solution given by theorem 9.11.66 . The potential $v_0+w$ is bounded and $H$-plurisubharmonic. Descent through the resolution $\pi $ (theorem 9.11.5 ) gives \[  u=(v_0+w)\circ \pi ^{-1}-\sup _ Y(v_0+w),  \] which satisfies the disk condition with the background $h$ itself. Since the normalization is a homeomorphism, $u$ is continuous. The definition of the extended measure and theorem 9.11.26 give the equation. Any other bounded solution pulls back to a bounded $H$-plurisubharmonic potential. Since $\pi $ is a Borel homeomorphism, equality of the pushforward measures means equality on $Y$. Subtracting $v_0$ and applying proposition 9.11.69 gives uniqueness. The mass identity of lemma 9.11.68 forces the scalar of every bounded solution to be $M/
u (X)=c$. The singular locus pulls back to the divisor $\{ p\} 	imes E_2	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n$, which has zero smooth volume. If a set is locally pluripolar, a local plurisubharmonic function equal to $-\infty $ on it pulls back to a plurisubharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, away from that divisor; its pole set has zero smooth volume. Thus $
u $ is non-pluripolar. On the regular locus, the change of variables formula gives the density $f/J$. Near the cusp $\alpha =0$, so \[  H^ n=n!ho \, \kappa _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \kappa _ n, \qquad \Omega =n!\lambda \, \kappa _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \kappa _ n.  \] The ratio gives the density $\lambda f/ho $; the generic degree of $\pi $ and both factorials have been accounted for. For the Hölder assertion, put $d=z-z'$ and $a=z+z'$. Then \[  z^2-z'^2=da,\qquad z^3-z'^3=d(3a^2+d^2)/4.  \] If $|a|\geq |d|/4$, the first modulus is at least $|d|^2/4$, which controls $|d|^3$ on a bounded chart. Otherwise the second modulus is at least $13|d|^3/64$. Hence $|z-z'|\leq C(|z^2-z'^2|+|z^3-z'^3|)^{1/3}$. The $C^1$ regularity of $v_0+w$ in $z$ and in the other product coordinates gives the asserted ambient estimate. Every resolution $\sigma :Z	o X$ factors through $Y$: in the cusp chart, the quotient $y/x$ is bounded off the exceptional set and extends holomorphically to the smooth source, giving the normalization coordinate. Write $\sigma =\pi \circ \mu $. The map $\mu $ is a proper modification. The bounded pullback products agree off its exceptional locus, and they give this analytic set zero mass by proposition 5.28.2 . Hence their pushforwards agree on all of $Y$. This proves the equation on every resolution, and the same argument applies to further common refinements. The full potential is exactly $u\circ \sigma $, which is constant on every fiber, and surjectivity preserves all ordinary comparisons. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.11.72
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Corollary 9.11.72 . 5F7DB1E779E6 For the same $X$ and $h$, every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p(Y,\Omega )$, $p>1$, admits a bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=\frac{M}{\int _ Yf\Omega }\, \pi _*(f\Omega ).  \] Proof. The torus $Y$ is Kähler, so it has bounded mass by lemma 19.9.12 . Since $k>0$, zero is an ordinary model for $k$: $P_ k[0]=0$. Its lower volume is $M>0$ by lemma 9.11.68 , because the potentials of the same ordinary type as zero are exactly the bounded ones. Hence theorem 10.31.3 , applied on $Y$ with background $k$ and reference zero, gives a bounded $k$-plurisubharmonic solution for the measure $f\Omega $, and its scalar is $M/\int f\Omega $. Adding $v_0$ and using theorem 9.11.5 , theorem 9.11.26 gives the normalized equation on $X$. The datum is non-pluripolar as in theorem 9.11.71 . Neither smallness nor strict positivity of $f$ is needed for this existence statement. $\square$

title: 1.1.2 Scope, attribution and conventions
text: Classical potential theory is developed through spherical means, harmonic measures, Green functions, capacities, sweeping, and Martin boundary representations. We work in real dimension $d\ge 2$, with ordinary Laplacian $\Delta $, unnormalized sphere area $s_{d-1}$, and unit ball volume $v_ d=s_{d-1}/d$. Put $\Phi (x)=|x|^{2-d}$ for $d\ge 3$ and $\Phi (x)=\log (1/|x|)$ for $d=2$. Then $-\Delta \Phi =c_ d\delta _0$, where $c_2=2\pi $ and $c_ d=(d-2)s_{d-1}$ for $d\ge 3$. Unless explicitly normalized otherwise, Green functions use this convention. Thus $G_{\rm Helms}=c_ dG_{\rm Foundations}$ and $C_{\rm Helms}=C_{\rm Foundations}/c_ d$. Superharmonic functions are lower semicontinuous, super-mean-valued and nontrivial on each component; positive means nonnegative unless strict positivity is stated. A potential is a nonnegative superharmonic function whose greatest harmonic minorant is zero. Measures are positive Radon measures unless signedness is specified. On noncompact spaces weak measure convergence in the source means vague convergence against $C_ c$. The prerequisites are multivariable calculus, Lebesgue integration, measure decomposition, and compact-metric measure representation. The harmonic and subharmonic results used below are established in the preceding Pome sections.

title: 3.3.1 Differentiating compact parameter integrals
text: Lemma 3.3.2 . 77E9E0297059 Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open, let $C$ be compact, and let $\mu $ be a finite signed Borel measure on $C$. Suppose $u$ and all the partial derivatives $\partial _{x_ j}u$ are jointly continuous on $U\times C$. Then $F(x)=\int _ Cu(x,y)\, d\mu (y)$ is of class $C^1$ on $U$, and \[  \partial _ jF(x)=\int _ C\partial _{x_ j}u(x,y)\, d\mu (y).  \] Proof. Choose a closed ball $K\subset U$ whose interior contains $x$. All the functions in the hypotheses are bounded and uniformly continuous on $K\times C$. For sufficiently small $h\neq 0$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  \frac{u(x+he_ j,y)-u(x,y)}h =\int _0^1\partial _{x_ j}u(x+she_ j,y)\, ds.  \] This converges to $\partial _{x_ j}u(x,y)$ uniformly in $y\in C$. Integrating the uniform error against the finite measure $|\mu |$ proves the differentiation formula. The same uniform continuity, now applied to $\partial _{x_ j}u$, proves continuity of the derivative integral as $x$ varies inside $K$. Joint continuity of $u$ also makes $F$ finite and continuous. The ball $K$ can be chosen about every point of $U$, proving the assertion. $\square$ Continuity of the $x$ derivatives alone is insufficient. For example, an $x$-independent measurable function $u(x,y)=g(y)$ can fail to be integrable on $C$ even though all those derivatives are zero. The compact-parameter Poisson kernels used below satisfy the corrected hypotheses.

title: 3.3.6 Measures on a compact metric boundary
search_title: Measures on a compact metric boundary
text: In this section we use the Riesz representation theorem for continuous linear functionals on $C(X)$, with $X$ compact metric: a bounded real functional is integration against a unique finite signed regular Borel measure, and its operator norm is the measure's total variation. This is an explicit measure-theory prerequisite, not an unproved potential-theoretic input. Theorem 3.3.7 (Compact-metric measure selection) . 2C91786CB405 Let $X$ be a compact metric space, and let $(\mu _ j)$ be finite signed Borel measures with $\sup _ j\| \mu _ j\| \leq M<\infty $. There is a subsequence and a finite signed Borel measure $\mu $, with $\| \mu \| \leq M$, such that \[  \int _ X f\, d\mu _{j_ k}\longrightarrow \int _ X f\, d\mu \qquad (f\in C(X)).  \] If all the $\mu _ j$ are positive, then $\mu $ is positive. Proof. If $X$ is empty or $M=0$, every measure is zero and the assertion is immediate. First construct a countable dense subset of $C(X)$. For each positive integer $n$, choose a finite $1/n$-net $x_{n,1},\ldots ,x_{n,N_ n}$, and put \[  p_{n,i}(x)=\frac{(2/n-\operatorname {dist}(x,x_{n,i}))^+}{\sum _{l=1}^{N_ n}(2/n-\operatorname {dist}(x,x_{n,l}))^+}.  \] The denominator is everywhere positive. These continuous functions form a partition of unity, and $p_{n,i}(x)>0$ implies $\operatorname {dist}(x,x_{n,i})<2/n$. For $f\in C(X)$, choose rational $q_{n,i}$ within $1/n$ of $f(x_{n,i})$. Then $\sum _ iq_{n,i}p_{n,i}$ converges uniformly to $f$ by uniform continuity. All rational combinations for all $n$ form a countable dense family. Enumerate that family as $(g_ l)$. For every $l$, the sequence $\int g_ l\, d\mu _ j$ is bounded by $M\| g_ l\| _\infty $. Successive subsequences and diagonal extraction yield a subsequence along which all these integrals converge. If $f\in C(X)$ and $g_ l$ is uniformly close to $f$, then \[  \left|\int f\, d\mu _{j_ k}-\int f\, d\mu _{j_{k'}}\right| \leq 2M\| f-g_ l\| _\infty + \left|\int g_ l\, d\mu _{j_ k}-\int g_ l\, d\mu _{j_{k'}}\right|.  \] Hence the integrals of every $f$ are Cauchy. Their limit $L(f)$ is a real linear functional with $|L(f)|\leq M\| f\| _\infty $. Riesz representation gives the required $\mu $ with $\| \mu \| \leq M$. If the original measures are positive, $L(f)\geq 0$ for $f\geq 0$; the positivity part of Riesz representation makes $\mu $ positive. $\square$ This form also applies to compactified boundaries, which need not be subsets of a fixed Euclidean space.

text:
Put $H=\{ x=(x',t)\in \mathbb R^{d-1}	imes \mathbb R:t>0\} $ and identify $\partial H$ with $\mathbb R^{d-1}$. For $z\in \mathbb R^{d-1}$ set 21F1298C637C 3.2.5  egin{equation}  P_ H(x,z)= rac{2}{s_{d-1}}  rac{t}{(|x'-z|^2+t^2)^{d/2}}. \end{equation} Theorem 3.2.6 (Half-space representation) . 6BC86EEF03A9 Every nonnegative harmonic function $h$ on $H$ has a representation F3ED29BBAD39 3.2.7  egin{equation}  h(x',t)=ct+\int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}P_ H((x',t),z)\, d
u (z), \end{equation} where $c\geq 0$ and $
u $ is a positive Radon measure satisfying 8F7C774A9D89 3.2.8  egin{equation}  \int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}(1+|z|^2)^{-d/2}\, d
u (z)<\infty . \end{equation} Conversely, any such pair defines a nonnegative harmonic function on $H$. The measure need not have finite total mass. Proof. We first derive the ball representation needed here from the ball Poisson formula and compactness of bounded positive measures on a compact set. Let $v\geq 0$ be harmonic on $B=B(b,R)$ and let $0<r<R$. On $\partial B$ define the measure \[  d\mu _ r(\zeta )=v igl (b+(r/R)(\zeta -b) igr )\, dS(\zeta ).  \] The mean-value property gives $\mu _ r(\partial B)=s_{d-1}R^{d-1}v(b)$. For a sequence $r_ j\uparrow R$, compactness therefore gives a subsequence converging weakly to a finite positive measure $\mu $ on $\partial B$. To apply the Euclidean measure-selection theorem, extend $\mu _{r_ j}$ by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$; their common compact support gives uniform tightness, and their weak limit is supported on that same closed sphere. For $|x-b|<r$, the ball Poisson formula, followed by the dilation from $\partial B$ to $\partial B(b,r)$, reads \[  v(x)=\int _{\partial B}\left( rac rRight)^{d-1}  rac{r^2-|x-b|^2}{s_{d-1}r\, |x-b-(r/R)(\zeta -b)|^ d}\, d\mu _ r(\zeta ).  \] For fixed $x\in B$ the integrands converge uniformly on $\partial B$ as $r\uparrow R$. The masses are uniformly bounded, so weak convergence gives 2009D781FC4A 3.2.9  egin{equation}  v(x)=\int _{\partial B} rac{R^2-|x-b|^2}{s_{d-1}R|x-\zeta |^ d}\, d\mu (\zeta ). \end{equation} This argument also covers $v(b)=0$, in which case all measures and $v$ vanish. Take $a=-e_ d$, $b=-e_ d/2$, $R=1/2$, and $T(x)=a+(x-a)/|x-a|^2$. Write $q=T(x)$ and $L=|x-a|$. Direct expansion gives B95428ABB7D8 3.2.10  egin{equation}  |q-a|=L^{-1},\qquad  rac14-|q-b|^2= rac{t}{L^2},\qquad |T(x)-T(y)|= rac{|x-y|}{|x-a||y-a|}. \end{equation} For the last identity, square both sides and expand the inner products; the numerator on the left becomes $|x-a|^2+|y-a|^2-2(x-a)\cdot (y-a)=|x-y|^2$ after multiplying by $|x-a|^2|y-a|^2$. The middle identity and $T^2=1$ show that $T$ maps $H$ onto $B(b,1/2)$ and maps $\partial H$ onto $\partial B\setminus \{ a\} $. By Theorem 3.2.2 , $v(q)=|q-a|^{2-d}h(T(q))$ is nonnegative and harmonic on $B$. Apply ( 3.2.9 ) and split $\mu =m\delta _ a+\mu _0$, where $\mu _0(\{ a\} )=0$. Since $h(x)=L^{2-d}v(T(x))$, the atom contributes $2mt/s_{d-1}$. Let $\sigma =T_*\mu _0$ on $\partial H$, and put \[  c=2m/s_{d-1},\qquad d
u (z)=|(z,0)-a|^ d\, d\sigma (z).  \] The measure $\sigma $ is finite and positive, and its continuous positive weight is bounded on compact sets. Hence $
u $ is a positive Radon measure. The distance identity in ( 3.2.10 ) transforms the remaining integral into \[  L^{2-d} rac{2}{s_{d-1}} \int _{\partial B\setminus \{ a\} }  rac{t/L^2}{|T(x)-\zeta |^ d}\, d\mu _0(\zeta ) = rac{2t}{s_{d-1}}\int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}  rac{d
u (z)}{|x-(z,0)|^ d}.  \] Also $|(z,0)-a|^ d=(1+|z|^2)^{d/2}$, so the integral in ( 3.2.8 ) equals $\sigma (\mathbb R^{d-1})<\infty $. This proves the required representation. For the converse, each kernel is smooth and harmonic as a function of $x\in H$. Indeed, with $r=|x-(z,0)|$, the radial differentiation formula used above gives $\Delta r^{-d}=2d r^{-d-2}$ and $\partial _ t r^{-d}=-dt r^{-d-2}$. Consequently $\Delta (t r^{-d})=2dt r^{-d-2}-2dt r^{-d-2}=0$. On a compact subset $K\subset H$, $t$ is bounded above and away from $0$, and $|x'|$ is bounded. Writing $v=x-(z,0)$, differentiation gives  egin{align*}  \partial _ i(t r^{-d})& =\delta _{id}r^{-d}-dtv_ i r^{-d-2},\  \partial _ j\partial _ i(t r^{-d}) & =-d(\delta _{id}v_ j+\delta _{jd}v_ i+t\delta _{ij})r^{-d-2} +d(d+2)tv_ iv_ j r^{-d-4}. \end{align*} For $|z|$ large, $r\geq |z|/2$ and $|v_ i|\leq r$, so these formulas bound the kernel and all its $x$ derivatives of orders at most two by $C_ K(1+|z|^2)^{-d/2}$. For bounded $z$, the lower bound on $t$ supplies the same estimate after increasing $C_ K$. These estimates also hold on a compact neighborhood of $K$ inside $H$, so dominated convergence justifies two differentiations under the integral. Condition ( 3.2.8 ) gives finiteness and harmonicity; positivity is immediate. $\square$ The weighted integrability condition and the converse above spell out the precise admissible class of measures.

title: 3.2.11 Bounded boundary data
text: Theorem 3.2.12 (Half-space Poisson integral) . 9ADD2DF19642 Let $f:\mathbb R^{d-1}\to \mathbb R$ be bounded and Lebesgue measurable, and let $c\in \mathbb R$. Then \[  u(x',t)=ct+\int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}P_ H((x',t),z)f(z)\, dz  \] is harmonic on $H$, and $|u(x',t)-ct|\leq \| f\| _\infty $. If $f$ is continuous at $z_0$, then $u(x',t)\to f(z_0)$ as $(x',t)\to (z_0,0)$ within $H$, with no restriction on the approach. Moreover $u(0,t)/t\to c$ as $t\to \infty $. Proof. We first verify the normalization AB2849CD8791 3.2.13 \begin{equation}  \int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}P_ H((x',t),z)\, dz=1. \end{equation} Translation and the substitution $z=x'+tw$ reduce the integral to $\frac{2}{s_{d-1}}\int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}(1+|w|^2)^{-d/2}\, dw$. The map \[  F(w)=\frac{(w,1)}{\sqrt{1+|w|^2}}  \] parametrizes the upper hemisphere. With $m=d-1$, its metric matrix is $DF^{\mathsf T}DF=(1+|w|^2)^{-1}I-(1+|w|^2)^{-2}ww^{\mathsf T}$. Its eigenvalues are $(1+|w|^2)^{-1}$ in the $m-1$ perpendicular directions and $(1+|w|^2)^{-2}$ in the direction of $w$. The square root of its determinant is $(1+|w|^2)^{-d/2}$. At $w=0$ this formula holds by continuity. The surface area formula and reflection in the equatorial plane show that the last integral is $s_{d-1}/2$, proving ( 3.2.13 ). This also treats $d=2$, when $m=1$ and there are no perpendicular directions. The weighted measure $|f(z)|\, dz$ satisfies ( 3.2.8 ), by the same integral at $(0,1)$. Applying the differentiation estimates in the proof of Theorem 3.2.6 to the positive and negative parts of $f$ proves harmonicity. The positivity and normalization of $P_ H$ give the stated bound. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. At a continuity point $z_0$, choose $\delta >0$ so that $|f(z)-f(z_0)|<\varepsilon $ for $|z-z_0|<\delta $. The contribution of this set to $|\int P_ H(x,z)(f(z)-f(z_0))\, dz|$ is at most $\varepsilon $. If $|x'-z_0|<\delta /2$ and $|z-z_0|\geq \delta $, then $|z-x'|\geq \delta /2$. Writing $s_{d-2}$ for the area of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ (in particular $s_0=2$), polar integration gives \[  \int _{|z-z_0|\geq \delta }P_ H(x,z)\, dz \leq \frac{2t}{s_{d-1}}s_{d-2}\int _{\delta /2}^{\infty }r^{-2}\, dr =\frac{4s_{d-2}}{s_{d-1}}\frac{t}{\delta }.  \] Thus \[  |u(x',t)-f(z_0)|\leq |c|t+\varepsilon + \frac{8s_{d-2}}{s_{d-1}}\| f\| _\infty \frac{t}{\delta }  \] near $(z_0,0)$. Letting $(x',t)\to (z_0,0)$ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the boundary limit. Finally $|u(0,t)/t-c|\leq \| f\| _\infty /t\to 0$. $\square$ For continuous bounded boundary data, varying $c$ gives distinct harmonic solutions with the same finite boundary values. This states nonuniqueness without a growth condition; it does not classify all such solutions.

title: Theorem 3.2.12 (Half-space Poisson integral)
text: Theorem 3.2.12 (Half-space Poisson integral) . 9ADD2DF19642 Let $f:\mathbb R^{d-1}\to \mathbb R$ be bounded and Lebesgue measurable, and let $c\in \mathbb R$. Then \[  u(x',t)=ct+\int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}P_ H((x',t),z)f(z)\, dz  \] is harmonic on $H$, and $|u(x',t)-ct|\leq \| f\| _\infty $. If $f$ is continuous at $z_0$, then $u(x',t)\to f(z_0)$ as $(x',t)\to (z_0,0)$ within $H$, with no restriction on the approach. Moreover $u(0,t)/t\to c$ as $t\to \infty $. Proof. We first verify the normalization AB2849CD8791 3.2.13 \begin{equation}  \int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}P_ H((x',t),z)\, dz=1. \end{equation} Translation and the substitution $z=x'+tw$ reduce the integral to $\frac{2}{s_{d-1}}\int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}(1+|w|^2)^{-d/2}\, dw$. The map \[  F(w)=\frac{(w,1)}{\sqrt{1+|w|^2}}  \] parametrizes the upper hemisphere. With $m=d-1$, its metric matrix is $DF^{\mathsf T}DF=(1+|w|^2)^{-1}I-(1+|w|^2)^{-2}ww^{\mathsf T}$. Its eigenvalues are $(1+|w|^2)^{-1}$ in the $m-1$ perpendicular directions and $(1+|w|^2)^{-2}$ in the direction of $w$. The square root of its determinant is $(1+|w|^2)^{-d/2}$. At $w=0$ this formula holds by continuity. The surface area formula and reflection in the equatorial plane show that the last integral is $s_{d-1}/2$, proving ( 3.2.13 ). This also treats $d=2$, when $m=1$ and there are no perpendicular directions. The weighted measure $|f(z)|\, dz$ satisfies ( 3.2.8 ), by the same integral at $(0,1)$. Applying the differentiation estimates in the proof of Theorem 3.2.6 to the positive and negative parts of $f$ proves harmonicity. The positivity and normalization of $P_ H$ give the stated bound. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. At a continuity point $z_0$, choose $\delta >0$ so that $|f(z)-f(z_0)|<\varepsilon $ for $|z-z_0|<\delta $. The contribution of this set to $|\int P_ H(x,z)(f(z)-f(z_0))\, dz|$ is at most $\varepsilon $. If $|x'-z_0|<\delta /2$ and $|z-z_0|\geq \delta $, then $|z-x'|\geq \delta /2$. Writing $s_{d-2}$ for the area of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ (in particular $s_0=2$), polar integration gives \[  \int _{|z-z_0|\geq \delta }P_ H(x,z)\, dz \leq \frac{2t}{s_{d-1}}s_{d-2}\int _{\delta /2}^{\infty }r^{-2}\, dr =\frac{4s_{d-2}}{s_{d-1}}\frac{t}{\delta }.  \] Thus \[  |u(x',t)-f(z_0)|\leq |c|t+\varepsilon + \frac{8s_{d-2}}{s_{d-1}}\| f\| _\infty \frac{t}{\delta }  \] near $(z_0,0)$. Letting $(x',t)\to (z_0,0)$ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the boundary limit. Finally $|u(0,t)/t-c|\leq \| f\| _\infty /t\to 0$. $\square$

title: 3.3.8 Radial boundary limits from symmetric densities
search_title: Radial boundary limits from symmetric densities
text: Theorem 3.3.9 . CAE5D89698DF Let $B=B(0,R)\subset \mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 2$, and let $\sigma $ be surface measure on $S=\partial B$. Let $\mu $ be a finite signed measure on $S$. For $\zeta \in S$ put $C_ s=\{ y\in S:|y-\zeta |\le s\} $. If $\mu (C_ s)/\sigma (C_ s)\to a\in \mathbb R$ as $s\downarrow 0$, then $P_ B\mu (t\zeta )\to a$ as $t\uparrow 1$. Proof. Subtract $a\sigma $, whose Poisson integral is the constant $a$. Thus $F(s)=\mu (C_ s)=o(A(s))$, where $A(s)=\sigma (C_ s)$. In particular $\mu (\{ \zeta \} )=0$. Fix $0<\delta <2R$ so that $|F(s)|\le \varepsilon A(s)$ for $0<s\le \delta $. The ball Poisson kernel at $t\zeta $ is a function of $s=|y-\zeta |$: \[  k_ t(s)=\frac{R^2(1-t^2)}{s_{d-1}R\, [R^2(1-t)^2+ts^2]^{d/2}}.  \] Here $s_{d-1}$ is the area of the unit sphere. This function is decreasing and smooth for $s\ge 0$, $0<t<1$. Integration of $k_ t(s)=k_ t(\delta )+\int _ s^\delta (-k_ t'(v))\, dv$ against the pushforward of $\mu |_{C_\delta }$, using finite signed Fubini, gives \[  \int _{C_\delta }k_ t(|y-\zeta |)\, d\mu =k_ t(\delta )F(\delta )+\int _0^\delta (-k_ t'(s))F(s)\, ds.  \] For each fixed $t$ all integrands are bounded and $\mu $ is finite, so this identity also holds when $F$ has jumps. Its absolute value is at most $\varepsilon \int _{C_\delta }k_ t\, d\sigma \le \varepsilon $, by positivity and normalization of the Poisson kernel. On $S\setminus C_\delta $, $\sup k_ t\to 0$, so the remaining integral tends to zero, bounded by $|\mu |(S)\sup _{s\ge \delta }k_ t(s)$. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: 3.3.10 Fine coverings and differentiation on a sphere

Lemma 3.3.11 . 3FB36EAD186A Let $X$ be a compact metric space and $A\subset X$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a family of closed sets of positive diameter such that every $x\in A$ belongs to members of arbitrarily small diameter. There is a finite or countably infinite disjoint sequence $F_ j\in \mathcal F$ such that, in the finite case, $A\subset  igcup _ jF_ j$, and, in the infinite case, for every $j$, \[  A\subset  igcup _{i\le j}F_ i\  \cup  igcup _{i>j}N(F_ i,3\operatorname {diam}F_ i).  \] Here $N(F,r)=\{ x:d(x,F)<r\} $. If a finite complete measure $m$ satisfies $0<m(F)$ and $m(N(F,3\operatorname {diam}F))\le C m(F)$ for all eligible members, the sequence covers $A$ except for an $m$-null set. Proof. If $A=\varnothing $, choose the empty sequence. Otherwise choose any $F_1$. After $F_1,\ldots ,F_ j$, stop if they cover $A$. If they do not, a point outside their closed union belongs to sufficiently small members $F$ with $N(F,\operatorname {diam}F)$ disjoint from that union. Let $e_ j>0$ be the supremum of their diameters, and choose such an $F_{j+1}$ with diameter $>2e_ j/3$. All chosen sets are disjoint. Fix $x\in A\setminus  igcup _{i\le j}F_ i$ and choose a member $F$ containing $x$ whose diameter is so small that its diameter-neighborhood avoids the first $j$ sets. It must meet a later chosen $F_ k$ in that neighborhood. Otherwise it remains eligible forever, so all subsequent chosen diameters exceed $2\operatorname {diam}F/3$; choosing a point in each yields an infinite uniformly separated subset of compact $X$, impossible. At the first such $k$, $\operatorname {diam}F_ k>2\operatorname {diam}F/3$. Some point of $F_ k$ is within $\operatorname {diam}F$ of $F$, hence $d(x,F_ k)<2\operatorname {diam}F<3\operatorname {diam}F_ k$. This proves the covering assertion. In the measure case the outer measure of the uncovered set is at most $C\sum _{i>j}m(F_ i)$ for every $j$; the tail tends to zero because the sets are disjoint and $m(X)<\infty $. Completeness makes every subset of the resulting null set measurable. $\square$ Theorem 3.3.12 . 5F363A880A82 Let $S=\partial B(0,R)\subset \mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 2$, with completed surface measure $\sigma $. A finite signed measure $\mu =f\sigma +\mu _ s$ has, for $\sigma $-almost every $\zeta $, the derivative \[  \lim _{\substack {\zeta \in K\ \operatorname {diam}K	o 0}}  rac{\mu (K)}{\sigma (K)}=f(\zeta ).  \] The sets $K$ are closed spherical caps of positive diameter less than a hemisphere. Moreover almost every $\zeta $ is a Lebesgue point: \[   rac1{\sigma (K)}\int _ K|f(y)-f(\zeta )|\, d\sigma (y)\longrightarrow 0 \quad (\zeta \in K,\  \operatorname {diam}K	o 0).  \] Proof. Small spherical caps satisfy uniform estimates $c r^{d-1}\le \sigma (K)\le C r^{d-1}$, $r=\operatorname {diam}K$, and $\sigma (N_ S(K,3r))\le C'\sigma (K)$. To verify them, cover $S$ by finitely many graph charts over tangent hyperplanes on which the graph map and its inverse have bounded derivatives and the surface Jacobian is bounded above and below by positive constants. A small cap centered at $z$ contains and is contained in chart balls of radii constant multiples of $r$; its $3r$-neighborhood is contained in a chart ball of radius a constant multiple of $r$. Euclidean volume scaling gives the estimates; compactness supplies uniform constants. These observations also show that any small cap containing $\zeta $ lies in a chart cube centered at $\zeta $ of side $Cr$, while its area is at least $cr^{d-1}$. u (K)/\sigma (K)>\lambda \} ,\qquad \lambda >0,  \] the good caps $
u (K)>\lambda \sigma (K)$ form a fine cover of $E_\lambda $. The lemma, applied to $m=\sigma $, gives disjoint good caps covering this set up to a surface null set. Thus its outer surface measure is at most $\sum \sigma (K)\le 
u (S)/\lambda $. This argument does not presume measurability of $E_\lambda $. If $
u $ is singular, choose a compact subset $L$ of a surface-null carrier with $
u (S\setminus L)<\varepsilon $, by regularity. Outside $L$, every sufficiently small cap sees only $

Precisely, for every fixed $A\ge 1$, it converges as $x	o \zeta $ in $B$ with $|x-\zeta |\le A(R-|x|)$. The same single full-measure set works for all finite $A$. Proof. title: 3.3.15 Harmonic reflection across a sphere
text: Lemma 3.3.16 . B0CFE200676D A nonnegative harmonic function $h$ on a punctured neighborhood of $a$ has the form $c\Phi (\cdot -a)+v$, where $c\ge 0$, $v$ is harmonic across $a$, and $\Phi (z)=\log (1/|z|)$ for $d=2$, $\Phi (z)=|z|^{2-d}$ for $d\ge 3$. Proof. This is a short consequence of the checked local Riesz decomposition. On a sufficiently small ball define $u=h+\Phi (\cdot -a)$ off $a$ and $u(a)=+\infty $. The fundamental function tends to infinity, and $h\ge 0$; thus $u$ is lsc and is superharmonic, using locality off $a$ and the trivial supermean inequality at $a$. It is locally integrable by the checked local integrability theorem. Its positive Riesz measure $-\Delta u$ is supported at $a$, so it equals $b\delta _ a$ with $b\ge 0$. Since $-\Delta \Phi =c_ d\delta _ a$, where $c_2=2\pi $ and $c_ d=(d-2)s_{d-1}$ otherwise, Weyl's lemma gives $u=(b/c_ d)\Phi +v$ almost everywhere. Equality holds everywhere off $a$ by continuity. Hence $h=(b/c_ d-1)\Phi +v$ there, and its nonnegativity near $a$ forces $c=b/c_ d-1\ge 0$. This also proves removability when $h$ is bounded, or when a one-sided bounded harmonic function has a finite limit along one approach to $a$. $\square$ Theorem 3.3.17 . 14F410C2E770 Let $0<r<R$ and let $h$ be continuous on the closed annulus $r\le |x-a|\le R$, harmonic on its interior, and zero on $|x-a|=R$. It has a harmonic extension across that sphere to $r<|x-a|<R+\varepsilon $ for some $\varepsilon >0$. Proof. First, odd reflection across a hyperplane preserves harmonicity for a harmonic function continuous and zero at that plane. The reflected function is continuous; at a center on the plane its spherical means vanish by the reflection symmetry, and away from the plane sufficiently small spheres have the usual harmonic mean property. The checked local mean characterization therefore proves harmonicity across the plane. Translate $a=0$. Add a sufficiently large positive multiple of $\log (R/|x|)$ if $d=2$, or of $|x|^{2-d}-R^{2-d}$ otherwise, so that the result is nonnegative on the inner sphere. The minimum principle makes it nonnegative throughout the annulus. These added functions already extend harmonically across the outer sphere, so it suffices to treat $h\ge 0$. Choose $b$ on the outer sphere and invert about a sphere centered at $b$. The outer sphere minus $b$ becomes a hyperplane, and the inner closed ball becomes a compact ball strictly in one of its half-spaces. The Kelvin transform is harmonic outside that compact ball in the half-space, continuous and zero at its planar boundary. Reflect it oddly. Applying the inverse Kelvin transform gives a harmonic extension on a neighborhood of the original closed annulus, except possibly at $b$. On its exterior side this extension is nonpositive, since the reflected function is nonpositive and the Kelvin multiplier is positive. On the interior side it tends to zero at $b$, so it is bounded above on a punctured neighborhood of $b$. Apply the preceding lemma to a constant minus this extension. Its singular coefficient must vanish because the extension has limit zero along the interior approach. Thus the singularity at $b$ is removable. Compactness of the outer sphere gives one $\varepsilon >0$ valid around the whole sphere. Finally subtract the added radial harmonic function. $\square$

The minimum principle makes it nonnegative throughout the annulus. These added functions already extend harmonically across the outer sphere, so it suffices to treat $h\ge 0$. title: 3.5.1 Harmonic lowering and greatest harmonic minorants
search_title: Harmonic lowering and greatest harmonic minorants
text: The following arguments use superharmonic functions in the nontrivial componentwise sense. Harmonic lowering $L_ Bu$ equals the Poisson integral of $u|_{\partial B}$ in $B\Subset \Omega $, and equals $u$ outside $B$. The checked comparison and Poisson boundary lower-limit statements show that $L_ Bu$ is superharmonic and $L_ Bu\le u$: at a boundary point it is lsc, and its sphere averages are at most those of $u$, with the same center value. In $B$ it is harmonic, and elsewhere locality applies. Lemma 3.5.2 . AC0C4669DCBF Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty family of superharmonic functions on an open set $\Omega $, closed under pairwise minimum and under every harmonic lowering. Its infimum is harmonic or identically $-\infty $ on each component. Proof. On a ball $B\Subset \Omega $ its infimum is also $\inf _{u\in \mathcal F}L_ Bu$, since $L_ Bu\le u$ and $L_ Bu\in \mathcal F$. The lowered harmonic functions form a downward directed family: $L_ B(\min (u,v))\le \min (L_ Bu,L_ Bv)$ by positivity of the Poisson kernel. A downward directed family of harmonic functions has harmonic infimum or infimum identically $-\infty $ on a ball. To see this from the checked Harnack convergence theorem, negate and restrict to the cofinal subfamily above one fixed member; its differences from that member are nonnegative harmonic. If bounded at one point, Harnack chains bound them on compact subsets, and harmonic compactness shows their directed supremum harmonic. If unbounded at a point, Harnack chains make the supremum infinity everywhere. Thus the infimum is locally harmonic or locally identically $-\infty $. The regions of these two alternatives are disjoint open sets; connectedness of each component leaves only one alternative. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.3 . 2791D284428C Let $u$ be superharmonic on $\Omega $ and $W\subset \Omega $ open. Choose balls $B_ j\Subset W$ covering $W$, with each chosen ball repeated infinitely often, and set $u_0=u$, $u_ j=L_{B_ j}u_{j-1}$. Then $u_ j$ decreases to $u_\infty $, equal to $u$ outside $W$, and harmonic or identically $-\infty $ on each component of $W$. If $u$ has a harmonic minorant on $W$, the restriction $u_\infty |_ W$ is its unique greatest harmonic minorant, independent of the ball sequence. This operation is additive on superharmonic functions having harmonic minorants. Proof. Lowering makes the sequence decrease and leaves it fixed outside $W$. On each fixed ball, the subsequence of stages just lowered there is harmonic and decreases to the same limit; the checked harmonic monotone convergence theorem makes that limit harmonic or $-\infty $. Connectedness propagates the alternative as in the preceding proof. If $v$ is any harmonic minorant on $W$, positivity of the Poisson kernel proves inductively $v\le u_ j$ there. Thus $v\le u_\infty \le u$, which excludes $-\infty $ and proves maximality and uniqueness. For two functions use the same sequence of balls. Linearity of each lowering gives $(u+v)_ j=u_ j+v_ j$; the limits are finite on $W$ when harmonic minorants exist, so their sum is the corresponding greatest harmonic minorant. No claim is made that the unregularized $u_\infty $ is superharmonic across $\partial W$. $\square$

title: 3.5.4 Minimal Green functions on general open sets
search_title: Minimal Green functions on general open sets
text: Write $\Phi _ a(x)=\Phi (x-a)$, with the normalization of Lemma 3.3.16 . A minimal Green function on an open set $\Omega $ is a nonnegative kernel $G$ such that $G(a,\cdot )=\Phi _ a+h_ a$, $h_ a$ harmonic on $\Omega $, and $G(a,\cdot )\le \Phi _ a+w$ whenever $w$ is superharmonic on $\Omega $ and $\Phi _ a+w\ge 0$. At $a$, both kernels have value infinity; differences of singular kernels below mean the harmonic extension of their difference off the pole. Theorem 3.5.5 . F3C6870EA9A8 For $a\in \Omega $ put $\mathcal B_ a=\{ \Phi _ a+w\ge 0:w\text{ superharmonic on }\Omega \} $. A minimal Green function exists exactly when all these classes are nonempty, and then $G(a,\cdot )=\inf \mathcal B_ a$ and it is unique. Existence holds for every open set if $d\ge 3$, every bounded open set if $d=2$, every open subset of a Greenian open set, and every planar open set which is not dense or is disconnected. The whole plane, and the plane minus a closed discrete set, have no Green function. In $\mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 3$, the Green function is $\Phi _ a$. Proof. The class $\mathcal B_ a$ is closed under minimum and lowering on balls away from $a$, since $\Phi _ a$ is harmonic there and lowering preserves superharmonicity of $w$. Its infimum $v$ is nonnegative and harmonic away from $a$ by Lemma 3.5.2 . On a ball about $a$, every member dominates the ball Green function: their harmonic singularities cancel and the superharmonic difference has nonnegative boundary lower limits. Hence $v$ also dominates that ball Green function. The local Bôcher lemma gives $v=c\Phi _ a+h$ with $c\ge 0$; the preceding domination forces $c\ge 1$. This expression defines harmonic $h$ across $a$ and on all of $\Omega $. Now $v/c=\Phi _ a+h/c\ge 0$ belongs to $\mathcal B_ a$, so $v\le v/c\le v$. If $c>1$, this would force $v=0$ off $a$, contradicting the ball domination. Thus $c=1$, and $v$ is the required minimal kernel. Uniqueness and necessity follow at once from the definition. For $d\ge 3$, $\Phi _ a\ge 0$ is an admissible member. For a bounded planar set, $\Phi _ a+C\ge 0$ for a sufficiently large constant. Restriction of an existing Green kernel supplies a member on any smaller open set. If a planar open set avoids a closed ball, translate and dilate so that it avoids $\overline{B(0,1)}$. For $a,y$ in it, \[  \log \frac{2|a||y|}{|a-y|} =\Phi _ a(y)+\log |y|+\log (2|a|)\ge 0,  \] since $|1/a-1/y|<2$. The last two terms are harmonic in $y$ there. For a disconnected planar open set, each component avoids a ball in another component and is Greenian. For a pole in one component, extend its harmonic correction by $-\Phi _ a$ on all the others; the resulting admissible member is zero on those other components. This proves existence for the union. A planar Green kernel would have a harmonic correction $h_ a\ge -\Phi _ a=\log |\cdot -a|$, which tends to infinity at infinity. On arbitrarily large circles the minimum principle would then force $h_ a(0)$ to exceed every constant, impossible. A minimal kernel is bounded outside every ball $B\Subset \Omega $ containing its pole. Indeed let $m=\max _{\partial B}G(a,\cdot )>0$, and replace it outside $B$ by $\min (G(a,\cdot ),2m)$. This agrees with $G$ near the sphere, is superharmonic, and after subtracting $\Phi _ a$ is superharmonic across the pole. Minimality bounds $G$ by this replacement. On a plane minus a closed discrete set, this bound and the Bôcher lemma remove every deleted point as a bounded harmonic singularity. The resulting nonnegative kernel has a harmonic correction on the whole plane, contradicting the preceding minimum-principle argument. Finally in dimension at least three on the whole space, $G=\Phi _ a+h_ a\le \Phi _ a$ makes $h_ a\le 0$ entire harmonic, hence constant by Liouville. Its constant must be zero because $G\ge 0$ and $\Phi _ a\to 0$ at infinity. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.6 . 9E37095B7A8A Minimal Green functions are monotone under inclusion of open sets and increase to $G_\Omega $ along an increasing exhaustion of a Greenian $\Omega $. They are symmetric, zero between different components, and strictly positive within one component. They are jointly continuous off the diagonal and tend to infinity jointly at the diagonal. For $\overline{B(b,r)}\subset \Omega $, the spherical average $\int _{\partial B(b,r)}G(z,y)\, d\sigma (y)$ is a finite continuous function of $z\in \Omega $. Proof. Restriction is admissible, proving domain monotonicity. Along an exhaustion the increasing limit is bounded above by $G_\Omega $ off the pole, hence harmonic there. The harmonic corrections $G_ j(a,\cdot )-\Phi _ a$ also increase and are bounded above by $h_ a$; harmonic monotone convergence across the pole makes their limit harmonic on all of $\Omega $. The limit is a nonnegative admissible kernel and is therefore $G_\Omega $ by minimality. Every harmonic minorant $v$ of $G(a,\cdot )$ satisfies $v\le 0$, since $G-v$ is admissible and minimality gives $G\le G-v$. Thus its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. In the simultaneous lowering process of the preceding theorem, applied to $G(a,\cdot )=\Phi _ a+h_ a$, the harmonic correction is invariant, so \[  0=(\Phi _ a)_\infty +h_ a,\qquad G(a,y)=\Phi _ a(y)-(\Phi _ a)_\infty (y).  \] We verify that $q(a,y)=(\Phi _ a)_\infty (y)$ is harmonic in $a$ for each fixed $y$. Choose a locally finite cover of $\Omega $ by relatively compact balls, and enumerate it with repetitions. Such a cover is obtained by covering the compact layers of a nested compact exhaustion by finitely many small balls lying in adjacent exhaustion layers; only finitely many distinct balls meet each compact subset. Its union of boundary spheres $C$ is relatively closed. At a finite lowering stage, integration of $\Phi _ a(z)$ against the successive compact-sphere Poisson kernels is harmonic in $a$ away from those spheres and, until a ball containing $y$ has been used, possibly away from $y$. Differentiation is justified locally by positive distance from the finite union of spheres and bounded derivatives of the fundamental kernel; iterated finite integrals preserve those bounds. Once a ball containing $y$ has been used, there is no remaining point-pole exception. Consequently, on $\Omega \setminus C$ the decreasing stage limits are harmonic or $-\infty $. They are finite because $q(a,y)=-h_ a(y)$ for all $a,y$, as the preceding identity shows; hence they are harmonic there. For any prescribed $a_0$, choose the locally finite covering balls so that none of their boundary spheres contains $a_0$. This is possible in each finite layer by perturbing radii while retaining the covering; the local finiteness construction is unchanged. Then $a_0\notin C$, and $q(\cdot ,y)$ is harmonic near $a_0$. The greatest-minorant characterization makes $q$ independent of the chosen cover. Thus it is harmonic on all of $\Omega $. For fixed $y$, $\Phi _ y-q(\cdot ,y)$ is nonnegative and admissible, so $G(a,y)\ge G(y,a)$; interchange $a,y$ for equality. On components not containing $a$, a competitor equal to zero there and unchanged on the pole component proves $G=0$ there. Within the pole component, the strong minimum principle on the punctured domain gives strict positivity. Take disjoint compact balls around two distinct points, lying in slightly larger disjoint balls in $\Omega $. Harnack bounds in the first variable and the established bound away from a pole in the second variable bound $G$ uniformly on their product. Harmonic interior derivative estimates in each variable then give uniform equicontinuity there, hence joint continuity by the triangle inequality. Near a diagonal point, domain monotonicity bounds $G$ below by the Green function of one fixed ball containing both variables. Its explicit formula tends to infinity there. Finally, away from the averaging sphere, joint continuity on a compact product gives continuity of the spherical integral. On the sphere itself, compare its normalized averages at radii $r+\eta $ and $r-\eta $. Superharmonic spherical-mean monotonicity places the radius-$r$ average between these two continuous functions of the pole $z$. At a fixed pole on the sphere, the radial averages converge as $\eta \to 0$: their continuity in radius follows from annular mean concavity, proved from the annular divergence formula and monotone smooth approximation. They are finite by local surface integrability of a superharmonic function on interior spheres. The squeeze gives continuity at the pole on the sphere. Multiply by the constant surface area to pass from means to the stated integrals. $\square$
