title: 3.5.7 Potentials and global Riesz decomposition
text:
Throughout this section $G_\Omega $ is the unnormalized minimal Green kernel, $-\Delta G_\Omega (\cdot ,y)=c_ d\delta _ y$. Measures are positive Radon measures; they need not have finite total mass. A potential means $p=G_\Omega \mu $ which is not identically infinity on any component. Theorem 3.5.8 . 977ECF0867E0 The integral $G_\Omega \mu $ is lsc and supermean, hence superharmonic on every component where it is nontrivial. Every finite measure has a potential. For any potential, \[  -\Delta (G_\Omega \mu )=c_ d\mu  \] in distributions. Its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. It is harmonic on an open set exactly when that set has $\mu $-measure zero. Two potentials whose difference is harmonic almost everywhere on an open set have equal measures there. If $S\subset \Omega $ is open, $\mu $ is supported in $S$ and $G_\Omega \mu $ is a potential, then $G_\Omega \mu =G_ S\mu +h$ on $S$ with $h\ge 0$ harmonic. Reciprocity $\int G\mu \, d
u =\int G
u \, d\mu $ holds in $[0,\infty ]$. Proof. Fatou's lemma applied to the nonnegative continuous extended kernel gives lsc; Tonelli and the supermean inequality for each pole give supermeans. If $\mu $ is finite and gives zero mass to a closed interior ball containing $x$, the bound for $G(x,\cdot )$ outside that ball makes its potential finite at $x$, hence superharmonic on that component. Split a finite measure into its part on a small interior ball and its complement. Each part misses some interior ball in the component, so both have superharmonic potentials and their sum is superharmonic. Apply this separately to every component, using that $G$ vanishes between components. A potential $p$ is locally integrable by superharmonic local integrability. For $\varphi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$, \[  \iint G(x,y)|\Delta \varphi (x)|\, dx\, d\mu (y) =\int p(x)|\Delta \varphi (x)|\, dx<\infty .  \] Thus signed Fubini is legitimate, and the fundamental-solution identity plus harmonicity of the correction gives $\int p\Delta \varphi =-c_ d\int \varphi \, d\mu $. In particular a harmonic potential has zero measure; more generally subtracting the distributional identities proves equality of measures wherever the difference is harmonic. If $\mu (U)=0$, Weyl's lemma gives a harmonic representative on $U$; canonical representative uniqueness identifies it pointwise with $p$. For the greatest minorant use the same sequence of harmonic lowerings for $p$ and for every kernel $G(\cdot ,y)$. Induction and nonnegative Tonelli show $p_ j(x)=\int G_ j(x,y)\, d\mu (y)$. For each $y$, $G_ j(x,y)\downarrow 0$, because the greatest harmonic minorant of the minimal Green kernel is zero. In each connected component choose $x_0$ with $p(x_0)<\infty $. Dominated convergence gives $p_\infty (x_0)=0$; its nonnegative harmonic minorant is therefore zero on that component by the minimum principle. This is a componentwise argument, even when $\Omega $ is disconnected. On $S$, domain monotonicity gives $0\le G_ S\mu \le p$. Both potentials are locally integrable; their distributional difference is harmonic and nonnegative almost everywhere, hence a nonnegative harmonic $h$. Equality $p=G_ S\mu +h$ holds everywhere by uniqueness of superharmonic representatives. Finally symmetry of $G$ and nonnegative Tonelli give reciprocity, including infinite values. None of these arguments separates divergent fundamental and harmonic-correction integrals. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.9 . 9453A8C660CC Let $u$ be superharmonic on a Greenian open set $\Omega $. Its unique Riesz measure is $
u =-\Delta u/c_ d$. For each open $W\Subset \Omega $, \[  u=G_ W(
u |_ W)+h_ W\quad \hbox{on }W,  \] where $h_ W$ is the greatest harmonic minorant there. If $u\ge 0$ on $\Omega $, the same formula holds globally with $W=\Omega $ and a nonnegative harmonic $h$. Thus a nonnegative superharmonic function is a Green potential exactly when its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. Proof. The checked distributional characterization gives the positive Radon measure $
u $. We first suppose $u$ is bounded below by a constant $m$ on its Greenian domain $D$ (either $D=W\Subset \Omega $, or $D=\Omega $ and $m=0$). For a compact $K\subset D$ put $p_ K=G_ D(
u |_ K)$, a potential of a finite measure. The locally integrable difference $u-p_ K$ has nonpositive Laplacian, so it has a superharmonic representative $w_ K$, and $u=w_ K+p_ K$ everywhere by canonical representative uniqueness. The function $p_ K$ is bounded outside some compact neighborhood $K'\Subset D$. Here is the required uniformity: cover $K$ by finitely many small balls whose closures lie in $D$. On each, Harnack chains bound $G_ D(x,y)$ for $y$ in its smaller concentric ball by a fixed multiple of $G_ D(x,y_ i)$, whenever $x$ lies outside the union of the larger balls. Each fixed-pole kernel is bounded away from its pole; integrating the resulting finite uniform bound against $
u |_ K$ proves the assertion. Choose $K'$ containing these larger closed balls. On $D\setminus K'$, $w_ K=u-p_ K\ge m-M$; on $K'$ it is bounded below by lsc and compactness. Hence $w_ K$ has a constant harmonic minorant on all of $D$. The greatest-minorant operation is additive, and $p_ K$ has greatest minorant zero. Thus $H_ Du=H_ Dw_ K\ge m$ because $u\ge m$. Consequently $w_ K\ge m$ and $p_ K\le u-m$. Exhaust $D$ by increasing compact $K_ j$. Monotone convergence gives $p=G_ D(
u |_ D)\le u-m$. This is finite almost everywhere, hence a potential. Its Riesz measure is $
u |_ D$, so $u-p$ is harmonic in distributions and has a harmonic representative $h$. Canonical uniqueness gives $u=p+h$ everywhere, and additivity of greatest minorants makes $h=H_ Du$. When $m=0$, $h\ge 0$. Applying this construction to every relatively compact $W$ proves the local assertion without assuming $u$ bounded below on the entire $\Omega $. Uniqueness of $
u $ follows from its distributional identity, and the last characterization follows from the zero-minorant property of potentials. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.5.8
text: Theorem 3.5.8 . 977ECF0867E0 The integral $G_\Omega \mu $ is lsc and supermean, hence superharmonic on every component where it is nontrivial. Every finite measure has a potential. For any potential, \[  -\Delta (G_\Omega \mu )=c_ d\mu  \] in distributions. Its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. It is harmonic on an open set exactly when that set has $\mu $-measure zero. Two potentials whose difference is harmonic almost everywhere on an open set have equal measures there. If $S\subset \Omega $ is open, $\mu $ is supported in $S$ and $G_\Omega \mu $ is a potential, then $G_\Omega \mu =G_ S\mu +h$ on $S$ with $h\ge 0$ harmonic. Reciprocity $\int G\mu \, d\nu =\int G\nu \, d\mu $ holds in $[0,\infty ]$. Proof. Fatou's lemma applied to the nonnegative continuous extended kernel gives lsc; Tonelli and the supermean inequality for each pole give supermeans. If $\mu $ is finite and gives zero mass to a closed interior ball containing $x$, the bound for $G(x,\cdot )$ outside that ball makes its potential finite at $x$, hence superharmonic on that component. Split a finite measure into its part on a small interior ball and its complement. Each part misses some interior ball in the component, so both have superharmonic potentials and their sum is superharmonic. Apply this separately to every component, using that $G$ vanishes between components. A potential $p$ is locally integrable by superharmonic local integrability. For $\varphi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$, \[  \iint G(x,y)|\Delta \varphi (x)|\, dx\, d\mu (y) =\int p(x)|\Delta \varphi (x)|\, dx<\infty .  \] Thus signed Fubini is legitimate, and the fundamental-solution identity plus harmonicity of the correction gives $\int p\Delta \varphi =-c_ d\int \varphi \, d\mu $. In particular a harmonic potential has zero measure; more generally subtracting the distributional identities proves equality of measures wherever the difference is harmonic. If $\mu (U)=0$, Weyl's lemma gives a harmonic representative on $U$; canonical representative uniqueness identifies it pointwise with $p$. For the greatest minorant use the same sequence of harmonic lowerings for $p$ and for every kernel $G(\cdot ,y)$. Induction and nonnegative Tonelli show $p_ j(x)=\int G_ j(x,y)\, d\mu (y)$. For each $y$, $G_ j(x,y)\downarrow 0$, because the greatest harmonic minorant of the minimal Green kernel is zero. In each connected component choose $x_0$ with $p(x_0)<\infty $. Dominated convergence gives $p_\infty (x_0)=0$; its nonnegative harmonic minorant is therefore zero on that component by the minimum principle. This is a componentwise argument, even when $\Omega $ is disconnected. On $S$, domain monotonicity gives $0\le G_ S\mu \le p$. Both potentials are locally integrable; their distributional difference is harmonic and nonnegative almost everywhere, hence a nonnegative harmonic $h$. Equality $p=G_ S\mu +h$ holds everywhere by uniqueness of superharmonic representatives. Finally symmetry of $G$ and nonnegative Tonelli give reciprocity, including infinite values. None of these arguments separates divergent fundamental and harmonic-correction integrals. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.5.9
text:
Theorem 3.5.9 . 9453A8C660CC Let $u$ be superharmonic on a Greenian open set $\Omega $. Its unique Riesz measure is $
u =-\Delta u/c_ d$. For each open $W\Subset \Omega $, \[  u=G_ W(
u |_ W)+h_ W\quad \hbox{on }W,  \] where $h_ W$ is the greatest harmonic minorant there. If $u\ge 0$ on $\Omega $, the same formula holds globally with $W=\Omega $ and a nonnegative harmonic $h$. Thus a nonnegative superharmonic function is a Green potential exactly when its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. Proof. The checked distributional characterization gives the positive Radon measure $
u $. We first suppose $u$ is bounded below by a constant $m$ on its Greenian domain $D$ (either $D=W\Subset \Omega $, or $D=\Omega $ and $m=0$). For a compact $K\subset D$ put $p_ K=G_ D(
u |_ K)$, a potential of a finite measure. The locally integrable difference $u-p_ K$ has nonpositive Laplacian, so it has a superharmonic representative $w_ K$, and $u=w_ K+p_ K$ everywhere by canonical representative uniqueness. The function $p_ K$ is bounded outside some compact neighborhood $K'\Subset D$. Here is the required uniformity: cover $K$ by finitely many small balls whose closures lie in $D$. On each, Harnack chains bound $G_ D(x,y)$ for $y$ in its smaller concentric ball by a fixed multiple of $G_ D(x,y_ i)$, whenever $x$ lies outside the union of the larger balls. Each fixed-pole kernel is bounded away from its pole; integrating the resulting finite uniform bound against $
u |_ K$ proves the assertion. Choose $K'$ containing these larger closed balls. On $D\setminus K'$, $w_ K=u-p_ K\ge m-M$; on $K'$ it is bounded below by lsc and compactness. Hence $w_ K$ has a constant harmonic minorant on all of $D$. The greatest-minorant operation is additive, and $p_ K$ has greatest minorant zero. Thus $H_ Du=H_ Dw_ K\ge m$ because $u\ge m$. Consequently $w_ K\ge m$ and $p_ K\le u-m$. Exhaust $D$ by increasing compact $K_ j$. Monotone convergence gives $p=G_ D(
u |_ D)\le u-m$. This is finite almost everywhere, hence a potential. Its Riesz measure is $
u |_ D$, so $u-p$ is harmonic in distributions and has a harmonic representative $h$. Canonical uniqueness gives $u=p+h$ everywhere, and additivity of greatest minorants makes $h=H_ Du$. When $m=0$, $h\ge 0$. Applying this construction to every relatively compact $W$ proves the local assertion without assuming $u$ bounded below on the entire $\Omega $. Uniqueness of $
u $ follows from its distributional identity, and the last characterization follows from the zero-minorant property of potentials. $\square$

title: 3.5.10 Continuity of potentials and bounded densities
search_title: Continuity of potentials and bounded densities
text: Theorem 3.5.11 . 64E880580F0E Let $\mu $ have compact support $K\Subset \Omega $. If $(G_\Omega \mu )|_ K$ is continuous at $a\in K$, then $G_\Omega \mu $ is continuous at $a$, in the extended sense. If $G_\Omega \mu $ is finite on $K$, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a compact $C\subset K$ with $\mu (K\setminus C)<\varepsilon $ for which $G_\Omega (\mu |_ C)$ is finite and continuous throughout $\Omega $. Proof. Near $K$ the Green potential differs from its fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Both potentials are locally integrable and have the same distributional Laplacian, so Weyl's lemma gives a harmonic difference. Adding that harmonic function preserves superharmonicity; canonical representatives then identify the equality everywhere, including infinite values. No joint continuity of a cancelled diagonal kernel is assumed. It suffices to prove the first assertion for $U\mu (x)=\int \Phi (x-y)d\mu (y)$. If $U\mu (a)=\infty $, lsc suffices. Otherwise choose a small ball $B$ about $a$ and split $\mu =\mu '+\mu ''$, with $\mu '=\mu |_ B$, so that the local singular integral $U\mu '(a)<\eta $. In the planar case take all relevant distances less than one so this local kernel is nonnegative. The remainder $U\mu ''$ is harmonic near $a$. If $z_ x\in K$ is a nearest point to $x$, then $z_ x\to a$ as $x\to a$, and $|z_ x-y|\le 2|x-y|$ for $y\in K$. For $d\ge 3$ this gives $U\mu '(x)\le 2^{d-2}U\mu '(z_ x)$. For $d=2$ it gives $U\mu '(x)\le U\mu '(z_ x)+(\log 2)\mu '(B)$. The restriction of $U\mu '$ to $K$ is continuous at $a$, being the difference of the assumed continuous restriction of $U\mu $ and the harmonic remainder. Thus the limsup of the local contribution is at most $2^{d-2}\eta $, or $\eta +(\log 2)\mu (B)$ in dimension two. In that case $\mu (\{ a\} )=0$ by finiteness of the potential, so $\mu (B)\to 0$ as the radius shrinks. The harmonic remainder is continuous; letting $\eta \to 0$ proves continuity. For the second assertion, Lusin's theorem gives compact $C\subset K$ with lost mass less than $\varepsilon $ and $G\mu |_ C$ finite continuous. On $C$, $G(\mu |_ C)=G\mu -G(\mu |_{K\setminus C})$ is upper semicontinuous, since the second term is lsc; it is also lsc. It is therefore continuous on $C$, and the first assertion gives continuity at every point of $C$. Off $C$ it is harmonic. This proves global finite continuity. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.12 . 9CF388990FE4 If $f\in L^1(\Omega )\cap L^\infty (\Omega )$, then $G_\Omega f$ is finite continuous on $\Omega $. For a ball and compactly supported measure its potential tends to zero at every boundary point. More generally suppose $\Omega $ is connected, has finite volume for $d\ge 3$, and is bounded for $d=2$. If $G_\Omega (x,y_0)\to 0$ as $x\to a\in \partial \Omega $ for one $y_0\in \Omega $, then $G_\Omega f(x)\to 0$ for every bounded measurable $f$. Proof. Separate the positive and negative parts of $f$. They are finite measures, so have superharmonic potentials. On an interior ball, the contribution from its complement is harmonic; the local contribution differs from a fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Its singular integral over a ball of radius $r$ is uniformly at most $\| f\| _\infty s_{d-1}r^2/2$ for $d\ge 3$, and $2\pi \| f\| _\infty \int _0^ r s\log (1/s)ds$ in the plane, after adding a harmless local constant. These bounds tend to zero. To justify that a ball centered elsewhere has no larger integral of the radial decreasing positive kernel, use its layer-cake representation: intersection with every centered superlevel ball has volume at most the smaller of the two ball volumes. The nonsingular part is continuous by dominated convergence, proving the first assertion and finiteness. For the boundary assertions, Harnack chains in the pole variable make $G(x,\cdot )\to 0$ uniformly on any fixed compact subset when it tends to zero at one pole. The explicit ball kernel supplies this condition at every ball boundary point, so compactly supported potentials tend to zero. Exhaust $\Omega $ by compact $K_ j$. In dimension at least three, $G(x,y)\le |x-y|^{2-d}$, and the layer-cake estimate just proved yields \[  \sup _ x\int _{\Omega \setminus K_ j}G(x,y)|f(y)|dy \le \tfrac 12s_{d-1}\| f\| _\infty (|\Omega \setminus K_ j|/v_ d)^{2/d}\longrightarrow 0.  \] For a bounded planar domain choose $D>\operatorname {diam}\Omega $; $G(x,y)\le \log (D/|x-y|)$ by minimality, and the same estimate is the integral of this radial kernel over a disk of the tail's area, tending to zero. Thus the compact-support integrals approximate $Gf$ uniformly in $x$, and their boundary limits are zero. $\square$

title: 3.5.13 The generalized Laplacian
text: For a continuous function $u$, write $\widetilde\Delta u(x)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0}2d(M_ ru(x)-u(x))/r^2$ whenever this finite limit exists, where $M_ r$ is the normalized sphere mean. Theorem 3.5.14 . 27ABF8BDD497 For bounded continuous $f\in L^1(\Omega )$ on a Greenian open set, $\widetilde\Delta (G_\Omega f)=-c_ df$ pointwise. If $u$ is continuous and $\widetilde\Delta u=0$ on an open set, then $u$ is harmonic there. Proof. Near a fixed $x$, the contribution of the measure outside a small closed ball is harmonic, and the local Green potential differs from its fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Harmonic functions contribute zero to the generalized Laplacian. The sphere average of $\Phi (\cdot -y)$ at center $x$ is $\Phi (r)$ when $|x-y|\le r$ and $\Phi (x-y)$ otherwise. For the second case this is the harmonic mean property. For the first, rotation invariance gives a radial harmonic function of $y$ inside the sphere, smooth there by differentiation, hence constant, with its value at the center equal to $\Phi (r)$. Here is uniform control at the sphere: its surface measure in any ball of radius $s$ centered on or near it is at most $Cs^{d-1}$, by finitely many bounded graph charts. Layer-cake integration therefore bounds its fundamental singular integral on such a cap by $Cs$ for $d\ge 3$, and by $Cs(1+|\log s|)$ for $d=2$. These bounds tend to zero uniformly in the pole. The remaining kernel is uniformly continuous, proving continuity across the sphere. Consequently \[  \frac{2d}{r^2}(M_ rGf(x)-Gf(x)) =\frac{2d}{r^2}\int _{|y-x|<r}[\Phi (r)-\Phi (x-y)]f(y)dy.  \] The bracket is nonpositive. Its absolute integral is $\pi r^2/2$ for $d=2$, since $2\pi \int _0^ r s\log (r/s)ds=\pi r^2/2$; for $d\ge 3$ it is $s_{d-1}r^2(1/2-1/d)$. Thus the expression for constant $f(x)$ is exactly $-c_ df(x)$, while the error is at most $c_ d\sup _{|y-x|<r}|f(y)-f(x)|$, tending to zero. For the converse fix a ball $B\Subset \Omega $, let $H$ be the continuous Poisson solution with boundary values $u$, and let $w=G_ B1$, continuous, zero at the boundary, with $\widetilde\Delta w=-c_ d$ by the first part. For $t>0$, both $u-H+tw$ and $H-u+tw$ have strictly negative generalized Laplacian. Hence at every point they satisfy the strict local supermean inequality for all sufficiently small radii. The elementary minimum principle for continuous locally supermean functions, proved by the open-and-closed minimum set argument, implies they are nonnegative on $B$ because their boundary values are zero. Let $t\downarrow 0$; then $u=H$. As $B$ was arbitrary, $u$ is harmonic. $\square$

title: 4.3.1 Global polar functions and exact compact pole sets
search_title: Global polar functions and exact compact pole sets
text: Theorem 4.3.2 . 253540032CE5 Every polar subset $A\subset \mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 2$, is contained in the infinite locus of an entire superharmonic function. If $a\notin A$, that function can be chosen finite at $a$. For $d\ge 3$ it can be chosen as a Newtonian potential of a finite positive measure. If $K\Subset \Omega $ is compact and polar in a Greenian open set, there is a finite compactly supported measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ with $G_\Omega \mu =\infty $ on $K$ and $G_\Omega \mu <\infty $ everywhere else in $\Omega $. Proof. We use the checked Foundations polar globalization : every bounded polar set has a finite compactly supported fundamental measure whose potential is infinite on that set. For the prescribed point put $A_ j=A\cap \{ 1/j\le |x-a|\le j\} $. Apply that result and restrict the resulting measure to $\{ |y-a|>1/(2j)\} $. The removed part has a bounded kernel at each point of $A_ j$, so the restricted fundamental potential $p_ j$ is still infinite on $A_ j$ and finite at $a$. In dimension at least three choose $b_ j>0$ so that $\sum b_ j(\mu _ j(\mathbb R^ d)+p_ j(a))<\infty $. Then $\mu =\sum b_ j\mu _ j$ is finite and its positive Newtonian potential is finite at $a$ and infinite on $A=\bigcup A_ j$, by Tonelli. In dimension two set $q_ j=p_ j-m_ j$, where $m_ j$ is the finite infimum of $p_ j$ on $\overline{B(a,j)}$. Such an infimum is finite by lsc and local integrability. Choose $b_ j>0$ with $\sum b_ jq_ j(a)<\infty $. For each fixed integer $k$, the tail $\sum _{j\ge k}b_ jq_ j$ is a monotone sum of nonnegative superharmonic functions on $B(a,k)$, finite at $a$; it is superharmonic there. Adding the finite initial sum gives an entire superharmonic function, finite at $a$ and infinite on $A$. Without a prescribed point, first choose $a$ outside the polar (hence null) set. For the last assertion first treat $K$ contained in an interior ball $B$. Its normalized ball capacity is zero by the checked polar zero capacity . Choose decreasing compact neighborhoods $K_ j\Subset B$ with intersection $K$; their capacitary potentials $v_ j$ lie in $[0,1]$, equal one near $K$, and decrease to zero off $K$. Indeed the limit is bounded harmonic off $K$, extends harmonically across $K$ by polar removability, and is dominated by the zero-minorant potential $v_1$, so is zero. On every compact subset of $B\setminus K$ this convergence is uniform by Dini. Pass to a subsequence such that both $\operatorname {cap}_ B(K_ j)<2^{-j}$ and $v_ j<2^{-j}$ on the first $j$ members of a compact exhaustion of $B\setminus K$ (and put every support in one fixed compact subset of $B$). This is possible by decreasing capacity continuity and the preceding uniform convergence. Write $v_ j=G_ B\mu _ j$, scaling the normalized Riesz measures by $1/c_ d$ for our kernel. Then $\sum \mu _ j(B)<\infty $. The potential of $\mu =\sum \mu _ j$ is $\sum v_ j$, infinite on $K$ and finite off $K$ in $B$. Its fundamental potential differs by a harmonic function on $B$; thus it has exactly the same finiteness set there. Off the common compact support it is finite automatically. The same distributional/harmonic-correction argument transfers it to $G_\Omega \mu $ without changing its poles. For general compact $K\Subset \Omega $, choose finitely many closed balls inside slightly larger interior balls whose interiors cover $K$; apply the construction to the polar compact intersections with these closed balls and add their measures. The sum is finite, compactly supported in $\Omega $, infinite on $K$ and finite at every point outside $K$. $\square$

title: 4.3.3 Boundary minimum principles with polar exceptions
search_title: Boundary minimum principles with polar exceptions
text: Theorem 4.3.4 . 09FD5942CD4F Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be Greenian and let $u$ be superharmonic and bounded below on $\Omega $. Suppose $\liminf _{\Omega \ni x\to z}u(x)\ge \alpha $ for every boundary point outside a polar set $Z$. Then $u\ge \alpha $ if $d=2$, or if $\Omega $ is bounded. For an unbounded domain in dimension at least three the same conclusion holds provided $\liminf _{x\in \Omega ,|x|\to \infty }u(x)\ge \alpha $. Proof. For a bounded $\Omega $, a global polar function infinite on $Z$ can be made nonnegative on $\overline\Omega $ by adding a constant. Call it $v$. Then $u+\varepsilon v$ has boundary lower limits at least $\alpha $ at all points, including $Z$, since $u$ is bounded below. The bounded-domain minimum principle gives $u+\varepsilon v\ge \alpha $. Average over a small interior ball; its average of $v$ is finite. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and then the radius decrease to zero to obtain $u\ge \alpha $ everywhere. The case with a condition at infinity follows by truncating with large balls, using $u\ge \alpha -\eta $ outside such a ball, and then letting $\eta \downarrow 0$. We need one planar fact: the boundary of a nonempty Greenian open set is not polar. If $\Omega $ is not dense and its boundary were polar, take an entire superharmonic polar function $v$ infinite there and replace it by infinity on one component of $\Omega $. The result is lsc, locally supermean (the boundary values are infinity), finite somewhere in the open complement, and hence superharmonic on the plane. It cannot be infinity on a nonempty open set, a contradiction. If $\Omega $ is dense, its complement equals its boundary. A fixed-pole Green function is bounded away from its pole, so polar removability extends it harmonically across the complement outside a small pole ball. Its harmonic correction then extends to the whole plane, and the resulting nonnegative fundamental-plus-harmonic function contradicts the whole-plane nonexistence proved earlier. Thus the planar fact holds. For unbounded planar $\Omega $, choose $z_0\in \partial \Omega \setminus Z$. For any $\eta >0$ choose $r>0$ with $u\ge \alpha -\eta $ on $\Omega \cap \overline{B(z_0,r)}$. Together with the inner ball inequality this proves the assertion on $\Omega $. $\square$

title: 4.3.5 Reduction and capacity on an admissible open set

text:
For a nonnegative superharmonic $u$ on a Greenian open set $\Omega $, let $R_ Eu$ be the infimum of nonnegative superharmonic majorants of $u$ on $E\subset \Omega $, and let $\widehat R_ Eu$ be its lsc regularization. Call $\Omega $ admissible if its compactly supported Green potentials tend to zero at every finite boundary point outside a polar set. In dimension at least three they also tend to zero at infinity, by $G\le \Phi $. The results in this section assert this hypothesis explicitly; its eventual verification for every Greenian set belongs to the boundary theory. Theorem 4.3.6 . C651523E22C3 For any $E$, $0\le \widehat R_ Eu\le R_ Eu\le u$, and the regularized reduction is superharmonic. It equals $u$ on the interior of $E$, is harmonic and equal to $R_ Eu$ outside $\overline E$, and differs from $R_ Eu$ only on a polar subset of $\partial E$. Reductions preserve order in $E,u$, positive scaling, and subadditivity in $u$. If $K\Subset \Omega $ is compact, then $\widehat R_ Ku$ is a Green potential, without assuming $u$ bounded on $K$. Proof. The family of majorants is nonempty (it contains $u$), closed under minimum and locally bounded below. The checked Foundations subharmonic envelope and polar limit discrepancy , applied after sign reversal, give superharmonic regularization and a polar discrepancy set. On $E$ the unregularized infimum equals $u$, and locality gives equality of the regularization on the interior. Outside $\overline E$, the family is saturated under ball lowering, so its infimum is harmonic by Lemma 3.5.2 ; it is nonnegative, excluding $-\infty $. Order and scaling follow from the defining families. Sums of majorants majorize the sum; the unregularized inequality passes to regularizations almost everywhere by the polar discrepancy assertion, and then everywhere by ball-average representatives. For bounded $u$ on $K$, in each component meeting $K$ choose a pole $a$. A multiple of $G(a,\cdot )$ majorizes $u$ on that component's compact intersection with $K$, since its positive lsc kernel has a positive minimum there. On all other components use $u$. This competitor shows $\widehat R_ Ku\le C G(a,\cdot )$ on the chosen component, so it has zero greatest harmonic minorant there. Components disjoint from $K$ have zero reduction. The global Riesz theorem makes the reduction a potential. For general $u=p+h$ with $p$ a potential and $h\ge 0$ harmonic, $h$ is bounded on $K$. The reduction of $p$ is dominated by $p$, hence has zero harmonic minorant; that of $h$ is a potential by the bounded case. Subadditivity bounds the reduction of $u$ by their sum, so it too has zero minorant and is a potential. $\square$ Theorem 4.3.7 . ABDF7610F7B2 Suppose $\Omega $ is admissible. For open sets strong subadditivity follows by decomposing each compact subset of their union into finitely many compact pieces in the respective opens, adding a compact subset of the intersection, and applying compact strong subadditivity. Taking almost optimal open majorants gives strong subadditivity of $C^*$. Repeated use gives the finite excess inequality \[  C^*( igcup _{i\le m}E_ i)-C^*( igcup _{i\le m}F_ i) \le \sum _{i\le m}(C^*(E_ i)-C^*(F_ i)),\quad F_ i\subset E_ i,  \] when the right side is finite; if a term is infinite use the equivalent inequality with sums on opposite sides. In a compact Hausdorff space, a set $D= igcap _ i igcup _ kK_{ik}$ with compact $K_{ik}$ is capacitable for any such outer capacity: replace each row by increasing unions and successively choose row bounds so that the capacity of the remaining part stays above any fixed number below $C^*(D)$. The graph is relatively closed in $D$ times the target, hence is again of the same compact-intersection form. Pull back capacity by the projection and apply the preceding argument. Continuous images commute with decreasing compact intersections because the closed fibers form nested nonempty compact sets. This proves capacitability of K-analytic sets in compact target neighborhoods; an increasing compact exhaustion and capacity continuity remove that restriction. Countable unions/intersections of these images are again of that form, by the product/equal-image construction for intersections and a disjoint union with one-point compactification for unions. If $A\Subset \Omega $ is polar, a finite compactly supported fundamental measure producing its poles can be localized to a compact neighborhood in $\Omega $; its Green potential $p$ is infinite on $A$. For $O_ t=\{ p>t\} $ and compact $L\subset O_ t$, reciprocity gives $C(L)\le t^{-1}\int p\, d\mu _ L\le \mu (\Omega )/t$. Thus $C^*(A)=0$, and exhaustions handle arbitrary polar $A$. Choose open $O_ j\supset A$ with $C(O_ j)<2^{-j}$, still separated from $a$. Increasing compact exhaustions of $O_ j$ have potentials increasing to $w_ j\le 1$, equal one on $O_ j$. The Green kernel at $a$ is bounded on the separated region, so $w_ j(a)\le M2^{-j}$. Hence $\sum _ jw_ j$ is superharmonic on that component, finite at $a$ and infinite on $A$. To perform the separation for a general local set, split it into its intersections with finitely many smaller closed neighborhoods, each avoiding a different interior ball; then use a countable local covering. Countable unions of polar sets are polar, proving the converse. $\square$

title: 3.5.15 A global extension finite outside a prescribed ball
search_title: A global extension finite outside a prescribed ball
text: Lemma 3.5.16 . 7C49056207BE If $u$ is superharmonic on $B(a,R)$ and $0<r<R$, there is an entire superharmonic function equal to $u$ on $B(a,r)$ and finite outside $\overline{B(a,r)}$. Proof. Shrink $R$ while keeping $r<R$, and subtract a lower bound so $u\ge 0$ on a neighborhood of the new closed ball. Reduce $u$ onto $K=\overline{B(a,r)}$ relative to $B(a,R)$. The regularized reduction $p$ equals $u$ inside $K$, is a potential with measure supported in $K$, and is harmonic outside $K$. Its measure is finite by compact support, so $p\to 0$ on the outer sphere. Harmonic reflection extends it to a slightly larger annulus; denote the extension again by $p$. Let $F(x)=\alpha (\Phi (x-a)-\Phi (Re_1))$. It is radial harmonic outside $a$ and zero on the outer sphere. The normal derivative of $\Phi $ is strictly negative there. Since $p$ is smooth on a compact collar of that sphere and zero on it, a sufficiently large $\alpha >0$ makes $F\ge p$ on the inner half of a thinner collar and $F\le p$ on its outer half: divide the radial differences by $|x-a|-R$ and use uniform continuity of the radial derivatives. Define $u^*=p$ inside the sphere and $u^*=F$ outside. In the collar it is the minimum of two harmonic functions, hence superharmonic, so locality proves it is entire superharmonic. It is finite outside $K$. Finally restore the subtracted constant. $\square$

section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: Let $D$ be a nonempty bounded open set. For extended boundary data $f$, let $\mathcal U_ f$ consist of componentwise superharmonic or identically infinite functions bounded below on $D$ with boundary lower limits at least $f$. Put $\overline H_ f=\inf \mathcal U_ f$ and $\underline H_ f=-\overline H_{-f}$. A function is resolutive when these coincide and are finite harmonic on every component. Theorem 4.4.2 . 09873BDAF3E0 Upper and lower solutions are componentwise harmonic or identically one of the two infinities, and $\underline H_ f\le \overline H_ f$. Each continuous boundary function is resolutive. There are probability measures $\omega _ x$ on $\partial D$, completed simultaneously for all $x\in D$, such that $f$ is resolutive exactly when it is measurable in all these completions and $\int |f|d\omega _ x<\infty $ for every $x$; then $H_ f(x)=\int f d\omega _ x$. For nonnegative measurable data the upper and lower solutions both equal the integral, possibly infinity. Within each component the measures are mutually absolutely continuous, their $L^ p$ spaces and weak/strong topologies agree, $1\le p<\infty $, and their norms are equivalent. The map $x\mapsto \omega _ x$ is weakly continuous. Proof. The finite superharmonic members of an upper class form a nonempty saturated family whenever that class has a member finite somewhere in the component: minimum and ball lowering preserve the boundary inequalities and the lower bound. The saturated-family lemma gives its harmonic or $-\infty $ infimum; if there is no such member the infimum is infinity. For $u$ in the lower and $v$ in the upper class, $v-u$ is superharmonic, bounded below, with nonnegative boundary lower limits, including where $f=\pm \infty $ (use the global bounds to avoid undefined subtraction). The bounded minimum principle gives $u\le v$. Order, constant translation, positive scaling, sign reversal and upper subadditivity follow from the defining classes, whenever sums are defined. For finite resolutive functions these prove linearity. A uniform change of boundary data by at most $\varepsilon $ changes each solution by at most $\varepsilon $, hence uniform limits of resolutive data are resolutive. The checked Foundations perron resolutivity supplies equality of the continuous upper and lower subsolution envelopes for continuous $f$. These classes are contained in our classes, so their common harmonic value lies between our lower and upper solutions; the reverse inequalities from class inclusion force equality here. Equivalently, approximate continuous data by smooth functions and split each smooth function as a difference of continuous subharmonic functions by adding a large multiple of $|x|^2$. We supply the required monotone limit argument. If $f_ j\uparrow f$ and $\overline H_{f_1}>-\infty $, then $\overline H_{f_ j}\uparrow \overline H_ f$. Work on one component. If the limit is infinity, order proves the claim. Otherwise the limit $h$ is harmonic by monotone harmonic convergence. text: A weak local barrier at $a\in \partial D$ is a strictly positive superharmonic function near $a$ in $D$ tending to zero at $a$. Theorem 4.4.5 . 2F74CBABB2A6 For bounded open $D$, a weak local barrier exists exactly when $a$ is regular for continuous Perron data. In that case the harmonic solution $H_ m$ for $m(z)=|z-a|$ is a global barrier, satisfies $H_ m(x)\ge |x-a|$, and has positive infimum away from every neighborhood of $a$. At such a point the upper boundary limsup of $\overline H_ f$ is at most the boundary limsup of $f$ for bounded-above $f$, and the analogous lower inequality holds for bounded-below data. Bounded data continuous at $a$ therefore attain their value there. Proof. The convex function $|x-a|$ is subharmonic by Jensen on harmonic coordinate functions, so lies in the lower class for $m$. Thus $H_ m\ge |x-a|>0$. Let $w$ be a weak local barrier, and choose a small sphere of radius $r$ centered at $a$ within its domain. Put $M=\max _{\partial D}|z-a|$. Choose compact $F\subset D\cap \partial B(a,r)$ whose complement in that open spherical set has normalized area less than $r/M$; if the open set is empty no $F$ is needed and comparison directly gives $H_ m\le r$ inside. Otherwise $k=\inf _ Fw>0$ (if $F$ is empty choose it nonempty by taking a smaller error). Let $b$ be the ball Poisson integral of boundary data $M$ on $(D\cap \partial B)\setminus F$ and zero elsewhere. It is nonnegative, continuous near the center, with $b(a)<r$. For every lower competitor $v$ for $m$, bounded comparison on $D\cap B$ gives \[  v\le r+(M/k)w+b.  \] On $F$ the $w$ term dominates the bound $v\le M$; on the remaining open sphere the Poisson limit is $M$; on the original boundary $v$ has upper limit at most $m\le r$. These verify every boundary piece. Taking the supremum and then approaching $a$ gives $\limsup H_ m\le 2r$. Let $r\to 0$. The global barrier and its positive-away-from-$a$ lower bound now follow from $H_ m\ge |x-a|$. For bounded-above data with local limsup $L$, the function $L+\varepsilon +cH_ m$ belongs to the upper class when $c$ is large enough to control the data outside a small neighborhood. Its limit at $a$ is $L+\varepsilon $. The case $L=-\infty $ is handled with any finite upper target instead. Negation gives the lower inequality. Conversely, regularity applied to continuous $m$ makes $H_ m$ a weak barrier. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.6 . 123C9AB7C052 Boundary regularity is inherited by open subsets at a common boundary point. An exterior tangent ball or an exterior truncated solid cone gives regularity. A planar exterior segment also gives regularity. Every open subset of $\mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 2$, has an increasing exhaustion by bounded regular open sets compactly contained in it. Proof. Restrict a weak barrier for inheritance. For an exterior ball tangent only at $a$ use minus its radial fundamental function after subtracting its value on the sphere; it is positive on the exterior and tends to zero at $a$. A smaller internally tangent ball removes other contact points. For a planar exterior segment choose the logarithm branch cut along its ray; on a sufficiently small slit ball $-\operatorname {Re}(1/\log (z-a))=-\log |z-a|/|\log (z-a)|^2$ is a positive harmonic barrier tending to zero. For a cone, shrink it and enlarge the domain locally to the truncated cone complement $D_\rho =B(a,\rho )\setminus C$. All its boundary points other than $a$ have exterior balls, hence are regular. On $D_{2\rho }$ let $u$ be the Perron solution for $|z-a|$. On the outer sphere it equals $2\rho $; on lateral cone boundary it equals $|z-a|$. It is bounded between zero and $2\rho $ and is strictly less than $2\rho $ inside. On the compact radius-$\rho $ spherical section (including its regular lateral endpoints) its maximum is $b<2\rho $. Choose $q$ with $\max \{ 1/2,b/(2\rho )\} <q<1$. On the boundary of $D_\rho $ except $a$, $u(x)\le q u(a+2(x-a))$: on the outer section use $b<q2\rho $ and on the lateral section use the factor two. Its finite nonnegative limsup $L$ at $a$ satisfies $L\le qL$, hence is zero. This is a weak local barrier and proves cone regularity. For exhaustion we give details of the finite-ball construction. Cover any compact $K$ in the open set by finitely many balls of a common radius $r$, with centers in $K$ and closures still inside the open set; choose the cover so a small interval of larger common radii still covers $K$ and has closures inside. Avoid finitely many critical radii: at a boundary point of the union, if the active outward normals had zero in their convex hull, that point would be the circumcenter in the affine span of some affinely independent subset of at most $d+1$ centers, by a minimal convex representation. Each such subset has at most one circumradius, giving a finite forbidden list. At an allowed radius the convex hull of the active normals avoids zero. Its nearest point to zero gives a direction with strictly positive scalar product with every active normal. A small solid cone in this direction avoids all active balls; the other finitely many balls have a positive gap locally. Thus every boundary point of the union has an exterior cone, and the union is bounded regular. Apply this to a compact exhaustion, including the closure of the previously constructed set at each step, to obtain the desired increasing exhaustion. $\square$

title: 4.4.7 Green boundary limits, Kellogg's theorem and planar Greenian sets

text: Theorem 4.4.8 . 52535FA416BF Every Greenian open set is admissible: one polar subset $Z$ of its finite boundary works for zero boundary limits of all compactly supported Green potentials. On a bounded connected open set a boundary point is regular exactly when a fixed interior-pole Green function tends to zero there. The irregular boundary points form a polar set. Bounded-density boundary limits hold with the same exception under the volume hypotheses of Theorem 3.5.12 . Proof. For a bounded open set, continuous boundary data $\Phi _ a$ have a finite harmonic Perron solution, and $G(a,\cdot )=\Phi _ a-H_{\Phi _ a}$. Indeed $\Phi _ a$ is an upper competitor, so the right side is nonnegative and admissible, hence at least $G$. Writing $G=\Phi _ a+h_ a$, the function $-h_ a$ is a lower competitor: it is bounded above by $\Phi _ a$ and bounded on a pole neighborhood by harmonicity, so bounded above throughout the bounded set. Its boundary upper limits are at most $\Phi _ a$. Thus $-h_ a\le H_{\Phi _ a}$, giving the opposite inequality. At regular points the formula gives zero boundary limit; conversely such a Green function is positive harmonic near a boundary point and supplies a weak local barrier. For arbitrary Greenian $\Omega $, exhaust by bounded regular open sets $D_ j\Subset \Omega $ containing a fixed pole $a$. Extend $G_{D_ j}(a,\cdot )$ by zero outside $D_ j$. On the complement of a small closed pole ball these are nonnegative continuous subharmonic functions: they are harmonic inside, zero outside, and at a boundary point their value zero is at most every sufficiently small sphere average. They increase to the zero extension $g$ of $G_\Omega (a,\cdot )$, bounded above there by the fixed-pole kernel bound. The checked subharmonic envelope/polar discrepancy theorem says $g=g^*$ outside a polar set. On $\partial \Omega $, $g=0$ and $g^*\ge \limsup _{\Omega \ni x\to z}G_\Omega (a,x)\ge 0$, so that limsup is zero off a polar set. Choose one pole in each component; there are at most countably many components. The union of their exceptions is polar. Harnack chains in the pole variable make the zero limit uniform on any compact subset of poles in a component. A compact subset meets only finitely many components, so the limit is uniform on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Integration against a finite compactly supported measure proves admissibility with one common exceptional set. The bounded-density statement is then precisely the compact-tail estimate already proved. On a bounded connected set, regularity and the fixed-pole condition are equivalent by the first part, so the irregular set is contained in that pole's polar exception. These arguments remove the temporary admissibility hypothesis in the capacity theorem without using that theorem to prove the boundary discrepancy. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.9 . 2C2E1569F3E2 For a nonempty planar open set $\Omega $, the following are equivalent: its complement is nonpolar; it supports a nonconstant strictly positive superharmonic function; and it has a Green function. Proof. A Greenian set has nonpolar boundary by the planar fact in the polar boundary minimum proof, hence nonpolar complement. Conversely, fix $a\in \Omega $. Countably many open disks tangent at $a$ cover the plane minus $a$. If the closed complement is nonpolar, one of its compact intersections $K$ with the corresponding closed disks is nonpolar. Take a larger tangent disk $B$ with $K\Subset B$ and $a\in \partial B$. The ball capacitary potential $p$ of $K$ is nonzero, lies in $[0,1]$, is harmonic off $K$ and zero at $\partial B$. Extend it by zero outside $B$. This is continuous subharmonic on the complement of $K$, by the same boundary mean argument as above. Then $2-p$ is strictly positive superharmonic on $\Omega $ and nonconstant near $a$: it equals two on the outer side of $\partial B$ and is strictly smaller on the adjacent inner component. This formulation also works if $B\setminus K$ has other components where $p=1$. It remains to obtain a Green kernel from a nonconstant positive superharmonic function $s$, first when $\Omega $ is connected. For any pole $a$, the strong minimum principle gives $b$ with $s(b)<s(a)$. Scale and truncate $s$ so it is at least one on a small closed ball $\overline{B(a,r)}$ and less than one at $b$. The regularized infimum $v$ of nonnegative superharmonic majorants of one on that ball lies in $[0,1]$, equals one inside, is harmonic outside, and is less than one at $b$; these use only saturated families and the checked polar discrepancy theorem, not a Green kernel on $\Omega $. It is continuous on the inner sphere: on a slightly larger concentric annulus its boundary values are continuous on the outer sphere, one on the inner sphere outside a polar exception; Perron comparison ignoring that exception and annulus regularity give inner limit one. Thus $w=1-v$ is continuous subharmonic, zero on the ball, and strictly positive on its complement. That complement is connected: any path crossing the ball may be detoured through a slightly larger sphere inside $\Omega $. Choose $t>r$ with $\overline{B(a,t)}\subset \Omega $, and $2\alpha =\min _{|x-a|=t}w(x)>0$. Define a subharmonic $q$ by $\log (|x-a|/r)$ on the inner ball, by $\max \{ \log (|x-a|/r),(w(x)/\alpha )\log (t/r)\} $ on the annulus, and by the second term outside the radius-$t$ ball. At the inner sphere the extension dominates the harmonic logarithm with the same value; its sphere submeans follow. Near the outer sphere the second term dominates strictly, so locality proves subharmonicity. It is bounded above and $q+\Phi _ a=-\log r$ near $a$. If $C$ bounds $q$, the nonnegative superharmonic function $C-q$ is $\Phi _ a$ plus a superharmonic correction extending across $a$. Thus the admissible class $\mathcal B_ a$ is nonempty, and the minimal-kernel construction gives a Green function. A disconnected planar open set is already Greenian by the earlier component construction, so the connected argument suffices. $\square$

Writing $G=\Phi _ a+h_ a$, the function $-h_ a$ is a lower competitor: it is bounded above by $\Phi _ a$ and bounded on a pole neighborhood by harmonicity, so bounded above throughout the bounded set. Its boundary upper limits are at most $\Phi _ a$. Thus $-h_ a\le H_{\Phi _ a}$, giving the opposite inequality. At regular points the formula gives zero boundary limit; conversely such a Green function is positive harmonic near a boundary point and supplies a weak local barrier. For arbitrary Greenian $\Omega $, exhaust by bounded regular open sets $D_ j\Subset \Omega $ containing a fixed pole $a$. Extend $G_{D_ j}(a,\cdot )$ by zero outside $D_ j$. On the complement of a small closed pole ball these are nonnegative continuous subharmonic functions: they are harmonic inside, zero outside, and at a boundary point their value zero is at most every sufficiently small sphere average. They increase to the zero extension $g$ of $G_\Omega (a,\cdot )$, bounded above there by the fixed-pole kernel bound. The checked subharmonic envelope/polar discrepancy theorem says $g=g^*$ outside a polar set. On $\partial \Omega $, $g=0$ and $g^*\ge \limsup _{\Omega \ni x\to z}G_\Omega (a,x)\ge 0$, so that limsup is zero off a polar set. Choose one pole in each component; there are at most countably many components. The union of their exceptions is polar. Harnack chains in the pole variable make the zero limit uniform on any compact subset of poles in a component. A compact subset meets only finitely many components, so the limit is uniform on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Integration against a finite compactly supported measure proves admissibility with one common exceptional set. The bounded-density statement is then precisely the compact-tail estimate already proved. On a bounded connected set, regularity and the fixed-pole condition are equivalent by the first part, so the irregular set is contained in that pole's polar exception. These arguments remove the temporary admissibility hypothesis in the capacity theorem without using that theorem to prove the boundary discrepancy. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.4.9
section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: Theorem 4.4.9 . 2C2E1569F3E2 For a nonempty planar open set $\Omega $, the following are equivalent: its complement is nonpolar; it supports a nonconstant strictly positive superharmonic function; and it has a Green function. Proof. A Greenian set has nonpolar boundary by the planar fact in the polar boundary minimum proof, hence nonpolar complement. Conversely, fix $a\in \Omega $. Countably many open disks tangent at $a$ cover the plane minus $a$. If the closed complement is nonpolar, one of its compact intersections $K$ with the corresponding closed disks is nonpolar. Take a larger tangent disk $B$ with $K\Subset B$ and $a\in \partial B$. The ball capacitary potential $p$ of $K$ is nonzero, lies in $[0,1]$, is harmonic off $K$ and zero at $\partial B$. Extend it by zero outside $B$. This is continuous subharmonic on the complement of $K$, by the same boundary mean argument as above. Then $2-p$ is strictly positive superharmonic on $\Omega $ and nonconstant near $a$: it equals two on the outer side of $\partial B$ and is strictly smaller on the adjacent inner component. This formulation also works if $B\setminus K$ has other components where $p=1$. It remains to obtain a Green kernel from a nonconstant positive superharmonic function $s$, first when $\Omega $ is connected. For any pole $a$, the strong minimum principle gives $b$ with $s(b)<s(a)$. Scale and truncate $s$ so it is at least one on a small closed ball $\overline{B(a,r)}$ and less than one at $b$. The regularized infimum $v$ of nonnegative superharmonic majorants of one on that ball lies in $[0,1]$, equals one inside, is harmonic outside, and is less than one at $b$; these use only saturated families and the checked polar discrepancy theorem, not a Green kernel on $\Omega $. It is continuous on the inner sphere: on a slightly larger concentric annulus its boundary values are continuous on the outer sphere, one on the inner sphere outside a polar exception; Perron comparison ignoring that exception and annulus regularity give inner limit one. Thus $w=1-v$ is continuous subharmonic, zero on the ball, and strictly positive on its complement. That complement is connected: any path crossing the ball may be detoured through a slightly larger sphere inside $\Omega $. Choose $t>r$ with $\overline{B(a,t)}\subset \Omega $, and $2\alpha =\min _{|x-a|=t}w(x)>0$. Define a subharmonic $q$ by $\log (|x-a|/r)$ on the inner ball, by $\max \{ \log (|x-a|/r),(w(x)/\alpha )\log (t/r)\} $ on the annulus, and by the second term outside the radius-$t$ ball. At the inner sphere the extension dominates the harmonic logarithm with the same value; its sphere submeans follow. Near the outer sphere the second term dominates strictly, so locality proves subharmonicity. It is bounded above and $q+\Phi _ a=-\log r$ near $a$. If $C$ bounds $q$, the nonnegative superharmonic function $C-q$ is $\Phi _ a$ plus a superharmonic correction extending across $a$. Thus the admissible class $\mathcal B_ a$ is nonempty, and the minimal-kernel construction gives a Green function. A disconnected planar open set is already Greenian by the earlier component construction, so the connected argument suffices. $\square$

text: Theorem 4.3.9 . 39A7F7684147 On a Greenian $\Omega $, a polar set $Z$ has a strictly positive superharmonic pole function finite at any prescribed $a\notin Z$. Consequently $R_ Eu=\widehat R_ Eu$ outside $E$, removing a polar subset from $E$ does not change the regularized reduction, and for increasing relatively closed $F_ j$ with union $F$, $\widehat R_{F_ j}u\uparrow \widehat R_ Fu$. For $W\Subset \Omega $ open, \[  \widehat R_{\Omega \setminus W}u=H^ W_{u|_{\partial W}}\quad \hbox{on }W.  \] For such $W$ the reduction is additive in $u$. Along an increasing exhaustion $W_ j$, these interior harmonic functions decrease to the greatest harmonic minorant of $u$, and their limit is zero exactly when $u$ is a potential. Proof. Work componentwise, choosing the prescribed point in its component and an arbitrary point in every other component outside the polar set. Cover $Z$ in the component by countably many small closed interior balls avoiding that point. The checked bounded-polar globalization with compact cutoffs gives finite measures supported in these balls, whose fundamental potentials are infinite on the covered polar pieces. Their Green potentials have the same poles by the local harmonic-correction identity, and are finite at the chosen point. Weight them so the sum of their masses and their potentials at that point is finite. The sum is a Green potential finite there and infinite on $Z$. Add the constant one for strict positivity, and glue the componentwise functions; superharmonicity is local. The discrepancy between $R_ Eu$ and its regularization is polar. For $a\notin E$ choose the pole function $p$ for its discrepancy on $E$, finite at $a$. Then $\widehat R_ Eu+\varepsilon p$ is a majorant of $u$ on $E$; evaluating at $a$ and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves equality there. If a polar subset is removed from $E$, adding its $\varepsilon $-pole function to any majorant on the remainder proves the opposite inequality almost everywhere; ball averages make it hold for the regularizations everywhere. For increasing $F_ j$, their increasing regularized reductions have a superharmonic limit $v\le \widehat R_ Fu$. On each $F_ j$ they equal $u$ outside a polar set; the union of these exceptions is polar. Thus $v$ majorizes $u$ on $F$ outside a polar set, and the polar-removal argument gives $v\ge \widehat R_ Fu$. Put $h=H^ W_ u$, which is finite harmonic because $0\le h\le u$ on $W$, and set $v=h$ on $W$, $v=u$ elsewhere. We justify the pasting even if $u$ has infinite boundary values. For any ball $B\Subset \Omega $, positivity of Perron solutions gives $H^ B_ v\le H^ B_ u\le u$ on $B\setminus W$. On $B\cap W$, compare the boundary values of $H^ B_ v$ and $v$, using the restriction lemma first from $B$ and then from $W$; both domains involved are bounded. This gives $H^ B_ v\le v$ there as well. If $\widehat v$ is the lsc regularization, $H^ B_{\widehat v}\le H^ B_ v\le v$; its harmonic continuity then gives $H^ B_{\widehat v}\le \widehat v$. The ball comparison characterization proves $\widehat v$ superharmonic. On $\partial W$, approximate the lsc boundary function $u$ increasingly by continuous functions. At regular points of $W$, their Perron solutions have the prescribed limits, so $\liminf _ W h\ge u$ there. The irregular set is polar. Hence $\widehat v\ge u$ on $\Omega \setminus W$ outside a polar set, proving $\widehat v\ge \widehat R_{\Omega \setminus W}u$. Conversely any defining majorant is in the upper Perron class for $u$ on $W$, so dominates $v$; regularization gives the reverse inequality. On $W$, $\widehat v=v=h$, proving the formula. Linearity of integrable boundary solutions proves additivity inside $W$; outside $W$, both reductions equal the original function off a polar set. Ball averages remove that exception from the additive identity. In an exhaustion the reductions decrease by set order. Their interior harmonic limit is nonnegative and at most $u$. Every global harmonic minorant of $u$ is a lower Perron competitor on each $W_ j$, since it is continuous near $\partial W_ j$; it is therefore at most this limit. This identifies the greatest harmonic minorant. The zero characterization is the global Riesz theorem. $\square$ Theorem 4.3.10 . C4F5D8B270EB Let $p=G_\Omega \mu $ be finite everywhere on a Greenian open set. If $w\ge 0$ is superharmonic and $w\ge p$ on $\operatorname {supp}\mu $ except for a polar set, then $w\ge p$ throughout $\Omega $. Proof. First let $\mu $ have compact support $K$ and $p$ be continuous. It is bounded on a compact neighborhood of $K$ and bounded outside it by the fixed-pole/Harnack bound, hence globally bounded. On $\Omega \setminus K$, $w-p$ is superharmonic and bounded below. At $K$ its lower boundary limits are nonnegative outside the stated polar exception by continuity of $p$ and lsc of $w$. At the ambient boundary the same holds because compact potentials tend to zero outside a polar set. If $d\ge 3$, at infinity $p\to 0$. The polar boundary minimum theorem gives $w\ge p$ off $K$; the inequality holds almost everywhere everywhere, and canonical ball averages give it at every point. For general compactly supported $\mu $, the finite potential permits the Lusin construction of pairwise disjoint compact restrictions $\mu _ j$ with continuous potentials and $\mu =\sum \mu _ j$. title: 4.4.10 Exterior Poisson kernels and Helms's point at infinity
search_title: Exterior Poisson kernels and Helms's point at infinity
section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: Let $\widehat{\mathbb R^ d}=\mathbb R^ d\cup \{ \infty \} $ have the one-point compactification topology. We use Helms's convention: superharmonicity at an interior infinity means lower semicontinuity there and $u(\infty )\ge M_{\partial B}u$ for every ball whose closed exterior lies in the domain. Harmonicity means the corresponding equality and both semicontinuities, in addition to ordinary harmonicity at finite points. This extra mean condition is part of the definition, and is not implied by ordinary bounded exterior harmonicity in dimension at least three. Theorem 4.4.11 . E16C09608A00 Let $B=B(a,R)$ and let $f\in L^1(\partial B,d\sigma )$. Put $m=(s_{d-1}R^{d-1})^{-1}\int f d\sigma $ and $r=|x-a|$. The exterior solution in this compactified convention is \[  H^{\rm ext}_ Bf(x)=\frac1{s_{d-1}R}\int _{\partial B} \left[\frac{r^2-R^2}{|x-z|^ d}+\frac1{R^{d-2}}-\frac1{r^{d-2}}\right] f(z)d\sigma (z),\qquad r>R,  \] with $H^{\rm ext}_ Bf(\infty )=m$. It is harmonic including at infinity, positive when $f\ge 0$, sends one to one, and tends to $f$ at every continuity point of $f$ on the sphere. More generally an ordinary exterior harmonic $h$, continuous to the sphere with finite limit $\alpha $ at infinity, satisfies \[  h(x)=K\bigl (H_ B(h|_{\partial B})\bigr )(x) +\alpha \bigl [1-(R/r)^{d-2}\bigr ].  \] For $d=2$ necessarily $\alpha =m$; for $d\ge 3$, it is harmonic in Helms's sense at infinity exactly when $\alpha =m$. Proof. Invert about the sphere and apply Kelvin covariance. For $d\ge 3$, the Kelvin transform of bounded $h$ is bounded in absolute value by a multiple of the fundamental pole near $a$. Adding a sufficiently large multiple of that pole makes it nonnegative, so the proved Bôcher lemma applies. Its singular coefficient is $\alpha R^{d-2}$, by taking the limit back at infinity. Subtracting this singularity leaves a harmonic function on $B$; its continuous boundary data identify it by the ball Poisson formula, giving the displayed representation. In dimension two the Kelvin transform is bounded near the center and extends harmonically there, with center value $\alpha =m$. For integrable $f$, define the right side with $\alpha =m$. The inverted ball Poisson integral is harmonic away from $a$ and its derivatives are controlled on compact subsets by the integrable boundary density. The inversion distance identity gives precisely the displayed kernel. Its first term is positive; for $d\ge 3$ so is the correction $R^{2-d}-r^{2-d}$, and for $d=2$ that correction is zero. Evaluating at $f=1$ shows the total kernel mass is one. Its limit at infinity is $m$, and the ball Poisson continuity-point estimate, together with the vanishing correction at $r=R$, proves the boundary assertion. The Kelvin identity for concentric spherical means gives, for a general finite-limit $h$, \[  M_{\partial B(a,t)}h=\alpha +(m-\alpha )(R/t)^{d-2}\quad (d\ge 3),  \] and the constant $m$ if $d=2$. For the chosen $\alpha =m$ these means are constant, so their radial flux is zero. The divergence theorem on the region between any large sphere containing $\overline B$ and a larger concentric sphere transfers this zero flux to the arbitrary sphere. The annular mean derivative formula then makes its subsequent spherical means constant; their limit is the limit at infinity, namely $m$. Thus every exterior-ball mean equals $h(\infty )$, as required. Conversely Helms's mean condition for the concentric spheres forces $\alpha =m$. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.12 . 8FA95EB71F47 On a connected compactified open set a superharmonic function attaining its infimum is constant. On a proper open subset, nonnegative boundary lower limits imply nonnegativity. Entire superharmonic functions on $\widehat{\mathbb R^ d}$ are constant. Positive scaling, sums and minima preserve superharmonicity. Harmonic lowering is valid on interior balls and on exterior balls, directed harmonic convergence holds, and a nonempty saturated family under both kinds of lowering has harmonic or $-\infty $ infimum on each component. The point infinity is polar for $d=2$ and is not polar for $d\ge 3$. Proof. At finite points the minimum-set argument is the checked Euclidean one. If the minimum is attained at infinity, each large sphere mean is at least the minimum and at most the value there. Lower semicontinuity and positivity of the surface measure of open patches force equality at every point of each such sphere. Thus the minimum set contains an exterior neighborhood and is open and closed. For a proper open set each component has a nonempty boundary in the connected compact ambient space. Extend by boundary liminf; compactness forces a negative minimum to be attained inside if any negative value exists. The strong minimum principle would make the component a negative constant, contradicting its nonnegative boundary limits. For the entire compact space a minimum is attained and the function is constant; one cannot infer a nonnegative constant from an empty boundary. For algebraic operations use the ordinary local result and the linear sphere inequalities at infinity; nontriviality follows from finite almost everywhere values on each Euclidean component. For exterior lowering, increasing continuous minorants of the lsc sphere data and the positive exterior Poisson kernel give a harmonic minorant bounded above by $u$ via compactified comparison. Finite interior values exclude an infinite limit. The same boundary-liminf/pasting proof as for interior lowering makes the replacement superharmonic at finite points. Near infinity it is the exterior harmonic solution with constant large-sphere means equal to its value there. For every other allowed sphere center, the finite-point superharmonic mean is concave as a function of $r^{2-d}$ (or $-\log r$ in the plane), and is constant at that value for all sufficiently large radii, by the zero-flux argument above. Concavity bounds its earlier means by the same value, giving the required inequality at infinity. Directed harmonic limits reduce to the Euclidean result away from infinity and the positive exterior kernel on a fixed sphere near infinity; directed monotone integration identifies the value and harmonicity there. The saturated-family proof then applies in both kinds of neighborhoods, exactly as for finite balls, with nonemptiness explicitly required. For $d=2$, $\log |x-a|$ on an exterior neighborhood, with value infinity at infinity, is a superharmonic pole function there. For $d\ge 3$, concentric sphere means of a superharmonic function on an exterior are finite and concave functions of $t=r^{2-d}$. A supporting affine upper bound at an interior $t$ bounds them above as $t\downarrow 0$. If the value at infinity were infinite, lsc would instead force all sufficiently distant sphere means to tend to infinity. This contradiction proves nonpolarity. $\square$ Lemma 4.4.13 . 58BE7FB3C948 Kelvin transformation preserves superharmonicity on domains avoiding its center. If $u$ is superharmonic on $B(a,R)$, harmonic near $a$, and $u(a)=0$, its Kelvin transform, extended by zero at infinity, is superharmonic on the compactified exterior. Proof. On compact subdomains avoiding the center, transform harmonic comparison functions, use positivity of the Kelvin multiplier and its involutivity, and transform the comparison back. This proves the superharmonic comparison property for the transformed lsc function. In the normalized case the transform is harmonic near infinity with zero large-sphere means: the original function is harmonic near $a$ with zero center value, so the concentric mean identity and the flux transfer in the exterior theorem apply. In particular its value at infinity is zero and it is continuous there. For any other exterior ball in the domain, its sphere means are concave in $r^{2-d}$ (or $-\log r$ in the plane), and are zero for all sufficiently large radii. Concavity makes them nonpositive at the smaller allowed radii. This is exactly the supermean condition at infinity. $\square$

text: Lemma 4.4.13 . 58BE7FB3C948 Kelvin transformation preserves superharmonicity on domains avoiding its center. If $u$ is superharmonic on $B(a,R)$, harmonic near $a$, and $u(a)=0$, its Kelvin transform, extended by zero at infinity, is superharmonic on the compactified exterior. Proof. On compact subdomains avoiding the center, transform harmonic comparison functions, use positivity of the Kelvin multiplier and its involutivity, and transform the comparison back. This proves the superharmonic comparison property for the transformed lsc function. In the normalized case the transform is harmonic near infinity with zero large-sphere means: the original function is harmonic near $a$ with zero center value, so the concentric mean identity and the flux transfer in the exterior theorem apply. In particular its value at infinity is zero and it is continuous there. For any other exterior ball in the domain, its sphere means are concave in $r^{2-d}$ (or $-\log r$ in the plane), and are zero for all sufficiently large radii. text: All domains in this section are proper open subsets of $\widehat{\mathbb R^ d}$ with nonpolar complement; harmonicity at an interior infinity has the exterior mean condition of the preceding section. Boundary limits and continuous data refer to this compactification. The upper class consists of bounded-below hyperharmonic functions whose boundary lower limits majorize the datum; lower classes are defined by sign reversal. We first construct the needed global pole functions, rather than presupposing their existence in a barrier argument. Lemma 4.4.15 . E0D6C3CD3750 If $\widehat{\mathbb R^ d}\setminus \overline\Omega $ is nonempty, continuous boundary data are resolutive. Every polar boundary set has a positive superharmonic blow-up function on $\Omega $. It can be chosen finite at any prescribed interior point. A finite boundary point is regular exactly when it admits a local weak barrier; the irregular set is polar. Infinity is always regular in $d\ge 3$ when it is a boundary point. Proof. Choose a closed ball disjoint from $\overline\Omega $ and invert about its sphere, sending $\Omega $ into a bounded ball. Continuous data, after subtracting a constant and a uniform approximation if necessary, can be assumed zero near infinity. The transformed data, divided by the positive Kelvin multiplier, then extend continuously with value zero near the inversion center. If infinity is interior, the center is separated from the transformed boundary and the same prescription is possible. Approximate uniformly by smooth functions $\varphi $ zero near that center. Such smooth approximation follows by extending a continuous function from the compact boundary, multiplying by a cutoff, and convolving; the uniform error on the boundary is controlled by uniform continuity. These approximants are differences of superharmonic functions harmonic and zero near the center. To verify this, take $q(x)=-A(|x-a|-r_0)_+^4$, with the support of $\Delta \varphi $ separated from $\overline{B(a,r_0)}$. Its Laplacian is nonpositive and strictly negative on that support; sufficiently large $A$ makes both $q$ and $\varphi +q$ superharmonic. For a polar boundary set, transform its finite points into the bounded ball and split it into countably many closed shells avoiding the center. title: Theorem 4.4.21
section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: Theorem 4.4.21 . D7E4078B4FE9 Let $u\ge 0$ be superharmonic on a Greenian domain, with $u(a)<\infty $, and suppose $u(a)>\sup _{\Omega \setminus V}u$ for every neighborhood $V$ of $a$. Then $E$ is thin at $a$ if and only if $\widehat R_ Eu(a)<u(a)$. The finiteness hypothesis is essential. The set of points of an arbitrary $E$ where $E$ is thin is polar. In particular $E$ is polar if and only if it is thin at each of its points. Proof. Remove $a$ from $E$, which does not alter regularized reduction. Outside $E$ raw and regularized reductions agree. A deficit at $a$ therefore gives a defining superharmonic majorant $v$ with $v(a)<u(a)$. Lower semicontinuity of $u$ and $v\ge u$ on $E$ give the strict-gap criterion. Conversely a thinness barrier can be chosen bounded near $a$ by truncation above its value there; local exact extension followed by compact reduction gives a bounded nonnegative superharmonic $v$ on $\Omega $, with $v(a)<\alpha <\liminf _ Ev$. On a neighborhood $V$ of $a$ we have $v>\alpha $ along $E$. The peaking assumption gives $\gamma =u(a)-\sup _{\Omega \setminus V}u>0$. For sufficiently small $\lambda >0$, the function $u(a)+\lambda (v-\alpha )$ is nonnegative, majorizes $u$ on all of $E$, and is strictly below $u(a)$ at $a$. This proves the deficit. Theorem 4.4.25 . 04CCB65ED650 Every endpoint of a nondegenerate planar segment is a nonthin point of that segment. If the complement of a planar open set is thin at $a$, arbitrarily small circles centered at $a$ lie in the open set. Consequently a boundary point belonging to a nondegenerate continuum in the complement is regular. In particular every bounded simply connected planar domain is regular. Proof. An interior point of a segment is regular for a disk slit along the segment by the explicit exterior-segment barrier. The boundary nonthinness theorem therefore makes the segment nonthin at that point. If it were thin at an endpoint, reflect an amplified barrier across the endpoint and add the two barriers. The doubled segment would then be thin at its interior point, a contradiction. The radial projection $y\mapsto a+|y-a|e_1$ is a contraction preserving distances from $a$. If every sufficiently small circle met a thin complement, its projection would contain a nondegenerate segment ending at $a$, contradicting contraction invariance of thinness. Hence the required circles exist. An exterior continuum containing $a$ and another point $b$ meets every circle of radius less than $|a-b|$, by connectedness of its distance image. This contradicts the circle conclusion if the complement were thin. Nonthinness gives regularity. All signed mutual integrals below are defined by finite positive-part energies, rather than by subtracting two infinities. Measures need not have finite total mass. The normalization is $-\Delta G\mu =c_ d\mu $. Theorem 4.5.2 . CC3D1AD9179B The mutual energy satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz. It extends to a positive definite inner product on $\mathcal E$. Measures of finite energy give every polar set outer measure zero. For Borel $Z$, vanishing of $\mu (Z)$ for every $\mu \in \mathcal E^+$ is equivalent to polarity of $Z$. If $G\lambda \le G\mu $ with $\mu \in \mathcal E^+$, then $\lambda \in \mathcal E^+$ and $\| \lambda \| \le \| \mu \| $. For compact $K$ and continuous real $f$ on $K$, the functional $I(\eta )-2\int f\, d\eta $ attains its minimum among positive measures on $K$. A minimizer has finite energy, satisfies $G\eta \le f$ on its support and $G\eta \ge f$ quasi-everywhere on $K$. Proof. The last assertion follows without Cauchy–Schwarz: $I(\lambda )\le I(\mu ,\lambda )=\int G\lambda \, d\mu \le I(\mu )$. On compact subsets $K$ of $P\cap \{ G\mu \le j\} $ the restricted measure has bounded potential on its support, so the everywhere-finite domination theorem, applied to $\varepsilon w$, gives $G(\mu |_ K)=0$.
