title: 4.5.7 The Martin boundary
text:
Throughout this section $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ is connected and Greenian, and $a\in \Omega $ is fixed. We use compact Hausdorff compactifications, finite Radon measures on compact spaces, Tychonoff's theorem, the compact-metric Riesz representation theorem, Tietze extension, and the lattice Stone–Weierstrass theorem as explicit general topology and functional analysis prerequisites. None of these is an assumed Martin representation theorem. Lemma 4.5.8 . D878F27BAB16 For any family $\mathcal Q$ of extended continuous functions on $\Omega $, there is a unique compactification in which these functions extend and separate boundary points. It is the closure of the evaluation map into $[-\infty ,\infty ]^{\mathcal Q\cup C_ c(\Omega )}$. Proof. Compact-support functions separate interior points and recover their original neighborhoods by positive bumps, so the evaluation map is an embedding. Each bump's nonzero set in the closure lies in the image of its compact support; thus the interior image is open and its complement is the boundary. All compact-support coordinates vanish on the boundary, so the remaining coordinates separate its points. For any other such compactification the coordinate extensions define a continuous injection into the same product, with exactly this closure as image by density. A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism, proving uniqueness fixing $\Omega $. $\square$ Choose $\alpha $ so large that $\{ G(\cdot ,a)\ge \alpha \} \Subset \Omega $; the Green bound away from its pole permits this choice. Take a smooth increasing concave function $\phi $ equal to $t$ for $t\le \alpha $ and constant for $t\ge \alpha +1$. Set $b=\phi (G(\cdot ,a))$. It is positive, smooth, superharmonic, constant near $a$, and a potential: it is bounded by the potential $G(\cdot ,a)$. Its Riesz measure has compact support. Put $k_ y(x)=G(y,x)/b(y)$. The compactification associated with the functions $y\mapsto k_ y(x)$ is denoted $M$, with boundary $\Delta $. Theorem 4.5.9 . 9D6B5CF5E0CF The extended kernel $K(y,x)$ on $M	imes \Omega $ is positive and jointly continuous, with extended values only on the interior diagonal. For $y\in \Delta $, $K_ y$ is harmonic and $K_ y(a)=1$. Distinct points of $M$ give nonproportional kernels. The space $M$ is compact metrizable: for a countable dense set $\{ x_ j\} $ in $\Omega $ the metric is \[  ho (y,z)=\sum _{j\ge 1}2^{-j} \left| rac{K(y,x_ j)}{1+K(y,x_ j)}-  rac{K(z,x_ j)}{1+K(z,x_ j)}ight|.  \] Proof. For $C\Subset W\Subset \Omega $ containing $a$, Harnack comparison in the pole variable, or sweeping onto a compact neighborhood of $C$, bounds $G(y,x)/G(y,a)$ uniformly for $x\in C$, $y
otin W$. For the sweeping proof, both pole functions equal their compact reductions off that neighborhood: they are bounded harmonic there and have the same boundary values outside a polar exception, so compactified uniqueness applies. Their boundary values on its compact interior boundary have uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds, giving the ratio bound. A general compact $C$ is enlarged to include $a$. Since $b=G(\cdot ,a)$ off a compact set, these bounds also hold for $k$. Normal convergence and the derivative estimates for bounded harmonic families show that every boundary kernel is harmonic, and that convergence in the compactification is locally uniform in $x$. This proves joint continuity at boundary points. Interior joint continuity is that of $G$, and $K_ y(a)=1$ on the boundary follows from the same identity off the cutoff compact. Positivity follows from the harmonic minimum principle. Interior kernels are distinguished by their poles. A boundary kernel has no interior pole. For two boundary points, proportionality and the value one at $a$ imply equality of every defining coordinate, hence equality of the points. More explicitly, $b=G\lambda _0$ with compactly supported $\lambda _0$; therefore $\int K(y,x)d\lambda _0(x)=1$, first for interior $y$, then on the boundary by joint continuity near that compact support. This supplies the normalization and the ratio representation of defining coordinates used in Helms 12.4 as well. The countable coordinates in the displayed formula separate points: density and extended continuity in $x$ recover every kernel. They define a continuous injection of compact $M$ into a countable cube, hence a homeomorphism onto its image. The uniformly convergent sum metric on that cube induces the given topology. No sequential compactness is assumed before this argument. $\square$ For a measure $\mu $ on $M$ write $K\mu (x)=\int K(y,x)d\mu (y)$ when not identically infinite. It is superharmonic. Its interior part is the Green potential of $b^{-1}\mu |_\Omega $, and its boundary part is harmonic by the compact kernel bounds. In particular equality of two $K$-potentials determines their interior measures, by the distributional Riesz identity. For $q\in C_ c^2(\Omega )$ put $\lambda =(-\Delta (qb)/c_ d)dx$. Then \[  q(y)=\int K(y,x)d\lambda (x),\qquad y\in \Omega .  \] This is the distributional Green identity for the compact test $qb$. The measure $\lambda $ has bounded density and compact support, so every defined $K$-potential is $|\lambda |$-integrable by local integrability. This also proves the test-function assertion 12.6 and the interior uniqueness assertion 12.7 without an undefined signed potential. Lemma 4.5.10 . B0A113187C30 For relatively closed $F\subset \Omega $ and $u\ge 0$ superharmonic, $\widehat R_ Fu=K\mu $ for a measure supported on its closure in $M$. Every positive harmonic function has such a representation supported on $\Delta $. For compact $C\Subset \Omega $, write $\mu _ C$ for the unique interior measure representing $\widehat R_ C(K\mu )$. For boundary $y$ write $\gamma _{y,C}=(\delta _ y)_ C$. The operator \[  T_ Cf(y)=\int f\, d\gamma _{y,C},\qquad y\in \Delta ,  \] maps $C(M)$ positively and continuously into $C(\Delta )$. If $C$ contains the cutoff compact in its interior, $T_ C1=1$ and $\| T_ C\| =1$. Proof. Exhaust $F$ by compact $F_ j$. The compact reductions are potentials $G
u _ j=K(b
u _ j)$, with supports in $F_ j$. At a point $x$ where $u(x)$ is finite the strictly positive minimum of $K(\cdot ,x)$ on $M$ bounds their masses. Choose a weak limit $\mu $. For a sphere compactly inside $\Omega $, its average of $K(y,\cdot )$ is a finite continuous function of $y\in M$: away from the sphere use joint bounded continuity; on it use the proved continuity of spherical Green averages after cancellation of the integrable fundamental singularity. Thus weak convergence and monotone convergence of reductions identify all spherical averages of $K\mu $ and $\widehat R_ Fu$. Fatou first bounds $K\mu \le u$, so it is defined. Let the sphere radius tend to zero to get equality everywhere. For harmonic $u=h$, take $F=\Omega $ and compact neighborhoods $F_ j$ exhausting it. The reduction equals $h$ on their interiors and its measure is supported on their boundaries; these escape every interior compact, so the limit measure lies on $\Delta $. The representing compact measure is unique by the interior Riesz identity. title: Lemma 4.5.8
text: Lemma 4.5.8 . D878F27BAB16 For any family $\mathcal Q$ of extended continuous functions on $\Omega $, there is a unique compactification in which these functions extend and separate boundary points. It is the closure of the evaluation map into $[-\infty ,\infty ]^{\mathcal Q\cup C_ c(\Omega )}$. Proof. Compact-support functions separate interior points and recover their original neighborhoods by positive bumps, so the evaluation map is an embedding. Each bump's nonzero set in the closure lies in the image of its compact support; thus the interior image is open and its complement is the boundary. All compact-support coordinates vanish on the boundary, so the remaining coordinates separate its points. For any other such compactification the coordinate extensions define a continuous injection into the same product, with exactly this closure as image by density. A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism, proving uniqueness fixing $\Omega $. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.5.9

title: 5.48 Stokes' formula and homotopies
text: We use the exterior derivative and pullback of differential forms with their usual graded rules. All manifolds in this section are smooth and Hausdorff with a countable basis. A compact domain with corners has, near a boundary point, an oriented coordinate description $\{ x_1\leq 0,\ldots ,x_ l\leq 0\} $ inside a coordinate neighborhood. Its boundary is the union of the codimension-one faces, with the outward normal first orientation. The intersections of two faces have measure zero in each face and are not counted twice in boundary integrals. The cutoff construction used for complex manifolds applies in every real coordinate dimension. Explicitly, if a compact set $C$ lies in an open set $U$, cover $C$ by finitely many smaller coordinate balls and choose smooth functions $0\leq b_ j\leq 1$ equal to one on those balls and compactly supported in larger coordinate balls contained in $U$. Then $1-\prod _ j(1-b_ j)$ is a smooth cutoff equal to one near $C$ and supported in $U$. To obtain a partition near a compact set subordinate to finitely many charts, first choose such chart cutoffs $b_ j$ with $h=\sum _ jb_ j>0$ near the compact set, and a further cutoff $\eta $ equal to one there and compactly supported in $\{ h>0\} $. The functions $\eta b_ j/h$, extended by zero, are smooth, compactly supported in their respective charts and sum to one near the compact set. Theorem 5.48.1 . 8F5E6DB87531 Let $M$ be an oriented real manifold of dimension $m\geq 1$ and let $K\subset M$ be a compact domain with corners. For every $(m-1)$-form $\alpha $ of class $C^1$ on a neighborhood of $K$, \[  \int _ K\mathrm d\alpha =\int _{\partial K}\alpha .  \] Proof. Choose a smooth partition of unity subordinate to finitely many interior and corner charts meeting $K$. The partition sums to one near $K$, so both sides are the sums of the corresponding expressions for the forms $\chi \alpha $. We may therefore assume that $\alpha $ has compact support in a single chart $V$ and write \[  \alpha =\sum _{j=1}^ m a_ j\,  \mathrm dx_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{\mathrm dx_ j} \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dx_ m.  \] Extend its coefficients by zero outside $V$. On the product write a form uniquely as $\eta =a(t,x)+\mathrm dt\wedge b(t,x)$, where $a,b$ contain only $M$ differentials. Such zero-forms are locally constant, hence constant on the connected manifold reached by the contraction. This proves the last assertion. $\square$

section: 5.49 Complex homotopy operators and Hartogs extension
text: Let $n\geq 1$. We use the existing distribution calculus and the fundamental solution $E_{2n}$ of $\Delta $ with $\Delta E_{2n}=\delta _0$. Write $e_ j\alpha = \mathrm d\bar z_ j\wedge \alpha $ and let $\iota _ j$ be contraction with $\partial /\partial \bar z_ j$, so that $e_ j\iota _ k+\iota _ ke_ j=\delta _{jk}\mathrm{Id}$, including on forms with holomorphic differentials. Put \[  D=-\sum _{j=1}^ n\iota _ j\partial _{z_ j},\qquad K\alpha =-4D(E_{2n}*\alpha ) =\sum _{j=1}^ n k_ j*\iota _ j\alpha ,\qquad k_ j(z)=\frac{(n-1)!}{\pi ^ n}\frac{\bar z_ j}{|z|^{2n}}.  \] The convolutions are defined coefficientwise for compactly supported currents. No metric adjoint convention is implicit in the definition of $D$. Proposition 5.49.1 . 7ACDC1AF162C For every compactly supported current $\alpha $ on $\mathbb C^ n$, \[  \bar\partial K\alpha +K\bar\partial \alpha =\alpha .  \] The operator $K$ lowers antiholomorphic degree by one and vanishes on antiholomorphic degree zero. If $\alpha $ is a compactly supported $C^ s$ form, $0\leq s\leq \infty $, then $K\alpha $ is $C^ s$; if $\alpha $ has order at most $s$, then $K\alpha $ has order at most $s$ locally. In particular, every compactly supported $\bar\partial $-closed $(p,q)$-current with $q\geq 1$ has the primitive $K\alpha $. Proof. The exterior anticommutation identity and commutation of scalar derivatives show directly that \[  \bar\partial D+D\bar\partial =-\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ j} =-\tfrac 14\Delta .  \] Differentiation commutes with convolution when one factor is compactly supported. Applying the preceding identity to $E_{2n}*\alpha $ gives $\bar\partial K\alpha +K\bar\partial \alpha =(\Delta E_{2n})*\alpha =\alpha $. Differentiating the explicit fundamental solution gives $4\partial _{z_ j}E_{2n}=k_ j$; for $n=1$ this is $1/(\pi z)$. Each kernel is locally integrable, since its size is at most a constant times $|z|^{1-2n}$. For a compactly supported $C^ s$ coefficient, derivatives of order at most $s$ can be moved onto that coefficient in the convolution. On a compact set of output points the integrals then range over a fixed bounded set of kernel arguments, and local integrability justifies continuity and differentiation. For an order-$s$ compact distribution $T$, its pairing with the convolution of a test function and the reflected kernel is bounded by derivatives of that test function of order at most $s$, times the integral of the absolute value of the kernel on the difference of the two fixed compact supports. A cutoff equal to one near the support of $T$ makes this pairing legitimate. This proves the order assertion. $\square$ For comparison with exterior-form notation, put \[  b_ n(z)=\frac{(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(n-1)!}{(2\pi \mathrm i)^ n} \sum _{j=1}^ n(-1)^{j-1}\frac{\bar z_ j}{|z|^{2n}} \mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n \wedge \mathrm d\bar z_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{\mathrm d\bar z_ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ n.  \] Then $\bar\partial b_ n=\delta _0$, where the right side is the integration current of the origin. Indeed, replace $|z|^{2n}$ by $(|z|^2+\varepsilon ^2)^ n$. The bar derivative is the positive density \[  \frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\frac{\varepsilon ^2}{(|z|^2+\varepsilon ^2)^{n+1}}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] Its integral is one: in polar coordinates the radial integral is $2n\int _0^\infty t^{2n-1}(1+t^2)^{-n-1}\, \mathrm dt=1$. Scaling shows concentration at zero, whereas the forms themselves converge locally in $L^1$ by the bound $|z|^{1-2n}$. Thus their bar derivatives tend to $\delta _0$. In dimension one the form is $\mathrm dz/(2\pi \mathrm i z)$, fixing the sign. Proposition 5.49.2 . 65D5B333E685 Let $U\Subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a domain with piecewise $C^1$ boundary, and let $v$ be a $C^1$ $(p,q)$-form on a neighborhood of $\overline U$. Here piecewise $C^1$ means finitely many faces whose closures are covered by finitely many $C^1$ hypersurface graph patches with bounded first derivatives. Their exceptional edges lie in finitely many compact $C^1$ submanifolds of codimension at least two. In particular the faces have finite surface measure. With outward boundary orientation, put \[  B_ Uv=K\bigl ((\bar\partial \mathbf1_ U)\wedge v\bigr ), \qquad T_ Uv=K(\mathbf1_ Uv).  \] Here the boundary derivative is a distribution. On $U$, \[  v=B_ Uv+\bar\partial T_ Uv+T_ U\bar\partial v.  \] In the smooth case this is an equality of ordinary forms; in general its meaning is the corresponding current identity, with all the displayed terms continuous in the interior whenever they have degree zero. Proof. Apply the preceding homotopy identity to the compactly supported current $\mathbf1_ Uv$ and use the distributional product rule \[  \bar\partial (\mathbf1_ Uv) =\mathbf1_ U\bar\partial v+(\bar\partial \mathbf1_ U)\wedge v.  \] Restrict to $U$, where $\mathbf1_ Uv=v$. The boundary term is smooth there, since its distributional support is on $\partial U$ and the kernel is smooth away from zero. Localizing the other two terms away from the boundary gives their stated interior regularity by the preceding kernel estimates and continuity of translations in $L^1$. For a test form $\phi $ of complementary degree, the boundary derivative is determined by $\langle \mathrm d\mathbf1_ U,\phi \rangle =-\int _ U\mathrm d\phi =-\int _{\partial U}\phi $. For a $C^1$ graph $x_ m=f(x')$ this Stokes identity follows by integrating first in $x_ m$: the boundary flux is $F_ m(x',f(x'))-\sum _{j<m}F_ j(x',f(x'))\partial _ jf$. A partition of unity proves it for $C^1$ boundaries. The same calculation on the finitely many faces of a piecewise $C^1$ boundary, with their outward orientations, gives the identity after removing a shrinking neighborhood of the edges. To justify this removal, such an edge set has an $\varepsilon $-neighborhood of volume $O(\varepsilon ^2)$, by its finite $C^1$ coordinate charts. Mollifying a Lipschitz cutoff of the distance to the edge set gives a smooth cutoff vanishing near it, with gradient $O(\varepsilon ^{-1})$. The extra volume term in Stokes' formula is consequently $O(\varepsilon )$ for the bounded test form; the omitted face integrals tend to zero because the edges have zero surface measure. Thus only the integration variable reaches the boundary. In particular, for $n=1,p=q=0$ the formula is \[  v(z)=\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{\partial U} \frac{v(\zeta )}{\zeta -z}\, \mathrm d\zeta -\frac1\pi \int _ U\frac{\partial _{\bar\zeta }v(\zeta )}{\zeta -z} \, \mathrm dV_2(\zeta ),  \] which also checks the boundary and volume signs. $\square$ Theorem 5.49.3 . 72B026809F75 Let $T$ be a $\bar\partial $-closed $(p,q)$-current near a point of $\mathbb C^ n$, with $q\geq 1$. On a smaller neighborhood there is a $(p,q-1)$-current $S$ with $\bar\partial S=T$. A $C^ s$ input has a $C^ s$ primitive, and an order-$s$ input has an order-$s$ primitive. Proof. First recall the smooth $(0,1)$ Cauchy construction. We spell out its extension to every positive antiholomorphic degree; no global pseudoconvexity is asserted. On a polydisc write a smooth closed $(0,q)$-form as $\alpha =\alpha _0+\mathrm d\bar z_ n\wedge \alpha _1$, where neither $\alpha _ i$ contains $\mathrm d\bar z_ n$. Convolve the coefficients of $\alpha _1$ in $z_ n$ with $1/(\pi z_ n)$ after inserting a cutoff in that variable equal to one on a smaller disc. The resulting form $\beta $ satisfies $\partial _{\bar z_ n}\beta =\alpha _1$ there. The closed remainder $\alpha -\bar\partial \beta $ contains no $\mathrm d\bar z_ n$, so its coefficients are holomorphic in $z_ n$. Induction on the number of remaining variables solves this remainder; the Cauchy operators in those variables preserve holomorphic dependence on $z_ n$. In dimension one the remainder is zero. The sum of the successive primitives solves the equation on a smaller polydisc. For $(p,q)$-forms apply this argument coefficientwise after factoring out $\mathrm dz_ I$; the uniform sign $(-1)^ p$ from moving $\bar\partial $ past these differentials is absorbed in the primitive. Now choose a cutoff $\chi $ equal to one on a neighborhood $V$ of the point and compactly supported in the domain of $T$. The homotopy identity and $\bar\partial T=0$ give on $V$ \[  T=\bar\partial K(\chi T)+R,\qquad R=K(\bar\partial \chi \wedge T).  \] The support of $\bar\partial \chi \wedge T$ misses $V$, so $R$ is smooth on $V$. It is closed there, by this identity. The smooth construction just given supplies $R=\bar\partial A$ on a smaller polydisc. Then $S=K(\chi T)+A$ is the required primitive and has the asserted regularity. $\square$ Theorem 5.49.4 . 4DB91EC236EA If $n\geq 2$, every compactly supported smooth closed $(p,1)$-form on $\mathbb C^ n$ has a compactly supported smooth primitive. If $n=1$ and $a$ is a compactly supported distribution on $\mathbb C$, then $\alpha =a\, \mathrm d\bar z$ has a compactly supported distributional primitive exactly when \[  \langle a,\zeta ^ j\rangle =0 \qquad \text{for every integer }j\geq 0.  \] For a $C^ s$ input this primitive is $C^ s$, and for an order-$s$ distribution it has order at most $s$. Proof. For $n\geq 2$ take $u=K\alpha $. This is a smooth $(p,0)$-form with $\bar\partial u=\alpha $. Each coefficient is holomorphic off the support of $\alpha $, and is $O(|z|^{1-2n})$ at infinity, by the explicit kernel and compact support. Choose $R$ with $\operatorname {Supp}\alpha \subset B(0,R)$. For fixed $z'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$ with $|z'|>R$, each coefficient of $u(z',z_ n)$ is entire in $z_ n$ and tends to zero as $|z_ n|\to \infty $. Liouville's theorem makes it zero. Since $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \overline{B(0,R)}$ is connected, the identity theorem gives $u=0$ there. Thus $u$ has compact support. For $n=1$ the canonical primitive is $K\alpha $; off the support it is $u(z)=\pi ^{-1}\langle a(\zeta ),(z-\zeta )^{-1}\rangle $. The pairing means insertion of a cutoff equal to one near the compact support and supported away from $z$; its value is independent of that cutoff. Outside a disc containing the support its normally convergent Laurent series has coefficients $\pi ^{-1}\langle a,\zeta ^ j\rangle $. Indeed the geometric series and all its derivatives in $\zeta $ converge uniformly on a fixed neighborhood of the support when $z$ ranges over a compact subset of that exterior. Pairing termwise with a finite-order distribution is therefore legitimate. All moments vanish if and only if this primitive vanishes outside that disc. Conversely, if any compactly supported primitive exists, integration by parts against $\zeta ^ j$ gives zero for each moment. The regularity and order assertions are those of the homotopy operator. $\square$ Theorem 5.49.5 (Hartogs extension) . 5617D4B2FDA2 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\geq 2$, and let $C\subset \Omega $ be compact with $\Omega \setminus C$ connected. Every holomorphic function on $\Omega \setminus C$ extends uniquely to a holomorphic function on $\Omega $. Proof. If $C$ or $\Omega $ is empty, there is nothing to extend. Otherwise choose a smooth compactly supported cutoff $\chi $ in $\Omega $ equal to one near $C$. Extend $g=(1-\chi )f$ as zero near $C$. The form $\alpha =\bar\partial g=-f\bar\partial \chi $, extended by zero to $\mathbb C^ n$, is smooth, closed and compactly supported. The preceding theorem gives a compactly supported solution $u=K\alpha $ of $\bar\partial u=\alpha $, so $F=g-u$ is holomorphic on $\Omega $. In fact $u=0$ outside any closed ball containing $\operatorname {Supp}\chi $, as in the preceding proof. There is a point of $\Omega $ outside such a ball chosen sufficiently tightly: the norm attains its maximum on the compact support of $\chi $, and openness of $\Omega $ permits a point of strictly larger norm. On a neighborhood of that point, $\chi =u=0$ and $F=f$. The identity theorem on the connected set $\Omega \setminus C$ gives $F=f$ everywhere there. Each component of $\Omega $ meets this set: a component contained in $C$ would be closed in the compact set $C$, hence compact, which is impossible for a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$. The identity theorem on each component therefore also proves uniqueness throughout $\Omega $. $\square$

For $n=1$ the canonical primitive is $K\alpha $; off the support it is $u(z)=\pi ^{-1}\langle a(\zeta ),(z-\zeta )^{-1}\rangle $. The pairing means insertion of a cutoff equal to one near the compact support and supported away from $z$; its value is independent of that cutoff. Outside a disc containing the support its normally convergent Laurent series has coefficients $\pi ^{-1}\langle a,\zeta ^ j\rangle $. Indeed the geometric series and all its derivatives in $\zeta $ converge uniformly on a fixed neighborhood of the support when $z$ ranges over a compact subset of that exterior. Pairing termwise with a finite-order distribution is therefore legitimate. All moments vanish if and only if this primitive vanishes outside that disc. Conversely, if any compactly supported primitive exists, integration by parts against $\zeta ^ j$ gives zero for each moment. The regularity and order assertions are those of the homotopy operator. $\square$

text: Theorem 5.49.5 (Hartogs extension) . 5617D4B2FDA2 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\geq 2$, and let $C\subset \Omega $ be compact with $\Omega \setminus C$ connected. Every holomorphic function on $\Omega \setminus C$ extends uniquely to a holomorphic function on $\Omega $. Proof. If $C$ or $\Omega $ is empty, there is nothing to extend. Otherwise choose a smooth compactly supported cutoff $\chi $ in $\Omega $ equal to one near $C$. Extend $g=(1-\chi )f$ as zero near $C$. The form $\alpha =\bar\partial g=-f\bar\partial \chi $, extended by zero to $\mathbb C^ n$, is smooth, closed and compactly supported. The preceding theorem gives a compactly supported solution $u=K\alpha $ of $\bar\partial u=\alpha $, so $F=g-u$ is holomorphic on $\Omega $. In fact $u=0$ outside any closed ball containing $\operatorname {Supp}\chi $, as in the preceding proof. There is a point of $\Omega $ outside such a ball chosen sufficiently tightly: the norm attains its maximum on the compact support of $\chi $, and openness of $\Omega $ permits a point of strictly larger norm. On a neighborhood of that point, $\chi =u=0$ and $F=f$. The identity theorem on the connected set $\Omega \setminus C$ gives $F=f$ everywhere there. Each component of $\Omega $ meets this set: a component contained in $C$ would be closed in the compact set $C$, hence compact, which is impossible for a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$. The identity theorem on each component therefore also proves uniqueness throughout $\Omega $. $\square$

title: 9.12 Separate holomorphy
text: Theorem 9.12.1 . 362351A63FB6 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. A function $f:\Omega \longrightarrow \mathbb C$ that is holomorphic in each variable when the other variables are fixed is holomorphic on $\Omega $. Proof. First suppose that $f$ is locally bounded. On a polydisc of polyradius $2r$ where $|f|\leq M$, the one-variable Cauchy derivative estimate bounds each separate derivative by $M/r$ on the concentric polydisc of polyradius $r$. Changing the coordinates successively and integrating along their line segments gives \[  |f(z)-f(w)|\leq (M/r)\sum _{j=1}^ n|z_ j-w_ j|.  \] Thus $f$ is continuous. Iterating the one-variable Cauchy formula on a smaller closed polydisc is now legitimate. Expanding its kernels gives a normally convergent power series there, so $f$ is holomorphic. We prove local boundedness by induction on $n$. The case $n=1$ is immediate. Write $z=(z',z_ n)$ and suppose that the conclusion is known in $n-1$ variables. Choose an open polydisc $P'$ with compact closure and a closed disc $\overline D$ such that $\overline{P'}\times \overline D\subset \Omega $. For $N\geq 1$, set \[  F_ N=\{ t\in \overline D: |f(z',t)|\leq N \text{ for every }z'\in \overline{P'}\} .  \] Each $F_ N$ is closed, because $f(z',\cdot )$ is continuous for each fixed $z'$. For fixed $t$, the induction hypothesis makes $f(\cdot ,t)$ holomorphic on a neighborhood of $\overline{P'}$; hence it is bounded there. Consequently $\bigcup _ NF_ N=\overline D$. Some $F_ N$ has nonempty relative interior. Indeed, otherwise one can choose successively closed discs in $D$, each in the interior of the preceding disc, of radii tending to zero, with the $N$th disc disjoint from $F_ N$. Completeness and nested compactness give a point in all these discs, contradicting their covering by the $F_ N$. The relative interior just obtained contains an open disc $D(b,r)\subset D$. Thus $f$ is bounded, and therefore holomorphic, on $P'\times D(b,r)$. We next propagate this bounded patch. Suppose that $P'\times D(b,R)\subset \Omega $ and that $|f|\leq M$ on $P'\times D(b,r)$ for some $0<r<R$. The Taylor coefficients \[  c_ j(z')=\frac{1}{j!}\partial _{z_ n}^ jf(z',b)  \] are holomorphic on $P'$, by the holomorphy on the smaller product. For every fixed $0<r_0<r$, Cauchy's estimate gives $|c_ j|\leq M r_0^{-j}$. For $j\geq 1$ let $v_ j=j^{-1}\log |c_ j|$, taking $v_ j\equiv -\infty $ if $c_ j\equiv 0$. These are subharmonic functions in the convention allowing the identically $-\infty $ function, and are locally uniformly bounded above. For each fixed $z'$, the separate Taylor series has radius at least $R$. Its coefficient formula therefore gives \[  \limsup _{j\to \infty }v_ j(z')\leq -\log R.  \] The subharmonic Hartogs lemma implies that, for every compact $L\subset P'$ and every $0<s<R$, eventually $|c_ j|\leq s^{-j}$ on $L$. For $0<t<s$ the series \[  \sum _{j=0}^\infty c_ j(z')(z_ n-b)^ j  \] therefore converges normally on $L\times \overline{D(b,t)}$. Its sum is holomorphic and agrees with $f$ by the one-variable Taylor formula. Varying $L,t,s$ proves holomorphy on the larger product. Finally take any $\zeta \in \Omega $ and a polydisc $P(\zeta ,2R)\subset \Omega $. Apply the bounded-patch construction with $P'=P(\zeta ',R)$ and $\overline D=\overline{D(\zeta _ n,R)}$. It gives a center $b\in D(\zeta _ n,R)$ and a bounded smaller disc there. Shrink its radius if necessary. Since $D(b,R)\subset D(\zeta _ n,2R)$, propagation applies to $P'\times D(b,R)$. This product contains $\zeta $, completing the induction and the proof. $\square$

section: 6.20 An obstruction to global decreasing approximation
text: Example 6.20.1 . 4BA55C74028C There is a bounded connected domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^2$ and a bounded plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $\Omega $ that is not the pointwise limit of any decreasing sequence of continuous plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $. Proof. For $j\geq 2$ put \[  a_ j=\frac{2^{-j}}{\log j},\qquad \varepsilon _ j=\exp (-8^ j),\qquad A=\bigcup _{j\geq 2}D(1/j,\varepsilon _ j).  \] All these discs lie in $D(0,1)$. They are pairwise disjoint: $8^ j>4j(j+1)$ for $j\geq 2$, by induction, so $\varepsilon _ j<1/(4j(j+1))$. The sum of the bounds for neighboring radii is less than $1/(j(j+1))$, the distance between their centers. The ordering of these disjoint intervals on the real axis then also separates every nonneighboring pair of discs. Define \[  \Omega =\bigl ((D(0,2)\setminus \{ |z|=1\} )\times D(0,1)\bigr ) \  \cup \  \bigl (\{ |z|=1\} \times A\bigr ).  \] This set is open: at a point of its added circles the second coordinate lies in the open set $A$, so a full product neighborhood is present. The inner and outer products are connected, and each added circle has such a neighborhood meeting both. Thus $\Omega $ is connected. On $\mathbb C$ consider \[  \psi (w)=\sum _{j\geq 2} a_ j\log |w-1/j|.  \] This defines a subharmonic function, with $\psi (0)=-\sum _{j\geq 2}2^{-j}=-1/2$. For completeness, on $D(0,R)$ with $R>1$, subtract $C_ R=\log (R+1)$ from every logarithm. The resulting finite sums are decreasing subharmonic functions and their values at zero have a finite limit, since $\sum a_ j<\infty $. The decreasing-limit theorem therefore applies. Adding back the convergent constant $C_ R\sum a_ j$ gives the displayed series; these local definitions agree. For $w\in D(1/j,\varepsilon _ j)$ the $j$th term is less than $-4^ j/\log j<-1$, and every other term is negative because $|w-1/k|<1$. Hence $\psi <-1$ on $A$. Put \[  u(z,w)= \begin{cases}  \max \{ \psi (w),-1\} ,&  |z|<1,\\  -1,&  |z|\geq 1, \end{cases}\qquad (z,w)\in \Omega .  \] Both pieces are plurisubharmonic. Near each bridge point they agree with the constant $-1$, so they define a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. It is bounded below by $-1$ and above because $\psi (w)\leq \log (3/2)\sum a_ j$ for $|w|<1$. In particular \[  u(0,0)=-1/2,\qquad u(z,0)=-1\quad (|z|=3/2).  \] Every continuous plurisubharmonic $v$ on $\Omega $ satisfies \[  v(0,0)\leq \sup _{|z|=3/2}v(z,0).  \] Indeed the entire disc $D(0,2)\times \{ 1/j\} $ lies in $\Omega $, and its subharmonic maximum principle gives $v(0,1/j)\leq \sup _{|z|=3/2}v(z,1/j)$. As $j\to \infty $, continuity gives convergence on the left and uniform convergence on the right: the latter follows from uniform continuity on the compact product of the outer circle with a small closed $w$-disc, which is contained in $\Omega $. Suppose now that continuous plurisubharmonic functions $v_ k$ decrease pointwise to $u$. On the compact outer circle, $v_ k(\cdot ,0)\downarrow -1$ implies $\sup _{|z|=3/2}v_ k(z,0)\downarrow -1$. To see this directly, the increasing open sets $\{ z:v_ k(z,0)<-1+\eta \} $ cover that circle for every $\eta >0$; a finite subcover and monotonicity give the uniform upper bound. The preceding inequality for $v_ k$ would then give $-1/2=u(0,0)\leq -1$, a contradiction. $\square$

Theorem 9.13.2 . 8FBCDB96A2E2 For an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ and any distance function $\delta $, the following conditions are equivalent: $\Omega $ is a domain of holomorphy; $\Omega $ is holomorphically convex; for every compact $K\subset \Omega $ and $f\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$, $|f|\leq \delta _\Omega $ on $K$ implies $|f|\leq \delta _\Omega $ on $\widehat K_\Omega $; $\Omega $ is a domain of existence of one holomorphic function. For $h\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$, $\xi \in B_\delta $ and $k\geq 0$, the function \[  A_{k,\xi }(z)= rac1{k!}D^ kh(z)(f(z)\xi )^ k  \] is holomorphic in $z$. For $0<r<1$, the points $z+t f(z)\xi $, with $z\in K$, $|t|\leq r$ and $\xi \in \overline B_\delta $, form a compact subset of $\Omega $. Indeed their $\delta $-displacement is at most $r\delta _\Omega (z)$; none can be in the complement. Cauchy's estimate on the parameter disc gives $|A_{k,\xi }|\leq M_ r r^{-k}$ on $K$, uniformly in $\xi $, where $M_ r$ bounds $h$ on that compact set. The hull inequalities transfer this bound to $\widehat K_\Omega $. At $a\in \widehat K_\Omega $ with $f(a)
e 0$, the homogeneous Taylor series for $h$ therefore converges normally on $a+f(a)B_\delta $: on every compact subset the ratio $\delta (z-a)/|f(a)|$ is bounded by some number less than $r<1$. It agrees with $h$ near $a$. This gives, for every $h$, an extension from a common neighborhood of $a$ to that connected balanced open set. The domain-of-holomorphy condition forces the latter to be contained in $\Omega $. Hence $|f(a)|\leq \delta _\Omega (a)$. The same conclusion is automatic if $f(a)=0$, proving the third condition. Taking constant $f$ of any modulus smaller than $\inf _ K\delta _\Omega $ also proves the final distance equality. In particular the hull has positive Euclidean distance from the complement. It is bounded and closed in $\Omega $, so compact. This proves the second condition; the third condition alone gives the same argument. Under the second condition the preceding proposition gives arbitrary discrete interpolation. We show that it supplies the fourth condition, including extension from just one local component. Give $\mathcal O(\Omega )$ its complete metrizable compact-open topology; completeness follows from the locally uniform Cauchy formula. Consider the countably many pairs of rational balls $b,B$ with $\overline b\subset B\cap \Omega $ and $B
ot\subset \Omega $. For an integer $N\geq 1$, let $E_{b,B,N}$ consist of functions admitting an extension from $b$ to $B$ bounded there by $N$. This set is closed: a convergent sequence of its functions has, by Montel on $B$, a subsequence of bounded extensions converging locally uniformly, with the correct restriction to $b$. It has empty interior. Let $W$ be the component of $B\cap \Omega $ containing $b$. It has a boundary point $a$ inside $B$, since it is a nonempty proper open subset of the connected ball $B$; such a point lies in $\partial \Omega $. Choose distinct $z_ j\in W$ tending to $a$. The Baire theorem now gives a function outside all these closed sets. Here Baire follows directly by choosing nested closed balls in a complete metric, with radii tending to zero and each ball disjoint from the next specified nowhere dense set. If this function extended from a nonempty open subset of $U\cap \Omega $ to a connected open $U$ crossing the boundary, identity would give equality on the corresponding component $W$ of $U\cap \Omega $. Choose $a\in \partial W\cap U$, a rational ball $B\Subset U$ containing $a$, and a rational ball $b\Subset W\cap B$. The extension is bounded on $B$ after choosing its closure in $U$, contrary to avoidance of $E_{b,B,N}$. This proves the fourth condition. It plainly implies the first. If the boundary is empty the condition is vacuous; the same proof or any entire function handles $\Omega =\mathbb C^ n$. The empty open set likewise has all four properties under the displayed definitions. $\square$

Moreover a domain of holomorphy satisfies $\inf _{\widehat K_\Omega }\delta _\Omega =\inf _ K\delta _\Omega $. Proof. Assume the first condition, and fix $K,f$ as in the third condition. For $h\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$, $\xi \in B_\delta $ and $k\geq 0$, the function \[  A_{k,\xi }(z)=\frac1{k!}D^ kh(z)(f(z)\xi )^ k  \] is holomorphic in $z$. For $0<r<1$, the points $z+t f(z)\xi $, with $z\in K$, $|t|\leq r$ and $\xi \in \overline B_\delta $, form a compact subset of $\Omega $. Indeed their $\delta $-displacement is at most $r\delta _\Omega (z)$; none can be in the complement. Cauchy's estimate on the parameter disc gives $|A_{k,\xi }|\leq M_ r r^{-k}$ on $K$, uniformly in $\xi $, where $M_ r$ bounds $h$ on that compact set. The hull inequalities transfer this bound to $\widehat K_\Omega $. At $a\in \widehat K_\Omega $ with $f(a)\ne 0$, the homogeneous Taylor series for $h$ therefore converges normally on $a+f(a)B_\delta $: on every compact subset the ratio $\delta (z-a)/|f(a)|$ is bounded by some number less than $r<1$. It agrees with $h$ near $a$. This gives, for every $h$, an extension from a common neighborhood of $a$ to that connected balanced open set. The domain-of-holomorphy condition forces the latter to be contained in $\Omega $. Hence $|f(a)|\leq \delta _\Omega (a)$. The same conclusion is automatic if $f(a)=0$, proving the third condition. For an integer $N\geq 1$, let $E_{b,B,N}$ consist of functions admitting an extension from $b$ to $B$ bounded there by $N$. This set is closed: a convergent sequence of its functions has, by Montel on $B$, a subsequence of bounded extensions converging locally uniformly, with the correct restriction to $b$. It has empty interior. Let $W$ be the component of $B\cap \Omega $ containing $b$. It has a boundary point $a$ inside $B$, since it is a nonempty proper open subset of the connected ball $B$; such a point lies in $\partial \Omega $. Choose distinct $z_ j\in W$ tending to $a$. They have no accumulation in $\Omega $, so interpolation gives $h(z_ j)=j$. This $h$ cannot extend from $b$ to $B$, since the identity theorem would make its extension equal to $h$ on $W$. If $E_{b,B,N}$ contained a neighborhood of $f_0$, then both $f_0$ and $f_0+t h$ would be in it for sufficiently small nonzero $t$; subtracting their extensions would extend $h$, a contradiction. Here Baire follows directly by choosing nested closed balls in a complete metric, with radii tending to zero and each ball disjoint from the next specified nowhere dense set. If this function extended from a nonempty open subset of $U\cap \Omega $ to a connected open $U$ crossing the boundary, identity would give equality on the corresponding component $W$ of $U\cap \Omega $. Choose $a\in \partial W\cap U$, a rational ball $B\Subset U$ containing $a$, and a rational ball $b\Subset W\cap B$. The extension is bounded on $B$ after choosing its closure in $U$, contrary to avoidance of $E_{b,B,N}$. This proves the fourth condition. It plainly implies the first. title: 6.21 Discrete interpolation from weighted estimates
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Proposition 6.21.1 . E7EBBDB6A293 On a pseudoconvex open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$, arbitrary complex values can be interpolated at a closed discrete set of distinct points. Consequently such an open set is holomorphically convex and is a domain of existence. Conversely a domain of holomorphy is pseudoconvex. Proof. Use the existing Oka theorem to choose a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion $s$. Around the discrete points $z_ j$ choose pairwise disjoint balls $B(z_ j,2r_ j)\Subset \Omega $ forming a locally finite family. For example, take $2r_ j$ smaller than one quarter of both the distance to the other points and the distance to the complement, and also take $r_ j\leq 1/j$. Let $\theta _ j$ be smooth, supported in $B(z_ j,r_ j)$ and equal to one near $z_ j$, and put $g=\sum _ j a_ j\theta _ j$. This is smooth; $\alpha =\bar\partial g$ vanishes near every $z_ j$. Choose smooth $\eta _ j$ supported in $B(z_ j,2r_ j)$, equal to one on $B(z_ j,r_ j)$, and set \[  L=n\sum _ j\eta _ j(z)\log \frac{|z-z_ j|^2}{r_ j^2}.  \] Off the discrete poles this is smooth. Its negative complex Hessian is bounded on each compact sublevel of $s$, since its only nonsmooth terms near a pole are plurisubharmonic logarithms with positive coefficient. There is a smooth convex increasing $\chi $ such that $p=\chi (s)+L$ is plurisubharmonic and \[  \int _\Omega |\alpha |^2\exp (-p-|z|^2)\, \mathrm dV<\infty .  \] Here is the simultaneous choice in detail. On each compact band $m\leq s\leq m+1$, let $C_ m$ bound the negative Hessian of $L$, and let $\lambda _ m>0$ be a lower bound for $H_ s$. The integral $I_ m=\int _{\{ m\leq s\leq m+1\} }|\alpha |^2 \exp (-L-|z|^2)\, \mathrm dV$ is finite, since $\alpha =0$ near the finitely many poles in the band. Choose a smooth nondecreasing nonnegative function $b$ such that $b\geq C_ m/\lambda _ m$ on $[m,m+1]$ and $\int _{m-1}^ m b\geq \log ^+(2^ m I_ m)$ for $m\geq 1$. Such a function is obtained by a locally finite sum of nondecreasing smooth steps, the $m$th step starting at $m-1$ and reaching a sufficiently large constant by $m-1/2$; include a sufficiently large initial constant for $m=0$. Put $\chi (t)=C+\int _0^ t b$ and choose $C$ for the band $0\leq s\leq 1$. The chain rule gives $H_{\chi (s)}\geq \chi '(s)H_ s$, proving positivity off the poles, and the integral on the $m$th band is at most $2^{-m}$. Near a pole, $p$ is the sum of $n\log |z-z_ j|^2$ and a smooth plurisubharmonic function, so it is PSH there as well. Apply the existing singular-weight $\bar\partial $ estimate with this $p$ and $q=|z|^2$, whose Hessian is the identity. It gives $\bar\partial v=\alpha $ and $\int |v|^2\exp (-p-|z|^2)<\infty $. Near $z_ j$, $v$ is holomorphic by the scalar distributional regularity theorem. The weight is a smooth positive factor times $|z-z_ j|^{-2n}$. A nonzero value $v(z_ j)$ would make its integral diverge, since the radial integral would contain $\int _0^ r t^{-1}\, dt$. Thus $v(z_ j)=0$ and $F=g-v$ is holomorphic with $F(z_ j)=a_ j$. If a holomorphic hull of a compact $K$ were noncompact, its boundedness and closedness in $\Omega $ would supply distinct hull points tending to the boundary. Interpolating the values $j$ there contradicts the defining bound $|F|\leq \sup _ K|F|$ of the hull. The hull is therefore compact, and the Cartan–Thullen theorem applies. Conversely that theorem and the hull-exhaustion proposition give a smooth PSH exhaustion on every domain of holomorphy, proving pseudoconvexity. $\square$

title: 9.14 Plurisubharmonic hulls and general boundary distances

section: 9.14 Plurisubharmonic hulls and general boundary distances
text: For compact $K\subset \Omega $, let \[  K_{\mathrm{psh}}=\{ z\in \Omega :u(z)\leq \sup _ Ku \text{ for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )\} .  \] Proposition 9.14.1 . D1E020BB8CEA For a proper open subset $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, the following are equivalent: pseudoconvexity; relative compactness of every $K_{\mathrm{psh}}$; compactness of every $K_{\mathrm{psh}}$; plurisubharmonicity of $-\log \delta _\Omega $ for any one of the distance functions defined above; and pseudoconvexity in a neighborhood of each boundary point. On a pseudoconvex open set the distance condition holds for every such $\delta $. Proof. The existing Oka proof establishes that the directional radius \[  d_\Omega (z,\xi )=\sup \{ r:z+\xi D(0,r)\subset \Omega \}   \] has $V(z,\xi )=-\log d_\Omega (z,\xi )$ upper semicontinuous and satisfying complex-disc submeans jointly in $(z,\xi )$; it may take the value $-\infty $. In particular each fixed-direction function satisfies those submeans. Directly from the definitions and complex homogeneity, \[  \delta _\Omega (z)=\inf _{|\xi |=1}\delta (\xi )d_\Omega (z,\xi ), \qquad -\log \delta _\Omega (z)=\sup _{|\xi |=1} \{ V(z,\xi )-\log \delta (\xi )\} .  \] For the first identity, each point of the complement supplies its radial direction, while each directional exit supplies such a point; take infima, also when a direction never exits. The supremum on the right has the submean property by bounding each summand by it in the circle integral. It is continuous and finite by continuity of $\delta _\Omega $, so it is plurisubharmonic. Conversely if this function is PSH, $|z|^2+\max \{ 0,-\log \delta _\Omega \} $ is a continuous PSH exhaustion. Indeed $\delta _\Omega \leq C d_\Omega ^{\rm Eucl}$, so its sublevels stay away from the boundary as well as infinity. Let $\rho $ be a continuous PSH exhaustion. Its inequality bounds $K_{\mathrm{psh}}$ in a compact sublevel. To prove closedness, we show that continuous PSH tests suffice in its definition. Suppose $u(a)>\sup _ Ku$. On a relatively compact sublevel $G=\{ \rho <c\} $ containing $K\cup \{ a\} $, convolve $u$ with a sufficiently small radial kernel on a neighborhood of $\overline G$. The smooth result $u_\varepsilon $ still separates $a$ from $K$: its values at $a$ decrease to $u(a)$, and $\sup _ Ku_\varepsilon \downarrow \sup _ Ku$. For the latter assertion, for each $M>\sup _ Ku$ the increasing open sets $\{ u_\varepsilon <M\} $ cover $K$ and hence one covers it by compactness. Choose $M_0>\sup _{\overline G}u_\varepsilon $ and $A$ so large that $A(\rho -c)+M_0<u_\varepsilon $ on $K\cup \{ a\} $. The function equal to $\max \{ u_\varepsilon ,A(\rho -c)+M_0\} $ on $G$ and $A(\rho -c)+M_0$ outside is continuous PSH by boundary gluing, and gives the same separation. Continuous tests define closed sets, so the hull is closed in $\Omega $, hence compact. Conversely suppose that all PSH hulls are relatively compact. In the existing directional Oka argument, the auxiliary analytic discs have their boundaries in a fixed compact $K\subset \Omega $. The subharmonic maximum principle for every PSH test puts their entire images in $K_{\mathrm{psh}}$. Its compact closure inside $\Omega $ allows the limiting disc and a slightly larger radius, which is exactly the continuation step in that proof. The rest of the same argument gives the Euclidean boundary-distance function PSH and a continuous PSH exhaustion. Thus relative compactness already suffices. Pseudoconvexity implies its boundary-local version by restricting to balls: add to $\rho $ the PSH barrier $1/(r^2-|z-a|^2)$ to exhaust the intersection with $B(a,r)$. For the converse, near each boundary point shrink a pseudoconvex neighborhood $W$ so that the Euclidean distances to the complements of $\Omega $ and $W\cap \Omega $ agree. Their negative logarithm is therefore PSH near the boundary. The remaining set $F$ may be chosen closed in $\mathbb C^ n$ and contained in $\Omega $; its intersection with each bounded ball is compact in $\Omega $. Choose a smooth convex increasing $b$ with $b(t)\geq t$ and $b(|z|^2)>-\log d_\Omega ^{\rm Eucl}(z)+1$ on $F$. Such a radial majorant exists by taking increasing slopes dominating the finite maxima on these compact intersections. Then \[  \max \{ b(|z|^2),-\log d_\Omega ^{\rm Eucl}(z)\}   \] is continuous PSH: off $F$ both terms are PSH, and near every point of $F$ the radial term strictly dominates. It is an exhaustion, which finishes all the equivalences. $\square$ Proposition 9.14.2 . CE8195E08F54 If $G$ is a pseudoconvex open subset of $\mathbb C^ N$ and $v$ is plurisubharmonic on $G$, then the open set $\{ v<c\} $ is pseudoconvex. The same holds with the identically $-\infty $ alternative on components. Proof. We spell out the continuation step needed to apply the existing Oka directional-radius proof to $H=\{ v<c\} $. In that proof the candidate discs have boundaries in one compact subset $K$ of $H$, and their images are in $H$ before a first possible exit. A continuous PSH exhaustion of $G$, composed with each disc, bounds all these images in one compact subset of $G$. The limiting disc is thus contained in $G$. Since $v$ is usc, $\max _ Kv<c$. Its composition with the limiting disc is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on a neighborhood of the closed parameter disc, so the maximum principle puts its whole image in $H$. Compactness and openness now allow a slightly larger radius. This is precisely the contradiction to a first exit in Oka's proof. The directional submean argument and its passage to the Euclidean boundary distance therefore apply to $H$, giving a continuous PSH exhaustion there. No continuity of $v$ is required. $\square$

title: 9.15 Complete Hartogs domains and Taylor coefficients

section: 9.15 Complete Hartogs domains and Taylor coefficients
text: Proposition 9.15.1 . 202C805DC8A2 Let $n\geq 2$, let $D\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$ be open and let $R:D\to (0,\infty ]$ be lower semicontinuous. The complete Hartogs open set \[  H=\{ (z,w):z\in D,\  |w|<R(z)\}   \] is pseudoconvex if and only if $D$ is pseudoconvex and $u=-\log R$ is PSH or identically $-\infty $ on each component. Every $f\in \mathcal O(H)$ has an expansion $f(z,w)=\sum _{j\geq 0}c_ j(z)w^ j$, with $c_ j\in \mathcal O(D)$, converging normally on $H$. If $H$ is a domain of existence of $f$, then \[  u=\left(\limsup _{j\to \infty }j^{-1}\log |c_ j|\right)^*.  \] Consequently every PSH function on an open set is locally of this form, with the identically zero coefficients assigned logarithm $-\infty $. Proof. If $H$ is pseudoconvex, restricting its continuous PSH exhaustion to the closed zero section gives an exhaustion of $D$. The existing Oka proof gives the joint directional submean property of $-\log d_ H((z,w),\xi )$. Its restriction to $w=0$ and the fixed vertical direction is $-\log R(z)$. It is usc; the submean and local alternative theorems make it PSH or identically $-\infty $ on each component. Conversely, on $D\times \mathbb C$ the function $v(z,w)=u(z)+\log |w|$ is PSH, with its natural pole values. Its sublevel $\{ v<0\} =H$ is pseudoconvex by the preceding proposition and the existing product property. Components where $u=-\infty $ give the entire product directly. Near every point of $D$, lower semicontinuity supplies a common positive fiber radius. Cauchy's formula there makes the Taylor coefficients holomorphic on the base, and these definitions agree on overlaps. On a compact subset of $H$ its circled fiberwise hull is compact in $H$, and a dilation by some fixed factor $t>1$ is still compact in $H$. The fiberwise Cauchy estimate gives $|c_ j(z)w^ j|\leq M t^{-j}$ on the original compact set (for $w=0$ the positive-degree terms vanish). This proves normal convergence. Put $a_ j=j^{-1}\log |c_ j|$ for $j\geq 1$. On relatively compact base neighborhoods Cauchy's estimate using a common inner fiber radius bounds the $a_ j$ uniformly above. The regularized limsup $a=(\limsup _ j a_ j)^*$ is PSH or identically $-\infty $ on each component; identically zero terms may be omitted from each envelope, with an empty tail giving $-\infty $. The fiberwise convergence radius gives $\limsup _ j a_ j\leq u$; since $u$ is usc, also $a\leq u$. The same series defines a holomorphic function on $H_ a=\{ (z,w):\log |w|+a(z)<0\} $. Indeed, near a point of this set, usc of $a$ gives a strict margin for a small product neighborhood, and the subharmonic Hartogs lemma applied to $a_ j$ gives a geometric normal majorant there. Its sum equals $f$ on $H$. If $a<u$ anywhere, $H_ a$ has a component strictly larger than the corresponding component of $H$, and is connected over that connected base component through its zero section. This extension contradicts the domain-of-existence hypothesis. Thus $a=u$. For the final assertion, restrict a PSH function $u$ to a ball $D$, put $R=\mathrm e^{-u}$, and use the already proved existence of a holomorphic function with domain of existence $H$. The formula just proved gives the claimed local representation, including poles of $u$. $\square$

This extension contradicts the domain-of-existence hypothesis. Thus $a=u$. title: 9.16 Local convexity and defining functions
text: Proposition 9.16.1 . 3269D913190D A nonempty closed connected locally convex subset $C$ of a finite dimensional real Euclidean space is convex. Consequently a connected open set $D$ is convex if and only if it admits a finite continuous locally convex exhaustion function. Proof. For the first assertion, any two points can be joined by a polygonal path in $C$. In fact, each equivalence class for polygonal reachability is relatively open, since near every point $C$ agrees with a convex set; its complement, a union of other classes, is relatively open too. Connectedness gives a single class. Fix $a,b\in C$ and a polygonal joining path of length $L$. Take paths whose lengths decrease to the infimum and are at most $L+1$. Parameterize them on $[0,1]$ with constant speed, inserting a constant path when needed. Their images lie in the compact set $C\cap \overline{B(a,L+1)}$ and their Lipschitz constants are at most $L+1$. A diagonal subsequence converges at every time in a countable dense subset of $[0,1]$, by compactness of the range. The common Lipschitz bound then makes it uniformly Cauchy, so it converges uniformly. Its limit joins $a$ to $b$ in $C$, and its length is at most the limiting lengths: for each finite partition the sum of successive distances passes to the uniform limit, and length is the supremum of these sums. It is therefore a shortest path. On every sufficiently short subarc around one of its points, local convexity permits replacement by the straight segment. Minimality forces equality between that subarc's length and the distance of its endpoints. In arclength parametrization it is consequently affine there: equality in the Euclidean triangle inequality places each intermediate point on that segment at its prescribed distance. The local affine directions agree on overlapping subarcs, so the whole path is the segment from $a$ to $b$. This proves convexity. Let $h$ be a finite continuous locally convex exhaustion on $D$. Its epigraph \[  E=\{ (x,t):x\in D,\  t\geq h(x)\}   \] is closed in the full Euclidean product: a convergent sequence in $E$ has its $x$-coordinates in one compact sublevel of the exhaustion, and continuity gives the limiting inequality. It is connected, being homeomorphic to $D\times [0,\infty )$, and is locally convex by local convexity of $h$. The first assertion makes $E$ convex, and its projection $D$ is convex. Conversely, if $D$ is a proper open convex set, its Euclidean boundary distance $d$ is concave. Indeed, the convex combinations of balls $B(x,r)\subset D$ and $B(y,s)\subset D$ give $B((1-t)x+ty,(1-t)r+ts)\subset D$; let $r\uparrow d(x)$, $s\uparrow d(y)$. Thus $-\log d$ is convex, and $|x|^2+\max \{ 0,-\log d(x)\} $ is a continuous convex exhaustion. For the full space use $|x|^2$. $\square$ Proposition 9.16.2 . 2822D619E8BC Let $D$ be a bounded connected domain in $\mathbb R^ m$ with a $C^2$ defining function $q$ on a neighborhood of $\overline D$: $D=\{ q<0\} $ there and $\mathrm dq\ne 0$ on $\partial D$. If $D^2q$ is positive definite on every real tangent space to $\partial D$, then $D$ is convex and every point of its boundary is an extreme point of $\overline D$. Proof. Near a boundary point replace $q$ by $\widetilde q=q+M q^2$. At the boundary its real Hessian is \[  D^2\widetilde q=D^2q+2M\, \mathrm dq\otimes \mathrm dq.  \] Write a vector as a tangential part plus a normal part. The tangential quadratic form is positive definite, mixed terms are bounded, and the last displayed term is a positive multiple of $M$ times the squared normal component. The inequality $2uv\leq \varepsilon u^2+\varepsilon ^{-1}v^2$ therefore makes the full Hessian positive definite for large enough $M$. It remains so on a smaller neighborhood by continuity, where $q$ and $q+Mq^2$ have the same sign. Thus $\overline D$ is locally convex at the boundary, being the nonpositive sublevel of a strictly convex function on a small ball. It is locally convex at its interior points as well. It is closed and connected, so the preceding proposition makes it convex. The regular defining function also gives $D=\operatorname {int}\overline D$: at a boundary point it has both signs locally, so that point cannot be in the interior of the closure. It follows that $D$ is convex. If a boundary point were interior to a nontrivial segment in $\overline D$, take two nearby points of that segment in the small strictly convex defining-function neighborhood. Their values of $\widetilde q$ are nonpositive; strict convexity makes its value at the intermediate boundary point negative, a contradiction. This is exactly the claimed extreme-point property. $\square$ Proposition 9.16.3 . 623CAE0176D7 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ have a $C^2$ defining function $q$ near $p\in \partial \Omega $, with $\mathrm dq(p)\ne 0$ and positive definite complex Hessian there. There exist a neighborhood $V$ of $p$ and a biholomorphic map on $V$ whose image of $\Omega \cap V$ is a bounded strongly convex domain with $C^2$ boundary. Proof. Translate $p$ to zero and make a complex linear change of coordinates so that the linear term of $q$ is $\operatorname {Re}z_ n$. Its Taylor expansion is \[  q(z)=\operatorname {Re}z_ n+\operatorname {Re}P(z)+H(z)+r(z), \qquad r(z)=o(|z|^2),  \] where $P$ is homogeneous holomorphic of degree two and $H$ is a positive definite Hermitian quadratic form. The map $w' =z'$, $w_ n=z_ n+P(z)$ is a local biholomorphism by the inverse theorem. In these coordinates the defining function becomes \[  Q(w)=\operatorname {Re}w_ n+H(w)+R(w), \qquad D^2R(w)\longrightarrow 0\quad (w\to 0),  \] with $R(0)=0$ and $\mathrm dR(0)=0$. In particular its real Hessian is positive definite near zero. Choose a smooth cap to obtain a complete bounded convex domain with a regular boundary. Take a small $r_0>0$ with $B(0,4r_0)$ in the coordinate neighborhood, and a smooth cutoff $\chi $ equal to one on $B(0,2r_0)$ and supported in $B(0,3r_0)$, whose derivatives of order $k\leq 2$ are bounded by $C_ k r_0^{-k}$. Taylor's estimates give $R=o(r_0^2)$, $\mathrm dR=o(r_0)$ and $D^2R=o(1)$ there. Hence the Hessian of $\chi R$ tends uniformly to zero as $r_0\downarrow 0$. For a small fixed choice, the globally defined \[  G_0(w)=\operatorname {Re}w_ n+H(w)+\chi (w)R(w)  \] has real Hessian bounded below by a positive multiple of the identity. For sufficiently large $M$, the function \[  G(w)=G_0(w)+M\bigl (\max \{ |w|^2-r_0^2,0\} \bigr )^3  \] is positive for $|w|\geq 2r_0$. Indeed the added nonnegative convex $C^2$ term grows to order six, is bounded below away from zero relative to any negative part of $G_0$ on $|w|\geq 2r_0$, and $G_0$ already has a positive quadratic lower bound minus a linear term. The real Hessian of $G$ is still uniformly positive definite. It has $G(0)=0$, nonzero differential at zero and negative values on the inward normal side. Thus $D=\{ G<0\} $ is nonempty, bounded and strongly convex, with closure inside $B(0,2r_0)$. Its boundary is $C^2$ and regular: a critical point of a strictly convex differentiable function is its unique global minimum, which here is strictly negative and cannot lie on the zero level. On $B(0,2r_0)$ we have $G\geq Q$, and on $B(0,r_0)$ we have $G=Q$. Consequently $D\subset \{ Q<0\} $ and for the open neighborhood $W=D\cup B(0,r_0)$ of zero, $W\cap \{ Q<0\} =D$. Pull $W$ back under the biholomorphic coordinate map. This gives precisely the required $V$ and the strongly convex image of $\Omega \cap V$. $\square$

section: 6.22 Relative smoothing with a variable strict lower bound
text: We use the normalized regularized maximum constructed in the existing Euclidean Richberg proof. For fixed positive parameters $\eta _ i$ it is smooth, convex, increasing in each variable and invariant under a common translation. It lies between $\max t_ i$ and $\max (t_ i+\eta _ i)$. A branch satisfying $t_ i+\eta _ i\leq \max _{j\ne i}(t_ j-\eta _ j)$ may be deleted without changing the function. Its nonnegative first derivatives sum to one. Consequently its composition with smooth functions having complex Hessians at least the same Hermitian form $\Gamma _ x$ also has complex Hessian at least $\Gamma _ x$: the chain-rule second-derivative term is positive semidefinite. These are the existing operator and proof, with their probability normalization retained. Theorem 6.22.1 (Relative Richberg smoothing) . 857A88CAB3FA Let $X$ be a second countable complex manifold and let $u$ be a continuous real-valued plurisubharmonic function on $X$. Suppose that on an open set $\Omega \subset X$ its distributional complex Hessian satisfies $H_ u\geq \gamma $, where $\gamma $ is a continuous positive definite Hermitian form on $TX|_\Omega $. For every continuous $\lambda :\Omega \to (0,\infty )$ there is a continuous PSH function $v$ on $X$, smooth and strictly PSH on $\Omega $, such that \[  v=u\text{ on }X\setminus \Omega ,\qquad u\leq v\leq u+\lambda \text{ on }\Omega ,\qquad H_ v\geq (1-\lambda )\gamma \text{ on }\Omega .  \] Proof. The cases $\Omega =\varnothing $ and $\dim X=0$ have the solution $v=u$. For positive dimension put $\kappa (x)=\min \{ \lambda (x),1/2\} $ and $\Gamma _ x=(1-\kappa (x))\gamma _ x$. This form is positive and dominates $(1-\lambda )\gamma $. Choose a countable locally finite family of coordinate balls $B_ i=B(c_ i,r_ i)\Subset \Omega $ whose concentric balls of radius $r_ i/3$ cover $\Omega $. One construction uses a compact exhaustion: cover each compact annulus by finitely many inner coordinate balls whose outer balls remain between the two neighboring larger annuli. The union is locally finite in $\Omega $; it need not be locally finite at points outside $\Omega $. For each ball choose a smooth function $0\leq b_ i\leq 1$ supported in it and positive on its inner ball. Extend these functions by zero to $X$. The series $b=\sum _{i\geq 1}2^{-i}b_ i$ converges uniformly on $X$, so it is continuous there, is positive on $\Omega $, and vanishes on its complement. Thus \[  e(x)=\min \{ \lambda (x)/2,1,b(x)\} \quad (x\in \Omega )  \] is continuous and positive on $\Omega $, and tends to zero at every boundary point in $X$. We will obtain $0\leq v-u\leq e$ there. In the $i$th coordinates let $A_ i>0$ be a lower bound on $\kappa (x)$ times the smallest eigenvalue of $\gamma _ x$ on $\overline B_ i$. Choose $\delta _ i>0$ with \[  \delta _ i<A_ i/4,\qquad \delta _ i r_ i^2<\min _{\overline B_ i}e, \qquad \eta _ i=\delta _ i r_ i^2/6.  \] For sufficiently small $h_ i>0$, the usual radial convolution is defined on a neighborhood of $\overline B_ i$ and satisfies \[  0\leq u*\rho _{h_ i}-u<\eta _ i,\qquad H_{u*\rho _{h_ i}}\geq \gamma -(A_ i/4)I \quad \text{on }B_ i.  \] The first assertion follows from continuity and the existing monotone PSH regularization. For the second, positivity of the distributional matrix $H_ u-\gamma $ survives convolution, whereas convolution of the continuous coefficient matrix $\gamma $ tends uniformly to $\gamma $ on this compact ball. Define \[  u_ i=u*\rho _{h_ i} +\delta _ i\bigl ((2r_ i/3)^2-|z-c_ i|^2\bigr ) \quad \text{on }B_ i.  \] Its complex Hessian is at least $\gamma -(A_ i/2)I$, hence at least $\Gamma $, since $\kappa \gamma \geq A_ i I$ in these coordinates. The same elementary radius estimates as in the Euclidean construction give \[  \begin{aligned}  u_ i& >u+\eta _ i& & \text{on }B(c_ i,r_ i/3),\\  u_ i& <u-\eta _ i& & \text{if }\sqrt7\, r_ i/3<|z-c_ i|<r_ i,\\  u_ i+\eta _ i& <u+e& & \text{on }B_ i. \end{aligned}  \] For the last inequality use $2\eta _ i+4\delta _ i r_ i^2/9=7\delta _ i r_ i^2/9<e$. At $x\in \Omega $, apply the fixed-parameter regularized maximum to the finitely many $u_ i(x)$ with $x\in B_ i$, and call the value $v(x)$. It is smooth near every point. Indeed an inner ball supplies a branch $u_ j-\eta _ j>u$ on a neighborhood of the point, while every branch whose domain boundary passes through the point satisfies $u_ i+\eta _ i<u$ in its nearby outer shell. Such branches may all be deleted by the operator's deletion property. Local finiteness then leaves one fixed finite set of smooth branches on a smaller neighborhood. The Hessian chain rule gives $H_ v\geq \Gamma $ intrinsically, since all branch lower bounds are the same tensor $\Gamma _ x$ in any coordinate system. The upper and lower operator bounds give $u\leq v\leq u+e$. Define $v=u$ on $X\setminus \Omega $. Because $e$ tends to zero at boundary points, this extension is continuous there. On $\Omega $ it is PSH, and its boundary limsup is $u$. The existing PSH boundary gluing proposition, applied to $\max \{ u,v\} =v$ on $\Omega $, therefore makes it PSH on all of $X$. Finally $H_ v\geq \Gamma \geq \gamma /2>0$ on $\Omega $, so it is strictly PSH there and satisfies the requested lower bound. The inequalities with $\lambda $ follow from $e\leq \lambda /2$. $\square$

title: 7.15 Integral leaves of constant-rank null distributions

section: 7.15 Integral leaves of constant-rank null distributions
text: Leaves in this section carry their intrinsic manifold topology. Their inclusion into the ambient manifold is an injective immersion; the image need not be an embedded submanifold. In a foliation chart it is the connected local plaques, rather than the entire intersection of a global leaf with the chart, that are fibers of a submersion. Proposition 7.15.1 (Frobenius) . 0E3D24D5541E Let $D$ be a constant-rank $C^ l$ real distribution on an open subset of $\mathbb R^ m$, where $1\leq l\leq \infty $. If the bracket of any two local $C^1$ sections is again in $D$, then there are local $C^ l$ coordinates in which $D$ is spanned by the first coordinate vectors. Its maximal connected integral leaves form a foliation by injectively immersed manifolds. Proof. We recall the local flow fact used in the argument. A $C^ l$ vector field $Z$ has a unique local $C^ l$ flow $F_ t(x)$, with inverse $F_{-t}$. On a compact coordinate ball, bound $|Z|$ by $M$ and $|\mathrm dZ|$ by $L$, and choose $T$ with $TM$ smaller than half the radius and $TL<1/2$. On continuous paths starting at a point in the inner ball, the operator $q\mapsto x+\int _0^ t Z(q(s))\, \mathrm ds$ maps the corresponding closed path ball to itself and contracts the supremum norm by at most $TL$. Its successive iterates converge geometrically to a solution; the same estimate gives uniqueness on this time interval, and hence the local group and inverse identities. Dependence on $x$ is $C^1$: the difference quotients satisfy the integral equation whose linear limit is $A(t)=I+\int _0^ t\mathrm dZ(F_ s(x))A(s)\, \mathrm ds$. Uniform continuity of $\mathrm dZ$ on the ball and the same integral estimate make these difference quotients converge to $A$. Repeated differentiation proves $C^ l$ dependence for larger $l$. The integral estimate may be iterated to give the bound $b(t)\leq c\sum _{j\geq 0}(L|t|)^ j/j!$ when $b(t)\leq c+L\int _0^{|t|}b(s)\, \mathrm ds$, so it also justifies these difference-quotient limits without an additional ODE theorem. Let the rank be $k$. The cases $k=0,m$ are immediate. After a real linear coordinate change at a fixed point, projection of $D$ to the first $k$ coordinates is an isomorphism nearby. Normalize a local frame to the form \[  Z_ i=\partial _{x_ i}+\sum _{a>k}b_{ia}(x)\partial _{x_ a}, \qquad 1\leq i\leq k.  \] The first $k$ coefficients of $[Z_ i,Z_ j]$ vanish, while the bracket belongs to $D$. The isomorphism of the projection implies $[Z_ i,Z_ j]=0$. Their local flows commute. To check this at $C^1$ regularity, put $M(t)=\mathrm dF_{i,t}|_ x$ and $Y(t)=Z_ j(F_{i,t}(x))$. The variational equation gives $M'=\mathrm dZ_ i(F_{i,t}(x))M$, while the zero bracket gives $Y'=\mathrm dZ_ i(F_{i,t}(x))Y$. Thus $M^{-1}Y$ is constant, so $F_{i,t}$ preserves $Z_ j$. Uniqueness of integral curves gives $F_{i,t}F_{j,s}=F_{j,s}F_{i,t}$ wherever both local compositions are defined. With the fixed point translated to zero, put \[  \Phi (t_1,\ldots ,t_ k,y) =F_{1,t_1}\circ \cdots \circ F_{k,t_ k}(0,\ldots ,0,y).  \] At zero its derivative is invertible. The inverse function theorem makes it a local $C^ l$ coordinate map, and flow commutation gives $\partial _{t_ i}\Phi =Z_ i\circ \Phi $. Its slices with fixed $y$ are the required local integral plaques. Join plaques by finite overlapping chains to obtain maximal connected leaves. The local normal form makes their plaques compatible, so these leaves are disjoint and cover the domain, with the indicated intrinsic manifold charts and immersion. They are Hausdorff because distinct points have disjoint ambient neighborhoods. They are second countable: use a countable foliation-chart cover of the ambient domain; a plaque meets another chart in at most countably many connected pieces, each lying in one plaque there. Starting with one plaque and iterating finite chains therefore reaches only countably many plaque charts covering its leaf. This completes the global leaf construction. $\square$ Proposition 7.15.2 . C2EBFD69CEA4 A $C^1$ real submanifold of $\mathbb C^ n$ whose tangent spaces are complex vector spaces is locally a complex submanifold. The same conclusion holds locally for an immersed real submanifold. Proof. At a fixed point let the complex tangent dimension be $k$ and choose a complex linear projection onto that tangent space. Its restriction to the submanifold has invertible real derivative, so the real inverse theorem writes a neighborhood as the graph of a $C^1$ map $g:W\subset \mathbb C^ k\to \mathbb C^{n-k}$. The graph of $\mathrm dg$ is a complex vector space at every point. This is equivalent to complex linearity of $\mathrm dg$, hence to $\bar\partial g=0$. The existing scalar distributional Cauchy–Riemann theorem makes $g$ holomorphic. The graph is therefore a complex submanifold. An immersion is an embedding on sufficiently small intrinsic coordinate neighborhoods, so the same argument applies there. $\square$ Theorem 7.15.3 . 8FE75D79B9CA Let $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ s$ be $C^ l$ complex-valued $(1,1)$-forms on an open subset $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, with $l\geq 1$. For real tangent vectors, let \[  D_ x=\{ v:\alpha _ j(v,w)=0\text{ for every real }w \text{ and every }j\} .  \] Assume that $D$ has constant dimension and that $\mathrm d\alpha _ j(X,Y,Z)=0$ whenever $X,Y$ lie in $D$. Then its maximal leaves form a $C^ l$ foliation by injectively immersed complex submanifolds, of complex dimension $\tfrac 12\dim _{\mathbb R}D$. In particular this holds for closed forms with constant-dimensional common nullspace. If the forms are $\mathrm dd^ c u_ j$ with $u_ j\in C^{l+2}(\Omega ,\mathbb C)$, then the real and imaginary parts of each $u_ j$ are pluriharmonic on each leaf. In any ambient holomorphic coordinates, all functions $\partial _{z_ a}\operatorname {Re}u_ j$ and $\partial _{z_ a}\operatorname {Im}u_ j$ restrict holomorphically to the leaves. Proof. For one form write $\alpha =(\mathrm i/2)\sum a_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$ and $A=(a_{jk})^{\mathsf T}$. With the Hermitian product linear in its first variable, its real nullspace is \[  N(\alpha )=\ker A\cap \ker A^*.  \] Indeed $\alpha (v,w)=0$ is equivalent to $\langle Av,w\rangle =\langle Aw,v\rangle $ for all $w$; applying this both to $w$ and to $\mathrm iw$ makes both sides zero. Thus $D$ is a complex vector space at every point. It is the kernel of the matrix obtained by stacking all $A_ j,A_ j^*$. Constant rank makes it a $C^ l$ distribution: near a point choose an invertible maximal minor and solve for its pivot variables in terms of the free ones to obtain a $C^ l$ frame. For local sections $X,Y$ of $D$ and any vector field $Z$, the formula for exterior differentiation gives $\mathrm d\alpha _ j(X,Y,Z)=-\alpha _ j([X,Y],Z)$, since all the other terms contain a null argument or derivatives of an identically zero pairing. The hypothesis therefore puts $[X,Y]$ in $D$. Frobenius gives real integral leaves, and their complex tangent spaces make them complex by the preceding proposition. For a potential, pullback to the leaf commutes with $\partial ,\bar\partial $. Its vanishing pulled-back $(1,1)$-form therefore says that both real and imaginary parts have zero complex Hessian on the leaf. They are pluriharmonic by the existing Hessian criterion. To check the gradient assertion, let $f$ be one of these real potentials and write a local holomorphic leaf parametrization $\psi $. The nullspace condition and Hermitian symmetry give \[  \partial _{\bar t_ b}(f_{z_ a}\circ \psi ) =\sum _ k f_{z_ a\bar z_ k}(\psi (t)) \overline{\partial _{t_ b}\psi _ k}=0.  \] This proves holomorphy. Let $p,q\geq 0$ with $p+q\leq n$ and assume everywhere that \[  \alpha ^ p\wedge \beta ^ q\ne 0,\qquad \alpha ^{p+1}=0,\qquad \alpha ^ p\wedge \beta ^{q+1}=0.  \] Here reducibility means $\ker A=\ker A^*$ for the coefficient matrix above. Then the common real nullspace has constant complex dimension $n-p-q$. Thus the preceding theorem applies if the forms are $C^1$ and their exterior derivatives satisfy its nullspace condition. Proof. The exterior-power expansion in the stated order is \[  \alpha ^ p=p!\, \frac{\mathrm i^{p^2}}{2^ p} \sum _{|J|=|K|=p}\det (a_{jk})_{j\in J,k\in K} \, \mathrm dz_ J\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ K.  \] It follows by expanding the product and moving all antiholomorphic factors past the later holomorphic factors; the phase is $(\mathrm i/2)^ p(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}=\mathrm i^{p^2}/2^ p$. Thus the first two assumptions imply $\operatorname {rank}A=p$. Reducibility splits the space orthogonally as its range $E$ and kernel $E^\perp $, with $A$ invertible on $E$. In these coordinates $\alpha ^ p$ is a nonzero multiple of the top complex volume on $E$. Consequently the other two wedge conditions say exactly that the compression $C=P_{E^\perp }B|_{E^\perp }$ of the Hermitian positive matrix of $\beta $ has rank $q$. For $v\in E^\perp $, positivity gives \[  Cv=0\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \langle Bv,v\rangle =0\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad Bv=0,  \] using a unitary eigenbasis of $B$. Hence $\ker A\cap \ker B=\ker C$ has dimension $n-p-q$. This is the common real nullspace since both forms are reducible. The argument includes $p=0$ or $q=0$ with the usual zeroth power. $\square$ In particular, a $C^3$ real plurisubharmonic function with constant complex Hessian rank $r$ has a null foliation of complex dimension $n-r$. The function is pluriharmonic along its leaves, and its ambient holomorphic partial derivatives restrict holomorphically. Rank $n-1$ gives Riemann surfaces. This follows directly from the constant-rank theorem, since $\mathrm dd^ c u$ is closed and semipositive. Example 7.15.5 . 849194DD5398 The semipositivity in the wedge criterion cannot be replaced by reducibility. In $\mathbb C^3$, put \[  \alpha =\frac{\mathrm i}{2}\mathrm dz_1\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_1, \qquad \beta =\frac{\mathrm i}{2} (\mathrm dz_1\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_2+ \mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_1+ \mathrm dz_3\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_3).  \] Both coefficient matrices are Hermitian, hence reducible, and $\alpha \wedge \beta \ne 0$, $\alpha ^2=0$ and $\alpha \wedge \beta ^2=0$. Nevertheless the matrix of $\beta $ is invertible, so the common nullspace is zero rather than a complex line. The lower-right compression of that matrix has rank one, whereas its kernel does not describe the kernel of the full indefinite matrix. For the corresponding potentials $u=|z_1|^2$ and $v=2\operatorname {Re}(z_1\bar z_2)+|z_3|^2$, there is no positive-dimensional complex leaf on which both are pluriharmonic and all their ambient holomorphic partial derivatives are holomorphic. An illustration of the intrinsic leaf convention is obtained on $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ by taking an irrational real $a$ and $h(z,w)=\log |w|-a\log |z|$. The smooth PSH function $h^2$ has complex Hessian $2(\partial h)\otimes \overline{\partial h}$ of constant rank one. Its leaves have parametrizations $t\mapsto (z_0\mathrm e^ t,w_0\mathrm e^{at})$. They are injective holomorphic immersions. Along $t=2\pi \mathrm i k$ the first coordinate is fixed and the second is dense on its circle; hence the leaf is not an embedded graph near a point, despite its nonzero first-coordinate tangent projection. This is why local plaques must be distinguished from entire global leaf intersections.
