title: 7.16 Relative extremals on bounded hyperconvex domains
search_title: Relative extremals on bounded hyperconvex domains
section: 7.16 Relative extremals on bounded hyperconvex domains
text: Let $n\geq 1$. For an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $E\subset \Omega $, write \[  h_{E,\Omega }=\sup \{ v\in \operatorname {PSH}(\Omega ):v\leq 0, \  v|_ E\leq -1\} , \qquad H_{E,\Omega }=h_{E,\Omega }^*.  \] This extends the existing ball notation. Taking the maximum with $-1$ does not change the supremum, so all competitors may be restricted to $[-1,0]$. We use the existing Bedford–Taylor products and their capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega $ on Borel sets, and outer capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*$ on arbitrary sets. We do not extend inner capacity subadditivity to arbitrary sets. All capacities may be infinite. Proposition 7.16.1 . 11F76749E371 The following properties hold. Set inclusion decreases $h$ and $H$; enlarging the ambient open set also decreases them wherever the smaller-domain function is defined. If $u\in \operatorname {PSH}(\Omega )$, $u\leq M$ on $\Omega $ and $u\leq m$ on $E$, for real numbers $m<M$, then \[  u\leq M+(M-m)h_{E,\Omega }.  \] If compact sets $K_ j\subset \Omega $ decrease to $K$, then $h_{K_ j,\Omega }\uparrow h_{K,\Omega }$ pointwise. Suppose $\Omega $ is bounded, connected and hyperconvex: it has a continuous negative PSH exhaustion $\rho $. For $E\Subset \Omega $, $h_{E,\Omega }$ and $H_{E,\Omega }$ tend to $0$ at every boundary point. If $K\Subset \Omega $ is compact and $H_{K,\Omega }=-1$ on $K$, then $h_{K,\Omega }=H_{K,\Omega }$ is continuous. In particular this holds if $K$ is a union of closed balls of positive radius. For any compact $K$, the raw extremal $h_{K,\Omega }$ is lower semicontinuous, and the continuous extremals of $K_\delta =\{ \operatorname {dist}(z,K)\leq \delta \} $ increase pointwise to it as $\delta \downarrow 0$ through sufficiently small radii. On an arbitrary open $\Omega $, $H_{K,\Omega }$ is maximal on $\Omega \setminus K$ for every compact $K\Subset \Omega $. Proof. The first assertions follow by inclusion of competitor families, and the two-constants inequality follows by applying the definition to $(u-M)/(M-m)$. Every competitor can be made strictly smaller than $-1$ on $K$ by subtracting a positive constant. If $v<-1$ on $K$, the open set $\{ v<-1\} $ contains all $K_ j$ for sufficiently large $j$: otherwise the decreasing compact sets $K_ j\setminus \{ v<-1\} $ would have nonempty intersection. Thus $v\leq h_{K_ j,\Omega }$ eventually. Take the supremum over these strict competitors to prove the second assertion. For the boundary claim choose $A>0$ with $A\rho \leq -1$ on $\overline E$. Then $A\rho \leq h_{E,\Omega }\leq H_{E,\Omega }\leq 0$. The exhaustion property implies $\rho \to 0$ at the boundary: for every $t<0$ its $t$-sublevel is relatively compact. This also gives the uniform boundary estimate needed below. If $H_ K=-1$ on $K$, the bounded PSH function $H_ K$ itself is a competitor, so $h_ K=H_ K$. Rescale $\rho $ to be at most $-1$ on $K$. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. For sufficiently small $\eta >0$, $K\subset \Omega _\eta $ and $\rho >-\varepsilon /2$ on $\Omega \setminus \Omega _\eta $, where $\Omega _\eta =\{ \operatorname {dist}(z,\partial \Omega )>\eta \} $. The radial convolutions $(H_ K)_ s$ are continuous PSH on $\Omega _\eta $ for $s<\eta $. They decrease to $-1$ on $K$; their continuous restrictions to the compact set $K$ therefore converge uniformly there by Dini. Choose $s$ with $(H_ K)_ s-\varepsilon \leq -1$ on $K$. The function \[  v_\varepsilon = \begin{cases}  \max \{ \rho ,(H_ K)_ s-\varepsilon \} ,& \Omega _\eta ,\\  \rho ,& \Omega \setminus \Omega _\eta \end{cases}  \] is continuous PSH: near the new interface the second branch is at most $-\varepsilon $ and $\rho >-\varepsilon /2$. It is a competitor and $H_ K-\varepsilon \leq v_\varepsilon \leq H_ K$, also outside $\Omega _\eta $. Thus $H_ K$ is continuous. We record the local ball barrier used for regularity of unions of balls. If $N$ is any complex norm, $0<r<R$, and $D=\{ N(z-a)<R\} $, the extremal of the closed inner norm ball is \[  \max \{ -1,\log (N(z-a)/R)/\log (R/r)\} .  \] Indeed $\log N$ is PSH. To verify this without an additional norm theorem, take a real supporting functional $L$ of $N$ at a nonzero point and put $\ell (z)=L(z)-iL(iz)$. Then $\ell $ is complex linear and $|\ell (z)|=\sup _{|\lambda |=1}L(\lambda z)\leq N(z)$; equality holds at the supporting point. Hence $\log N$ is the supremum of the PSH functions $\log |\ell |$ and is already upper semicontinuous, including its value $-\infty $ at $0$. The displayed candidate is therefore PSH and continuous. On each line $a+tb$, $N(b)=1$, any competitor is bounded above by it by harmonic comparison on $r<|t|<R$. This proves the formula. If $b\in \partial K$ belongs to a closed ball $\overline{B(a,r)}\subset K$, choose $R>r$ with $\overline{B(a,R)}\subset \Omega $. Such a choice is possible because the inner closed ball is compact in $\Omega $. Monotonicity bounds $h_ K$ above by the preceding local continuous extremal, which equals $-1$ at $b$. Consequently $H_ K=-1$ on $K$, and the continuity criterion applies. Each sufficiently small $K_\delta $ is a compact union of closed balls contained in $\Omega $. Its continuous extremals increase to $h_ K$ by the second assertion, proving lower semicontinuity. Finally, choose increasing bounded competitors $v_ j$ tending almost everywhere to $H_ K$ by the existing Choquet selection. On a ball $D\Subset \Omega \setminus K$ replace $v_ j$ by its homogeneous PSH balayage. The replacements still equal $v_ j$ on $K$ and are nonpositive by the maximum principle. They remain competitors, increase, and lie between $v_ j$ and $H_ K$, so they tend almost everywhere to $H_ K$. Increasing BT continuity shows that its Monge–Ampere measure vanishes on $D$. The existing bounded maximality theorem proves the assertion. $\square$ Proposition 7.16.2 . 0667BDD8ADC8 Let $\Omega $ be bounded and hyperconvex, let $K\Subset \Omega $ be compact, and let open subsets $\Omega _ j$ increase to $\Omega $, with $K\subset \Omega _1$. Then $h_{K,\Omega _ j}\downarrow h_{K,\Omega }$ pointwise. Proof. Choose a continuous negative PSH exhaustion $\psi $ with $\psi <-1$ on $K$. For $0<\varepsilon <1$, the closure of $\{ \psi <-\varepsilon \} $ lies in $\Omega _ j$ for all large $j$. If $v$ is a competitor on such $\Omega _ j$, glue $\max \{ v-\varepsilon ,\psi \} $ on this sublevel to $\psi $ elsewhere. The boundary inequality follows from $v\leq 0$. The result is a competitor on $\Omega $. At a point in the sublevel it is at least $v-\varepsilon $; outside, $\psi \geq -\varepsilon \geq v-\varepsilon $ wherever $v$ is defined. Consequently $h_{K,\Omega _ j}-\varepsilon \leq h_{K,\Omega }$ on $\Omega _ j$. Monotonicity gives the opposite inequality without $\varepsilon $. Let $j\to \infty $, then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$ Proposition 7.16.3 . 86AFECC63967 Let $\Omega $ be a bounded connected open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$. For $E\subset \Omega $ the following conditions are equivalent: $H_{E,\Omega }=0$; $E$ is pluripolar; $\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*(E)=0$; and $E$ is contained in the pole set of one negative PSH function on $\Omega $. Countable unions of sets with zero extremal again have zero extremal. If $E_ j$ increase to $E$, then $H_{E_ j,\Omega }\downarrow H_{E,\Omega }$ pointwise. Proof. If $H_ E=0$, the raw supremum is zero almost everywhere by the existing envelope theorem. Choose $a$ where $h_ E(a)=0$, and competitors $v_ j\in [-1,0]$ with $v_ j(a)>-2^{-j}$. Their sum has decreasing partial sums and is finite at $a$; subtracting $1$ from its limit gives a proper strictly negative PSH function which is $-\infty $ on $E$. Conversely, if such a function $v$ exists, $tv$ is a competitor for every $t>0$. Thus $h_ E=0$ almost everywhere and $H_ E=0$. A negative global pole function proves local pluripolarity. For the reverse implication use the existing Josefson theorem on $\mathbb C^ n$, after the existing locality theorem extends pluripolarity from $\Omega $ to $\mathbb C^ n$. The resulting global PSH function is bounded above on $\overline\Omega $; subtract a larger constant to make it negative on $\Omega $. Its restriction is not identically $-\infty $ because it is locally integrable. The existing local pole-capacity theorem and a compact exhaustion give outer capacity zero in $\Omega $ for every pluripolar set. Conversely, if that capacity is zero, fix a ball $B\Subset \Omega $. On compact subsets of $B$, the existing local comparability of capacities bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*$ by a constant times $\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*$. Exhaust $B$ by such compact sets to see that $E\cap B$ has zero outer capacity in $B$. The existing ball zero-capacity theorem makes it pluripolar there. This proves all four equivalences. Countable unions follow from the existing countable-union theorem for pluripolar sets. For increasing $E_ j$, the bounded PSH functions $H_{E_ j}$ decrease to a bounded PSH function $H\geq H_ E$. Each set $E_ j\cap \{ H_{E_ j}>-1\} $ is pluripolar by the existing envelope discrepancy theorem. Outside their countable union $F$, the limit equals $-1$ on $E$. Choose a negative PSH function $v$ with poles on $F$ by the equivalences just proved. Then $H+tv$ is a competitor for $E$ for every $t>0$. Let $t\downarrow 0$ at the almost-everywhere finite points of $v$ and use uniqueness of canonical PSH representatives to get $H\leq H_ E$ everywhere. CF1B00103D5B Let $\Omega '\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be open and $E\subset \Omega '$. If $f:\Omega \to \Omega '$ is holomorphic, then $h_{E,\Omega '}\circ f\leq h_{f^{-1}(E),\Omega }$. If it has full target rank generically on every component of $\Omega $, then also $H_{E,\Omega '}\circ f\leq H_{f^{-1}(E),\Omega }$. For a proper surjective holomorphic map between open subsets of the same $\mathbb C^ n$, both inequalities are equalities. Proof. Pull back bounded competitors to prove the raw inequality. On the full-rank locus $f$ is locally open by the holomorphic submersion normal form, so taking upper regularizations commutes there with composition. The two regularizations are bounded PSH functions and the exceptional analytic set is null. Their equality there extends everywhere by uniqueness of canonical representatives, proving the regularized inequality. A proper map as in the last assertion has finite fibers: they are compact analytic subsets of a Euclidean domain. It is open by the existing finite-map theorem. For a bounded PSH competitor $v$ upstairs the fiber maximum $w(y)=\max _{f(x)=y}v(x)$ is PSH. To recall the checked argument, off the proper analytic critical image it is the maximum of finitely many inverse-branch pullbacks. For continuous $v$ it is continuous by properness and openness, so the existing bounded analytic-removal theorem extends this PSH function. For general $v$, on a relatively compact target neighborhood convolve $v$ decreasingly on a neighborhood of its compact inverse image. The continuous fiber maxima decrease to $w$, since each fiber is finite; hence $w$ is PSH. These local arguments agree on overlaps. It is a downstairs competitor and $v\leq w\circ f$, proving the reverse raw inequality. Openness also makes upper regularization commute with composition at every point, giving the regularized equality. $\square$ Theorem 7.16.5 . 08DA18E923C1 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be bounded, connected and hyperconvex. For every $E\Subset \Omega $, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*(E) =\int _\Omega (dd^ cH_{E,\Omega })^ n<\infty .  \] For compact $K\Subset \Omega $ the measure is carried by $K\cap \{ H_ K=-1\} $ and $\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (K)=\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*(K)$. In particular $H_ K>-1$ everywhere on $K$ implies capacity zero. Outer capacity is continuous on decreasing compact sets and on increasing sequences of arbitrary subsets of $\Omega $, with extended values allowed. Proof. For compact $K$, Proposition 7.16.1 proves that the measure of $H_ K$ is carried by $K$. Its subset $K\cap \{ H_ K>-1\} $ lies in the exceptional set $\{ h_ K<H_ K\} $, whose outer capacity is zero by the existing envelope theorem, valid on every bounded open set. The competitor $H_ K+1$ shows that this subset also has zero measure for $(dd^ cH_ K)^ n$. Thus the support assertion holds. The existing ball proof of the compact capacity formula now applies with the barrier $A\rho $ in place of the quadratic ball barrier. Here are its two inequalities. Since $H_ K+1$ is a capacity competitor, $\int (dd^ cH_ K)^ n\leq \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (K)$. For a capacity competitor $0\leq v\leq 1$, let $w=(1-2\varepsilon )(v-1)-\varepsilon $, $0<\varepsilon <1/2$. Then $-1+\varepsilon \leq w\leq -\varepsilon $, the set $K\cap \{ H_ K\geq w\} $ is null for $(dd^ cw)^ n$, and the boundary comparison between $H_ K$ and $w$ gives \[  (1-2\varepsilon )^ n\int _ K(dd^ cv)^ n \leq \int _{\{ H_ K<w\} }(dd^ cH_ K)^ n \leq \int _\Omega (dd^ cH_ K)^ n.  \] Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and take the supremum over $v$. For $K_ j\downarrow K$, raw extremal convergence implies $H_{K_ j}\uparrow H_ K$ almost everywhere. Increasing BT continuity and the fixed compact support $K_1$ give convergence of their total masses, and hence of their capacities. Apply this to $K_\delta \downarrow K$: $\operatorname {Cap}^*(K)\leq \operatorname {Cap}(\operatorname {Int}K_\delta ) \leq \operatorname {Cap}(K_\delta )$ proves equality of inner and outer capacity on $K$. All these numbers are finite by local CLN. For an open $G\Subset \Omega $, exhaust $G$ by compact sets $K_ j$ with $K_ j\subset \operatorname {Int}K_{j+1}$. Then $H_{K_ j}\downarrow h_ G=H_ G$: the limit is PSH, equals $-1$ on $G$, and the two competitor inequalities identify it. Decreasing BT continuity, common compact support $\overline G$ and the existing Borel capacity continuity from below give \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (G)=\int _\Omega (dd^ cH_ G)^ n.  \] For arbitrary $E\Subset \Omega $, choose a relatively compact open neighborhood $U$ of $\overline E$. Monotonicity gives $H_ U\leq H_ E$. If $E\ne \varnothing $ we may assume $U$ nonempty; then $H_ U<0$ on the connected domain by the maximum principle, since it is $-1$ on $U$. Thus $(1+\varepsilon )H_ U<H_ E$ everywhere. Both extremals tend to zero on the boundary, so comparison gives \[  \int _\Omega (dd^ cH_ E)^ n \leq (1+\varepsilon )^ n\int _\Omega (dd^ cH_ U)^ n =(1+\varepsilon )^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (U).  \] The same argument works for any relatively compact open neighborhood of $E$. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and take the infimum. Such neighborhoods suffice in the outer-capacity definition, by intersecting with one fixed relatively compact neighborhood of $\overline E$. For the reverse inequality, choose bounded competitors $v_ j\uparrow H_ E$ almost everywhere, and replace them by $\max \{ v_ j,A\rho \} $, where $A\rho \leq -1$ on $\overline E$. They still have the same limit and boundary value zero. Put $G_ j=\{ (1+1/j)v_ j<-1\} $. These open sets decrease, contain $E$, and have closures in the fixed compact sublevel $\{ A\rho \leq -1/2\} \Subset \Omega $, since $v_ j\geq v_1\geq A\rho $. Their extremals increase, and \[  (1+1/j)v_ j\leq H_{G_ j}\leq H_ E  \] identifies their limit almost everywhere with $H_ E$. All their measures are supported in one compact subset of $\Omega $; increasing BT continuity therefore gives \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*(E)\leq \lim _ j\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (G_ j) =\lim _ j\int _\Omega (dd^ cH_{G_ j})^ n =\int _\Omega (dd^ cH_ E)^ n.  \] For $E=\varnothing $, all functions and capacities are zero, so the formula also holds. We finish with increasing arbitrary sets. First suppose each $E_ j$ is relatively compact, without assuming a common compact neighborhood, and let $E=\bigcup _ jE_ j$. The exceptional sets $E_ j\cap \{ H_{E_ j}>-1\} $ are pluripolar by the existing envelope discrepancy theorem. Their union $F$ has outer capacity zero by the existing pluripolar capacity theorem on bounded open sets. Choose open $G\supset F$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (G)<\varepsilon $. For $0<\delta <1$ put $U_ j=\{ H_{E_ j}<-1+\delta \} $ and $V_ j=U_ j\cup G$. The $U_ j$ are relatively compact by the boundary barrier, increase with $j$, and $E_ j\subset V_ j$. If $H_{E_ j}=0$, then $U_ j$ is empty and the following inequality is immediate. Otherwise $H_{E_ j}<0$ everywhere, so total-mass comparison applies with a factor tending to one. Since $H_{E_ j}/(1-\delta )\leq H_{U_ j}$, the same total-mass comparison as above and the extremal formula give \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (U_ j) \leq (1-\delta )^{-n}\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*(E_ j).  \] The $V_ j$ are open, so Borel subadditivity and continuity from below yield \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*(E) \leq \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega \Bigl (\bigcup _ jV_ j\Bigr ) \leq \varepsilon +(1-\delta )^{-n} \lim _ j\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*(E_ j).  \] Let $\varepsilon ,\delta \downarrow 0$; the opposite inequality is monotonicity. For general increasing $E_ j$, take a compact exhaustion $L_ j$ with increasing interiors and apply the proved case to $E_ j\cap L_ j$. These are relatively compact, increase to $E$, and their capacities are bounded by those of $E_ j$. This proves the asserted continuity, including infinite limits. $\square$ Already in the unit disc this capacity can be infinite on the whole domain. The logarithmic profile above and its radial derivative give, in Pome's normalization, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\mathbb D}(\overline{\mathbb D(0,r)}) =\frac{1}{2\log (1/r)}\longrightarrow \infty \qquad (r\uparrow 1).  \] Indeed its distributional Laplacian has total mass $2\pi /\log (1/r)$, and in one complex dimension $4\pi \, dd^ c u=\Delta u$ as measures. This is why the capacity and its continuity statements use values in $[0,\infty ]$.

title: Proposition 7.16.1
section: 7.16 Relative extremals on bounded hyperconvex domains
text: Proposition 7.16.1 . 11F76749E371 The following properties hold. Set inclusion decreases $h$ and $H$; enlarging the ambient open set also decreases them wherever the smaller-domain function is defined. If $u\in \operatorname {PSH}(\Omega )$, $u\leq M$ on $\Omega $ and $u\leq m$ on $E$, for real numbers $m<M$, then \[  u\leq M+(M-m)h_{E,\Omega }.  \] If compact sets $K_ j\subset \Omega $ decrease to $K$, then $h_{K_ j,\Omega }\uparrow h_{K,\Omega }$ pointwise. Suppose $\Omega $ is bounded, connected and hyperconvex: it has a continuous negative PSH exhaustion $\rho $. For $E\Subset \Omega $, $h_{E,\Omega }$ and $H_{E,\Omega }$ tend to $0$ at every boundary point. If $K\Subset \Omega $ is compact and $H_{K,\Omega }=-1$ on $K$, then $h_{K,\Omega }=H_{K,\Omega }$ is continuous. In particular this holds if $K$ is a union of closed balls of positive radius. For any compact $K$, the raw extremal $h_{K,\Omega }$ is lower semicontinuous, and the continuous extremals of $K_\delta =\{ \operatorname {dist}(z,K)\leq \delta \} $ increase pointwise to it as $\delta \downarrow 0$ through sufficiently small radii. On an arbitrary open $\Omega $, $H_{K,\Omega }$ is maximal on $\Omega \setminus K$ for every compact $K\Subset \Omega $. Proof. The first assertions follow by inclusion of competitor families, and the two-constants inequality follows by applying the definition to $(u-M)/(M-m)$. Every competitor can be made strictly smaller than $-1$ on $K$ by subtracting a positive constant. If $v<-1$ on $K$, the open set $\{ v<-1\} $ contains all $K_ j$ for sufficiently large $j$: otherwise the decreasing compact sets $K_ j\setminus \{ v<-1\} $ would have nonempty intersection. Thus $v\leq h_{K_ j,\Omega }$ eventually. Take the supremum over these strict competitors to prove the second assertion. For the boundary claim choose $A>0$ with $A\rho \leq -1$ on $\overline E$. Then $A\rho \leq h_{E,\Omega }\leq H_{E,\Omega }\leq 0$. The exhaustion property implies $\rho \to 0$ at the boundary: for every $t<0$ its $t$-sublevel is relatively compact. This also gives the uniform boundary estimate needed below. If $H_ K=-1$ on $K$, the bounded PSH function $H_ K$ itself is a competitor, so $h_ K=H_ K$. Rescale $\rho $ to be at most $-1$ on $K$. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. For sufficiently small $\eta >0$, $K\subset \Omega _\eta $ and $\rho >-\varepsilon /2$ on $\Omega \setminus \Omega _\eta $, where $\Omega _\eta =\{ \operatorname {dist}(z,\partial \Omega )>\eta \} $. The radial convolutions $(H_ K)_ s$ are continuous PSH on $\Omega _\eta $ for $s<\eta $. They decrease to $-1$ on $K$; their continuous restrictions to the compact set $K$ therefore converge uniformly there by Dini. Choose $s$ with $(H_ K)_ s-\varepsilon \leq -1$ on $K$. The function \[  v_\varepsilon = \begin{cases}  \max \{ \rho ,(H_ K)_ s-\varepsilon \} ,& \Omega _\eta ,\\  \rho ,& \Omega \setminus \Omega _\eta \end{cases}  \] is continuous PSH: near the new interface the second branch is at most $-\varepsilon $ and $\rho >-\varepsilon /2$. It is a competitor and $H_ K-\varepsilon \leq v_\varepsilon \leq H_ K$, also outside $\Omega _\eta $. Thus $H_ K$ is continuous. We record the local ball barrier used for regularity of unions of balls. If $N$ is any complex norm, $0<r<R$, and $D=\{ N(z-a)<R\} $, the extremal of the closed inner norm ball is \[  \max \{ -1,\log (N(z-a)/R)/\log (R/r)\} .  \] Indeed $\log N$ is PSH. To verify this without an additional norm theorem, take a real supporting functional $L$ of $N$ at a nonzero point and put $\ell (z)=L(z)-iL(iz)$. Then $\ell $ is complex linear and $|\ell (z)|=\sup _{|\lambda |=1}L(\lambda z)\leq N(z)$; equality holds at the supporting point. Hence $\log N$ is the supremum of the PSH functions $\log |\ell |$ and is already upper semicontinuous, including its value $-\infty $ at $0$. The displayed candidate is therefore PSH and continuous. On each line $a+tb$, $N(b)=1$, any competitor is bounded above by it by harmonic comparison on $r<|t|<R$. This proves the formula. If $b\in \partial K$ belongs to a closed ball $\overline{B(a,r)}\subset K$, choose $R>r$ with $\overline{B(a,R)}\subset \Omega $. Such a choice is possible because the inner closed ball is compact in $\Omega $. Monotonicity bounds $h_ K$ above by the preceding local continuous extremal, which equals $-1$ at $b$. Consequently $H_ K=-1$ on $K$, and the continuity criterion applies. Each sufficiently small $K_\delta $ is a compact union of closed balls contained in $\Omega $. Its continuous extremals increase to $h_ K$ by the second assertion, proving lower semicontinuity. Finally, choose increasing bounded competitors $v_ j$ tending almost everywhere to $H_ K$ by the existing Choquet selection. On a ball $D\Subset \Omega \setminus K$ replace $v_ j$ by its homogeneous PSH balayage. The replacements still equal $v_ j$ on $K$ and are nonpositive by the maximum principle. They remain competitors, increase, and lie between $v_ j$ and $H_ K$, so they tend almost everywhere to $H_ K$. Increasing BT continuity shows that its Monge–Ampere measure vanishes on $D$. The existing bounded maximality theorem proves the assertion. $\square$

text: Theorem 7.16.5 . 08DA18E923C1 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be bounded, connected and hyperconvex. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and take the infimum. Such neighborhoods suffice in the outer-capacity definition, by intersecting with one fixed relatively compact neighborhood of $\overline E$. The exceptional sets $E_ j\cap \{ H_{E_ j}>-1\} $ are pluripolar by the existing envelope discrepancy theorem. Their union $F$ has outer capacity zero by the existing pluripolar capacity theorem on bounded open sets. Choose open $G\supset F$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (G)<\varepsilon $. For $0<\delta <1$ put $U_ j=\{ H_{E_ j}<-1+\delta \} $ and $V_ j=U_ j\cup G$. The $U_ j$ are relatively compact by the boundary barrier, increase with $j$, and $E_ j\subset V_ j$. Since $H_{E_ j}/(1-\delta )\leq H_{U_ j}$, the same total-mass comparison as above and the extremal formula give \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (U_ j) \leq (1-\delta )^{-n}\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*(E_ j).  \] The $V_ j$ are open, so Borel subadditivity and continuity from below yield \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*(E) \leq \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega \Bigl (\bigcup _ jV_ j\Bigr ) \leq \varepsilon +(1-\delta )^{-n} \lim _ j\operatorname {Cap}_\Omega ^*(E_ j).  \] Let $\varepsilon ,\delta \downarrow 0$; the opposite inequality is monotonicity. Use the existing plurifine topology and its thin-complement neighborhood criterion. Write $h_{A,\Omega }$ for the raw relative extremal, with values in $[-1,0]$. We use the checked Bedford–Taylor amplification: if $A$ is plurithin at an accumulation point $a$, a global PSH function $b$, finite at $a$ and locally bounded off $a$, tends to $-\infty $ along $A\setminus \{ a\} $ at $a$. Its existing proof also gives $b(z)=c\log |z-a|+C$ outside a ball, with $c>0$; division by $c$ gives logarithmic growth with coefficient one. Theorem 5.50.1 . 0313727814DD Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be bounded and open, $a\in \Omega $, and $A\subset \Omega $. Suppose $a$ is a Euclidean accumulation point of $A\setminus \{ a\} $. E34D223CA44D Let $F\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be closed and plurithin at $a$, let $V$ be a Euclidean neighborhood of $a$, and let $v\leq 0$ be PSH on $V\setminus F$. otin F$, use the plurifine continuity of PSH functions. If $a$ is an isolated point of $F$, bounded-above point removability gives the same conclusion. title: 16.30 Polynomial descriptions of logarithmic envelopes
text:
Use the existing class $\mathcal L=\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb C^ n):u\leq \log ^+|z|+C_ u\} $ and write $V_ A=\sup \{ u\in \mathcal L:u|_ A\leq 0\} $. The obstacle is pointwise and $V_ A$ denotes the raw supremum. The existing projective correspondence and logarithmic pole theorem retain their canonical entries. Proposition 16.30.1 . F5C5050EEDEB For a complex norm $N$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, $r>0$, and $K=\{ N(z-a)\leq r\} $, \[  V_ K(z)=\log ^+ rac{N(z-a)}r.  \] For every polynomial $P$ of degree $d\geq 1$, \[  |P(z)|\leq \| P\| _ K\max \{ 1,N(z-a)/r\} ^ d.  \] Proof. The existing complex-norm support argument proves $\log N$ PSH, so the displayed profile is a competitor. For any other competitor $u$ and a point $w$ with $N(w-a)>r$, put $R=N(w-a)/r$ and consider \[  q(\zeta )=u(a+\zeta ^{-1}(w-a))+\log |\zeta |-\log R, \qquad 0<|\zeta |<R.  \] This is SH or identically $-\infty $, is bounded above at zero by the growth condition, and has boundary upper limits at most zero. Point removability and the maximum principle give $q(1)\leq 0$. Inside $K$ the constraint and the zero competitor give $V_ K=0$. Apply the result to $d^{-1}\log (|P|/\| P\| _ K)$; the zero polynomial is immediate. $\square$ Proposition 16.30.2 . F983146D5FCD For decreasing compact sets $K_ j\downarrow K$, $V_{K_ j}\uparrow V_ K$ pointwise. For compact $K$, $V_ K$ is lower semicontinuous. If $K
e \varnothing $ and $V_ K^*=0$ on $K$, then $V_ K=V_ K^*$ is continuous. In particular, for nonempty compact $K$ and $\eta >0$, the closed thickening $K_\eta =\{ \operatorname {dist}(z,K)\leq \eta \} $ has a continuous extremal, and $V_{K_\eta }\uparrow V_ K$ as $\eta \downarrow 0$. Proof. If $u\in \mathcal L$, $u\leq 0$ on $K$, and $\epsilon >0$, upper semicontinuity and compactness put $K_ j$ in $\{ u<\epsilon \} $ for large $j$. Thus $u-\epsilon \leq V_{K_ j}$, proving the first assertion. If $K$ is empty, some $K_ j$ is empty and all the assertions concerning this limit have the evident value $+\infty $. Radial convolution $u_ t$ remains in $\mathcal L$ and decreases to $u$. For small $t$, $u_ t<\epsilon $ on $K$: the decreasing continuous functions have no common point of the compact sets $K\cap \{ u_ t\geq \epsilon \} $. Hence $u_ t-\epsilon $ is a continuous competitor. Letting $t,\epsilon \downarrow 0$ expresses $V_ K$ as the supremum of its continuous competitors, proving lower semicontinuity. Suppose $K
e \varnothing $ and $V_ K^*=0$ on $K$. Near one point of $K$, $V_ K$ is bounded above on a ball, by the definition of this regularization. Applying the norm-ball bound to every competitor, after a common constant subtraction, bounds the entire family above locally and gives its regularization growth at most one. Thus $V_ K^*$ is PSH and in $\mathcal L$. Its constraint on $K$ makes it a competitor, so $V_ K^*=V_ K$; combine upper and lower semicontinuity. Every point of $K_\eta $ belongs to a closed radius-$\eta $ ball centered on $K$ and contained in $K_\eta $. The norm-ball formula, including continuity at that point, gives $V_{K_\eta }^*=0$ there. This proves the remaining assertions without a polynomial representation as input. $\square$ Theorem 16.30.3 . 19CBC18237E5 Let $h:\mathbb C^ m	o [0,\infty )$ be PSH, not identically zero, with $h(\lambda z)=|\lambda |h(z)$. Then \[  h=\left(\limsup _{j	o \infty }|Q_ j|^{1/j}ight)^*  \] for homogeneous polynomials $Q_ j$ of degree exactly $j$ whenever nonzero. Conversely any such finite-valued, nonzero regularized limit has these properties. In particular $\log h\in \mathcal L(\mathbb C^ m)$: upper semicontinuity on the unit sphere and homogeneity give $h\leq C|z|$. If, in addition, $h$ is continuous and vanishes only at zero, then \[  h(z)=\sup \{ |Q(z)|^{1/d}:Q	ext{ homogeneous of degree }d\geq 1, \  |Q|^{1/d}\leq h	ext{ on }\mathbb C^ m\} .  \] Proof. The checked homogeneous-gauge argument gives $\log h$ PSH: apply the product-tube minimum principle to $h(e^ w z)-\operatorname {Re}w$; its infimum in $\operatorname {Re}w$ is $1+\log h(z)$, including value $-\infty $ at zeros. Hence $D=\{ h<1\} $ is a balanced pseudoconvex domain containing zero, by the checked gauge/Oka criterion. It is proper because $h
ot\equiv 0$. The domain-of-existence theorem gives $f\in \mathcal O(D)$ with no extension from a local component across its boundary. Its Taylor expansion at zero groups into homogeneous polynomials $f=\sum _{j\geq 0}Q_ j$. The expansion is normal on $D$: for a compact $L\subset D$, a fixed dilation greater than one of its circular hull is still compact in $D$, and Cauchy's formula in the dilation parameter bounds the terms by a geometric sequence on $L$. The coefficient formula agrees near zero with the Taylor polynomial and then everywhere by the identity theorem. Cauchy's bounds on a ball at zero make $j^{-1}\log |Q_ j|$ locally uniformly bounded above on all of $\mathbb C^ m$. Let $q$ be their regularized limsup. The same bounds on every circular orbit inside $D$ give $q\leq \log h$, also where $h=0$. The functions $q$ and $e^ q$ are logarithmically homogeneous and homogeneous of degree one, respectively. On $\{ q<0\} $ Hartogs' lemma gives local geometric bounds on the Taylor terms, so the series extends $f$ normally there. This balanced domain is connected and contains $D$. If it were larger, it would contradict the domain-of-existence property. The case $q\equiv -\infty $ would extend $f$ to all of $\mathbb C^ m$ and gives the same contradiction. Thus $\{ q<0\} =D$; homogeneity gives $e^ q=h$ everywhere, including the zero directions. For the converse, finite-valued regularized limsup implies pointwise boundedness of $|Q_ j|^{1/j}$. The closed sets where all these functions are at most an integer cover $\mathbb C^ m$. Baire gives a ball with one common bound. The norm-ball polynomial inequality then gives local uniform upper bounds everywhere. Upper-envelope/limsup closure gives PSH for the regularized root limit; its homogeneity follows from the exact matching degrees. It is nonzero by hypothesis. For the pointwise supremum assume $h$ continuous with zero set $\{ 0\} $. Its sublevels $K_ t=\{ h\leq t\} $, $t<1$, are compact. Fix $a$ with $h(a)=1$. The points $s_ k a$ for distinct $s_ k\uparrow 1$ form a closed discrete subset of $D$. The checked interpolation theorem gives $f(s_ k a)=k$. If $f=\sum Q_ j$ is its homogeneous Taylor expansion, the one-variable series $f(\lambda a)$ has radius precisely one; otherwise it would be bounded near $\lambda =1$. Thus $\limsup _ j|Q_ j(a)|^{1/j}=1$. For $0<t<1$, put $M_ t=\sup _{K_ t}|f|>0$. Cauchy's parameter formula on $K_ t$ gives $|Q_ j(z)|\leq M_ t(h(z)/t)^ j$ for every $z$, by homogeneity. Consequently $t^ jQ_ j/M_ t$ is admissible and its root values at $a$ have limsup $t$. Let $t\uparrow 1$. The opposite inequality is the constraint itself; homogeneity handles every nonzero point, and both sides vanish at zero. This proof uses discrete interpolation directly and needs no additional polynomial-approximation theorem. $\square$ Theorem 16.30.4 . FBAB51FD36FB A function $u:\mathbb C^ n	o [-\infty ,\infty )$, not identically $-\infty $, belongs to $\mathcal L$ if and only if \[  u=\left(\limsup _{j	o \infty }j^{-1}\log |P_ j|ight)^* \quad 	ext{for polynomials }\deg P_ j\leq j.  \] Proof. For $u\in \mathcal L$, homogenize by $\log H(\zeta ,z)=\log |\zeta |+u(z/\zeta )$ off $\{ \zeta =0\} $. The growth bound makes this PSH function locally bounded above there, so canonical zero-set extension gives $\log H$ globally. Its exponential is nonnegative PSH, homogeneous of degree one and not zero. Apply the preceding theorem and set $P_ j(z)=Q_ j(1,z)$. Near $\zeta =1$ use the coordinates $(\zeta ,w=z/\zeta )$: the identity $j^{-1}\log |Q_ j(\zeta ,z)|=\log |\zeta |+j^{-1}\log |P_ j(w)|$ shows explicitly that regularized limsup restricts to the claimed regularized limsup on the slice. Conversely Baire gives a ball on which all $|P_ j|^{1/j}$ are bounded. The degree bound and the norm-ball inequality give a common logarithmic majorant of slope one everywhere. The regularized limsup is therefore PSH, and has that growth. Its assumed nondegeneracy excludes the constant $-\infty $. $\square$ Theorem 16.30.5 . E171A0405847 For nonempty compact $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$, set \[  \Phi _ K(z)=\sup \{ |P(z)|^{1/\deg P}:\deg P\geq 1,\  \| P\| _ K\leq 1\} .  \] Then $V_ K=\log \Phi _ K=V_{\widehat K}$ for the polynomial hull $\widehat K$. For nonempty compact $E\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $F\subset \mathbb C^ m$, \[  V_{E	imes F}(z,w)=\max \{ V_ E(z),V_ F(w)\} .  \] Proof. The definition gives $\log \Phi _ K\leq V_ K$. Also $\Phi _ K\geq 1$: normalize polynomials $1+\epsilon z_1$ on $K$ and let $\epsilon 	o 0$. Fix $\eta >0$ and put $u=V_{K_\eta }$, which is continuous, nonnegative and in $\mathcal L$, by the earlier norm-ball and regularity results. For $j\geq 2$ define, off $\zeta =0$, \[  H_ j(\zeta ,z)=|\zeta |\exp ((1-j^{-1})u(z/\zeta )) +j^{-1}|(\zeta ,z)|,  \] and put $H_ j(0,z)=j^{-1}|z|$. The growth bound makes the first term tend to zero locally uniformly as $\zeta 	o 0$: it is bounded by $C_ j|\zeta |^{1/j}|(\zeta ,z)|^{1-1/j}$. Thus $H_ j$ is continuous, homogeneous of degree one, positive off zero and PSH. To see the last assertion, its logarithm off the hyperplane is the convex log-sum-exp of the two PSH logarithms; bounded-above zero-set extension agrees with the displayed continuous values. Exponentiation preserves PSH. On $K$, $H_ j(1,z)=1+j^{-1}|(1,z)|\leq 1+\epsilon $ for large $j$. For each homogeneous polynomial $Q$ of degree $d$ with $|Q|^{1/d}\leq H_ j$, the polynomial $P(z)=Q(1,z)$ has degree at most $d$ and norm at most $(1+\epsilon )^ d$ on $K$. Therefore $|P(z)|^{1/d}\leq (1+\epsilon )\Phi _ K(z)$. This also holds for constant $P$, since $\Phi _ K\geq 1$; for positive degree less than $d$, use $x^{1/d}\leq \max (1,x^{1/\deg P})$. Take the pointwise homogeneous supremum to obtain $H_ j(1,z)\leq (1+\epsilon )\Phi _ K(z)$. Let $j	o \infty $, then $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ and $\eta \downarrow 0$. This proves $e^{V_ K}\leq \Phi _ K$, without assuming regularized and raw envelopes agree on $K$. Polynomial norms agree on $K$ and $\widehat K$, proving the hull identity. For the product identity let $G_ r$ and $H_ r$ be the unions of open radius-$r$ polydiscs centered on $E$ and $F$. Gram–Schmidt on monomials ordered by total degree gives orthonormal polynomial bases $p_\alpha $ and $q_ eta $ in their polynomial $L^2$ spaces, with degrees $|\alpha |$ and $| eta |$. The polydisc submean inequality gives $\| p_\alpha \| _ E\leq (\pi r^2)^{-n/2}$ and $\| q_ eta \| _ F\leq (\pi r^2)^{-m/2}$. Hence, writing $A=\Phi _ E(z)$ and $B=\Phi _ F(w)$, each product at $(z,w)$ is bounded by $C_ r A^{|\alpha |}B^{| eta |}$, including constants. For a polynomial $P$ of total degree $k$, only products with $|\alpha |+| eta |\leq k$ occur in its orthogonal expansion: they form a basis of that degree filtration. Every coefficient is bounded by $\| P\| _{L^2(G_ r	imes H_ r)}$. If $A,B$ are finite, it follows that \[  |P(z,w)|\leq C'_ r inom {n+m+k}{n+m} \| P\| _{G_ r	imes H_ r}\max (A,B)^ k.  \] Apply this to $P^ t$, take the $kt$-th root and let $t	o \infty $; the binomial factor has subexponential growth. Then let $r\downarrow 0$. For $\| P\| _{E	imes F}\leq 1$ the limiting norm bound is at most one, so $|P(z,w)|^{1/k}\leq \max (A,B)$. If either $A$ or $B$ is infinite, the upper bound is automatic. Pulling back polynomials from either factor gives the reverse inequality for $\Phi $; take logarithms. $\square$ Proposition 16.30.6 . F453BE749AEC For a nonempty compact $K$, $V_ K$ is continuous if and only if for every $t>1$ there are an open neighborhood $U$ of $K$ and $M>0$ such that \[  \| P\| _ U\leq M t^{\deg P}\| P\| _ K  \] for every polynomial $P$. In that case one can take $M=1$. Proof. If $V_ K$ is continuous, it vanishes on $K$, so $V_ K<\log t$ on some bounded open neighborhood $U$. The polynomial identity gives the estimate with $M=1$ for nonzero $P$ of positive $K$-norm. If a nonzero polynomial vanished on $K$, its arbitrary scalar multiples would force $\Phi _ K$ to be infinite off its zero set, contradicting finite $V_ K$. Constants and the zero polynomial satisfy the estimate directly. Conversely apply the given estimate to $P^ k$, take the $k$-th root and let $k	o \infty $. It follows that $\| P\| _ U\leq t^{\deg P}\| P\| _ K$. Thus $\Phi _ K\leq t$ on $U$ and $V_ K^*\leq \log t$ on $K$. Let $t\downarrow 1$ and use $V_ K\geq 0$ to obtain $V_ K^*=0$ there. The compact-envelope regularity proposition proves continuity everywhere. $\square$

F5C5050EEDEB For a complex norm $N$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, $r>0$, and $K=\{ N(z-a)\leq r\} $, \[  V_ K(z)=\log ^+\frac{N(z-a)}r.  \] For every polynomial $P$ of degree $d\geq 1$, \[  |P(z)|\leq \| P\| _ K\max \{ 1,N(z-a)/r\} ^ d.  \] Proof. The existing complex-norm support argument proves $\log N$ PSH, so the displayed profile is a competitor. For any other competitor $u$ and a point $w$ with $N(w-a)>r$, put $R=N(w-a)/r$ and consider \[  q(\zeta )=u(a+\zeta ^{-1}(w-a))+\log |\zeta |-\log R, \qquad 0<|\zeta |<R.  \] This is SH or identically $-\infty $, is bounded above at zero by the growth condition, and has boundary upper limits at most zero. Point removability and the maximum principle give $q(1)\leq 0$. Inside $K$ the constraint and the zero competitor give $V_ K=0$. Apply the result to $d^{-1}\log (|P|/\| P\| _ K)$; the zero polynomial is immediate. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.30.2
text: Proposition 16.30.2 . F983146D5FCD For decreasing compact sets $K_ j\downarrow K$, $V_{K_ j}\uparrow V_ K$ pointwise. For compact $K$, $V_ K$ is lower semicontinuous. If $K\ne \varnothing $ and $V_ K^*=0$ on $K$, then $V_ K=V_ K^*$ is continuous. In particular, for nonempty compact $K$ and $\eta >0$, the closed thickening $K_\eta =\{ \operatorname {dist}(z,K)\leq \eta \} $ has a continuous extremal, and $V_{K_\eta }\uparrow V_ K$ as $\eta \downarrow 0$. Proof. If $u\in \mathcal L$, $u\leq 0$ on $K$, and $\epsilon >0$, upper semicontinuity and compactness put $K_ j$ in $\{ u<\epsilon \} $ for large $j$. Thus $u-\epsilon \leq V_{K_ j}$, proving the first assertion. If $K$ is empty, some $K_ j$ is empty and all the assertions concerning this limit have the evident value $+\infty $. Radial convolution $u_ t$ remains in $\mathcal L$ and decreases to $u$. For small $t$, $u_ t<\epsilon $ on $K$: the decreasing continuous functions have no common point of the compact sets $K\cap \{ u_ t\geq \epsilon \} $. Hence $u_ t-\epsilon $ is a continuous competitor. Letting $t,\epsilon \downarrow 0$ expresses $V_ K$ as the supremum of its continuous competitors, proving lower semicontinuity. Suppose $K\ne \varnothing $ and $V_ K^*=0$ on $K$. Near one point of $K$, $V_ K$ is bounded above on a ball, by the definition of this regularization. Applying the norm-ball bound to every competitor, after a common constant subtraction, bounds the entire family above locally and gives its regularization growth at most one. Thus $V_ K^*$ is PSH and in $\mathcal L$. Its constraint on $K$ makes it a competitor, so $V_ K^*=V_ K$; combine upper and lower semicontinuity. Every point of $K_\eta $ belongs to a closed radius-$\eta $ ball centered on $K$ and contained in $K_\eta $. The norm-ball formula, including continuity at that point, gives $V_{K_\eta }^*=0$ there. This proves the remaining assertions without a polynomial representation as input. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.30.3
text: Theorem 16.30.3 . 19CBC18237E5 Let $h:\mathbb C^ m\to [0,\infty )$ be PSH, not identically zero, with $h(\lambda z)=|\lambda |h(z)$. Then \[  h=\left(\limsup _{j\to \infty }|Q_ j|^{1/j}\right)^*  \] for homogeneous polynomials $Q_ j$ of degree exactly $j$ whenever nonzero. Conversely any such finite-valued, nonzero regularized limit has these properties. In particular $\log h\in \mathcal L(\mathbb C^ m)$: upper semicontinuity on the unit sphere and homogeneity give $h\leq C|z|$. If, in addition, $h$ is continuous and vanishes only at zero, then \[  h(z)=\sup \{ |Q(z)|^{1/d}:Q\text{ homogeneous of degree }d\geq 1, \  |Q|^{1/d}\leq h\text{ on }\mathbb C^ m\} .  \] Proof. The checked homogeneous-gauge argument gives $\log h$ PSH: apply the product-tube minimum principle to $h(e^ w z)-\operatorname {Re}w$; its infimum in $\operatorname {Re}w$ is $1+\log h(z)$, including value $-\infty $ at zeros. Hence $D=\{ h<1\} $ is a balanced pseudoconvex domain containing zero, by the checked gauge/Oka criterion. It is proper because $h\not\equiv 0$. The domain-of-existence theorem gives $f\in \mathcal O(D)$ with no extension from a local component across its boundary. Its Taylor expansion at zero groups into homogeneous polynomials $f=\sum _{j\geq 0}Q_ j$. The expansion is normal on $D$: for a compact $L\subset D$, a fixed dilation greater than one of its circular hull is still compact in $D$, and Cauchy's formula in the dilation parameter bounds the terms by a geometric sequence on $L$. The coefficient formula agrees near zero with the Taylor polynomial and then everywhere by the identity theorem. Cauchy's bounds on a ball at zero make $j^{-1}\log |Q_ j|$ locally uniformly bounded above on all of $\mathbb C^ m$. Let $q$ be their regularized limsup. The same bounds on every circular orbit inside $D$ give $q\leq \log h$, also where $h=0$. The functions $q$ and $e^ q$ are logarithmically homogeneous and homogeneous of degree one, respectively. On $\{ q<0\} $ Hartogs' lemma gives local geometric bounds on the Taylor terms, so the series extends $f$ normally there. This balanced domain is connected and contains $D$. If it were larger, it would contradict the domain-of-existence property. The case $q\equiv -\infty $ would extend $f$ to all of $\mathbb C^ m$ and gives the same contradiction. Thus $\{ q<0\} =D$; homogeneity gives $e^ q=h$ everywhere, including the zero directions. For the converse, finite-valued regularized limsup implies pointwise boundedness of $|Q_ j|^{1/j}$. The closed sets where all these functions are at most an integer cover $\mathbb C^ m$. Baire gives a ball with one common bound. The norm-ball polynomial inequality then gives local uniform upper bounds everywhere. Upper-envelope/limsup closure gives PSH for the regularized root limit; its homogeneity follows from the exact matching degrees. It is nonzero by hypothesis. For the pointwise supremum assume $h$ continuous with zero set $\{ 0\} $. Its sublevels $K_ t=\{ h\leq t\} $, $t<1$, are compact. Fix $a$ with $h(a)=1$. The points $s_ k a$ for distinct $s_ k\uparrow 1$ form a closed discrete subset of $D$. The checked interpolation theorem gives $f(s_ k a)=k$. If $f=\sum Q_ j$ is its homogeneous Taylor expansion, the one-variable series $f(\lambda a)$ has radius precisely one; otherwise it would be bounded near $\lambda =1$. Thus $\limsup _ j|Q_ j(a)|^{1/j}=1$. For $0<t<1$, put $M_ t=\sup _{K_ t}|f|>0$. Cauchy's parameter formula on $K_ t$ gives $|Q_ j(z)|\leq M_ t(h(z)/t)^ j$ for every $z$, by homogeneity. Consequently $t^ jQ_ j/M_ t$ is admissible and its root values at $a$ have limsup $t$. Let $t\uparrow 1$. The opposite inequality is the constraint itself; homogeneity handles every nonzero point, and both sides vanish at zero. This proof uses discrete interpolation directly and needs no additional polynomial-approximation theorem. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.30.4
text: Theorem 16.30.4 . FBAB51FD36FB A function $u:\mathbb C^ n\to [-\infty ,\infty )$, not identically $-\infty $, belongs to $\mathcal L$ if and only if \[  u=\left(\limsup _{j\to \infty }j^{-1}\log |P_ j|\right)^* \quad \text{for polynomials }\deg P_ j\leq j.  \] Proof. For $u\in \mathcal L$, homogenize by $\log H(\zeta ,z)=\log |\zeta |+u(z/\zeta )$ off $\{ \zeta =0\} $. The growth bound makes this PSH function locally bounded above there, so canonical zero-set extension gives $\log H$ globally. Its exponential is nonnegative PSH, homogeneous of degree one and not zero. Apply the preceding theorem and set $P_ j(z)=Q_ j(1,z)$. Near $\zeta =1$ use the coordinates $(\zeta ,w=z/\zeta )$: the identity $j^{-1}\log |Q_ j(\zeta ,z)|=\log |\zeta |+j^{-1}\log |P_ j(w)|$ shows explicitly that regularized limsup restricts to the claimed regularized limsup on the slice. Conversely Baire gives a ball on which all $|P_ j|^{1/j}$ are bounded. The degree bound and the norm-ball inequality give a common logarithmic majorant of slope one everywhere. The regularized limsup is therefore PSH, and has that growth. Its assumed nondegeneracy excludes the constant $-\infty $. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.30.5
text: Theorem 16.30.5 . E171A0405847 For nonempty compact $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$, set \[  \Phi _ K(z)=\sup \{ |P(z)|^{1/\deg P}:\deg P\geq 1,\  \| P\| _ K\leq 1\} .  \] Then $V_ K=\log \Phi _ K=V_{\widehat K}$ for the polynomial hull $\widehat K$. For nonempty compact $E\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $F\subset \mathbb C^ m$, \[  V_{E\times F}(z,w)=\max \{ V_ E(z),V_ F(w)\} .  \] Proof. The definition gives $\log \Phi _ K\leq V_ K$. Also $\Phi _ K\geq 1$: normalize polynomials $1+\epsilon z_1$ on $K$ and let $\epsilon \to 0$. Fix $\eta >0$ and put $u=V_{K_\eta }$, which is continuous, nonnegative and in $\mathcal L$, by the earlier norm-ball and regularity results. For $j\geq 2$ define, off $\zeta =0$, \[  H_ j(\zeta ,z)=|\zeta |\exp ((1-j^{-1})u(z/\zeta )) +j^{-1}|(\zeta ,z)|,  \] and put $H_ j(0,z)=j^{-1}|z|$. The growth bound makes the first term tend to zero locally uniformly as $\zeta \to 0$: it is bounded by $C_ j|\zeta |^{1/j}|(\zeta ,z)|^{1-1/j}$. Thus $H_ j$ is continuous, homogeneous of degree one, positive off zero and PSH. To see the last assertion, its logarithm off the hyperplane is the convex log-sum-exp of the two PSH logarithms; bounded-above zero-set extension agrees with the displayed continuous values. Exponentiation preserves PSH. On $K$, $H_ j(1,z)=1+j^{-1}|(1,z)|\leq 1+\epsilon $ for large $j$. For each homogeneous polynomial $Q$ of degree $d$ with $|Q|^{1/d}\leq H_ j$, the polynomial $P(z)=Q(1,z)$ has degree at most $d$ and norm at most $(1+\epsilon )^ d$ on $K$. Therefore $|P(z)|^{1/d}\leq (1+\epsilon )\Phi _ K(z)$. This also holds for constant $P$, since $\Phi _ K\geq 1$; for positive degree less than $d$, use $x^{1/d}\leq \max (1,x^{1/\deg P})$. Take the pointwise homogeneous supremum to obtain $H_ j(1,z)\leq (1+\epsilon )\Phi _ K(z)$. Let $j\to \infty $, then $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ and $\eta \downarrow 0$. This proves $e^{V_ K}\leq \Phi _ K$, without assuming regularized and raw envelopes agree on $K$. Polynomial norms agree on $K$ and $\widehat K$, proving the hull identity. For the product identity let $G_ r$ and $H_ r$ be the unions of open radius-$r$ polydiscs centered on $E$ and $F$. Gram–Schmidt on monomials ordered by total degree gives orthonormal polynomial bases $p_\alpha $ and $q_\beta $ in their polynomial $L^2$ spaces, with degrees $|\alpha |$ and $|\beta |$. The polydisc submean inequality gives $\| p_\alpha \| _ E\leq (\pi r^2)^{-n/2}$ and $\| q_\beta \| _ F\leq (\pi r^2)^{-m/2}$. Hence, writing $A=\Phi _ E(z)$ and $B=\Phi _ F(w)$, each product at $(z,w)$ is bounded by $C_ r A^{|\alpha |}B^{|\beta |}$, including constants. For a polynomial $P$ of total degree $k$, only products with $|\alpha |+|\beta |\leq k$ occur in its orthogonal expansion: they form a basis of that degree filtration. Every coefficient is bounded by $\| P\| _{L^2(G_ r\times H_ r)}$. If $A,B$ are finite, it follows that \[  |P(z,w)|\leq C'_ r\binom {n+m+k}{n+m} \| P\| _{G_ r\times H_ r}\max (A,B)^ k.  \] Apply this to $P^ t$, take the $kt$-th root and let $t\to \infty $; the binomial factor has subexponential growth. Then let $r\downarrow 0$. For $\| P\| _{E\times F}\leq 1$ the limiting norm bound is at most one, so $|P(z,w)|^{1/k}\leq \max (A,B)$. If either $A$ or $B$ is infinite, the upper bound is automatic. Pulling back polynomials from either factor gives the reverse inequality for $\Phi $; take logarithms. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.30.6
text: Proposition 16.30.6 . F453BE749AEC For a nonempty compact $K$, $V_ K$ is continuous if and only if for every $t>1$ there are an open neighborhood $U$ of $K$ and $M>0$ such that \[  \| P\| _ U\leq M t^{\deg P}\| P\| _ K  \] for every polynomial $P$. In that case one can take $M=1$. Proof. If $V_ K$ is continuous, it vanishes on $K$, so $V_ K<\log t$ on some bounded open neighborhood $U$. The polynomial identity gives the estimate with $M=1$ for nonzero $P$ of positive $K$-norm. If a nonzero polynomial vanished on $K$, its arbitrary scalar multiples would force $\Phi _ K$ to be infinite off its zero set, contradicting finite $V_ K$. Constants and the zero polynomial satisfy the estimate directly. Conversely apply the given estimate to $P^ k$, take the $k$-th root and let $k\to \infty $. It follows that $\| P\| _ U\leq t^{\deg P}\| P\| _ K$. Thus $\Phi _ K\leq t$ on $U$ and $V_ K^*\leq \log t$ on $K$. Let $t\downarrow 1$ and use $V_ K\geq 0$ to obtain $V_ K^*=0$ there. The compact-envelope regularity proposition proves continuity everywhere. $\square$

title: 16.31 Logarithmic families and a fixed-ball capacity
search_title: Logarithmic families and a fixed-ball capacity
section: 16.31 Logarithmic families and a fixed-ball capacity
text: Use the canonical logarithmic growth class $\mathcal L$ and the raw extremals $V_ E$; use the existing Josefson theorem with upper growth $\log ^+|z|$. Thus a set is pluripolar exactly when it is contained in the pole set of a member of $\mathcal L$. This equivalence and its countable-union assertion keep their existing entries. Theorem 16.31.1 . 62CEBBF93786 Let $\mathcal U\subset \mathcal L$ be nonempty and put $F=\sup _{u\in \mathcal U}u$. If $\{ F<\infty \} $ is non-pluripolar, then $\mathcal U$ is locally uniformly bounded above and $F^*\in \mathcal L$. For any $E\subset \mathbb C^ n$, either $E$ is pluripolar and $V_ E^*\equiv +\infty $, or $V_ E^*\in \mathcal L$. Proof. If local uniform bounds fail, choose a closed ball $B=\overline{B(a,r)}$ and $u_ j\in \mathcal U$ with $M_ j=\sup _ Bu_ j\geq 2^ j$. The norm-ball formula gives \[  w_ j=u_ j-M_ j\leq p:=\log ^+(|z-a|/r)\quad \hbox{on }\mathbb C^ n.  \] There is $z_0$ with $\limsup _ jw_ j(z_0)>-\infty $. Otherwise Hartogs' lemma, using the common local upper bound $p$, would give $\sup _ Bw_ j\to -\infty $, contrary to its value zero. Pass to a subsequence with $w_ j(z_0)\geq -C$, retaining $M_ j\geq 2^ j$ after relabeling. The sum $w=\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}w_ j$ is PSH on the whole space and finite at $z_0$: on each ball subtract a constant from every $w_ j$ to make the series decrease, then use its finite value at $z_0$ on a larger connected ball. It satisfies $w\leq p$ and hence belongs to $\mathcal L$. At any point where $F(z)<\infty $, \[  \sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}w_ j(z) \leq \Bigl (\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}\Bigr )F(z)-N\longrightarrow -\infty .  \] The case $F(z)=-\infty $ is immediate as well. Thus $\{ F<\infty \} $ is pluripolar, a contradiction. Once local bounds hold, a common bound $M$ on one ball gives $F\leq M+p$ by the same formula. The upper-envelope theorem proves $F^*\in \mathcal L$. If $E$ is non-pluripolar, the extremal family is finite (indeed zero) on $E$, so the first assertion applies. If $E$ is pluripolar, let $b\in \mathcal L$ have poles on $E$. Every $b+C$ is a competitor; their supremum is infinite wherever $b$ is finite, hence almost everywhere. Its regularization is identically infinite. $\square$ Proposition 16.31.2 . A76B9D558430 For bounded $E$ and pluripolar $P$, $V_{E\cup P}^*=V_ E^*$. If $E_ j\uparrow E$ with bounded union, then $V_{E_ j}^*\downarrow V_ E^*$ pointwise. For arbitrary $E$, the points $a\in E$ at which $V_ E$ is not continuous form a pluripolar set. Proof. If $E$ is pluripolar, so is $E\cup P$, and both regularizations are infinite. Otherwise choose a logarithmic pole $b$ on $P$, subtracting a constant so that $b\leq 0$ on the bounded set $E$. For every competitor $u$ of $V_ E$, \[  u_\epsilon =\frac{u+\epsilon b}{1+\epsilon }  \] remains in $\mathcal L$ and is nonpositive on $E\cup P$. It tends to $u$ almost everywhere, giving $u\leq V_{E\cup P}^*$ everywhere by canonical PSH representatives. Supremum and regularization give one inequality; monotonicity gives the other. Applying this to $E\setminus P$ also proves invariance on deleting a pluripolar subset of a bounded obstacle. No unnormalized slope-$(1+\epsilon )$ sum is used. For increasing sets, if all $E_ j$ are pluripolar, so is their union and all values are infinite. Otherwise discard finitely many indices so every $E_ j$ is non-pluripolar. Enclose $E$ in a closed ball $B$. The decreasing sequence $V_{E_ j}^*$ is bounded below by $V_ B$ and above by $V_{E_1}^*$. Its limit $v$ is PSH in $\mathcal L$. For each $j$, the canonical envelope discrepancy theorem makes $E_ j\cap \{ V_{E_ j}^*>0\} $ pluripolar. Off their countable union $P$, we have $v\leq 0$ on $E$. Polar obstacle invariance therefore gives $v\leq V_{E\setminus P}^*=V_ E^*$; monotonicity gives equality. Finally, if arbitrary $E$ is pluripolar, any subset of it is pluripolar. Otherwise the family theorem gives $V_ E^*\in \mathcal L$, and $\{ V_ E<V_ E^*\} $ is pluripolar by the canonical discrepancy theorem. At $a\in E$ outside this set we have $0=V_ E(a)=V_ E^*(a)$. Since $0\leq V_ E\leq V_ E^*$, upper semicontinuity of the last function proves continuity of the raw envelope at $a$. $\square$ Theorem 16.31.3 . E215D05E52EC Fix a closed Euclidean ball $B$ of positive radius. For arbitrary $E$ put \[  \alpha _ B(E)=\exp \bigl (-\sup _ B V_ E^*\bigr ),\qquad e^{-\infty }=0.  \] Then $0\leq \alpha _ B\leq 1$, its zero sets are exactly the pluripolar sets, and it is monotone. It is continuous on increasing sequences with bounded union and on decreasing sequences of compact sets. Consequently its restriction to the subsets of any bounded open set is a generalized capacity with these three continuity/monotonicity axioms. Proof. The bounds, zero sets and monotonicity follow from the family theorem and $V_ E\geq 0$. For $E_ j\uparrow E$ with bounded union, the preceding proposition gives decreasing upper semicontinuous functions on the compact test ball. Their suprema decrease to the supremum of their limit: if the limit were smaller, points of maximum have a convergent subsequence and upper semicontinuity of each fixed earlier function gives a contradiction. If the union is non-pluripolar, countable-union polarity permits discarding finitely many infinite terms; otherwise every capacity is zero. Exponentiation proves increasing continuity. Let $K_ j\downarrow K$ be compact and set $u_ j=V_{K_ j}^*$. If any $K_ j$ is pluripolar then $K$ is pluripolar and all later capacities vanish. Otherwise the $u_ j$ are nonnegative finite PSH functions increasing with $j$. The raw compact-limit theorem gives $V_{K_ j}\uparrow V_ K$, whence $(\sup _ j u_ j)^*=V_ K^*$, with the value $+\infty $ allowed. Write $B^\circ $ for the open test ball. For any PSH function $u$ defined near $B$, $\sup _ Bu=\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B^\circ }u$. The submean inequality proves the assertion at interior points. At a boundary point, small balls have an asymptotically positive fraction inside $B^\circ $; if $u$ exceeded the interior supremum there, upper semicontinuity bounds the remaining fraction by $u$'s value plus an arbitrarily small error, contradicting the submean inequality. If $\sup _ j\sup _ Bu_ j$ is infinite, then so is $\sup _ BV_ K^*$ by monotonicity, and the desired limit follows. If it is finite, the increasing family is uniformly bounded on $B^\circ $. There its regularized supremum equals $V_ K^*$ and agrees with the pointwise supremum almost everywhere by the local upper-envelope theorem. This local bound on $V_ K^*$, followed by the global norm-ball majorant for its raw competitors, makes $V_ K^*$ a finite PSH function on a neighborhood of $B$. The interior/boundary supremum identity therefore applies to it as well. Thus \[  \sup _ BV_ K^* =\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B^\circ }\sup _ j u_ j =\sup _ j\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B^\circ }u_ j =\sup _ j\sup _ Bu_ j.  \] Exponentiation now proves decreasing compact continuity, including the case of a pluripolar intersection. $\square$ Proposition 16.31.4 . 4146861A3795 Define \[  \gamma (E)=\limsup _{|z|\to \infty }(V_ E^*(z)-\log |z|), \qquad c(E)=e^{-\gamma (E)}.  \] Use $e^{-\infty }=0$ and $e^{+\infty }=+\infty $. Then $c$ is monotone, vanishes exactly on pluripolar sets, and is continuous on increasing sequences with bounded union. For the unit test ball, $\alpha _{\overline B(0,1)}(E)\leq c(E)$. Proof. If $E$ is non-pluripolar, the growth bound on $V_ E^*$ makes $\gamma (E)$ bounded above, so $c(E)>0$; the polar case has $V_ E^*\equiv +\infty $ and $c(E)=0$. Monotonicity is immediate from the obstacle inequalities. For non-pluripolar $E$, put $\chi =\log (1+|z|^2)$ and use the canonical correspondence to extend $p_ E=V_ E^*-\chi /2$ to a $\tfrac 12\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-PSH function on $\mathbb P^ n$. For the hyperplane at infinity $H$, canonical extension and compactness give $\gamma (E)=\sup _ Hp_ E$: $\chi /2-\log |z|\to 0$ at infinity, every sequence approaching $H$ obeys the upper bound by upper semicontinuity, and the canonical limsup realizes every boundary value. Let $E_ j\uparrow E$ have bounded union. If all $E_ j$ are pluripolar, all capacities are zero. Otherwise discard finitely many indices and use the preceding extremal continuity. The corresponding $p_{E_ j}$ decrease on $\mathbb P^ n$, and are bounded below by the bounded projective potential of one enclosing norm ball. Their limit is therefore a proper PSH potential, equals $p_ E$ on the affine chart, and hence equals its canonical extension everywhere. Suprema on the compact $H$ decrease to $\sup _ Hp_ E$ by the same compact upper semicontinuity argument as above. This proves the asserted continuity. Finally, for non-pluripolar $E$, set $M=\sup _{\overline B(0,1)}V_ E^*$. The global norm-ball formula gives $V_ E^*\leq M+\log ^+|z|$. Thus $\gamma (E)\leq M$ and the claimed inequality follows; for pluripolar $E$ both sides are zero. $\square$

Their suprema decrease to the supremum of their limit: if the limit were smaller, points of maximum have a convergent subsequence and upper semicontinuity of each fixed earlier function gives a contradiction. If the union is non-pluripolar, countable-union polarity permits discarding finitely many infinite terms; otherwise every capacity is zero. Exponentiation proves increasing continuity. Let $K_ j\downarrow K$ be compact and set $u_ j=V_{K_ j}^*$. If any $K_ j$ is pluripolar then $K$ is pluripolar and all later capacities vanish. Otherwise the $u_ j$ are nonnegative finite PSH functions increasing with $j$. The raw compact-limit theorem gives $V_{K_ j}\uparrow V_ K$, whence $(\sup _ j u_ j)^*=V_ K^*$, with the value $+\infty $ allowed. Write $B^\circ $ for the open test ball. For any PSH function $u$ defined near $B$, $\sup _ Bu=\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B^\circ }u$. The submean inequality proves the assertion at interior points. At a boundary point, small balls have an asymptotically positive fraction inside $B^\circ $; if $u$ exceeded the interior supremum there, upper semicontinuity bounds the remaining fraction by $u$'s value plus an arbitrarily small error, contradicting the submean inequality. If $\sup _ j\sup _ Bu_ j$ is infinite, then so is $\sup _ BV_ K^*$ by monotonicity, and the desired limit follows. If it is finite, the increasing family is uniformly bounded on $B^\circ $. There its regularized supremum equals $V_ K^*$ and agrees with the pointwise supremum almost everywhere by the local upper-envelope theorem. This local bound on $V_ K^*$, followed by the global norm-ball majorant for its raw competitors, makes $V_ K^*$ a finite PSH function on a neighborhood of $B$. The interior/boundary supremum identity therefore applies to it as well. Thus \[  \sup _ BV_ K^* =\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B^\circ }\sup _ j u_ j =\sup _ j\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{B^\circ }u_ j =\sup _ j\sup _ Bu_ j.  \] Exponentiation now proves decreasing compact continuity, including the case of a pluripolar intersection. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.31.4
section: 16.31 Logarithmic families and a fixed-ball capacity
text: Proposition 16.31.4 . 4146861A3795 Define \[  \gamma (E)=\limsup _{|z|\to \infty }(V_ E^*(z)-\log |z|), \qquad c(E)=e^{-\gamma (E)}.  \] Use $e^{-\infty }=0$ and $e^{+\infty }=+\infty $. Then $c$ is monotone, vanishes exactly on pluripolar sets, and is continuous on increasing sequences with bounded union. For the unit test ball, $\alpha _{\overline B(0,1)}(E)\leq c(E)$. Proof. If $E$ is non-pluripolar, the growth bound on $V_ E^*$ makes $\gamma (E)$ bounded above, so $c(E)>0$; the polar case has $V_ E^*\equiv +\infty $ and $c(E)=0$. Monotonicity is immediate from the obstacle inequalities. For non-pluripolar $E$, put $\chi =\log (1+|z|^2)$ and use the canonical correspondence to extend $p_ E=V_ E^*-\chi /2$ to a $\tfrac 12\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-PSH function on $\mathbb P^ n$. For the hyperplane at infinity $H$, canonical extension and compactness give $\gamma (E)=\sup _ Hp_ E$: $\chi /2-\log |z|\to 0$ at infinity, every sequence approaching $H$ obeys the upper bound by upper semicontinuity, and the canonical limsup realizes every boundary value. Let $E_ j\uparrow E$ have bounded union. If all $E_ j$ are pluripolar, all capacities are zero. Otherwise discard finitely many indices and use the preceding extremal continuity. The corresponding $p_{E_ j}$ decrease on $\mathbb P^ n$, and are bounded below by the bounded projective potential of one enclosing norm ball. Their limit is therefore a proper PSH potential, equals $p_ E$ on the affine chart, and hence equals its canonical extension everywhere. Suprema on the compact $H$ decrease to $\sup _ Hp_ E$ by the same compact upper semicontinuity argument as above. This proves the asserted continuity. Finally, for non-pluripolar $E$, set $M=\sup _{\overline B(0,1)}V_ E^*$. The global norm-ball formula gives $V_ E^*\leq M+\log ^+|z|$. Thus $\gamma (E)\leq M$ and the claimed inequality follows; for pluripolar $E$ both sides are zero. $\square$

section: 16.32 Maps and regularity of global extremals
text: Use the existing raw global extremal $V_ E$, raw relative extremal $h_{E,\Omega }\in [-1,0]$ and their upper regularizations. For bounded $E$ write $K=\widehat{\overline E}$, the polynomial hull of its compact closure. All dimensions and polynomial degrees below are positive. Theorem 16.32.1 . 68FB8247AB5A Let $f:\mathbb C^ n\to \mathbb C^ n$ be holomorphic and let $\alpha ,\beta $ be positive integers. The following are equivalent: $f$ is polynomial of degree at most $\beta $, and $\liminf _{|z|\to \infty }|f(z)|/|z|^\alpha >0$; $f$ is proper and, for every $E\subset \mathbb C^ n$, \[  \alpha V_{f^{-1}E}\leq V_ E\circ f\leq \beta V_{f^{-1}E}.  \] If $\alpha =\beta =d$, these conditions are also equivalent to $f$ being polynomial of degree at most $d$ with degree-$d$ homogeneous part $f_ d$ satisfying $f_ d^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $. In that case every component has degree $d$, and $V_ E\circ f=dV_{f^{-1}E}$. Proof. The growth lower bound makes $f$ proper, and the checked finite/open proper-map theorem makes it surjective. If $u\in \mathcal L$ is nonpositive on $f^{-1}E$, the fiber maximum $v(y)=\alpha \max _{f(x)=y}u(x)$ is PSH. The growth lower bound gives $v(y)\leq \log ^+|y|+C$, so $v\in \mathcal L$ and $v\leq 0$ on $E$. Thus $\alpha u\leq V_ E\circ f$. Conversely, for a competitor $u$ of $V_ E$, the degree upper bound gives $\beta ^{-1}u\circ f\in \mathcal L$ and makes it a competitor for $f^{-1}E$. Take both suprema. For the reverse implication put $E=\overline B(0,1)$ and $A=f^{-1}E$. Properness and surjectivity make $A$ compact with nonempty interior. Thus $V_ A^*\in \mathcal L$. The upper inequality and norm-ball formula give $\log ^+|f(z)|\leq \beta (\log ^+|z|+C)$. Cauchy's coefficient estimates on growing polydiscs force every Taylor coefficient of degree greater than $\beta $ to vanish. Enclose $A$ in $\overline B(0,R)$. The other inequality gives $\alpha \log ^+(|z|/R)\leq \log ^+|f(z)|$, proving the growth lower bound. When the two exponents are $d$, uniform leading-term asymptotics on the unit sphere give $|f_ d(\xi )|\geq c>0$. Conversely this positive minimum gives the lower growth bound, since $f-f_ d=O(|z|^{d-1})$. The leading map is then proper and surjective itself; no component can be identically zero, so every original component has degree $d$. $\square$ Proposition 16.32.2 . 94014DB9102B Let $f_ j$ have positive degrees $d_ j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, and suppose their highest homogeneous parts have no common zero except zero. For $A=\{ z:|f_ j(z)|\leq 1\text{ for all }j\} $, \[  V_ A(z)=\max _ j d_ j^{-1}\log ^+|f_ j(z)|.  \] In particular $V_ A$ is continuous. Invertible affine maps also preserve raw extremals by composition. Proof. Take a common multiple $D$ of the $d_ j$ and put $g_ j=f_ j^{D/d_ j}$. The preceding theorem applies with degree $D$ to $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ n)$. The closed polydisc is the unit ball of the complex maximum norm, whose extremal is $\max _ j\log ^+|z_ j|$. Pull it back and divide by $D$. The affine assertion is the degree-one case of the same theorem. $\square$ Proposition 16.32.3 . D63431730901 Let $E$ be bounded and $\Omega $ a bounded open neighborhood of $K$. There is $m>0$ with \[  m(h_{E,\Omega }+1)\leq V_ E\quad \hbox{on }\Omega .  \] If $E$ is non-pluripolar there is also a finite $M>0$ such that $V_ E\leq M(h_{E,\Omega }+1)$. Both inequalities hold after regularization. For every bounded $E$, including polar $E$, \[  \{ V_ E=0\} =\{ h_{E,\Omega }=-1\} .  \] If $E$ is non-pluripolar and $c>\sup _ KV_ E^*$, then for $\Omega =\{ V_ E^*<c\} $, \[  V_ E^*=c(h_{E,\Omega }^*+1)\quad \hbox{on }\Omega .  \] Proof. The empty obstacle case is immediate, so assume $E\ne \varnothing $. The raw extremal $V_{\overline E}$ is positive outside $K$, by the polynomial identity and polynomial separation. Its compact thickening extremals increase pointwise to it and are continuous. A finite open cover of $\partial \Omega $ therefore supplies a small thickening $F$ and $m>0$ with $V_ F\geq m$ there; choose the thickening inside $\Omega $. For each relative competitor $v$, glue $\max \{ m(v+1),V_ F\} $ inside $\Omega $ to $V_ F$ outside. The boundary inequality justifies PSH gluing. This function agrees with $V_ F$ near infinity, lies in $\mathcal L$, and is zero on $E$. It is a global competitor, proving the lower bound after taking the supremum. Also $V_ E\geq V_{\overline E}$ puts its zero set inside $K$. This uses the compact closure only for the barrier, and makes no false lower semicontinuity assertion for raw $V_ E$ when $E$ is not closed. For non-pluripolar $E$, choose $M>\sup _\Omega V_ E^*$, which is finite. Every global competitor $u$ gives the relative competitor $u/M-1$; this proves the upper bound. Even for polar $E$, this argument works for each individual $u$ with its own finite positive upper bound $M_ u$. Consequently $h=-1$ implies that every $u\leq 0$ at the point, hence $V_ E=0$. The lower bound proves the converse. Taking upper regularizations gives the stated star inequalities. For the last assertion, $\Omega $ is bounded by the enclosing-ball lower profile, is open, and contains $K$. The preceding upper argument uses $c$ itself because every global competitor is below $V_ E^*<c$ there. Conversely glue $\max \{ c(v+1),V_ E^*\} $ inside to $V_ E^*$ outside; at every boundary point the latter is at least $c$. The glued function belongs to $\mathcal L$ and is zero on $E$ except possibly on the pluripolar discrepancy subset where $V_ E^*>0$. The checked polar-obstacle invariance makes it at most $V_ E^*$. Thus $c(h+1)\leq V_ E^*$; regularization and the upper inequality give equality. This uses the normalized polar perturbation already proved internally, without leaving the growth class. $\square$ Proposition 16.32.4 . 59F7B1095E20 If $E$ is compact and $\Omega $ is an open neighborhood of its polynomial hull, then its PSH hull in $\Omega $ equals that polynomial hull. Proof. Logarithms of polynomial absolute values show that the PSH hull is contained in the polynomial hull. For the reverse inclusion, if a PSH test $v$ separated a point $a$ of the polynomial hull from $E$, truncate it from below to make $\sup _ Ev$ finite while preserving the strict gap. Choose a bounded $W\Subset \Omega $ containing the hull and $M>\sup _ Wv$. The relative competitor $(v-M)/(M-\sup _ Ev)$ has value greater than $-1$ at $a$. The preceding zero-set equivalence then gives $V_ E(a)>0$, contrary to the polynomial identity. No compact approximation of an arbitrary PSH test is assumed. $\square$ Theorem 16.32.5 . 15FA5C21941D Let $E$ be bounded and let $f:U\to \mathbb C^ n$ be holomorphic on an open $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$. Suppose $f^{-1}K$ is compact in $U$. Put $Z_ E=\{ V_ E=0\} $ and take all inverse images within $U$. Then \[  V_{f^{-1}E}=V_{f^{-1}Z_ E}.  \] If $a\in f^{-1}E$ and $V_ E$ is continuous at $f(a)$, then $V_{f^{-1}E}$ is continuous at $a$. For compact $E$, in particular, $f^{-1}\widehat E\subset \widehat{f^{-1}E}$ and these two inverse images have the same polynomial hull. If instead $f$ is defined near $K$ with values in $\mathbb C^ m$, $a\in E$, $E$ is L-regular at $a$, and $f$ has full target rank generically near $a$, then $f(E)$ is L-regular at $f(a)$. Proof. First localize the compact inverse image: choose a relatively compact open neighborhood $O$ of it in $U$, whose boundary image misses $K$. A bounded open neighborhood $W$ of $K$ disjoint from $f(\partial O)$ makes $f:O\cap f^{-1}W\to W$ proper. Its image $W_1$ is open by finiteness of Euclidean proper fibers and is closed in $W$ by properness. Put $W_2=W\setminus W_1$ and $O_1=O\cap f^{-1}W$. All original inverse images of points in $K$ lie in $O_1$. Each $K_ i=K\cap W_ i$ is compact and polynomially convex. Indeed its polynomial hull lies in $K$; the preceding PSH-hull theorem on $W_1\cup W_2$ and a locally constant PSH test exclude the other piece. The relative extremal $h_{E,W}$ restricts on $W_1$ to $h_{E\cap W_1,W_1}$, because bounded competitors on the disjoint open pieces can be chosen independently. Proper-map raw extremal equality therefore gives \[  h_{f^{-1}E,O_1}=h_{E,W}\circ f\quad \hbox{on }O_1.  \] For $b\in f^{-1}Z_ E$, zero-set equivalence on $W$ makes this value $-1$. Any global competitor $u$ for $A=f^{-1}E$ is bounded above on the bounded relatively compact $O_1$; using $u/M_ u-1$ as a relative competitor proves $u(b)\leq 0$. Hence $A\subset f^{-1}Z_ E\subset \{ V_ A=0\} $. Every competitor for $A$ already satisfies the constraint on the last set, proving the raw envelope identity. For compact $E$, apply the polynomial identity to both compact inverse images to obtain the hull consequence. This does not assert that a local holomorphic inverse image is itself polynomially convex. Suppose now $E$ is regular at $f(a)$. The global/relative lower bound on $W$ gives $h_{E,W}^*(f(a))=-1$. Proper maps are open, so upper regularization commutes with composition: images of neighborhoods are neighborhoods, which gives both limsup inequalities. If $A$ were pluripolar, its regularized relative extremal would vanish, contradicting the equality at $a$. Thus $A$ is non-pluripolar and $M_ A>\sup _{O_1}V_ A^*$ is finite. The relative upper estimate for $A$ needs no hull assumption on $O_1$. Combining it with the lower estimate for $E$ gives, near $a$, \[  0\leq V_ A^*\leq (M_ A/m_ E)V_ E^*\circ f.  \] The right side is zero at $a$; the raw/star sandwich proves continuity. For the image assertion choose a bounded neighborhood $O\Subset \operatorname {Dom}f$ of $K$ and a large target ball $B$ containing $f(\overline O)$ and the polynomial hull of $f(E)$. Holomorphic relative pullback and the generic rank hypothesis give $h_{f(E),B}^*\circ f\leq h_{E,O}^*$ near $a$. The latter has value $-1$ there by the lower comparison and regularity. Thus the target relative extremal is $-1$ at $f(a)$. The image cannot be pluripolar, since its regularized relative extremal would then be zero. Its finite global-family upper bound and the relative upper comparison give $V_{f(E)}^*(f(a))=0$, as required. $\square$ Example 16.32.6 . 446A0A9CF0BF The compact inverse-image and hull-neighborhood hypotheses are substantive. For $f(z_1,z_2)=(z_1,z_1z_2^2-z_2)$ take $E=\{ |w_1|=|w_2|=1\} \cup \{ (1/3,0)\} $. Its polynomial hull is the closed unit polydisc, by the maximum principle in each variable. The inverse torus lies in $|z_1|=1$, $|z_2|<2$: for $|z_2|\geq 2$, $|z_1z_2^2-z_2|\geq |z_2|^2-|z_2|>1$. The remaining fiber is $\{ (1/3,0),(1/3,3)\} $. Thus $f^{-1}E$ is compact, but its isolated point $b=(1/3,3)$ is not regular. Indeed deleting it leaves a compact subset of the radius-two polydisc; polar invariance and the norm profile give $V_{f^{-1}E}^*(b)\geq \log (3/2)>0$, whereas the raw value is zero. The target is regular at $f(b)$, since its extremal equals the continuous unit-polydisc profile. The inverse image of the target hull is not compact: it contains $(1/j,j)$ for every positive integer $j$. For the missing hull neighborhood, take $E=\{ |z|=1\} \cup \{ 1/2\} $ and $f(z)=1/z$. The target set $f(E)=\{ |z|=1\} \cup \{ 2\} $ has raw extremal zero at $2$, but its regularization is $\log ^+|z|$ by polar invariance. The original $E$ has the continuous closed-disc profile. The map is undefined at zero in its hull. Regularity of an image does not force regularity of an arbitrary set mapping onto it. Let $B=\overline B((1,0),1)\subset \mathbb C^2$, $E=B\cup ([-1,1]\times \{ 0\} )$ and $f(z_1,z_2)=(z_1^2,z_2)$. The added segment maps into $f(B)$, so $f(E)=f(B)$ is regular by the image theorem. The segment is pluripolar, being contained in $\{ z_2=0\} $. Hence $V_ E^*=V_ B$, which is strictly positive at every point of the added segment outside $B$, although $V_ E=0$ there. Proposition 16.32.7 . 5886156A306E Let $h$ be holomorphic near $[0,1]$. If $V_ E$ is continuous and zero at every point $h(t)$, $0<t\leq 1$, then it is continuous and zero at $h(0)$. Consequently the closure of a bounded open set with $C^1$ boundary is L-regular. Proof. The hypothesis at one point excludes a pluripolar $E$ and makes $V_ E^*$ proper and finite. Its pullback along $h$ is nonnegative SH. It vanishes on $(0,1]$; nonthinness of a planar interval forces its value at zero to vanish as well. A constant map is already covered by the hypothesis. Upper semicontinuity and $0\leq V_ E\leq V_ E^*$ give the conclusion. This is a zero-contact assertion even if $h(0)$ belongs only to the closure of $E$. At a $C^1$ boundary point a normal affine segment lies inside the open set except at its endpoint, by a local defining function with nonzero normal derivative. Interior points are zero-contact points by the contained-ball profile. Apply the first assertion to that segment. The raw compact lower semicontinuity and zero-star criterion then give continuity globally for the compact closure. $\square$ Proposition 16.32.8 . 7C8B2A4D660E Every compact $K\subset \mathbb R^ m$ has bounded open neighborhoods $D_ j$ with smooth boundary such that $\overline D_{j+1}\subset D_ j$ and $\bigcap _ jD_ j=K$. In $\mathbb C^ n$ their closures are L-regular. Proof. We first give the needed equal-dimensional critical-value argument. If $F:U\subset \mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ m$ is $C^1$, its critical values have measure zero. On a fixed compact cube in $U$, partition into small side-$h$ cubes meeting the critical set. At a critical point in such a cube, $DF$ has rank at most $m-1$. Uniform continuity of $DF$ bounds the Taylor error throughout the cube by $\epsilon h$ for small $h$. If $\| DF\| \leq M$, its image therefore lies in a box with at most $m-1$ side lengths $C_ m(M+1)h$ and one side length $C_ m\epsilon h$. Its outer volume is at most $C_{m,M}\epsilon h^ m$. There are $O(h^{-m})$ cubes. Letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the assertion on this compact cube; a countable interior cube cover proves it on $U$. It suffices to construct $K\subset D\Subset \{ \operatorname {dist}(x,K)<\eta \} $ for arbitrary $\eta >0$. The empty case uses $D=\varnothing $. For nonempty $K$, convolve its distance function with a smooth kernel of radius $\delta <\eta /8$ to obtain $g\in C^\infty (\mathbb R^ m)$ with $|g-\operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,K)|\leq \delta $. For $|a|<1/2$, $g_ a=g-a\cdot x$ tends to infinity uniformly as $|x|\to \infty $, since $g_ a\geq |x|/2-\sup _ K|x|-\delta $. Choose a large fixed ball outside which all these functions exceed $\eta $, and then restrict $a$ further so $|a\cdot x|<\eta /8$ on that ball. The preceding critical-value argument applied to $F=\nabla g$ supplies such an arbitrarily small regular value $a$. Every critical point of $g_ a$ then has invertible Hessian and is isolated. There are only finitely many critical points in the compact band $\{ \eta /3\leq g_ a\leq 2\eta /3\} $, because an accumulation would be a nonisolated critical point. Choose a value $c\in (\eta /3,2\eta /3)$ avoiding their values. The set $D=\{ g_ a<c\} $ has smooth boundary by the implicit-function theorem. On $K$, $g_ a<\eta /4$; where the distance to $K$ is at least $\eta $, $g_ a>3\eta /4$ on the fixed ball and exceeds $\eta $ outside it. Thus $D$ has the required compact containment. Choose each next $\eta $ also small enough that the corresponding closed distance neighborhood of $K$ lies in the preceding $D_ j$, and make $\eta \downarrow 0$. This gives the nested sequence and its intersection. Its L-regularity follows from the preceding $C^1$ boundary assertion. Only the proved equal-dimensional $C^1$ critical-value lemma is needed, not a general Sard theorem as an unverified reference. $\square$
