text: Theorem 16.32.5 . 15FA5C21941D Let $E$ be bounded and let $f:U\to \mathbb C^ n$ be holomorphic on an open $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$. Suppose $f^{-1}K$ is compact in $U$. Put $Z_ E=\{ V_ E=0\} $ and take all inverse images within $U$. Then \[  V_{f^{-1}E}=V_{f^{-1}Z_ E}.  \] If $a\in f^{-1}E$ and $V_ E$ is continuous at $f(a)$, then $V_{f^{-1}E}$ is continuous at $a$. For compact $E$, in particular, $f^{-1}\widehat E\subset \widehat{f^{-1}E}$ and these two inverse images have the same polynomial hull. If instead $f$ is defined near $K$ with values in $\mathbb C^ m$, $a\in E$, $E$ is L-regular at $a$, and $f$ has full target rank generically near $a$, then $f(E)$ is L-regular at $f(a)$. Proof. First localize the compact inverse image: choose a relatively compact open neighborhood $O$ of it in $U$, whose boundary image misses $K$. A bounded open neighborhood $W$ of $K$ disjoint from $f(\partial O)$ makes $f:O\cap f^{-1}W\to W$ proper. Its image $W_1$ is open by finiteness of Euclidean proper fibers and is closed in $W$ by properness. Put $W_2=W\setminus W_1$ and $O_1=O\cap f^{-1}W$. All original inverse images of points in $K$ lie in $O_1$. Each $K_ i=K\cap W_ i$ is compact and polynomially convex. Indeed its polynomial hull lies in $K$; the preceding PSH-hull theorem on $W_1\cup W_2$ and a locally constant PSH test exclude the other piece. The relative extremal $h_{E,W}$ restricts on $W_1$ to $h_{E\cap W_1,W_1}$, because bounded competitors on the disjoint open pieces can be chosen independently. Proper-map raw extremal equality therefore gives \[  h_{f^{-1}E,O_1}=h_{E,W}\circ f\quad \hbox{on }O_1.  \] For $b\in f^{-1}Z_ E$, zero-set equivalence on $W$ makes this value $-1$. Any global competitor $u$ for $A=f^{-1}E$ is bounded above on the bounded relatively compact $O_1$; using $u/M_ u-1$ as a relative competitor proves $u(b)\leq 0$. Hence $A\subset f^{-1}Z_ E\subset \{ V_ A=0\} $. Every competitor for $A$ already satisfies the constraint on the last set, proving the raw envelope identity. For compact $E$, apply the polynomial identity to both compact inverse images to obtain the hull consequence. This does not assert that a local holomorphic inverse image is itself polynomially convex. Suppose now $E$ is regular at $f(a)$. The global/relative lower bound on $W$ gives $h_{E,W}^*(f(a))=-1$. Proper maps are open, so upper regularization commutes with composition: images of neighborhoods are neighborhoods, which gives both limsup inequalities. If $A$ were pluripolar, its regularized relative extremal would vanish, contradicting the equality at $a$. Thus $A$ is non-pluripolar and $M_ A>\sup _{O_1}V_ A^*$ is finite. The relative upper estimate for $A$ needs no hull assumption on $O_1$. Combining it with the lower estimate for $E$ gives, near $a$, \[  0\leq V_ A^*\leq (M_ A/m_ E)V_ E^*\circ f.  \] The right side is zero at $a$; the raw/star sandwich proves continuity. For the image assertion choose a bounded neighborhood $O\Subset \operatorname {Dom}f$ of $K$ and a large target ball $B$ containing $f(\overline O)$ and the polynomial hull of $f(E)$. Holomorphic relative pullback and the generic rank hypothesis give $h_{f(E),B}^*\circ f\leq h_{E,O}^*$ near $a$. The latter has value $-1$ there by the lower comparison and regularity. Thus the target relative extremal is $-1$ at $f(a)$. The image cannot be pluripolar, since its regularized relative extremal would then be zero. Its finite global-family upper bound and the relative upper comparison give $V_{f(E)}^*(f(a))=0$, as required. $\square$

title: Example 16.32.6
section: 16.32 Maps and regularity of global extremals
text: Example 16.32.6 . 446A0A9CF0BF The compact inverse-image and hull-neighborhood hypotheses are substantive. For $f(z_1,z_2)=(z_1,z_1z_2^2-z_2)$ take $E=\{ |w_1|=|w_2|=1\} \cup \{ (1/3,0)\} $. Its polynomial hull is the closed unit polydisc, by the maximum principle in each variable. The inverse torus lies in $|z_1|=1$, $|z_2|<2$: for $|z_2|\geq 2$, $|z_1z_2^2-z_2|\geq |z_2|^2-|z_2|>1$. The remaining fiber is $\{ (1/3,0),(1/3,3)\} $. Thus $f^{-1}E$ is compact, but its isolated point $b=(1/3,3)$ is not regular. Indeed deleting it leaves a compact subset of the radius-two polydisc; polar invariance and the norm profile give $V_{f^{-1}E}^*(b)\geq \log (3/2)>0$, whereas the raw value is zero. The target is regular at $f(b)$, since its extremal equals the continuous unit-polydisc profile. The inverse image of the target hull is not compact: it contains $(1/j,j)$ for every positive integer $j$. For the missing hull neighborhood, take $E=\{ |z|=1\} \cup \{ 1/2\} $ and $f(z)=1/z$. The target set $f(E)=\{ |z|=1\} \cup \{ 2\} $ has raw extremal zero at $2$, but its regularization is $\log ^+|z|$ by polar invariance. The original $E$ has the continuous closed-disc profile. The map is undefined at zero in its hull. Regularity of an image does not force regularity of an arbitrary set mapping onto it. Let $B=\overline B((1,0),1)\subset \mathbb C^2$, $E=B\cup ([-1,1]\times \{ 0\} )$ and $f(z_1,z_2)=(z_1^2,z_2)$. The added segment maps into $f(B)$, so $f(E)=f(B)$ is regular by the image theorem. The segment is pluripolar, being contained in $\{ z_2=0\} $. Hence $V_ E^*=V_ B$, which is strictly positive at every point of the added segment outside $B$, although $V_ E=0$ there.

title: Proposition 16.32.7
section: 16.32 Maps and regularity of global extremals
text: Proposition 16.32.7 . 5886156A306E Let $h$ be holomorphic near $[0,1]$. If $V_ E$ is continuous and zero at every point $h(t)$, $0<t\leq 1$, then it is continuous and zero at $h(0)$. Consequently the closure of a bounded open set with $C^1$ boundary is L-regular. Proof. The hypothesis at one point excludes a pluripolar $E$ and makes $V_ E^*$ proper and finite. Its pullback along $h$ is nonnegative SH. It vanishes on $(0,1]$; nonthinness of a planar interval forces its value at zero to vanish as well. A constant map is already covered by the hypothesis. Upper semicontinuity and $0\leq V_ E\leq V_ E^*$ give the conclusion. This is a zero-contact assertion even if $h(0)$ belongs only to the closure of $E$. At a $C^1$ boundary point a normal affine segment lies inside the open set except at its endpoint, by a local defining function with nonzero normal derivative. Interior points are zero-contact points by the contained-ball profile. Apply the first assertion to that segment. The raw compact lower semicontinuity and zero-star criterion then give continuity globally for the compact closure. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.32.8
section: 16.32 Maps and regularity of global extremals
text: Proposition 16.32.8 . 7C8B2A4D660E Every compact $K\subset \mathbb R^ m$ has bounded open neighborhoods $D_ j$ with smooth boundary such that $\overline D_{j+1}\subset D_ j$ and $\bigcap _ jD_ j=K$. In $\mathbb C^ n$ their closures are L-regular. Proof. We first give the needed equal-dimensional critical-value argument. If $F:U\subset \mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ m$ is $C^1$, its critical values have measure zero. On a fixed compact cube in $U$, partition into small side-$h$ cubes meeting the critical set. At a critical point in such a cube, $DF$ has rank at most $m-1$. Uniform continuity of $DF$ bounds the Taylor error throughout the cube by $\epsilon h$ for small $h$. If $\| DF\| \leq M$, its image therefore lies in a box with at most $m-1$ side lengths $C_ m(M+1)h$ and one side length $C_ m\epsilon h$. Its outer volume is at most $C_{m,M}\epsilon h^ m$. There are $O(h^{-m})$ cubes. Letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the assertion on this compact cube; a countable interior cube cover proves it on $U$. It suffices to construct $K\subset D\Subset \{ \operatorname {dist}(x,K)<\eta \} $ for arbitrary $\eta >0$. The empty case uses $D=\varnothing $. For nonempty $K$, convolve its distance function with a smooth kernel of radius $\delta <\eta /8$ to obtain $g\in C^\infty (\mathbb R^ m)$ with $|g-\operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,K)|\leq \delta $. For $|a|<1/2$, $g_ a=g-a\cdot x$ tends to infinity uniformly as $|x|\to \infty $, since $g_ a\geq |x|/2-\sup _ K|x|-\delta $. Choose a large fixed ball outside which all these functions exceed $\eta $, and then restrict $a$ further so $|a\cdot x|<\eta /8$ on that ball. The preceding critical-value argument applied to $F=\nabla g$ supplies such an arbitrarily small regular value $a$. Every critical point of $g_ a$ then has invertible Hessian and is isolated. There are only finitely many critical points in the compact band $\{ \eta /3\leq g_ a\leq 2\eta /3\} $, because an accumulation would be a nonisolated critical point. Choose a value $c\in (\eta /3,2\eta /3)$ avoiding their values. The set $D=\{ g_ a<c\} $ has smooth boundary by the implicit-function theorem. On $K$, $g_ a<\eta /4$; where the distance to $K$ is at least $\eta $, $g_ a>3\eta /4$ on the fixed ball and exceeds $\eta $ outside it. Thus $D$ has the required compact containment. Choose each next $\eta $ also small enough that the corresponding closed distance neighborhood of $K$ lies in the preceding $D_ j$, and make $\eta \downarrow 0$. This gives the nested sequence and its intersection. Its L-regularity follows from the preceding $C^1$ boundary assertion. Only the proved equal-dimensional $C^1$ critical-value lemma is needed, not a general Sard theorem as an unverified reference. $\square$

Proposition 16.33.1 . C39B105D9256 Every compact $K\subset \mathbb R^ n\subset \mathbb C^ n$ is polynomially convex. At a point $a\in K$, global L-regularity is equivalent to regularity at $a$ of $K\cap \overline B(a,r)$ for every $r>0$. Proof. For real $a
otin K$, put $q(z)=\sum _ j(z_ j-a_ j)^2$ and choose $R>\sup _ Kq$. The polynomial $1-q/R$ is one at $a$ and has absolute value strictly less than one on $K$. For nonreal $a=x+iy$, instead put $q(z)=\sum _ j(z_ j-x_ j)^2$ and take $R>\sup _ Kq$ positive. The same polynomial has absolute value at most one on $K$ and value $1+|y|^2/R>1$ at $a$. These degree-two separators prove the hull assertion directly, without polynomial approximation as a prerequisite. Local regularity implies global regularity by obstacle monotonicity. Conversely suppose $V_ K^*(a)=0$ and set $F=K\cap \overline B(a,r)$. If $F$ were not regular at $a$, choose a finite PSH function $\phi $ on $\mathbb C^ n$ with $\phi (a)>0$ and $\phi =0$ on $F\setminus P$ for some pluripolar $P\subset F$. If $F$ is non-pluripolar, take $\phi =V_ F^*$ and its discrepancy set. If $F$ is pluripolar, take $\phi =1$ and $P=F$. Put $M=\sup _ K\phi >0$ and \[  w(z)=\phi (z)- rac M{r^2}\operatorname {Re}\sum _ j(z_ j-a_ j)^2.  \] Then $w(a)>0$ and $w\leq 0$ on $K\setminus P$, because the quadratic is $|x-a|^2$ on real points. On a large bounded ball $\Omega $ containing $K$, normalize $w$ to a negative relative competitor $v=w/C-1$ with $v(a)>-1$ for $K\setminus P$. Relative regularized envelopes are unchanged by deleting a pluripolar subset of an obstacle: choose a negative PSH pole $b$ on $P$ in $\Omega $. For every bounded competitor $u$ of $K\setminus P$, $u+\epsilon b$ is a competitor of $K$, tends to $u$ almost everywhere, and canonical representatives give $u\leq h_{K,\Omega }^*$. Monotonicity gives the reverse inequality after taking suprema. Thus $h_{K,\Omega }^*(a)>-1$. The global-relative lower comparison gives $V_ K^*(a)>0$, a contradiction. The raw/star sandwich identifies regularity at $a$ with zero-star contact throughout this argument. $\square$ Example 16.33.2 . 2B1312D361AC For $K=\{ |z|=1\} \cup \{ 0\} \subset \mathbb C$, the global extremal is $\log ^+|z|$, so $K$ is regular at zero. But its intersection with a sufficiently small closed ball about zero is the polar singleton, whose regularized extremal is infinite. Hence the preceding local equivalence uses the real-subspace hypothesis. Write $J_\pm (\zeta )=(\zeta \pm \zeta ^{-1})/2$ and $J=J_+$. The map $J$ sends $|\zeta |>1$ biholomorphically to $\mathbb C\setminus [-1,1]$. Indeed its quadratic inverse roots have product one, and a root on the unit circle gives a point in $[-1,1]$. Off that segment exactly one root has modulus greater than one; $J'$ has no zero there, giving a holomorphic inverse $h(z)=z+\sqrt{z^2-1}$ with $h(t)>1$ for $t>1$. Define \[  g(z)= egin{cases} \log |h(z)|,& z
otin [-1,1],\ 0,& z\in [-1,1],\end{cases} \qquad H(t)=t+\sqrt{t^2-1}\quad (t\geq 1).  \] The function $g$ is continuous, nonnegative and harmonic off the cut, with $g(z)=\log |z|+\log 2+o(1)$ at infinity. It is SH on the whole plane: at a cut point its value zero is below every local mean. The ellipses \[  J(re^{it})=J_+(r)\cos t+iJ_-(r)\sin t,\qquad r>1,  \] give both continuity at the cut and $|z+1|+|z-1|=2J_+(r)$ when $g(z)=\log r$. Proposition 16.33.3 . 227A1367C31C For scalar $z$ put $A_ z(\zeta )=(\overline\zeta z-\zeta ^{-1}\overline z)/2$. Then \[  |A_ z(\zeta )|=|A_ z(|\zeta |)|,\qquad 2|A_{J(\zeta )}(|\zeta |)|=|J_-(|\zeta |^2)|.  \] For every nonzero $c\in \mathbb C^ n$, the vector map $J_ c(\zeta )=(\zeta c+\zeta ^{-1}\overline c)/2$ is injective for $|\zeta |>1$ and has continuous inverse on its image. If image points approach a point of $J_ c(\{ |\zeta |=1\} )$, their parameter moduli tend to one. Proof. For $r=|\zeta |$ direct expansion gives $4|A_ z(\zeta )|^2=|z|^2(r^2+r^{-2})-2\operatorname {Re}z^2$. If $\zeta =re^{it}$, then $A_{J(\zeta )}(r)=(r^2-r^{-2})e^{it}/4$, proving the absolute-value identity, including $r<1$. Also \[  2(J_ c(\zeta _1)-J_ c(\zeta _2)) =(\zeta _1-\zeta _2)(c-(\zeta _1\zeta _2)^{-1}\overline c).  \] Distinct parameters giving the same image would have product of modulus one, impossible when both are outside the unit disc. Image convergence bounds the parameters, since $|J_ c(\zeta )|	o \infty $ as $|\zeta |	o \infty $. The same identity excludes a unit-circle cluster parameter for an exterior image point and excludes an exterior cluster parameter for a boundary image point. This proves the claims. $\square$ Proposition 16.33.4 . D47F294B7F7D If a holomorphic $f:\mathbb C^*	o \mathbb C$ satisfies \[  2f(|\zeta |)=|f(\zeta )+1|+|f(\zeta )-1|,  \] then it is either constant with value in $[1,\infty )$, or $f(\zeta )=J((a\zeta )^ p)$ for $a>0$ and an integer $p\geq 1$. Every listed function satisfies the identity. Proof. The identity on the positive axis forces $f(r)\geq 1$ and real. The ellipse identity shows that $g(f(\zeta ))=\log H(f(|\zeta |))$. For a nonconstant $f$, $g\circ f$ is continuous radial SH on $\mathbb C^*$, harmonic on each circle where $f(r)>1$. Its profile in $\log r$ is convex, by harmonic annular comparison. If it never vanished, it would be harmonic on all of $\mathbb C^*$ and equal to $A\log r+B$. Nonnegativity forces $A=0$, so the image of $f$ would lie in one ellipse, contradicting the local inverse theorem at a point with $f'
e 0$. Thus it has a zero radius $r_0$. There cannot be two: convexity would make the whole intervening annulus map into $[-1,1]$, again forcing constancy. For $r>r_0$ radial harmonicity now gives $g(f(\zeta ))=p\log (r/r_0)$ with $p>0$. On this annulus the nonvanishing holomorphic function $q=h\circ f$ has modulus $(r/r_0)^ p$. Differentiating its logarithmic modulus shows $\zeta q'/q=p$; integration around a circle makes $p$ an integer. Thus $q=C\zeta ^ p$, and its positive real values on the positive axis give $C=r_0^{-p}$. Hence $f=J((\zeta /r_0)^ p)$ on the annulus and, by the identity theorem, on $\mathbb C^*$. The constants and the converse follow directly from the ellipse identity. $\square$ Proposition 16.33.5 . F36E879B8976 Let $D\subset \mathbb C$ be bounded, let $E\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be compact, and let $f:\overline D	o \mathbb C^ n$ be continuous and holomorphic on $D$, with $f(\partial D)\subset E$. Suppose that $v$ is continuous and nonnegative on $f(\overline D)$, vanishes on $f(\partial D)$, and $-v\circ f$ is SH on $D$. Then $V_ E\leq v$ on $f(D)$. Proof. For every global competitor $u$, the function $(u-v)\circ f$ is SH or identically $-\infty $ on each component and has nonpositive boundary upper limits. The bounded-domain maximum principle makes it nonpositive. Take the supremum over all competitors. $\square$ Theorem 16.33.6 . A1B73D6E87D0 Let $E\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be compact, convex, symmetric about zero, with zero in its real interior, and let $E^\circ =\{ y\in \mathbb R^ n:x\cdot y\leq 1	ext{ for all }x\in E\} $. Extend real linear functionals complex linearly. Then \[  V_ E(z)=\max _{y\in E^\circ }g(y\cdot z) =\sup _{y\in \operatorname {Extr}(E^\circ )}g(y\cdot z).  \] Both equal the maximum over the closure of the extreme points. Proof. Finite-dimensional separation gives the bipolar identity and compactness of $E^\circ $. Every point of a finite-dimensional compact convex set is a finite convex combination of its extreme points: boundary points lie in lower-dimensional exposed faces; use induction on their affine dimension, and express an interior point on a segment between boundary points. An extreme point of an exposed face is extreme in the whole set. The sublevel sets of $g$ are the filled ellipses just described, including the degenerate segment at level zero, so they are convex. Applied to $y\mapsto y\cdot z$, this shows that its maximum over the polar equals its supremum over extreme points. Closure does not change the supremum, and supplies a compact set for attainment. Each $g(y\cdot z)$ is PSH of logarithmic growth, nonpositive on $E$; the zero functional gives the admissible zero function. Thus $V_ E$ is at least the displayed maximum. For $z_0
otin E$ this maximum is $\log r>0$: real separation detects a real point outside $E$, and the polar's real span detects any nonzero imaginary part. Choose $y_0$ attaining it and $\zeta $ with $|\zeta |=r$ and $y_0\cdot z_0=J(\zeta )$. Set \[  c= rac{2(\overline\zeta z_0-\zeta ^{-1}\overline z_0)}{r^2-r^{-2}}.  \] Then $J_ c(\zeta )=z_0$ and $y_0\cdot c=1$. For every $y\in E^\circ $, $g(y\cdot z_0)\leq \log r$. The real-linear map $w\mapsto (\zeta w+\zeta ^{-1}\overline w)/2$ takes the closed unit disc bijectively onto this filled ellipse. Its inverse formula is exactly the displayed formula for $y\cdot c$, so $|y\cdot c|\leq 1$. Consequently $J_ c(e^{it})=\operatorname {Re}(e^{it}c)$ lies in $E$ by bipolarity and symmetry. For every global competitor $u$, the function $u(J_ c(\xi ))-\log |\xi |$ is SH, or identically $-\infty $, on $|\xi |>1$. Its growth is bounded above at infinity and its boundary upper limits are nonpositive. Inversion gives a bounded-above removable puncture in the unit disc; the maximum principle therefore bounds it by zero. Thus $u(z_0)\leq \log r$. Take the supremum over $u$. On $E$ both sides are zero. This exterior argument supplies the growth condition missing from an invocation of the bounded-disc lemma. $\square$ Proposition 16.33.7 . E41A4DC7736D Let $B\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be the closed unit ball, let $S=\{ x_ j\geq 0,\  \sum _ jx_ j\leq 1\} $ and let $C=[-1,1]\cup [-i,i]\subset \mathbb C$. Then \[   egin{aligned}  V_{[-1,1]^ n}(z)& =\max _ j g(z_ j),\  V_ B(z)& =	frac 12\log H\left(|z|^2+\left|\sum _ jz_ j^2-1ight|ight),\  V_ S(z)& =\log H\left(\sum _ j|z_ j|+\left|\sum _ jz_ j-1ight|ight),\  V_ C(z)& =	frac 14\log H\left(|z|^4+|z^4-1|ight). \end{aligned}  \] Proof. The cube formula is the already proved Cartesian maximum theorem applied to the one-dimensional case of the body formula. Equivalently the extreme points of the cube's polar, the unit l1 ball, are $\pm e_ j$. For the real ball use the preceding construction and take a maximizing unit real $y_0$. Such a maximizer exists on the sphere by the extreme- point formula. Write $c=a+ib$. We have $a\cdot y_0=1$, $b\cdot y_0=0$, and $|y\cdot c|\leq 1$ for every unit real $y$. Testing $y=a/|a|$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|a|=1$ and $a=y_0$; testing $y=b/|b|$ when $b
e 0$ gives $|b|\leq 1$. Hence $a\perp b$ and \[  z_0=aJ_+(\zeta )+ibJ_-(\zeta ),\quad |z_0|^2=|J_+(\zeta )|^2+|b|^2|J_-(\zeta )|^2,  \] while $\sum _ jz_{0,j}^2-1=(1-|b|^2)J_-(\zeta )^2$. Their indicated sum is $J_+(r^2)$, since $|J_+(\zeta )|^2+|J_-(\zeta )|^2=(r^2+r^{-2})/2$. Thus $r^2=H(|z_0|^2+|\sum _ jz_{0,j}^2-1|)$, proving the ball formula outside $B$; on $B$ the argument equals one and the value is zero. The degree-two regular polynomial map $f(z)=(z_1^2,\ldots ,z_ n^2)$ has $f^{-1}S=B$, including the requirement that every coordinate be real. The polynomial covariance theorem gives $V_ S(f(z))=2V_ B(z)$. Choose square roots of arbitrary coordinates to obtain the simplex formula. Likewise $z\mapsto z^2$ has inverse image $C$ of $[-1,1]$; use covariance and the one-dimensional ball formula for the last identity. All displayed arguments of $H$ are at least one by the triangle inequality; $H(1)=1$ includes the cut/boundary values continuously. $\square$

D47F294B7F7D If a holomorphic $f:\mathbb C^*\to \mathbb C$ satisfies \[  2f(|\zeta |)=|f(\zeta )+1|+|f(\zeta )-1|,  \] then it is either constant with value in $[1,\infty )$, or $f(\zeta )=J((a\zeta )^ p)$ for $a>0$ and an integer $p\geq 1$. Every listed function satisfies the identity. Proof. The identity on the positive axis forces $f(r)\geq 1$ and real. The ellipse identity shows that $g(f(\zeta ))=\log H(f(|\zeta |))$. For a nonconstant $f$, $g\circ f$ is continuous radial SH on $\mathbb C^*$, harmonic on each circle where $f(r)>1$. Its profile in $\log r$ is convex, by harmonic annular comparison. If it never vanished, it would be harmonic on all of $\mathbb C^*$ and equal to $A\log r+B$. Nonnegativity forces $A=0$, so the image of $f$ would lie in one ellipse, contradicting the local inverse theorem at a point with $f'\ne 0$. Thus it has a zero radius $r_0$. There cannot be two: convexity would make the whole intervening annulus map into $[-1,1]$, again forcing constancy. For $r>r_0$ radial harmonicity now gives $g(f(\zeta ))=p\log (r/r_0)$ with $p>0$. On this annulus the nonvanishing holomorphic function $q=h\circ f$ has modulus $(r/r_0)^ p$. Differentiating its logarithmic modulus shows $\zeta q'/q=p$; integration around a circle makes $p$ an integer. Thus $q=C\zeta ^ p$, and its positive real values on the positive axis give $C=r_0^{-p}$. Hence $f=J((\zeta /r_0)^ p)$ on the annulus and, by the identity theorem, on $\mathbb C^*$. The constants and the converse follow directly from the ellipse identity. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.33.5
section: 16.33 Real compact sets and explicit extremal formulas
text: Proposition 16.33.5 . F36E879B8976 Let $D\subset \mathbb C$ be bounded, let $E\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be compact, and let $f:\overline D\to \mathbb C^ n$ be continuous and holomorphic on $D$, with $f(\partial D)\subset E$. Suppose that $v$ is continuous and nonnegative on $f(\overline D)$, vanishes on $f(\partial D)$, and $-v\circ f$ is SH on $D$. Then $V_ E\leq v$ on $f(D)$. Proof. For every global competitor $u$, the function $(u-v)\circ f$ is SH or identically $-\infty $ on each component and has nonpositive boundary upper limits. The bounded-domain maximum principle makes it nonpositive. Take the supremum over all competitors. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.33.6
section: 16.33 Real compact sets and explicit extremal formulas
text: Theorem 16.33.6 . A1B73D6E87D0 Let $E\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be compact, convex, symmetric about zero, with zero in its real interior, and let $E^\circ =\{ y\in \mathbb R^ n:x\cdot y\leq 1\text{ for all }x\in E\} $. Extend real linear functionals complex linearly. Then \[  V_ E(z)=\max _{y\in E^\circ }g(y\cdot z) =\sup _{y\in \operatorname {Extr}(E^\circ )}g(y\cdot z).  \] Both equal the maximum over the closure of the extreme points. Proof. Finite-dimensional separation gives the bipolar identity and compactness of $E^\circ $. Every point of a finite-dimensional compact convex set is a finite convex combination of its extreme points: boundary points lie in lower-dimensional exposed faces; use induction on their affine dimension, and express an interior point on a segment between boundary points. An extreme point of an exposed face is extreme in the whole set. The sublevel sets of $g$ are the filled ellipses just described, including the degenerate segment at level zero, so they are convex. Applied to $y\mapsto y\cdot z$, this shows that its maximum over the polar equals its supremum over extreme points. Closure does not change the supremum, and supplies a compact set for attainment. Each $g(y\cdot z)$ is PSH of logarithmic growth, nonpositive on $E$; the zero functional gives the admissible zero function. Thus $V_ E$ is at least the displayed maximum. For $z_0\notin E$ this maximum is $\log r>0$: real separation detects a real point outside $E$, and the polar's real span detects any nonzero imaginary part. Choose $y_0$ attaining it and $\zeta $ with $|\zeta |=r$ and $y_0\cdot z_0=J(\zeta )$. Set \[  c=\frac{2(\overline\zeta z_0-\zeta ^{-1}\overline z_0)}{r^2-r^{-2}}.  \] Then $J_ c(\zeta )=z_0$ and $y_0\cdot c=1$. For every $y\in E^\circ $, $g(y\cdot z_0)\leq \log r$. The real-linear map $w\mapsto (\zeta w+\zeta ^{-1}\overline w)/2$ takes the closed unit disc bijectively onto this filled ellipse. Its inverse formula is exactly the displayed formula for $y\cdot c$, so $|y\cdot c|\leq 1$. Consequently $J_ c(e^{it})=\operatorname {Re}(e^{it}c)$ lies in $E$ by bipolarity and symmetry. For every global competitor $u$, the function $u(J_ c(\xi ))-\log |\xi |$ is SH, or identically $-\infty $, on $|\xi |>1$. Its growth is bounded above at infinity and its boundary upper limits are nonpositive. Inversion gives a bounded-above removable puncture in the unit disc; the maximum principle therefore bounds it by zero. Thus $u(z_0)\leq \log r$. Take the supremum over $u$. On $E$ both sides are zero. This exterior argument supplies the growth condition missing from an invocation of the bounded-disc lemma. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.33.7
section: 16.33 Real compact sets and explicit extremal formulas
text: Proposition 16.33.7 . E41A4DC7736D Let $B\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be the closed unit ball, let $S=\{ x_ j\geq 0,\  \sum _ jx_ j\leq 1\} $ and let $C=[-1,1]\cup [-i,i]\subset \mathbb C$. Then \[  \begin{aligned}  V_{[-1,1]^ n}(z)& =\max _ j g(z_ j),\\  V_ B(z)& =\tfrac 12\log H\left(|z|^2+\left|\sum _ jz_ j^2-1\right|\right),\\  V_ S(z)& =\log H\left(\sum _ j|z_ j|+\left|\sum _ jz_ j-1\right|\right),\\  V_ C(z)& =\tfrac 14\log H\left(|z|^4+|z^4-1|\right). \end{aligned}  \] Proof. The cube formula is the already proved Cartesian maximum theorem applied to the one-dimensional case of the body formula. Equivalently the extreme points of the cube's polar, the unit l1 ball, are $\pm e_ j$. For the real ball use the preceding construction and take a maximizing unit real $y_0$. Such a maximizer exists on the sphere by the extreme- point formula. Write $c=a+ib$. We have $a\cdot y_0=1$, $b\cdot y_0=0$, and $|y\cdot c|\leq 1$ for every unit real $y$. Testing $y=a/|a|$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|a|=1$ and $a=y_0$; testing $y=b/|b|$ when $b\ne 0$ gives $|b|\leq 1$. Hence $a\perp b$ and \[  z_0=aJ_+(\zeta )+ibJ_-(\zeta ),\quad |z_0|^2=|J_+(\zeta )|^2+|b|^2|J_-(\zeta )|^2,  \] while $\sum _ jz_{0,j}^2-1=(1-|b|^2)J_-(\zeta )^2$. Their indicated sum is $J_+(r^2)$, since $|J_+(\zeta )|^2+|J_-(\zeta )|^2=(r^2+r^{-2})/2$. Thus $r^2=H(|z_0|^2+|\sum _ jz_{0,j}^2-1|)$, proving the ball formula outside $B$; on $B$ the argument equals one and the value is zero. The degree-two regular polynomial map $f(z)=(z_1^2,\ldots ,z_ n^2)$ has $f^{-1}S=B$, including the requirement that every coordinate be real. The polynomial covariance theorem gives $V_ S(f(z))=2V_ B(z)$. Choose square roots of arbitrary coordinates to obtain the simplex formula. Likewise $z\mapsto z^2$ has inverse image $C$ of $[-1,1]$; use covariance and the one-dimensional ball formula for the last identity. All displayed arguments of $H$ are at least one by the triangle inequality; $H(1)=1$ includes the cut/boundary values continuously. $\square$

section: 16.34 Logarithmic total mass and bounded-obstacle support
text: Proposition 16.34.1 . B5EE2E185F5F Let $u,v$ be locally bounded PSH functions on $\mathbb C^ n$, with $v(z)\to +\infty $ and $u(z)/v(z)\to 1$ as $|z|\to \infty $. Then \[  \int _{\mathbb C^ n}(dd^ cu)^ n\leq \int _{\mathbb C^ n}(dd^ cv)^ n,  \] where infinite nonnegative integrals are allowed. Proof. Fix $\epsilon >0$ and $c>0$, and put $w_ c=(1+\epsilon )v-c$ and $G_ c=\{ w_ c<u\} $. For sufficiently large $|z|$, we have $u\leq (1+\epsilon /2)v$ and $(\epsilon /2)v>c+1$. Thus $w_ c>u+1$ there, so $G_ c$ is contained in a bounded ball. Apply the canonical bounded-domain comparison principle on a larger ball, where the boundary ordering is strict. It gives \[  \int _{G_ c}(dd^ cu)^ n\leq \int _{G_ c}(dd^ cw_ c)^ n \leq (1+\epsilon )^ n\int _{\mathbb C^ n}(dd^ cv)^ n.  \] As $c\uparrow \infty $, the Borel sets $G_ c$ increase to all of $\mathbb C^ n$, since both potentials are finite. Monotone convergence and then $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ prove the assertion. Properness of $v$ is essential to this proof of boundedness; positivity near infinity alone does not establish it. $\square$ Proposition 13.5.1 . 06A36B9354A5 With Pome's normalization, every $u\in \mathcal L_1^+$ has total mass $2^{-n}$. More explicitly, for $\gamma (z)=\tfrac 12\log (1+|z|^2)$, \[  (dd^ c\gamma )^ n= \frac{n!}{2^ n\pi ^ n}(1+|z|^2)^{-n-1}\, dV_{2n}.  \] Proof. The existing Fubini–Study Hessian matrix has eigenvalues $(1+|z|^2)^{-1}$ in the $n-1$ tangential directions and $(1+|z|^2)^{-2}$ in the radial direction. Divide each by two for $\gamma $ and apply the canonical determinant normalization to obtain the displayed density, including the same values at zero. Using $|S^{2n-1}|=2\pi ^ n/(n-1)!$ and the substitution $t=r^2/(1+r^2)$, we have \[  \int _0^\infty \frac{r^{2n-1}}{(1+r^2)^{n+1}}\, dr =\frac12\int _0^1t^{n-1}\, dt=\frac1{2n}.  \] The density therefore integrates to $2^{-n}$. For $u\in \mathcal L_1^+$, both $u$ and $\gamma $ are locally bounded, tend to infinity, and have ratio tending to one. Apply the proper mass comparison in both orders. This conclusion also follows directly from the checked affine/projective dictionary and bounded cohomological mass: $u-\gamma $ extends to a bounded $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}/2$-PSH function on $\mathbb P^ n$. The bounded product gives zero mass to the pluripolar hyperplane at infinity; its cohomological mass equals that of $\gamma $. Thus the mass statement is a consequence of existing canonical inputs, with the explicit radial calculation supplying its normalization. $\square$ Proposition 16.34.2 . 01D4425BEF42 Let $E\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be bounded and non-pluripolar. Then $V_ E^*\in \mathcal L_1^+$ is locally bounded, is maximal on $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \overline E$, and \[  \mu _ E=(dd^ cV_ E^*)^ n,\qquad \mu _ E(\mathbb C^ n\setminus \overline E)=0,\qquad \mu _ E(\overline E)=2^{-n}.  \] No measurability of $E$ itself is required for these closed-set statements. Proof. The ball profile below $V_ E$ gives the lower logarithmic bound. The checked non-pluripolar family bound gives the global upper bound, so $V=V_ E^*\in \mathcal L_1^+$. In particular it is locally bounded. The discrepancy set $P=\{ x\in E:V(x)>0\} $ is pluripolar, since the raw obstacle envelope is zero on $E$. Let $U\Subset \mathbb C^ n\setminus \overline E$ and let $q$ be PSH on $U$ with boundary upper limits at most $V$. The gluing lemma makes $w=\max (q,V)$ on $U$, and $w=V$ off $U$, a global PSH function in $\mathcal L_1$. Since $w=V=0$ on $E\setminus P$, take the checked logarithmic pole $b\in \mathcal L_1$ with $b\leq 0$ on $E$ and $b=-\infty $ on $P$. For $\epsilon >0$ the function \[  w_\epsilon =\frac{w+\epsilon b}{1+\epsilon }  \] belongs to $\mathcal L_1$ and is nonpositive on all of $E$. Consequently $w_\epsilon \leq V_ E\leq V$. Letting $\epsilon \to 0$ off the pole set gives $w\leq V$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere by canonical PSH representatives. Thus $q\leq V$ on $U$, proving maximality on the stated open complement. The checked locally bounded maximality theorem makes its Monge–Ampere measure zero there. The full-mass identity just proved gives the remaining equality. $\square$

title: 16.35 Polynomial families and equilibrium-null obstacles
text:
Say that $(E,\mu )$ has the polynomial $L^*$ property at $a$ if every family $\mathcal F$ of polynomials with \[  \mu \{ x\in E:\sup _{p\in \mathcal F}|p(x)|=+\infty \} =0  \] satisfies the following: for every $b>1$ there are a neighborhood $U$ of $a$ and $M>0$ with $\sup _ U|p|\leq M b^{\deg p}$ for all nonzero $p\in \mathcal F$. Constants have degree zero and the zero polynomial requires no estimate. The exceptional set is relatively Borel even for an uncountable family: the supremum of continuous functions is lower semicontinuous, and its infinity set is a countable intersection of open sets, intersected with $E$. Proposition 16.35.1 . B76C0AE2777D Let $E$ be bounded and $V_ E^*(a)=0$. Let $\mu $ be a nonnegative function on the relative Borel subsets of $E$, zero on the empty set and positive on every non-pluripolar such set. Then $(E,\mu )$ has $L^*$ at $a$. For a nonempty compact $K$ and $a\in K$, the property with counting measure is equivalent to L-regularity at $a$. Proof. For a family as above put $F_ j=\{ x\in E:\sup _{p\in \mathcal F}|p(x)|\leq j\} $ and $F= igcup _{j\geq 1}F_ j$. The omitted subset $E\setminus F$ is pluripolar by the hypothesis on $\mu $. The checked polar-invariance and increasing-obstacle results give \[  V_{F_ j}^*\downarrow V_ F^*=V_ E^*.  \] The set $E$ is non-pluripolar, since $V_ E^*(a)=0$. At least one $F_ j$ is non-pluripolar, since otherwise their union and then $E$ would be pluripolar. Discard earlier indices so that all displayed regularized extremals are finite PSH functions. Choose a compact ball $Q$ about $a$ on which $V_ F^*<	frac 12\log b$. The increasing open sets $\{ V_{F_ j}^*<\log b\} $ cover $Q$; compactness gives one index $j$ covering it. For every nonconstant $p\in \mathcal F$ of degree $d$, the global PSH function $d^{-1}\log (|p|/j)$ is a competitor for $V_{F_ j}$. Thus $|p|\leq j b^ d$ on $Q$. Every constant in the family has modulus at most $j$ because $F_ j$ is nonempty. Take $U$ inside $Q$ and $M>j$. No measure additivity or unstated uniform Dini theorem is used. For the converse on $K$, apply $L^*$ to the family of all nonconstant polynomials of norm at most one on $K$. It is pointwise bounded by one there. Every power of each such polynomial is in the same family, so taking its kth power in the estimate and letting $k	o \infty $ gives $d^{-1}\log |p|\leq \log b$ on $U$. The checked compact Siciak identity implies $V_ K\leq \log b$ on $U$, hence $V_ K^*(a)\leq \log b$. Let $b\downarrow 1$. Nonnegativity gives zero, equivalent to regularity at a point of $K$. The forward direction uses counting measure in the first assertion. $\square$ Proposition 16.35.2 . 884332AF4253 Let $K$ be compact in a bounded hyperconvex domain $D$, and set $h=h_{K,D}^*$ and $
u _{K,D}=(dd^ ch)^ n$. If a Borel subset $N\subset K$ has $
u _{K,D}(N)=0$, then $h_{K\setminus N,D}^*=h$. The same holds for subsets of completed measure-zero Borel sets. Proof. The polar case has both envelopes zero. Otherwise put $v=h_{K\setminus N,D}^*\geq h$. Both bounded potentials tend to zero at the boundary of $D$. The measure $
u _{K,D}$ is supported on $K$ and gives zero mass to pluripolar sets. On $K$, except for the union of two pluripolar discrepancy sets, $h=-1$, and $v=-1$ on $K\setminus N$. Therefore $
u _{K,D}\{ v>h\} \leq 
u _{K,D}(N)=0$. The canonical local domination principle and the common boundary limit give $v\leq h$ everywhere. This proves equality, also for a subset of a completed null set by obstacle monotonicity. $\square$ Proposition 16.35.3 . 6E38A7B6271A Let $K$ be compact and non-pluripolar. For bounded hyperconvex domains $D_1\subset D_2$ containing $K$, one has $
u _{K,D_2}\leq 
u _{K,D_1}$ on $D_1$. If $D_1$ contains the polynomial hull $\widehat K$, then also $c

Both are zero on $K$ except for a pluripolar set, and their Monge–Ampere measures are supported on $K$ and do not charge that set. Apply the canonical bounded ordered-contact inequality with $a=U_2$, $b=U_1$. It gives $
u _{K,D_2}\leq 
u _{K,D_1}$. This needs no continuity of the potentials or strict boundary gap. If $D_1$ contains $\widehat K$, the checked global-relative comparisons give $mU_1\leq V_ K^*\leq MU_2$ on $D_1$, with $m,M>0$. Apply the same contact inequality to $(m/M)U_1\leq U_2$ on their common zero set outside the polar discrepancy union. It yields the reverse bound with $c=(m/M)^ n$. For the global statement use $mU\leq V_ K^*\leq MU$ on $D$, where $U=h_{K,D}^*+1$. Contact comparison in both orders gives the constants $m^ n$ and $M^ n$. All the compared measures are carried by $K$, by the checked relative and global maximality/support results. In particular, the book's Levenberg comparison is already the same canonical contact consequence: if $u_1\geq u_2$ and both vanish on compact $K$, while $(dd^ cu_2)^ n$ is supported there, then $(dd^ cu_1)^ n\geq (dd^ cu_2)^ n$. Its additional continuity and boundary strictness are unnecessary for this reduction. $\square$ Proposition 16.35.4 . 1C591D5634BA If a compact $K$ is L-regular at $a\in K$, then $(K,\mu _ K)$ has $L^*$ at $a$. The same is true for $(K,
u _{K,D})$ when $D$ is a bounded hyperconvex neighborhood of $\widehat K$. Proof. For a family whose exceptional set $N$ is $
u _{K,D}$-null, the null- deletion proposition identifies its two relative envelopes. By the global-relative lower comparison and $V_ K^*(a)=0$, their common value at $a$ is $-1$. This also shows that $K\setminus N$ is non-pluripolar, since a polar obstacle would have relative envelope zero. The finite global-relative upper comparison therefore gives $V_{K\setminus N}^*(a)=0$. The family is pointwise bounded on $K\setminus N$, so apply the first proposition with counting measure. For $\mu _ K$ use a ball $D$ containing $\widehat K$ and $c
u _{K,D}\leq \mu _ K$: a global-null exceptional set is relative-null. The hull-neighborhood hypothesis in the source's relative assertion is retained; its hat is present in the original image. $\square$ Proposition 16.35.5 . 6F70A6B34439 Let $g$ be real $C^1$ on an open set, with $G=\{ g<0\} $ relatively compact and $dg
e 0$ on $\partial G=g^{-1}(0)$. Orient $\partial G$ by the outward-normal convention. Then $T(\alpha )=\int _{\partial G}d^ cg\wedge \alpha $ is a positive $(1,1)$-current. Proof. The compact boundary has finitely many $C^1$ graph charts, so this integral defines an order-zero current. At any boundary point a complex unitary affine change and a positive rescaling normalize $dg=-dy_ n$. The tangent half-space for $G$ is $y_ n>0$, whose induced boundary orientation is $dx_ n\wedge dx_1\wedge dy_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dy_{n-1}$. In Pome's convention $d^ c(-y_ n)=dx_ n/(4\pi )$. For a positive $(n-1,n-1)$ test form, only its tangential diagonal coefficient survives after wedging with $dx_ n$ and restriction to this hyperplane; that coefficient is nonnegative by the canonical positivity cone test. Thus the integrand is nonnegative at every point. This proves positivity, including $n=1$; changing back preserves the complex orientation. $\square$

u _{K,D_1}$. This needs no continuity of the potentials or strict boundary gap. title: Proposition 16.35.4
text:
Proposition 16.35.4 . 1C591D5634BA If a compact $K$ is L-regular at $a\in K$, then $(K,\mu _ K)$ has $L^*$ at $a$. The same is true for $(K,
u _{K,D})$ when $D$ is a bounded hyperconvex neighborhood of $\widehat K$. Proof. For a family whose exceptional set $N$ is $
u _{K,D}$-null, the null- deletion proposition identifies its two relative envelopes. By the global-relative lower comparison and $V_ K^*(a)=0$, their common value at $a$ is $-1$. title: Proposition 16.35.5
text: Proposition 16.35.5 . 6F70A6B34439 Let $g$ be real $C^1$ on an open set, with $G=\{ g<0\} $ relatively compact and $dg\ne 0$ on $\partial G=g^{-1}(0)$. Orient $\partial G$ by the outward-normal convention. Then $T(\alpha )=\int _{\partial G}d^ cg\wedge \alpha $ is a positive $(1,1)$-current. Proof. The compact boundary has finitely many $C^1$ graph charts, so this integral defines an order-zero current. At any boundary point a complex unitary affine change and a positive rescaling normalize $dg=-dy_ n$. The tangent half-space for $G$ is $y_ n>0$, whose induced boundary orientation is $dx_ n\wedge dx_1\wedge dy_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dy_{n-1}$. In Pome's convention $d^ c(-y_ n)=dx_ n/(4\pi )$. For a positive $(n-1,n-1)$ test form, only its tangential diagonal coefficient survives after wedging with $dx_ n$ and restriction to this hyperplane; that coefficient is nonnegative by the canonical positivity cone test. Thus the integrand is nonnegative at every point. This proves positivity, including $n=1$; changing back preserves the complex orientation. $\square$

title: 7.17 Isolated-pole Green envelopes and continuity
text: For a domain $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $a\in D$, let $g_ D(z,a)$ be the supremum of negative PSH functions $u$ satisfying $u(z)\leq \log |z-a|+C$ near $a$. Put $g_ D=-\infty $ when the family is empty. The pole coefficient is one relative to $\log |z-a|$. Monge–Ampere products below are used only away from the pole. Proposition 7.17.1 . 3360BE3E2E50 If $D$ is bounded and $B(a,r)\subset D\subset B(a,R)$, then $g_ D$ is negative PSH, finite and locally bounded off $a$, and \[  \log (|z-a|/R)\leq g_ D(z,a)\leq \log (|z-a|/r).  \] It is maximal off $a$, so $(dd^ cg_ D)^ n=0$ there. Enlarging the domain decreases the envelope; deleting a relatively closed pluripolar set not containing $a$ does not change it. Holomorphic maps satisfy \[  g_{D'}(f(z),f(a))\leq g_ D(z,a).  \] On an arbitrary domain the envelope is either identically $-\infty $ or negative PSH. Contraction and domain comparisons retain the empty-family convention. Proof. The lower logarithm is a competitor on a bounded domain. To bound every competitor above on $B(a,r)$, restrict to any complex line through $a$. If the restriction is identically $-\infty $, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise subtract the line's logarithmic pole, remove the bounded-above puncture and apply the SH maximum principle on circles of radii tending to $r$. This gives the upper bound; outside that ball it follows from negativity. The upper envelope is locally bounded above by zero, and its regularization retains the same pole bound. It is PSH and negative by the maximum principle, hence itself a competitor. Therefore it equals the raw supremum. The two logarithmic bounds imply local boundedness off $a$. On an arbitrary domain with a nonempty family, a single competitor gives a nontrivial lower bound; the same local upper pole bound and envelope argument give a negative PSH representative. No local boundedness away from the pole is asserted in that generality. For $U\Subset D\setminus \{ a\} $ and a PSH test with boundary upper limits at most $g_ D$, the maximum principle first makes the test negative on $U$. Glue its maximum with $g_ D$ inside $U$ to $g_ D$ outside. The result is still a competitor, so it cannot exceed the envelope. This proves maximality; use the canonical bounded maximality theorem only off the pole. Domain monotonicity is competitor inclusion. On a domain with a relatively closed pluripolar subset removed, every negative competitor extends canonically across that subset by the removable-set theorem. Its logarithmic condition at the retained pole is unchanged; the two competitor comparisons give equality. For a target competitor $u$, its composition with $f$ is either PSH or identically $-\infty $. The latter case contributes only a trivial inequality. In the former case the local holomorphic Lipschitz estimate $|f(z)-f(a)|\leq C|z-a|$ gives the required upper logarithmic pole. Thus $u\circ f$ is a source competitor. Taking the supremum proves contraction, including an empty target family. Applying contraction to a biholomorphism and its inverse gives invariance. $\square$ Proposition 7.17.2 . 7B9EA3C07531 Suppose that $h:\mathbb C^ n\to [0,\infty )$ is finite USC, $h^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $, and $h(\lambda z)=|\lambda |h(z)$. On the balanced domain $D=\{ h<1\} $ one has $g_ D(z,0)\leq \log h(z)$. Equality holds if $\log h$ is PSH. In particular, \[  g_{B(0,R)}(z,w)=\log |A_{w/R}(z/R)|, \quad g_{P(0,R)}(z,w)=\max _ j\log \left| \frac{R(z_ j-w_ j)}{R^2-z_ j\overline w_ j}\right|.  \] Here $A$ is the canonical smooth centered ball automorphism, with $A_0$ the identity, and $P$ is the open polydisc. Its negative is the source's nonzero-parameter involution and gives the same norm. Proof. Upper semicontinuity on the unit sphere and homogeneity give $h(z)\leq C|z|$. In particular $D$ is open, contains a ball and is connected by its radial segments. For any competitor $u$ and $z\ne 0$ in $D$, restrict to the line $\zeta z$, whose parameter disc has radius $1/h(z)>1$. Subtract $\log |\zeta |+\log h(z)$ and remove the puncture. Circle maximum principles as the radius tends to $1/h(z)$ give $u(z)\leq \log h(z)$. This works for each competitor and does not assume beforehand that the Green envelope is PSH on this possibly unbounded domain. If $\log h$ is PSH, it is itself a negative competitor by the bound $h\leq C|z|$, proving equality. The ball/polydisc formulas follow by applying this to the norm/max norm at zero and then using the checked ball and coordinate-disc biholomorphisms. For $0<\epsilon <1$, the explicit nonconvex example has $h(z_1,z_2)=\max \{ |z_1|,|z_2|,\sqrt{|z_1z_2|/\epsilon }\} $. Its logarithm is the maximum of the two coordinate logarithms and their half-sum minus $\tfrac 12\log \epsilon $, hence PSH. Its sublevel is pseudoconvex, since $-\log (1-h)+|z|^2$ is a PSH exhaustion there. It is nonconvex: for a real $t$ just below one, the points $(t,t\epsilon )$ and $(t\epsilon ,t)$ belong to the domain while their midpoint has coordinate product $t^2(1+\epsilon )^2/4>\epsilon $. $\square$ Proposition 7.17.3 . 2CC830293978 Let $f:D\to D'$ be a proper holomorphic map of bounded domains in $\mathbb C^ n$, and let $\alpha ,\beta >0$. The following are equivalent: \[  f^{-1}(f(a))=\{ a\} ,\qquad c|z-a|^\alpha \leq |f(z)-f(a)|\leq C|z-a|^\beta \quad \hbox{near }a  \] for some $c,C>0$, and \[  \alpha g_ D(z,a)\leq g_{D'}(f(z),f(a))\leq \beta g_ D(z,a).  \] Proof. Proper Euclidean fibers are finite, and the map is open and surjective, by the canonical finite-map results. Its proper fiber maximum $v(y)=\alpha \max _{f(x)=y}g_ D(x,a)$ is PSH. Near $f(a)$ all inverse points approach $a$, by properness and the single-fiber assumption. The lower growth estimate and the local Green upper bound give $v(y)\leq \log |y-f(a)|+C'$. It is negative, hence a target competitor. Thus $\alpha g_ D\leq v\circ f\leq g_{D'}\circ f$, with the factor $\alpha $ retained. The upper growth estimate makes $\beta ^{-1}g_{D'}\circ f$ a source competitor, proving the other bound. Conversely the lower Green inequality excludes any other inverse point of $f(a)$, since $g_ D$ is finite off $a$. At $a$ both Green functions equal the corresponding logarithm up to bounded terms. Substituting those local bounds into the two inequalities gives exactly the two growth estimates. $\square$ Proposition 7.17.4 . 5A3A24549BAA For bounded hyperconvex $D$, $g_ D$ tends to zero at every boundary point, is continuous off its pole, and is jointly continuous on $\overline D\times D$ with values in $[-\infty ,0]$, extended by zero on $\partial D\times D$. Proof. Fix $B(a,r)\Subset D\subset B(a,R)$ and $0<\delta <r$. The relative extremal $h_\delta =h_{\overline B(a,\delta ),D}$ is continuous, equals $-1$ on that ball, and tends to zero at the boundary, by the checked hyperconvex compact-obstacle theorem. Put $A=\log (r/\delta )$ and $B=\log (R/\delta )$. The Green upper bound gives $g_ D/A\leq -1$ on the obstacle, so $g_ D\leq A h_\delta $. Also $\ell =\log (|z-a|/R)$ satisfies $\ell /B\leq h_\delta $ everywhere. Glue $B h_\delta $ outside the closed $\delta $-ball to $\ell $ inside it. Their values agree on the sphere; the outside branch is at least $\ell $, so the canonical maximum pasting lemma, with base $\ell $ and outside open set, makes the glued function PSH. It is a negative logarithmic-pole competitor. Consequently \[  B h_\delta \leq g_ D\leq A h_\delta \quad \hbox{outside }\overline B(a,\delta ).  \] For fixed $\delta $, the left bound proves the zero boundary limit. On a compact set away from $a$, $g_ D\geq -C$ by its lower logarithmic bound, so $|h_\delta |\leq C/A$. Hence \[  0\leq A h_\delta -g_ D\leq \log (R/r)\, C/A\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $g_ D$ is a locally uniform limit of continuous relative extrema off $a$. This supplies continuity without the source's defective five-piece lower-semicontinuity patch. We verify uniformity in the pole. Given $a$, a neighborhood $U$ of it, and $\eta >0$, choose a small closed ball about $a$ in $U$, a uniform inner radius $r_0$ for its poles, and $R_0$ larger than all distances to points of $D$. Choose $t>0$ small enough that $B(a,t)\Subset U$ and \[  (1+\eta )\log (3t/(2r_0))<\log (t/(2R_0)).  \] For $x,y\in B(a,t/2)$, keep $\log (|z-y|/R_0)$ inside $B(a,t)$ and outside take its maximum with $(1+\eta )g_ D(z,x)$. On the interface, the uniform ball upper bound gives a strict gap putting the logarithmic branch above the other branch. The resulting negative PSH function has a logarithmic pole at $y$, so it is at most $g_ D(z,y)$. On $D\setminus U$ it is at least $(1+\eta )g_ D(z,x)$. Interchanging $x,y$ gives \[  (1+\eta )^{-1}\leq \frac{g_ D(z,y)}{g_ D(z,x)}\leq 1+\eta \qquad (z\in D\setminus U).  \] Fixed-pole continuity and this ratio estimate prove joint continuity off the diagonal and at the outer boundary. Near an interior diagonal point, a uniform inner-ball upper bound $g_ D(z,a)\leq \log (|z-a|/r_0)$ tends to $-\infty $. This is exactly continuity into the extended-real interval. $\square$ Proposition 7.17.5 . 518349DA23E4 If domains $D_ j$ increase to $D$, then $g_{D_ j}(z,a)\downarrow g_ D(z,a)$ where defined. On any pseudoconvex domain, $g_ D$ is jointly upper semicontinuous, with the same empty-family convention. Proof. The decreasing limit is either identically $-\infty $ or PSH, by the canonical decreasing-limit theorem on the exhaustion. In the former case domain monotonicity already gives equality with $g_ D$. In the latter case it is nonpositive and retains a uniform logarithmic upper pole bound from any fixed inner ball. It is strictly negative by the maximum principle, so it is a competitor and equality follows in the other direction too. An empty intermediate family gives the same immediate equality. For a pseudoconvex domain use the checked PSH exhaustion and its increasing bounded hyperconvex sublevel components. They cover the connected domain: every compact path to a fixed base point eventually lies in a sublevel. Their jointly continuous Green functions decrease to $g_ D$ on each local product neighborhood, proving upper semicontinuity. $\square$ Proposition 7.17.6 . B016253F39B4 For a bounded planar domain, $g_ D$ is minus its canonical Helms-normalized positive Green function, equivalently $-2\pi $ times the Foundations- normalized positive kernel. In particular it is symmetric in its two arguments, and for a conformal map $f:D\to \mathbb D$ one has $g_ D(z,a)=\log |\varphi _{f(a)}(f(z))|$. Proof. On a bounded regular planar domain, the positive Helms kernel $G$ has zero boundary limits and singularity $-\log |z-a|$ plus a harmonic function. Thus $-G$ is a competitor. For any other competitor $u$, $u+G$ is subharmonic off $a$ and bounded above near $a$, so its puncture is removable. Its boundary upper limits are nonpositive, hence $u\leq -G$ by the maximum principle. For a general bounded domain, use the checked increasing exhaustion by bounded regular open sets, choosing the pole's component. Canonical positive Green exhaustion and the preceding negative envelope exhaustion pass this equality to the limit. The normalization factor is the existing identity $G_{\rm Helms}=2\pi G_{\rm Foundations}$ in real dimension two. Symmetry follows from canonical Green symmetry; the conformal formula is the already proved disc formula and invariance. No Riemann mapping existence theorem is a premise of that conditional formula. $\square$ Proposition 7.17.7 . 465EA6ED94FB On a bounded hyperconvex domain, $g_ D(\cdot ,a)$ is the unique negative PSH function $u$ that is locally bounded off $a$, is maximal there, tends to zero at the boundary, and satisfies $u=\log |z-a|+O(1)$ at $a$. Proof. Fix $\epsilon ,\delta >0$. The function $(1+\epsilon )u-\delta $ lies below $g_ D$ near $a$, since their difference is $\epsilon \log |z-a|+O(1)$. It also lies strictly below near the outer boundary, where both unshifted functions tend to zero. On the intervening compact annulus use maximality of $g_ D$ to obtain $(1+\epsilon )u-\delta \leq g_ D$ throughout. Let $\delta $ and then $\epsilon $ decrease to zero. Interchange the two functions and use maximality of $u$ to get the reverse inequality. Neither an isolated-pole Monge–Ampere product nor an excluded-page proof is an input. $\square$ Example 7.17.8 . 34EFBF9EA39F Strict real convexity, even a positive real boundary Hessian with $C^2$ boundary, does not imply a smooth isolated-pole Green function. Take $p=5/2$, $h(z)=(|z|^2+\| z\| _ p^2)^{1/2}$ on $\mathbb C^2$, and $D=\{ h<1\} $. It is a complex norm, so $\log h$ is PSH by the canonical norm support-functional proof and $g_ D(z,0)=\log h(z)$. The continuous negative PSH exhaustion $h-1$ makes $D$ hyperconvex. The function $h^2$ is $C^2$ off zero and its real Hessian is at least twice the identity, since $\| z\| _ p^2$ is convex. Its gradient is nonzero on the unit level by Euler homogeneity. Thus $D$ has strongly convex $C^2$ boundary. At $(t,1/2)$ the logarithm is a real analytic function of $t^2$ and $|t|^{5/2}$ with a strictly positive coefficient of the latter; its third derivative is unbounded as $t\to 0$. Hence it is not $C^3$ at the interior point $(0,1/2)$. The uniqueness just proved excludes a different smooth maximal zero-boundary solution with the same pole. The source's unqualified smoothness survey statement therefore needs the boundary regularity hypotheses of its cited Lempert theorem.

title: Proposition 7.17.7
text: Proposition 7.17.7 . 465EA6ED94FB On a bounded hyperconvex domain, $g_ D(\cdot ,a)$ is the unique negative PSH function $u$ that is locally bounded off $a$, is maximal there, tends to zero at the boundary, and satisfies $u=\log |z-a|+O(1)$ at $a$. Proof. Fix $\epsilon ,\delta >0$. The function $(1+\epsilon )u-\delta $ lies below $g_ D$ near $a$, since their difference is $\epsilon \log |z-a|+O(1)$. It also lies strictly below near the outer boundary, where both unshifted functions tend to zero. On the intervening compact annulus use maximality of $g_ D$ to obtain $(1+\epsilon )u-\delta \leq g_ D$ throughout. Let $\delta $ and then $\epsilon $ decrease to zero. Interchange the two functions and use maximality of $u$ to get the reverse inequality. Neither an isolated-pole Monge–Ampere product nor an excluded-page proof is an input. $\square$

title: Example 7.17.8
text: Example 7.17.8 . 34EFBF9EA39F Strict real convexity, even a positive real boundary Hessian with $C^2$ boundary, does not imply a smooth isolated-pole Green function. Take $p=5/2$, $h(z)=(|z|^2+\| z\| _ p^2)^{1/2}$ on $\mathbb C^2$, and $D=\{ h<1\} $. It is a complex norm, so $\log h$ is PSH by the canonical norm support-functional proof and $g_ D(z,0)=\log h(z)$. The continuous negative PSH exhaustion $h-1$ makes $D$ hyperconvex. The function $h^2$ is $C^2$ off zero and its real Hessian is at least twice the identity, since $\| z\| _ p^2$ is convex. Its gradient is nonzero on the unit level by Euler homogeneity. Thus $D$ has strongly convex $C^2$ boundary. At $(t,1/2)$ the logarithm is a real analytic function of $t^2$ and $|t|^{5/2}$ with a strictly positive coefficient of the latter; its third derivative is unbounded as $t\to 0$. Hence it is not $C^3$ at the interior point $(0,1/2)$. The uniqueness just proved excludes a different smooth maximal zero-boundary solution with the same pole. The source's unqualified smoothness survey statement therefore needs the boundary regularity hypotheses of its cited Lempert theorem.

section: 7.18 Classical Monge–Ampere measures at one exceptional point
text: The following is a proof expansion for the single-point self-product case of the existing small-pole product theorem. It uses only bounded Bedford–Taylor products and their annular weighted continuity; it makes no assertion about the full general Hausdorff-zero mixed-current theorem. Proposition 7.28.1 . 1BBBF8109419 Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $a\in D$, and let $u$ be PSH and locally bounded on $D\setminus \{ a\} $. There is a unique positive Radon measure $M_ u$ such that for every decreasing locally bounded PSH sequence $u_ j\downarrow u$, \[  (dd^ cu_ j)^ n\longrightarrow M_ u\quad \hbox{locally weakly}.  \] It agrees with the bounded product off $a$, is local on open sets, and commutes with positive scaling and addition of constants. More generally, if $v_ j$ are PSH and locally bounded off $a$, and $v_ j\downarrow u$, then $M_{v_ j}\to M_ u$. The measure can charge $a$; it is the classical extension, not the product which deletes pluripolar mass. Proof. Smooth compactly supported tests constant near $a$ are uniformly dense in continuous compactly supported tests, with a common compact support. Indeed first use canonical smooth approximation. For a smooth $\phi $, replace it by $\phi _\delta =\eta _\delta \phi +(1-\eta _\delta )\phi (a)$, where the smooth cutoff $\eta _\delta $ is zero on $B(a,\delta )$ and one outside $B(a,2\delta )$. The uniform difference tends to zero by continuity, and the extra support lies in one fixed compact ball in $D$. Choose first $u_ j=\max (u,-j)$. For a smooth test $\phi $ constant near $a$, bounded recursion and weighted continuity on the compact support of $dd^ c\phi $, which misses $a$, give \[  \lim _ j\int \phi (dd^ cu_ j)^ n =\lim _ j\int u_ j(dd^ cu_ j)^{n-1}\wedge dd^ c\phi =\int u(dd^ cu)^{n-1}\wedge dd^ c\phi .  \] The last product is used only OFF the point. For every compact $K\Subset D$, choose a nonnegative smooth cutoff $\chi =1$ near $K\cup \{ a\} $. Its derivative support is separated from $a$, and all $u_ j$ are uniformly bounded there between $u$ and $\max (u,-1)$. Both signs of $dd^ c\chi $ are bounded by a constant times a positive Euclidean form. The canonical annular CLN estimate therefore bounds $\int \chi (dd^ cu_ j)^ n$ uniformly. In particular the masses on $K$ are bounded. The dense-test limits thus extend to every continuous compact test: uniform approximation and this common mass bound make the integral sequence Cauchy. Its limit is positive, so the canonical Riesz theorem represents it by a positive Radon measure $M_ u$. The same identity and bounds apply to any decreasing locally bounded approximation, using its first member as an upper bound and $u$ as a lower bound on the derivative annulus. Hence the limit is independent of the approximation. Bounded locality identifies it off $a$. General open- set locality, scaling and constants follow by applying the same operations to the truncations and their locally weak limits. Finally the displayed identity holds for every $v$ in the same one-point class, by its bounded approximations. Apply it to $v_ j\downarrow u$: on the derivative annulus all functions are uniformly locally bounded, so the same weighted BT limit applies. The same cutoff bounds and density then give $M_{v_ j}\to M_ u$, without requiring $v_ j$ bounded at $a$. $\square$ Proposition 5.27.18 . F7D352207205 Suppose that $u,v$ belong to this one-point class and $u(a)=-\infty $. If $u\leq v+C$ near $a$, then $M_ v(\{ a\} )\leq M_ u(\{ a\} )$. If $u-v$ is bounded near $a$, the atom masses are equal. If both have value $-\infty $ at $a$ and $\limsup _{z\to a}u(z)/v(z)\leq 1$, then $M_ u(\{ a\} )\leq M_ v(\{ a\} )$. Proof. This is the point case of the canonical residual-invariance argument, now with its decreasing-continuity input proved above. For $\epsilon >0$ and $c>0$ put $w_ c=\max \{ v-c,(1+\epsilon )u\} $. Near $a$, upper semicontinuity makes $u<-(C+c)/\epsilon $, and the assumed order gives $v-c-(1+\epsilon )u>0$ off $a$. At $a$ the second branch is minus infinity. Thus $w_ c=v-c$ on a neighborhood of $a$ and $M_{w_ c}(\{ a\} )=M_ v(\{ a\} )$ by ordinary locality. As $c\uparrow \infty $, $w_ c\downarrow (1+\epsilon )u$. Compact-set upper mass semicontinuity of positive measures gives $M_ v(\{ a\} )\leq (1+\epsilon )^ nM_ u(\{ a\} )$. Let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. A bounded difference gives the reverse inequality too, since both functions then have a pole. For the ratio assertion, both functions are negative near $a$. For each $\eta >0$ the limsup condition gives $v\leq u/(1+\eta )$ there. Apply the first assertion with these two functions and let $\eta \downarrow 0$. This is stronger than the source's ordered ratio-one special case. $\square$ Proposition 7.18.1 . 00C5CD9B3208 Let $D$ be a bounded domain and let $u,v$ be PSH, continuous and finite on $\overline D\setminus \{ a\} $, with both taking value $-\infty $ at $a$. If $u<v$ on $D\setminus \{ a\} $ and $u-v\to 0$ at the boundary, then $M_ v(D)\leq M_ u(D)$, allowing infinite total mass. Proof. Truncating such a function below a sufficiently negative constant preserves its total mass. To see this, the changed sublevel is compactly contained in $D$. Choose a smooth cutoff equal to one on a neighborhood of that sublevel, with derivative support where the function and its truncation agree. The constant-near-point identity in the first proof makes their cutoff integrals equal. Off the compact change set their measures agree by locality. Thus their total masses agree, also when the shared exterior mass is infinite. Choose $m$ large and put $u_ m=\max (u,-m-1)$ and $v_ m=\max (v,-m)$. They agree with the original functions near the boundary, have boundary difference tending to zero, and satisfy $u_ m<v_ m$ everywhere, including at $a$. Canonical bounded comparison on $D$, with its strict comparison set equal to $D$, gives $\int _ D(dd^ cv_ m)^ n\leq \int _ D(dd^ cu_ m)^ n$. Use the mass-preserving truncation identities to conclude. $\square$ Proposition 7.18.2 . AD17D2D77F97 For $R>0$, $M_{\log (|z-a|/R)}=2^{-n}\delta _ a$. If $D$ is bounded and hyperconvex, its Green function satisfies \[  M_{g_ D(\cdot ,a)}=2^{-n}\delta _ a.  \] It is the unique PSH solution continuous and finite off $a$, with $u=\log |z-a|+O(1)$ at $a$, zero boundary limit, and this prescribed classical measure. Proof. The existing bounded spherical-product formula states $(dd^ c\log \max \{ |z-a|^2,r^2\} )^ n=\sigma _{a,r}$, normalized surface measure on the radius-$r$ sphere. Therefore the bounded truncations of $\log |z-a|$ have measures $2^{-n}\sigma _{a,r}$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Their weak limit is $2^{-n}\delta _ a$ by continuity of compact tests. Adding $-\log R$ does not change the measure. The Green ball bounds give $g_ D-\log |z-a|=O(1)$ near $a$. The proved residual invariance identifies its atom as $2^{-n}$. Off $a$ its local boundedness and maximality give zero bounded MA measure, so no other part remains. The continuity and zero boundary limit follow from Proposition 7.17.4 . Conversely the prescribed measure makes any proposed solution maximal off $a$. Its zero boundary limit and logarithmic pole make it negative by the maximum principle. The zero-boundary uniqueness in Proposition 7.17.7 then identifies it with $g_ D$. $\square$

title: 7.19 Symmetric envelopes and finite collections of poles
search_title: Symmetric envelopes and finite collections of poles
section: 7.19 Symmetric envelopes and finite collections of poles
text: Throughout this section $D$ is a bounded domain in $\mathbb C^ n$. Proposition 7.19.1 . 9261026A57C2 On every bounded domain $D$, the isolated-pole Green function is jointly upper semicontinuous on $D\times D$. Proof. Suppose $(z_ j,a_ j)\to (z,a)$. A uniform inner-ball bound gives convergence to minus infinity if $z=a$, so assume $z\ne a$. Write $u_ j=g_ D(\cdot ,a_ j)$. They are PSH, bounded above by zero. For a fixed $R>\operatorname {diam}D$, the lower bound $u_ j(x)\geq \log (|x-a_ j|/R)$ prevents collapse at a fixed point away from $a$. Canonical PSH compactness therefore supplies an $L^1_{\rm loc}$ convergent subsequence along any subsequence attaining the upper limit. Call its proper PSH limit $u$. A uniform inner radius $r>0$ gives $u_ j(x)\leq \log (|x-a_ j|/r)$ near the moving poles. Off $a$ the right sides converge locally uniformly; passing to the $L^1$ limit and then canonical representatives gives $u(x)\leq \log (|x-a|/r)$ near $a$, so $u$ is a negative competitor for $g_ D(\cdot ,a)$. For a fixed small radial convolution kernel, the submean inequality gives $u_ j(z_ j)\leq (u_ j*\rho _\epsilon )(z_ j)$. The $L^1$ convergence makes the convolutions converge locally uniformly. Thus $\limsup _ j u_ j(z_ j)\leq (u*\rho _\epsilon )(z)$; letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ gives at most $u(z)\leq g_ D(z,a)$. This proves the assertion without a pseudoconvexity hypothesis. $\square$ Proposition 7.19.2 . ABA8792055E8 For bounded $D$, $g_ D(z,w)=g_ D(w,z)$ if and only if it is PSH in its second variable for each fixed first variable. Proof. Symmetry and the known first-variable property give one direction. Conversely, for fixed $z$ and an inner ball $B(z,r)\subset D$, ball comparison gives $g_ D(z,w)\leq g_{B(z,r)}(z,w)=\log (|w-z|/r)$ near $z$. The assumed negative PSH function of $w$ is therefore a competitor for $g_ D(w,z)$. It is at most that envelope. Interchanging $z,w$ proves equality. $\square$ Put $d(z)=\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus D)$ and \[  H(z,w)=\log |z-w|-\log \max \{ d(z),d(w)\} .  \] Let $W_ D$ be the supremum of jointly SH functions on $D\times D$ that are nonpositive, are separately PSH in the two $n$-variable groups, and are at most $H$. Joint SH is part of this definition; joint PSH is not being imposed. Proposition 7.19.3 . 557F24B2F2DD The raw envelope $W_ D$ is jointly USC and SH, separately PSH, symmetric, and satisfies $W_ D\leq g_ D$. It equals $g_ D$ exactly when $g_ D$ is symmetric. For each pole $a$, $W_ D(\cdot ,a)$ is locally bounded off $a$ and differs from $\log |z-a|$ by a bounded term near $a$. Its classical Monge–Ampere atom at $a$ is consequently $2^{-n}$, and its total mass is at least $2^{-n}$. Proof. Choose $R>\operatorname {diam}D$. The jointly PSH function $\ell (z,w)=\log (|z-w|/R)$ is an admissible lower bound, since $d(z),d(w)<R$. The family is bounded above by zero, so its joint USC regularization $F$ is SH by the canonical real envelope theorem. It retains the bound by $H$, which is continuous off the diagonal and tends to minus infinity at the diagonal. For fixed $w_0$, take the USC regularization in $z$ of $\sup _{|w-w_0|<\epsilon }W_ D(z,w)$. This is PSH by the canonical PSH envelope theorem. As $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, these functions decrease to $F(z,w_0)$: the iterated upper limits are the same as joint upper limits over shrinking rectangles. The lower bound $\ell $ prevents an identically-minus-infinity limit. Thus $F$ is PSH in $z$; interchange variables for the other group. It is an admissible member of the original family, so $F\leq W_ D\leq F$, proving equality. Swapping the variables preserves that family, hence $W_ D$ is symmetric. For fixed $a$, its upper pole bound and negativity make it a competitor for $g_ D(\cdot ,a)$. The bounds $\ell \leq W_ D\leq H$ also give the asserted local boundedness and logarithmic type. Apply the proved one-point residual invariance to obtain its atom and the total-mass lower bound. If $g_ D$ is symmetric, it is separately PSH and jointly USC by the preceding propositions. Separate radial convolutions are smooth joint SH functions, since their two partial Laplacians are nonnegative. They decrease to $g_ D$: separate submeans bound them below by $g_ D$, and joint USC bounds their upper limit. Local integrability follows also from $\ell \leq g_ D\leq 0$. Therefore $g_ D$ is joint SH. Its two inner-ball upper bounds give $g_ D\leq H$, so it belongs to the defining family and $W_ D=g_ D$. The converse follows from symmetry of $W_ D$. $\square$ Proposition 7.19.4 . 0FDD375AF53F For bounded $D$, set \[  e_ D(z,w)=-\sup _{f\in \mathcal O(D,\mathbb C),\  f\  \mathrm{nonconstant}} g_{f(D)}(f(z),f(w)).  \] Then $e_ D$ is symmetric, has value $+\infty $ on the diagonal, is finite and strictly positive off it, and $-e_ D\leq g_ D$. In dimension one, $e_ D=-g_ D$. Proof. We first fix the planar target convention, including unbounded images. A nonempty negative SH logarithmic-pole family supplies a nonconstant positive superharmonic function. The canonical planar Greenian criterion therefore gives a positive Helms-normalized classical Green kernel. Conversely its negative is a pole competitor. Exhaustion by bounded regular open sets and the proved negative-envelope exhaustion identify $g$ with minus that classical kernel. If the domain is not Greenian, every pole family is empty and $g$ is identically minus infinity. Thus all the planar target kernels in the definition are symmetric, with the empty-family convention included. Holomorphic contraction gives each target value at most $g_ D$, proving $-e_ D\leq g_ D$. Off the diagonal a bounded separating coordinate function has bounded planar image and distinct values, giving one finite target Green value. Hence the supremum is finite, while its upper bound $g_ D<0$ makes $e_ D$ strictly positive. On the diagonal every target value is minus infinity. If $D$ is planar, the identity map supplies equality. $\square$ Proposition 7.19.5 . A3DBF2B9E6B2 Let $a_1,\ldots ,a_ N$, $N\geq 1$, be distinct points of $D$ and let $\alpha _ j>0$. The envelope $g_ A$ of negative PSH functions with $u\leq \alpha _ j\log |z-a_ j|+O(1)$ at every $a_ j$ is a negative PSH function, locally bounded and maximal off this finite set, with exact logarithmic types $\alpha _ j\log |z-a_ j|+O(1)$. Its classical measure is \[  M_{g_ A}=2^{-n}\sum _{j=1}^ N\alpha _ j^ n\delta _{a_ j}.  \] If $D$ is hyperconvex it has zero boundary limits and is the unique PSH function locally bounded off these points, of these logarithmic types, with zero boundary limits and this prescribed classical measure. Proof. A sum of sufficiently shifted negative logarithms is a competitor. Each competitor is at most $\alpha _ jg_ D(\cdot ,a_ j)$ for every $j$. These uniform local pole bounds survive regularization, so the raw supremum is PSH and itself a competitor. The sum lower bound and the individual upper bounds give exact pole types and local boundedness away from the finite set. A compact maximum replacement away from all poles remains a competitor, proving maximality there. The one-point measure construction applies on a neighborhood of each pole; it agrees with the bounded product elsewhere. The local limits of global bounded truncations therefore glue to a positive Radon measure. Residual invariance and positive scaling give atom $2^{-n}\alpha _ j^ n$ at $a_ j$; maximality makes the remaining part zero. In the hyperconvex case, $\sum _ j\alpha _ jg_ D(\cdot ,a_ j)$ is a competitor with zero boundary limit, so the envelope has that limit too. Any proposed solution is negative by the maximum principle and maximal off the poles by its prescribed measure and canonical bounded maximality. For uniqueness, compare $(1+\epsilon )u-\delta $ with the envelope near each of the finitely many poles and near the outer boundary. The excess set is then compact and avoids all poles, so maximality proves the inequality. Let the parameters decrease to zero and interchange the functions, as in the one-pole proof. No interior continuity theorem for this multipole envelope is needed or asserted by this locally bounded formulation. $\square$

In a local parametrization $F$ at $a$, $F'(0)
e 0$. The outer-ball Green lower bound gives $E(F(\zeta ))\geq c|\zeta |^2$ near zero. Equality of the two Levi forms and the curve limits thus give $v/E	o 1$ at $a$. Proposition 9.17.2 . 6BCDD3D7DD27 The function \[  q(\zeta ,\eta )=\operatorname {atanh}|\phi _\eta (\zeta )|  \] is a distance on $\Delta $, invariant under its automorphisms, and contracts under every holomorphic self-map $f$ of $\Delta $. On the disc, Schwarz–Pick and the identity disc give $c_\Delta = \delta _\Delta =q$, and its triangle inequality gives $k_\Delta =q$. Use $d^ c=\mathrm i( ar\partial -\partial )/(4\pi )$, so that $dd^ c=\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial /(2\pi )$, and put $m_ n=2^{-n}$. Proposition 7.20.1 . 1359A4B6C1D8 Let $u$ be $C^2$, PSH and maximal on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$. If $c$ is a regular value and $S=\{ u=c\} $ is compact, then \[  (dd^ c\max (u,c))^ n=[S]\wedge d^ cu\wedge (dd^ cu)^{n-1},  \] where $S$ is oriented as the boundary of $\{ u<c\} $. In particular the right side is a positive measure. Proof. Off $S$ the asserted measure is zero, by locality and maximality. Choose smooth convex increasing $F_\epsilon $ decreasing to $\max (t,c)$, with derivative zero below $c-\epsilon $, one above $c+\epsilon $, and between zero and one elsewhere. Such functions are the even one-dimensional convolutions of the maximum. The chain rule and $(dd^ cu)^ n=0$ give \[  (dd^ cF_\epsilon (u))^ n =n(F_\epsilon '(u))^{n-1}F_\epsilon ''(u) du\wedge d^ cu\wedge (dd^ cu)^{n-1}.  \] This identity holds for $C^2$ potentials by the determinant formula. In regular-level coordinates, integration of a continuous compactly supported test $h$ on the right is integration in $t$ of \[  n(F_\epsilon '(t))^{n-1}F_\epsilon ''(t) \int _{\{ u=t\} }h\, d^ cu\wedge (dd^ cu)^{n-1}.  \] The level integral is continuous near $c$, by the local flow of a vector field transverse to the level and the continuity of the coefficients. The nonnegative scalar coefficient is the derivative of $(F_\epsilon ')^ n$, has integral one and is supported near $c$. It therefore converges to evaluation at $c$. Bounded decreasing Bedford–Taylor continuity identifies the left limit. The orientation is the outward one because the transverse coordinate is $u$. $\square$ Let $D$ be a bounded hyperconvex domain, $a\in D$, $g=g_ D(\cdot ,a)$, $g_ r=\max (g,r)$ and $B(r)=\{ g<r\} $ for $r<0$. The measures $ eta _ r=(dd^ cg_ r)^ n$ are supported on $\{ g=r\} $ and have total mass $m_ n$. Indeed locality/maximality gives the support; the compact-change cutoff argument for the classical point measure gives mass preservation under truncation, and $M_ g=m_ n\delta _ a$. The domain $B(r)$ is connected. A component not containing $a$ would be relatively compact away from $a$ and have boundary values $r$ for the continuous maximal function $g$; comparison with the constant $r$ would contradict $g<r$ there. Its negative continuous PSH exhaustion $\max (g-r,-1)$ proves hyperconvexity. Zero-boundary logarithmic uniqueness therefore gives \[  g_{B(r)}(z,a)=g_ D(z,a)-r\qquad (z\in B(r)).  \] Proposition 7.20.2 . 351C8FCB17FF For $v\in \operatorname {PSH}(D)\cap C(D)$ there is a positive classical mixed measure $
u =dd^ cv\wedge (dd^ cg)^{n-1}$, defined by decreasing truncations, and \[  \int _ D v\, d eta _ r-m_ n v(a) =\int _{B(r)}(r-g)\, d
u \qquad (r<0).  \] In particular all integrals on the right are finite and $r\mapsto \int v\, d eta _ r$ is increasing. Proof. For $s<0$ put $
u _ s=dd^ cv\wedge (dd^ cg_ s)^{n-1}$. The bounded polynomial expansion of $(dd^ c(g_ s+t v))^ n$ has positive mixed coefficients. For any fixed $t\geq 0$, $g_ s+t v$ decreases to a PSH function locally bounded off $a$. The proved one-point classical continuity theorem gives a limit for its top measure. Evaluating at $n+1$ distinct nonnegative $t$ and inverting the Vandermonde matrix therefore gives weak limits for every mixed coefficient, still positive. The coefficient of $t$ is $n
u _ s$, defining the asserted $
u $. For $n=1$ it is simply $dd^ cv$. On $D\setminus \{ a\} $ this agrees with the ordinary bounded mixed product by locality. For $s<t<0$, we claim \[  
u _ s(B(t))=
u (B(t)).  \] For $n=1$ the claim is immediate. For $n\geq 2$ and $s'<s$, the difference $
u _ s-
u _{s'}$ is $dd^ c$ of a bounded mixed current supported in the compact set $\{ g\leq s\} \subset B(t)$: use the telescoping sum with factor $g_ s-g_{s'}$ and the closed factors $dd^ cv$, $dd^ cg_ s$, $dd^ cg_{s'}$. A smooth cutoff equal to one on a neighborhood of that compact set integrates this difference to zero. Let $s'	o -\infty $ with this same cutoff. Locality shows that $
u _ s-
u $ is still supported there, and its cutoff integral is zero. This proves the claim without assuming that $\{ g=t\} $ has zero measure in a weak-limit argument. Write $F(r)=\int v\, d eta _ r$. For $s<r<0$, bounded compactly supported integration by parts and the telescoping product give \[  F(r)-F(s) =\int _ D(g_ r-g_ s)\, dd^ cv\wedge \sum _{k=0}^{n-1}(dd^ cg_ r)^ k\wedge (dd^ cg_ s)^{n-1-k} =\int _ D(r-g_ s)_+\, d

The smooth differences are still supported in one fixed compact set, so no outer boundary term occurs. In the second equality every $k\geq 1$ term vanishes where its weight is positive, because $g_ r$ is constant on $\{ g<r\} $; on the remaining level the continuous weight is zero. Layer cake and the preceding claim give \[  F(r)-F(s)=\int _ s^ r
u _ s(B(t))\, dt =\int _ s^ r
u (B(t))\, dt.  \] As $s	o -\infty $, the supports of $ eta _ s$ shrink to $a$ and their common mass is $m_ n$, so continuity of $v$ gives $F(s)	o m_ n v(a)$. Positivity proves monotonicity. $\square$ Proposition 7.20.3 . EC62871F80C4 The measures $ eta _ r$, extended by zero outside $D$, converge weakly as $r\uparrow 0$ to a positive measure $\mu _{D,a}$ on $\partial D$ of mass $m_ n$. For $v\in \operatorname {PSH}(D)\cap C(\overline D)$, \[  v(a)=2^ n\int _{\partial D}v\, d\mu _{D,a} +2^ n\int _ Dg\, dd^ cv\wedge (dd^ cg)^{n-1}.  \] For pluriharmonic $v$ the second term vanishes. text: Proposition 7.20.1 . 1359A4B6C1D8 Let $u$ be $C^2$, PSH and maximal on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$. If $c$ is a regular value and $S=\{ u=c\} $ is compact, then \[  (dd^ c\max (u,c))^ n=[S]\wedge d^ cu\wedge (dd^ cu)^{n-1},  \] where $S$ is oriented as the boundary of $\{ u<c\} $. In particular the right side is a positive measure. Proof. Off $S$ the asserted measure is zero, by locality and maximality. Choose smooth convex increasing $F_\epsilon $ decreasing to $\max (t,c)$, with derivative zero below $c-\epsilon $, one above $c+\epsilon $, and between zero and one elsewhere. Such functions are the even one-dimensional convolutions of the maximum. The chain rule and $(dd^ cu)^ n=0$ give \[  (dd^ cF_\epsilon (u))^ n =n(F_\epsilon '(u))^{n-1}F_\epsilon ''(u) du\wedge d^ cu\wedge (dd^ cu)^{n-1}.  \] This identity holds for $C^2$ potentials by the determinant formula. In regular-level coordinates, integration of a continuous compactly supported test $h$ on the right is integration in $t$ of \[  n(F_\epsilon '(t))^{n-1}F_\epsilon ''(t) \int _{\{ u=t\} }h\, d^ cu\wedge (dd^ cu)^{n-1}.  \] The level integral is continuous near $c$, by the local flow of a vector field transverse to the level and the continuity of the coefficients. The nonnegative scalar coefficient is the derivative of $(F_\epsilon ')^ n$, has integral one and is supported near $c$. It therefore converges to evaluation at $c$. Bounded decreasing Bedford–Taylor continuity identifies the left limit. The orientation is the outward one because the transverse coordinate is $u$. $\square$
