title: 16.36 The real cube equilibrium density
text: Proposition 16.36.1 . 6BA3C254E28C The classical equilibrium measure of $K=[-1,1]^ n$ in the present normalization is \[  (dd^ cV_ K)^ n=2^{-n}\pi ^{-n} \prod _{j=1}^ n(1-x_ j^2)^{-1/2}\, dx_1\cdots dx_ n  \] on the real cube. For $n\geq 2$ its density is not bounded above by a constant times $\operatorname {dist}(x,\partial K)^{-1/2}$. Proof. Let $J(\zeta )=(\zeta +\zeta ^{-1})/2$ on $\mathbb C^*$, and $F=J^ n$. The quadratic inverse equation shows that $J$ is proper of degree two: above a compact target its two roots are bounded and bounded away from zero. Thus $F$ is proper of degree $2^ n$. The proved Joukowski and product extremal formulas give \[  V_ K\circ F=U(\zeta )=\max _ j|\log |\zeta _ j||.  \] This is continuous and locally bounded. Its top measure is supported on the unit real torus. To see this, use local logarithmic coordinates with real parts $t_ j$. Away from $t=0$, the active slopes of $\max _ j|t_ j|$ contain at most one of the two signs for each coordinate. There is a common affine direction on which all these slopes equal one. Subtract its real pluriharmonic coordinate and make a complex-linear change of variables. The remaining maximum depends on at most $n-1$ complex variables, so its top product vanishes by bounded smoothing. Off the analytic critical sets of $F$ and their analytic images, biholomorphic bounded-product invariance applies on the finitely many inverse branches. Neither top measure charges those analytic sets, because the potentials are locally bounded and analytic sets are pluripolar. Consequently \[  F_*((dd^ cU)^ n)=2^ n(dd^ cV_ K)^ n.  \] The previously proved logarithmic total mass is $m_ n$ for $V_ K$; properness and the displayed identity therefore give total mass one for $U$. Its independent rotational invariance and torus support identify it with product normalized angular measure, by averaging continuous tests. Finally $J(e^{\mathrm it})=\cos t$ sends circle probability to the arcsine density $dx/(\pi \sqrt{1-x^2})$; this follows by the two inverse arcs and the ordinary change of variables. Push forward the product and divide by $2^ n$ to get the formula. At $x_ j=1-t$, $t\downarrow 0$, the density is asymptotic to a positive constant times $t^{-n/2}$, whereas the real distance to the cube boundary is $t$. For $n\geq 2$ its ratio to $t^{-1/2}$ is unbounded; continuity of the density in the cube interior makes the violations persist on open sets. This disproves a universal square-root boundary bound at corners; it makes no assertion about a correctly qualified smooth-body theorem. $\square$

title: 7.21 Boundary peaks and the symmetric-envelope mass criterion

section: 7.21 Boundary peaks and the symmetric-envelope mass criterion
text: Proposition 7.21.1 . DBAB6E03ACC7 Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be bounded with $C^2$ strongly pseudoconvex boundary. For every $\xi \in \partial D$ there is $p\in \mathcal O(D)\cap C(\overline D)$ such that $p(\xi )=1$ and $|p|<1$ on $\overline D\setminus \{ \xi \} $. Proof. We give the boundary and solvability details. A $C^2$ defining function $q$ can be made strictly PSH on a boundary collar by replacing it by $q+Aq^2$ and shrinking the collar. On the boundary the added Hessian is a positive multiple of $A\partial q\otimes \bar\partial q$; the tangential Levi form is positive and the bounded mixed terms are absorbed by the normal square. Compactness makes the constants uniform. Write the resulting function as $\rho $. Small outward domains $D_ t$, obtained by adjoining the collar $0\leq \rho <t$, contain $\overline D$ compactly and are pseudoconvex. Explicitly, near their boundary $1/(t-\rho )$ is PSH; its maximum with a sufficiently large constant glues to that constant in the interior, giving a continuous PSH exhaustion. The Levi Taylor polynomial at $\xi $ gives a holomorphic polynomial $L$, with $L(\xi )=0$, for which \[  \operatorname {Re}L(z)\leq -c|z-\xi |^2 \quad (z\in \overline D\text{ near }\xi ).  \] Indeed subtract the holomorphic linear and pure quadratic Taylor terms from $\rho $; the remainder has a positive definite Hermitian quadratic part and an $o(|z-\xi |^2)$ error. On a small outward domain the same calculation gives $\operatorname {Re}L\leq t-c|z-\xi |^2$. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi $, equal to one on $B(\xi ,r)$ and supported on $B(\xi ,2r)$ in this neighborhood, with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. For sufficiently small $t>0$, $L$ has no zero on the support of $\bar\partial \chi $ in $\overline{D_ t}$. The form $\alpha =(\bar\partial \chi )/L$, extended by zero, is smooth, $\bar\partial $-closed and bounded on $D_ t$. The exact canonical Hörmander theorem, with smooth weight $|z|^2$ and Hessian the identity, gives $b\in L^2(D_ t)$ with $\bar\partial b=\alpha $. It is smooth inside $D_ t$: locally its Laplacian is smooth, and a smooth local Newton potential followed by the harmonic distribution theorem gives this regularity. In particular $b$ is bounded on $\overline D$. The function \[  B=\chi /L-b-C  \] is holomorphic on $D$. Choose $C>1+\sup _{\overline D}|b|$. The local Levi inequality shows $\operatorname {Re}(\chi /L)\leq 0$ where $\chi \ne 0$, so $\operatorname {Re}B<-1$ throughout $D$ and on its boundary away from $\xi $. Thus $p=\exp (1/B)$ is holomorphic there and has modulus less than one. Near $\xi $, $B=1/L-b-C$, hence $1/B\to 0$ and $p\to 1$. There are no other zeros of $L$ on the relevant closed local domain, and away from the cutoff its expression is smooth. This proves the continuous extension and the peak property. $\square$ Proposition 7.21.2 . FAE7CB808668 On a domain $D$ as above, the symmetric envelope $W_ D$ has zero boundary limits in each variable. For every $a\in D$, its classical slice measure has mass at least $m_ n=2^{-n}$, and \[  M_{W_ D(\cdot ,a)}(D)=m_ n \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad W_ D(\cdot ,a)=g_ D(\cdot ,a).  \] The total mass equals that of every sufficiently negative bounded truncation. In particular, equality for every pole is equivalent to $W_ D=g_ D$, or equivalently to symmetry of $g_ D$. Proof. For a nonconstant holomorphic $p:D\to \Delta $ the symmetric kernel \[  K_ p(z,w)=\log \left|\frac{p(z)-p(w)}{1-p(z)\overline{p(w)}}\right|  \] is an admissible member of the defining family of $W_ D$. It is nonpositive, separately PSH and jointly SH: its numerator is a holomorphic logarithm on the product, and the denominator logarithm is smooth and harmonic in each variable group, hence jointly harmonic. For each fixed pole the local Lipschitz bound on $p$ gives the upper logarithmic pole. Thus $K_ p\leq g_ D(z,w)$ and, by symmetry, $K_ p\leq g_ D(w,z)$. The centered-ball estimates imply \[  K_ p(z,w)\leq \log |z-w|-\log \max \{ d(z),d(w)\}   \] on all pairs: outside the relevant centered ball that individual bound is nonnegative, so follows from $K_ p\leq 0$. This verifies the exact distance constraint, including pairs with $p(z)=p(w)$. Fix $a$ and a boundary point $\xi $, and choose its peak $p$ from the preceding proposition. Then $p(z)\to 1$, $|p(a)|<1$, and $K_ p(z,a)\to 0$ as $z\to \xi $. Since $K_ p\leq W_ D\leq 0$, the slice has zero boundary limit. Its two-sided logarithmic bounds and local boundedness off $a$ were proved in the basic-envelope proposition; the classical one-point residual invariance gives atom $m_ n$ at $a$. This proves the total lower bound. For $w=W_ D(\cdot ,a)$, a sufficiently negative truncation $w_ s$ changes $w$ only on a compact set, since $w\to 0$ on the boundary. The smooth test identity constant near the pole gives equal integrals of $M_ w$ and $(dd^ cw_ s)^ n$ against a cutoff which is one on that change set. Off it the measures agree by locality. Their total masses agree, allowing infinite exterior mass; no interior continuity of $w$ is required. If its total mass is $m_ n$, positivity and its known atom force $M_ w=m_ n\delta _ a$. The bounded maximality criterion makes $w$ maximal off $a$. The zero-boundary scaled comparison with finitely many pole neighborhoods, here just one, then identifies $w$ with $g_ D(\cdot ,a)$. Conversely equality of the functions gives the known Green Dirac measure. Apply this at all poles and use the proved symmetry criterion $W_ D=g_ D$ iff $g_ D$ is symmetric. $\square$

For a nonconstant holomorphic $p:D\to \Delta $ the symmetric kernel \[  K_ p(z,w)=\log \left|\frac{p(z)-p(w)}{1-p(z)\overline{p(w)}}\right|  \] is an admissible member of the defining family of $W_ D$. It is nonpositive, separately PSH and jointly SH: its numerator is a holomorphic logarithm on the product, and the denominator logarithm is smooth and harmonic in each variable group, hence jointly harmonic. For each fixed pole the local Lipschitz bound on $p$ gives the upper logarithmic pole. Thus $K_ p\leq g_ D(z,w)$ and, by symmetry, $K_ p\leq g_ D(w,z)$. The centered-ball estimates imply \[  K_ p(z,w)\leq \log |z-w|-\log \max \{ d(z),d(w)\}   \] on all pairs: outside the relevant centered ball that individual bound is nonnegative, so follows from $K_ p\leq 0$. This verifies the exact distance constraint, including pairs with $p(z)=p(w)$. Fix $a$ and a boundary point $\xi $, and choose its peak $p$ from the preceding proposition. Then $p(z)\to 1$, $|p(a)|<1$, and $K_ p(z,a)\to 0$ as $z\to \xi $. Since $K_ p\leq W_ D\leq 0$, the slice has zero boundary limit. Its two-sided logarithmic bounds and local boundedness off $a$ were proved in the basic-envelope proposition; the classical one-point residual invariance gives atom $m_ n$ at $a$. This proves the total lower bound. For $w=W_ D(\cdot ,a)$, a sufficiently negative truncation $w_ s$ changes $w$ only on a compact set, since $w\to 0$ on the boundary. The smooth test identity constant near the pole gives equal integrals of $M_ w$ and $(dd^ cw_ s)^ n$ against a cutoff which is one on that change set. Off it the measures agree by locality. Their total masses agree, allowing infinite exterior mass; no interior continuity of $w$ is required. If its total mass is $m_ n$, positivity and its known atom force $M_ w=m_ n\delta _ a$. The bounded maximality criterion makes $w$ maximal off $a$. The zero-boundary scaled comparison with finitely many pole neighborhoods, here just one, then identifies $w$ with $g_ D(\cdot ,a)$. Conversely equality of the functions gives the known Green Dirac measure. Apply this at all poles and use the proved symmetry criterion $W_ D=g_ D$ iff $g_ D$ is symmetric. $\square$

section: 7.22 A smooth strictly pseudoconvex domain with asymmetric Green function
text: Proposition 7.22.1 . 8B924AA3ED4A There is a bounded strongly pseudoconvex domain in $\mathbb C^2$ with real analytic boundary whose pluricomplex Green function is asymmetric. On some such domain and at some pole, the total symmetric-envelope slice mass is strictly greater than $2^{-2}$, possibly infinite. Proof. Fix $a=1/2$ and choose $\epsilon >0$ sufficiently small. Put \[  P(z,w)=w^2-z^2(z-a),\qquad u(z,w)=\max \left\{ \tfrac 12\log \frac{|P(z,w)|}{\epsilon ^2}, \log |z|\right\} ,\qquad D=\{ u<0\} .  \] This is bounded, since $|z|<1$ and $|P|<\epsilon ^2$ bound $w$. It is connected: the proper finite holomorphic map $(z,w)\mapsto (z,P/\epsilon ^2)$ maps it onto $\Delta ^2$, and every component maps openly and properly, hence onto that connected target. Each component would therefore contain a preimage of $(0,0)$, whose only preimage is $(0,0)$. There can be only one component. The maximum $u$ is continuous off $(0,0)$, zero at the boundary, and $u=\log |(z,w)|+O(1)$ at zero. The last assertion follows from $|P|\leq C|(z,w)|^2$ near zero and $|w|^2\leq |P|+C|z|^2$. It is maximal off zero: if one holomorphic factor is zero, its logarithm is inactive locally; otherwise take their local holomorphic logarithms, subtract one pluriharmonic term, and express the maximum as a convex function of the real part of one holomorphic scalar function. Its smooth approximations have complex Hessian rank at most one, so their top products in dimension two vanish. Bounded continuity passes this to $u$. Also $\max (u,-1)$ is a continuous negative PSH exhaustion of $D$. Green uniqueness therefore gives $u=g_ D(\cdot ,0)$, in particular $g_ D((a,0),0)=\log a$. Let $L=\log (1/\epsilon )$ and $c_\epsilon =1/2+L^{-1/2}<1$. The corrected competitor for the other pole is \[  v(z,w)= \begin{cases}  \log (|w|/2),& |z-a|\leq \epsilon ,\\  \max \{ \log (|w|/2),c_\epsilon \log |(z-a)/(1-az)|\} , & |z-a|\geq \epsilon . \end{cases}  \] On the gluing circle, points of $D$ satisfy the actual lower estimate \[  |w|^2\geq (a-\epsilon )^2\epsilon -\epsilon ^2\geq C_0\epsilon  \] for a fixed $C_0>0$ and small $\epsilon $. Therefore the first branch is at least $-L/2-C_1$. On this circle $\log |(z-a)/(1-az)|=-L+O(1)$ uniformly, so the other branch is at most $-L/2-\sqrt L+C_2$. For small $\epsilon $ the first strictly dominates, proving PSH gluing. Also $|w|<2$ on $D$, so both branches are negative. Near $(a,0)$ the expression is $\log (|w|/2)$, at most the required logarithmic pole in the full Euclidean norm. It is thus a Green competitor, and \[  g_ D(0,(a,0))\geq v(0,0)=c_\epsilon \log a >\log a=g_ D((a,0),0).  \] To obtain smooth strictly pseudoconvex domains explicitly, let \[  Q_ j(z,w)=|z|^{4j}+|P(z,w)/\epsilon ^2|^{2j} +\delta _ j(|z|^2+|w|^2), \qquad \delta _ j\downarrow 0,  \] and choose regular values $b_ j\uparrow 1$ in $(1/2,1)$. Proposition 16.37.1 provides them. Each $Q_ j$ is a strictly PSH real polynomial. Its sublevel $Q_ j<b_ j$ is relatively compact in $D$, with strongly pseudoconvex real analytic boundary. Let $D_ j$ be its component containing zero. On $D$, $Q_{j+1}\leq Q_ j$ and $b_{j+1}>b_ j$, so these components increase, with compact containment. They exhaust $D$: on every compact joining path in $D$, $Q_ j\to 0$ uniformly. If every $g_{D_ j}$ were symmetric, the domain-exhaustion limit $g_{D_ j}\downarrow g_ D$ would be symmetric, contradicting the strict inequality above. One $D_ j$ has the stated asymmetry. On that domain $W\ne g$ at some pair because $W$ is symmetric. The preceding mass criterion gives strictly greater total mass at a corresponding pole. $\square$

title: 9.18 Disc interpolation on convex domains
Theorem 9.18.1
text: Theorem 9.18.1 . 7F33F823B79C On a bounded convex domain $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$, the one-disc distance $\delta _ D$ is a complete metric inducing the Euclidean topology, and $\delta _ D=k_ D$. Every pair of distinct points has an extremal disc: there are $f:\Delta \to D$ holomorphic and $0<t<1$ such that $f(0)=a$, $f(t)=b$ and $\delta _ D(a,b)=q(0,t)$. Proof. We first prove the triangle inequality. Discs used in the infimum can be chosen holomorphic on a neighborhood of $\overline\Delta $ with image in $D$, at arbitrarily small additional distance cost. Indeed, replace a given disc $f$ by $f(r\zeta )$ with $r\uparrow 1$, and replace its two interpolation nodes by their quotients by $r$. Both nodes remain in $\Delta $ for $r$ sufficiently close to one; their distance converges to its old value. Disc automorphisms then give discs $f,g$ and real nodes $0<A<B<1$ such that \[  f(0)=a,\quad f(A)=g(A)=b,\quad g(B)=d,  \] with $q(0,A)$ and $q(A,B)$ as close as desired to $\delta _ D(a,b)$ and $\delta _ D(b,d)$. To obtain these nodes, send the first pair to $0,A$ and the first node of the second pair to $A$; a rotation in its stabilizer places its second node on the real geodesic beyond $A$. This is the explicit disc-automorphism formula for $B=(A+s)/(1+As)$ when the second distance is $q(0,s)$. Put \[  L(\zeta )=\frac{(\zeta -B)(\zeta -B^{-1})}{(\zeta -A)(\zeta -A^{-1})},\qquad h=g+L(f-g).  \] The apparent pole at $A$ is removable because $f(A)=g(A)$. Moreover $L(0)=1$, $L(B)=0$, and on $|\zeta |=1$ \[  L(\zeta )=\frac{B+B^{-1}-2\operatorname {Re}\zeta }{A+A^{-1}-2\operatorname {Re}\zeta }\in (0,1).  \] Thus $h(\partial \Delta )\subset D$ by convexity. Its boundary image is compact; its convex hull is a compact subset of $D$. The harmonic mean formula in each real coordinate puts $h(\Delta )$ in that convex hull. Since $h(0)=a$ and $h(B)=d$, \[  \delta _ D(a,d)\leq q(0,B)=q(0,A)+q(A,B).  \] Let the two approximation errors tend to zero. Zero or repeated points are immediate. The coordinate-disc lower bounds for $c_ D$ give separation, since $c_ D\leq \delta _ D$, and symmetry follows by interchanging the disc nodes. The previously proved characterization of $k_ D$ as the greatest pseudodistance below $\delta _ D$ now gives $k_ D=\delta _ D$. For the topology, fix $a$ and $B(a,r)\subset D$. The affine disc $\zeta \mapsto a+r\zeta (b-a)/|b-a|$ gives $\delta _ D(a,b)\leq q(0,|b-a|/r)$ when $|b-a|<r$. Conversely, a fixed $R$ with $|z_ j|<R$ on $D$ gives $c_ D(a,b)\geq q(a_ j/R,b_ j/R)$ for every coordinate. The explicit disc formula therefore makes convergence in $\delta _ D$ equivalent to Euclidean convergence. An extremizing sequence can be normalized as $f_ j(0)=a$, $f_ j(t_ j)=b$, $t_ j>0$. The infimum is finite by the disc-joining theorem, and positive by coordinate separation, so $t_ j\to t\in (0,1)$ after choosing the sequence appropriately. Boundedness and Montel's theorem give a compact-uniform limit $f:\Delta \to \overline D$ with $f(0)=a$, $f(t)=b$. It actually maps into $D$: if $f(\zeta _0)\in \partial D$, a real supporting hyperplane there has equation $\operatorname {Re}\ell (z)=s$ with $\operatorname {Re}\ell <s$ on $D$. The harmonic function $\operatorname {Re}\ell \circ f\leq s$ would attain its maximum at $\zeta _0$, contradicting $f(0)=a\in D$. This proves attainment. Finally, a $\delta _ D$-Cauchy sequence is Euclidean Cauchy by the coordinate bounds, with limit in $\overline D$. If its limit $\xi $ were on the boundary, choose a supporting complex linear functional $\ell $ there, and set $F=s-\ell $, so $F:D\to \{ \operatorname {Re}w>0\} $ and $\operatorname {Re}F(\xi )=0$. Holomorphic contraction and a half-plane-to-disc automorphism give \[  \delta _ D(a,z)\geq q\left(0,\left|\frac{F(z)-F(a)}{F(z)+\overline{F(a)}}\right|\right).  \] The modulus tends to one as $z\to \xi $, so the distance tends to infinity, contrary to the Cauchy property. The limit lies in $D$, and the local affine-disc bound proves metric convergence. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.18.2
3.6 Separate harmonicity and subharmonicity
text: Theorem 3.6.1 . 58AAF98CC15E Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ p$ and $V\subset \mathbb R^ q$ be domains. Suppose $u:U\times V\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ is subharmonic in each group of variables separately, allowing identically $-\infty $ slices. If $u$ has a locally integrable pointwise majorant, it is subharmonic on $U\times V$. In particular, it is enough to assume directly that $u$ is locally bounded above. Proof. We first derive a local upper bound from the majorant $M$. For small fixed radii $r,s$ and $(x,y)$ in a smaller product of balls, the two successive submean inequalities give \[  u(x,y)\leq \frac1{|B_ r|}\int _{B(x,r)}u(t,y)\, dt \leq \frac1{|B_ r||B_ s|} \int _{B(x,r)}\int _{B(y,s)}M^+(t,w)\, dw\, dt.  \] For the second inequality, first apply the $y$-submean inequality at each $t$ for which the slice of $M^+$ is integrable, then integrate the measurable function $u(\cdot ,y)$. Exceptional $t$ form a null set by Fubini applied to $M^+$. All balls lie in a fixed compact product, so its $L^1$ norm bounds the last expression uniformly. This step does not assume joint measurability of $u$. We now assume a local upper bound and prove joint upper semicontinuity. Let $(x_ j,y_ j)\to (x,y)$. The functions $v_ j=u(x_ j,\cdot )$ are locally uniformly bounded above on a ball about $y$, and for each fixed $w$ separate upper semicontinuity gives $\limsup _ jv_ j(w)\leq u(x,w)$. If a subsequence contradicted the desired upper bound at $y_ j$, subharmonic compactness would give a further subsequence converging in $L^1$ to a subharmonic $v$; the alternative of locally uniform convergence to $-\infty $ cannot contradict the bound. A further almost-everywhere subsequence gives $v\leq u(x,\cdot )$ almost everywhere and hence everywhere by canonical subharmonic representatives. Hartogs' lemma for the moving points $y_ j$ then gives $\limsup _ jv_ j(y_ j)\leq v(y)\leq u(x,y)$, a contradiction. If $u(x,\cdot )\equiv -\infty $, the nondegenerate $L^1$ alternative is impossible by the same almost-everywhere inequality. Thus $u$ is jointly upper semicontinuous, in particular Borel measurable. Either $u\equiv -\infty $, or every open product of balls contains a point where $u$ is finite: if it vanished to $-\infty $ on an open product, first the $x$-slice nondegeneracy theorem and then its $y$ counterpart would propagate this to the whole connected product. Fix a smaller product and choose such a point $(a,b)$ sufficiently near its center. Choose an $x$-ball $B(a,R)$ containing its smaller $x$-projection and still in the larger product. With an upper bound $C\geq 0$ there, the $x$-submean inequality implies, for almost every $y$ in the smaller $y$-ball, \[  \int _{B(a,R)}u^-(t,y)\, dt \leq |B_ R|\bigl (C+u^-(a,y)\bigr ).  \] The slice $u(a,\cdot )$ is nondegenerate because $u(a,b)$ is finite, so it is locally integrable. Integrating the displayed bound proves local integrability of $u$ on the product. This argument works about every point by taking sufficiently small nested product balls. Fubini and the slice distribution inequalities now give $\Delta _ xu\geq 0$ and $\Delta _ yu\geq 0$, hence $\Delta u\geq 0$. Convolve on smaller products with the product of the two canonical nonnegative radial mollifiers. The resulting smooth functions are jointly subharmonic. Successive submeans give $u_\epsilon \geq u$; joint upper semicontinuity gives $u_\epsilon \to u$ pointwise. The one-variable radial convolution monotonicity in each factor shows that these approximants decrease as both radii decrease. The canonical decreasing-limit theorem proves joint subharmonicity, including the identically $-\infty $ case. $\square$ We need a precise real-trace consequence of pluripolar discrepancy. Let $Q\subset \mathbb R^ m\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be a closed cube in a complex ball $B$. Its explicitly computed global extremal is continuous and zero on $Q$. The proved global-relative comparison therefore gives $h_{Q,B}^*=-1$ on $Q$. Deleting a pluripolar subset does not change this relative regularization. Consequently, if a PSH function $w$ on $B$ is at most $A$ on $Q\setminus E$, where $E$ is pluripolar, then $w\leq A$ on $Q$. Indeed, take a smaller ball containing $Q$, an upper bound $C>A$ for $w$ there, and use $(w-A)/(C-A)-1$ as a relative competitor. The assertion is immediate if $w\leq A$ already on the ball. It follows that if $v_ j$ are PSH on a complex neighborhood of a real open set, locally uniformly bounded above, and $\limsup _ jv_ j(x)\leq A$ at every real point, then for every compact real cube $K$ in that set and $\epsilon >0$, \[  v_ j(x)\leq A+\epsilon \quad (x\in K,\  j\geq j_0).  \] To see this, set $w_ k=(\sup _{j\geq k}v_ j)^*$. Canonical envelope discrepancy and countable pluripolar unions give $w=\lim _ kw_ k=\limsup _ jv_ j$ off a pluripolar set. Locally $w$ is PSH or identically $-\infty $. The preceding real-cube observation makes $w\leq A$ on each larger real cube. On a smaller compact cube, the decreasing closed sets $\{ w_ k\geq A+\epsilon \} $ have empty intersection and hence are eventually empty. If some $v_ j$ is identically $-\infty $, it can simply be omitted. Theorem 3.6.2 . 95AFE3B73B3D A real-valued function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^ p\times \mathbb R^ q$ that is harmonic in each group separately is jointly harmonic. The assertion extends to finitely many groups. Proof. It suffices to work on a product of balls. If one group has dimension one, harmonicity in its interval means affinity there; two fixed values determine the affine coefficients, which are harmonic in the other group. Assume therefore $p,q\geq 2$. We first prove propagation from a bounded strip. Suppose $f$ is jointly bounded on compact subsets of $X\times B(P,\rho )$, where $X$ is an $x$-ball, $P\in V$ and $\rho >0$. The preceding theorem makes $f$ jointly subharmonic there. It is locally integrable, and Fubini gives $\Delta f=0$ because both slice Laplacians vanish. Weyl's lemma gives a harmonic representative. Its partial Laplacians also vanish, since it represents the same distribution; its slices are therefore harmonic. It agrees with $f$ everywhere: equality almost everywhere and harmonic slice uniqueness first give equality for all $x$ at almost every $y$, and then for all $y$ at every fixed $x$. For each fixed $x$, expand the harmonic function in the other group about $P$: \[  f(x,P+r\theta )=\sum _{s\geq 0}a_ s(x,\theta )r^ s, \qquad |\theta |=1.  \] The coefficients are homogeneous harmonic polynomials in $r\theta $. They are harmonic in $x$, by the joint harmonicity on the original strip and the Poisson coefficient formula on a small $y$-sphere. If $R=\operatorname {dist}(P,\partial V)$, that same formula on any radius $r<R$ gives, for each fixed real $x$, \[  \limsup _{s\to \infty }\frac1s \log \sup _{|\theta |=1}|a_ s(x,\theta )|\leq -\log R.  \] Here the Poisson kernel expansion has coefficients bounded by a polynomial in $s$ times $r^{-s}$: expand $(1-2t\cos \gamma +t^2)^{-q/2}$; its absolute coefficients are bounded by the coefficients of $(1-t)^{-q}$, namely $\binom {s+q-1}{q-1}$, and the numerator $1-t^2$ adds only two terms. Taking $s$-th roots and then $r\uparrow R$ proves the bound. On any smaller $x$-ball the original bounded strip gives uniform geometric bounds for all $a_ s(x,\theta )$. Harmonic functions on a fixed real ball extend holomorphically to a fixed smaller complex ball, with a uniform supremum estimate. This follows directly by complexifying its Poisson kernel: for a unit sphere the denominator $\sum _ j(\xi _ j-z_ j)^2$ stays in a disc about one avoiding zero when $|z|$ is sufficiently small, uniformly in $\xi $; choose its branch there and integrate. The numerator and denominator are bounded uniformly on a smaller complex ball, so the extension norm is at most a fixed constant times the real boundary supremum. The extension is unique on overlaps by the holomorphic identity theorem on a real open set, obtained by applying the one-variable identity theorem successively to the coordinates. Thus the holomorphic extensions $a_ s(z,\theta )$ have a common complex neighborhood and locally uniform geometric bounds. The functions \[  v_ s(z)=\max \left\{ \frac1s\log \sup _{|\theta |=1} |a_ s(z,\theta )|,-s\right\}  \quad (s\geq 1)  \] are PSH there: the coefficients form a finite holomorphic tuple, and the supremum over the real sphere is a complex norm on its finite-dimensional space of homogeneous harmonic polynomials. Use the canonical complex-norm logarithm and maxima. The real-trace estimate just proved gives, uniformly for real $x$ on a smaller cube, $\sup _\theta |a_ s(x,\theta )|\leq (e^\epsilon /R)^ s$ for large $s$. The harmonic series therefore converges absolutely and uniformly on its product with every $B(P,r)$, $r<R$, after choosing $\epsilon >0$ so that $re^\epsilon <R$. This bounds $f$ jointly there. The preceding local boundedness, distribution and Weyl argument now proves joint harmonicity on $X\times B(P,R)$. To start a strip, take any closed $x$-ball $\overline X$ inside the given $x$-domain and a closed $y$-ball $\overline Y$ inside $V$. The closed sets \[  E_ j=\{ y\in \overline Y: |f(x,y)|\leq j \text{ for all }x\in \overline X\}   \] cover $\overline Y$, since each $x$-slice is continuous on the compact ball. Baire's theorem gives a $y$-ball inside some $E_ j$. This is the required bounded strip on $X$. The propagation step extends it from its center $P$ to $B(P,\operatorname {dist}(P,\partial V))$. Along a compact path in the connected domain $V$, its distance from the boundary has a positive lower bound. Repeatedly choose the next center inside the preceding ball and move by less than half that lower bound. Finitely many propagation steps reach any specified point of $V$. Hence $f$ is harmonic on $X\times V$. The ball $X$ was arbitrary, proving the two-group theorem. Local induction combines any finite number of groups. $\square$

Successive submeans give $u_\epsilon \geq u$; joint upper semicontinuity gives $u_\epsilon \to u$ pointwise. The one-variable radial convolution monotonicity in each factor shows that these approximants decrease as both radii decrease. title: Theorem 3.6.2
text: Theorem 3.6.2 . 95AFE3B73B3D A real-valued function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^ p\times \mathbb R^ q$ that is harmonic in each group separately is jointly harmonic. The assertion extends to finitely many groups. Proof. It suffices to work on a product of balls. If one group has dimension one, harmonicity in its interval means affinity there; two fixed values determine the affine coefficients, which are harmonic in the other group. Assume therefore $p,q\geq 2$. We first prove propagation from a bounded strip. Suppose $f$ is jointly bounded on compact subsets of $X\times B(P,\rho )$, where $X$ is an $x$-ball, $P\in V$ and $\rho >0$. The preceding theorem makes $f$ jointly subharmonic there. It is locally integrable, and Fubini gives $\Delta f=0$ because both slice Laplacians vanish. Weyl's lemma gives a harmonic representative. Its partial Laplacians also vanish, since it represents the same distribution; its slices are therefore harmonic. It agrees with $f$ everywhere: equality almost everywhere and harmonic slice uniqueness first give equality for all $x$ at almost every $y$, and then for all $y$ at every fixed $x$. For each fixed $x$, expand the harmonic function in the other group about $P$: \[  f(x,P+r\theta )=\sum _{s\geq 0}a_ s(x,\theta )r^ s, \qquad |\theta |=1.  \] The coefficients are homogeneous harmonic polynomials in $r\theta $. They are harmonic in $x$, by the joint harmonicity on the original strip and the Poisson coefficient formula on a small $y$-sphere. If $R=\operatorname {dist}(P,\partial V)$, that same formula on any radius $r<R$ gives, for each fixed real $x$, \[  \limsup _{s\to \infty }\frac1s \log \sup _{|\theta |=1}|a_ s(x,\theta )|\leq -\log R.  \] Here the Poisson kernel expansion has coefficients bounded by a polynomial in $s$ times $r^{-s}$: expand $(1-2t\cos \gamma +t^2)^{-q/2}$; its absolute coefficients are bounded by the coefficients of $(1-t)^{-q}$, namely $\binom {s+q-1}{q-1}$, and the numerator $1-t^2$ adds only two terms. Taking $s$-th roots and then $r\uparrow R$ proves the bound. On any smaller $x$-ball the original bounded strip gives uniform geometric bounds for all $a_ s(x,\theta )$. Harmonic functions on a fixed real ball extend holomorphically to a fixed smaller complex ball, with a uniform supremum estimate. This follows directly by complexifying its Poisson kernel: for a unit sphere the denominator $\sum _ j(\xi _ j-z_ j)^2$ stays in a disc about one avoiding zero when $|z|$ is sufficiently small, uniformly in $\xi $; choose its branch there and integrate. The numerator and denominator are bounded uniformly on a smaller complex ball, so the extension norm is at most a fixed constant times the real boundary supremum. The extension is unique on overlaps by the holomorphic identity theorem on a real open set, obtained by applying the one-variable identity theorem successively to the coordinates. Thus the holomorphic extensions $a_ s(z,\theta )$ have a common complex neighborhood and locally uniform geometric bounds. The functions \[  v_ s(z)=\max \left\{ \frac1s\log \sup _{|\theta |=1} |a_ s(z,\theta )|,-s\right\}  \quad (s\geq 1)  \] are PSH there: the coefficients form a finite holomorphic tuple, and the supremum over the real sphere is a complex norm on its finite-dimensional space of homogeneous harmonic polynomials. Use the canonical complex-norm logarithm and maxima. The real-trace estimate just proved gives, uniformly for real $x$ on a smaller cube, $\sup _\theta |a_ s(x,\theta )|\leq (e^\epsilon /R)^ s$ for large $s$. The harmonic series therefore converges absolutely and uniformly on its product with every $B(P,r)$, $r<R$, after choosing $\epsilon >0$ so that $re^\epsilon <R$. This bounds $f$ jointly there. The preceding local boundedness, distribution and Weyl argument now proves joint harmonicity on $X\times B(P,R)$. To start a strip, take any closed $x$-ball $\overline X$ inside the given $x$-domain and a closed $y$-ball $\overline Y$ inside $V$. The closed sets \[  E_ j=\{ y\in \overline Y: |f(x,y)|\leq j \text{ for all }x\in \overline X\}   \] cover $\overline Y$, since each $x$-slice is continuous on the compact ball. Baire's theorem gives a $y$-ball inside some $E_ j$. This is the required bounded strip on $X$. The propagation step extends it from its center $P$ to $B(P,\operatorname {dist}(P,\partial V))$. Along a compact path in the connected domain $V$, its distance from the boundary has a positive lower bound. Repeatedly choose the next center inside the preceding ball and move by less than half that lower bound. Finitely many propagation steps reach any specified point of $V$. Hence $f$ is harmonic on $X\times V$. The ball $X$ was arbitrary, proving the two-group theorem. Local induction combines any finite number of groups. $\square$

section: 3.7 Polynomial approximation and a separate-subharmonic example
text: Proposition 3.7.1 . 6D285B395FD0 Let $K\subset \mathbb C$ be compact with connected complement. Every function holomorphic on a neighborhood of $K$ is a uniform limit on $K$ of polynomials. Proof. The empty set is immediate. For nonempty $K$, choose a sufficiently fine finite grid of squares in the neighborhood, including an extra layer around the squares meeting $K$. Their union contains $K$ in its interior and has boundary disjoint from $K$. Summing the Cauchy formula over the squares cancels interior edges and gives an integral representation of $f(z)$ for $z\in K$ over the remaining oriented edges, whose winding number is one there. On this boundary times $K$ the Cauchy integrand is uniformly continuous. Its Riemann sums therefore approximate $f$ uniformly by rational functions with poles outside $K$. Let $A$ be the uniform closure of polynomials in $C(K)$; it is a closed algebra. The set of $a\in \mathbb C\setminus K$ for which $(z-a)^{-1}\in A$ is relatively closed by uniform continuity of the resolvent in $a$. It is relatively open by the convergent geometric expansion about such an $a$ for $|b-a|<\operatorname {dist}(a,K)$. It contains all sufficiently large $a$, by expansion in $z/a$. Connectedness makes it the whole complement. Products then put every higher resolvent power in $A$, so all rational approximants above belong to $A$. This proves the assertion. $\square$ There is a finite nonnegative function on $\mathbb C^2$ that is subharmonic in each complex variable separately and is not jointly subharmonic. Use the argument branch $0<\arg z\leq 2\pi $ and set \[  a_ j=j^{-1}e^{i/(j+1)},\qquad K_ j=\{ z:|z|\leq j,\  1/j\leq \arg z\leq 2\pi \} \cup \{ 0\} .  \] These are compact, $a_ j\notin K_ j$, and their complements are connected: the missing open sector connects every complementary point to the exterior of the disc. Removing the additional point $a_ j$ preserves connectedness, by detouring a path around it in a small disc. Approximate the locally constant holomorphic function zero near $K_ j$ and $j+1$ near $a_ j$ on $K_ j\cup \{ a_ j\} $ by a polynomial $Q_ j$ with error $\eta _ j<1/8$. After the constant correction $P_ j=Q_ j+j+1-Q_ j(a_ j)$, we have $P_ j(a_ j)=j+1$ and $\| P_ j\| _{K_ j}<1/4<1/2$. Put $b_ j=\max (|P_ j|-1,0)$ and \[  F(z,w)=\sum _{j\geq 1}b_ j(z)b_ j(w).  \] Each $b_ j$ is continuous nonnegative subharmonic. Every fixed $z$ belongs to $K_ j$ for all sufficiently large $j$, including zero and the positive real ray with argument $2\pi $. Thus $b_ j(z)=0$ eventually and $F$ is finite. At fixed $w$ its sum has only finitely many nonzero coefficients, so it is subharmonic in $z$, and likewise in $w$. But $F(0,0)=0$, whereas $F(a_ j,a_ j)\geq j^2$ and $a_ j\to 0$. Joint upper semicontinuity fails. The total two-variable function has the single name $F$; an index $j$ on it would confuse the summation index with a free parameter.

title: 9.19 Boundary-distance counterexamples in higher dimension
text: Proposition 9.19.1 . EF227A55DB12 For every real dimension $m\geq 3$ there is a bounded nonconvex domain $T\subset \mathbb R^ m$ for which minus the boundary distance is subharmonic throughout $T$. There is also a proper domain $D$ with nonconvex complement whose boundary distance is subharmonic on an interior neighborhood of its boundary. Proof. Write $x=(x_1,x_2,y)\in \mathbb R^2\times \mathbb R^{m-2}$, $\rho =(x_1^2+x_2^2)^{1/2}$, and choose $R>2r>0$. Let \[  C=\{ (R\cos t,R\sin t,0):t\in \mathbb R\} ,\qquad s=\operatorname {dist}(x,C) =\sqrt{(\rho -R)^2+|y|^2},\qquad T=\{ s<r\} .  \] The distance formula follows by maximizing the scalar product with $(\cos t,\sin t)$; it remains valid on $\rho =0$. The set $T$ is bounded and connected, since each point joins its nearest point on the connected circle by a segment in $T$. It is nonconvex: the points $(R,0,0)$ and $(-R,0,0)$ belong to $T$, while their midpoint does not. The boundary is $\{ s=r\} $ and the interior distance equals $r-s$. Indeed $s$ is one-Lipschitz, giving the lower bound $r-s$ for the distance to that level. If $s>0$, continue the normal segment from its nearest circle point until its normal length is $r$. Along this segment $\rho >0$ and the same circle point remains nearest, because $r<R$. It reaches the level in distance $r-s$. At $s=0$ any circle-normal segment of length $r$ proves the upper bound. On $T$ we have $\rho >R-r>R/2$. The smooth functions $s_\epsilon =\sqrt{(\rho -R)^2+|y|^2+\epsilon ^2}$ decrease to $s$, and the cylindrical-coordinate Laplacian gives \[  \Delta s_\epsilon =\frac{m-1-R/\rho }{s_\epsilon } +\frac{\epsilon ^2}{s_\epsilon ^3}>0.  \] For completeness, the variables $(\rho -R,y)$ have dimension $m-1$, so their Laplacian of $\sqrt{|v|^2+\epsilon ^2}$ is $(m-2)/s_\epsilon +\epsilon ^2/s_\epsilon ^3$; the remaining cylindrical term is $(\rho -R)/(\rho s_\epsilon )$. Since $m\geq 3$ and $\rho >R/2$, the displayed sign is positive. The canonical decreasing-limit theorem makes $s-r$, which is minus the boundary distance of $T$, subharmonic even on the core circle. No removability theorem for that circle is required. Now put $D=\mathbb R^ m\setminus \overline T=\{ s>r\} $. This open set is connected for $m\geq 3$. In the half-space $(\rho ,y)\in [0,\infty )\times \mathbb R^{m-2}$ its image is the complement of the closed radius-$r$ ball centered at $(R,0)$. From any point there, increase $|y|$ along its ray to a value greater than $r+1$; when $y=0$ choose any fixed unit direction, which exists because $m-2\geq 1$. This only increases $s$. Then move $\rho $ to $R+2r$ while keeping that $y$ fixed, and finally move $y$ to zero. The whole path stays outside the ball. Lift it with a fixed polar angle; the lift is continuous even if its initial $\rho $ is zero. At $(\rho ,y)=(R+2r,0)$ join angles along the full circle, which lies in $D$. Thus $D$ is a proper domain, and its complement $\overline T$ is nonconvex by the same two circle points. Choose $\delta >0$ with $r+\delta <R/2$ and work on the interior collar $r<s<r+\delta $. There $\rho >R/2$ and $s$ is smooth. The distance to $\partial D$ is $s-r$: the Lipschitz lower bound is attained by shortening the same normal segment to length $r$. The preceding formula with $\epsilon =0$ gives $\Delta (s-r)>0$ throughout this collar. This proves the second assertion, including every even dimension $m=2n\geq 4$ relevant to several complex variables. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.37.1
section: 16.37 Robin capacity and its quantitative comparison
text: Proposition 16.37.1 . 5CD6FC21D2D4 If $f$ is a real $C^\infty $ function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^ m$, the image of $\{ df=0\} $ has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. In particular every nonempty real interval contains a regular value. Proof. Put $C_ k=\{ D^\alpha f=0:1\leq |\alpha |\leq k\} $. First, $f(C_ m)$ is null. Work on a compact cube inside the domain, with a slightly larger compact neighborhood still in the domain. Divide it into cubes of side $h$. If a small cube meets $C_ m$, choose $a$ in that intersection. Uniform continuity of the derivatives of order $m$, and Taylor's formula at $a$, give \[  |f(y)-f(a)|\leq \epsilon h^ m  \] on that cube for all sufficiently small $h$, after absorbing the fixed dimension constant in the choice of the modulus of continuity. There are $O(h^{-m})$ cubes, so these intervals cover the image of $C_ m$ with total length at most $C\epsilon $. Let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ and exhaust the domain by countably many such cubes. This also proves the assertion for $m=1$. Proceed by induction on $m$. At a point of $C_ k\setminus C_{k+1}$, $1\leq k<m$, there is a derivative $g=D^\beta f$, $|\beta |=k$, with $dg\ne 0$. The implicit function theorem makes $\{ g=0\} $ a smooth hypersurface near that point. The points of $C_ k$ on it are critical points of the restriction of $f$, since $df=0$ there. The induction hypothesis in a coordinate chart on this hypersurface makes their values null. A countable subcover of these neighborhoods, for each $k$, together with the already treated $C_ m$, covers $C_1$. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.37.2
section: 16.37 Robin capacity and its quantitative comparison
text: Proposition 16.37.2 . 13360BBA8D19 Let $u,v\in \mathcal L^+$ and $u\geq v$. If $b=\limsup _{|z|\to \infty }(u-v)$, then all the following integrals are finite and \[  \int _{\mathbb C^ n}u\, d\mu _ v- \int _{\mathbb C^ n}v\, d\mu _ u\leq n b m_ n.  \] Proof. On $X=\mathbb P^ n$ use $\omega =dd^ c\Gamma $ on the affine chart, where $\Gamma =\tfrac 12\log (1+|z|^2)$. The canonical growth correspondence extends $a=u-\Gamma $ and $d=v-\Gamma $ as bounded $\omega $-PSH potentials. Put \[  T_ u=\omega +dd^ ca,\quad T_ v=\omega +dd^ cd,\quad h=a-d\geq 0, \qquad S=\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}T_ v^ jT_ u^{n-1-j}.  \] All mixed top masses are $m_ n$ by bounded cohomological mass. Let $H=\{ Z_0=0\} $ and $t=|Z_0|^2/\| Z\| ^2$. For $\eta >0$ set \[  g_\eta =-\tfrac 12\log (t+\eta ),\qquad B_\eta =\omega -dd^ cg_\eta .  \] The form $B_\eta $ is smooth and positive: it is half the curvature of the positive quadratic form $|Z_0|^2+\eta \| Z\| ^2$. It represents $\{ \omega \} $, tends smoothly to zero off $H$, and $\int _ X B_\eta \wedge S=nm_ n$. The weighted Chern–Levine–Nirenberg theorem with base current $1$ and $n$ bounded potentials makes $\log |s|$ integrable against every mixed top product here, in a chart in which $s$ defines $H$. Consequently $\Gamma $ is integrable against $T_ u^ n,T_ v^ n$ and the displayed affine integrals are finite. This uses integrability against bounded products, without forming a product with the divisor current. Bounded global integration by parts and $T_ v^ n-T_ u^ n=-dd^ ch\wedge S$ give \begin{align*}  I_\eta & :=\int _ X(a+g_\eta )T_ v^ n-\int _ X(d+g_\eta )T_ u^ n\\ & =-\sum _{l=1}^{n-1}\int _ Xh\, T_ v^ lT_ u^{n-l} +\int _ Xh B_\eta \wedge S \leq \int _ Xh B_\eta \wedge S. \end{align*} For example, this follows by first writing $I_\eta =\int hT_ v^ n-\int h\, dd^ c(d+g_\eta )\wedge S$ and using $dd^ c(d+g_\eta )=T_ v-B_\eta $. For any $\delta >0$, $h\leq b+\delta $ on a sufficiently small punctured neighborhood of $H$. Bounded products with the smooth $B_\eta $ do not charge $H$. On its compact complement, $h$ is bounded and $B_\eta \to 0$ smoothly. Thus \[  \limsup _{\eta \downarrow 0}I_\eta \leq n(b+\delta )m_ n.  \] On the affine chart $g_\eta \uparrow \Gamma $; the preceding integrability, or monotone convergence after adding a constant, passes both integrals to the limit. Let $\delta \downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.37.3
section: 16.37 Robin capacity and its quantitative comparison
text: Theorem 16.37.3 . 27353237EC80 There is a constant $C_ n>0$ such that every compact $K\subset \overline B(0,1)$ satisfies \[  \alpha (K)\leq c(K)\leq C_ n\alpha (K)^{1/n},\qquad \alpha (K)=\exp \bigl (-\sup _{\overline B(0,1)}V_ K^*\bigr ).  \] The same upper bound holds with any exponent $0<\delta \leq 1/n$. Proof. The polar case has both capacities zero. Otherwise put $u=V_ K^*$ and $M=\sup _{\overline B(0,1)}u$. The norm-ball formula gives \[  0\leq \log ^+|z|\leq u(z)\leq M+\log ^+|z|.  \] In particular $\gamma (u)\leq M$, proving $\alpha \leq c$. The normalized family $w=u-M$ is bounded above by $\log ^+|z|$ and satisfies $\sup _{\overline B(0,1)}w=0$. The canonical subharmonic compactness alternative gives a uniform $L^1$ bound on $B(0,2)$ for this family. Indeed any sequence without that bound has, by the common local upper bounds and compactness, either an $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergent subsequence or a subsequence tending locally uniformly to $-\infty $; the first contradicts the missing bound and the second contradicts the normalized supremum on the closed unit ball. The sphere average of a subharmonic function is at least its concentric ball average. Hence \[  M\leq \mathop{\mathrm{avg}}_{|z|=2}u+C'_ n.  \] Take $v=\log ^+(|z|/2)\leq u$. Its measure is $m_ n$ times normalized surface measure on that sphere. The equilibrium support theorem gives $\operatorname {supp}\mu _ u\subset K$, where $v=0$. The preceding proposition, with $b=\gamma (u)+\log 2$, therefore gives \[  \mathop{\mathrm{avg}}_{|z|=2}u\leq n(\gamma (u)+\log 2).  \] Thus $M\leq n\gamma (u)+C''_ n$, which is the upper estimate after exponentiation. Finally $0\leq \alpha \leq 1$ implies $\alpha ^{1/n}\leq \alpha ^\delta $ for the stated exponents. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.37.4
section: 16.37 Robin capacity and its quantitative comparison
text: Proposition 16.37.4 . 786CD8A5F7AA If $u\in \mathcal L^+$ and $\epsilon >0$, there is $q>0$ and arbitrarily large $R$ such that the fraction of the sphere $|z|=R$ occupied by \[  F_\epsilon =\{ u-\log ^+|z|>\gamma (u)-\epsilon \}   \] is at least $q$. Proof. Let $M(R)=\max _{|z|=R}u$. The norm-ball formula shows that $M(R)-\log R$ decreases to $\gamma (u)$ for $R>1$. Choose $0<t<1/2$ with $\log (1+t)<\epsilon /2$. For large $R$, put $s=R/(1+t)$ and choose $z_0$ on $|z|=s$ with $u(z_0)=M(s)$. On $B(z_0,ts)\subset B(0,R)$, \[  u\leq u(z_0)+\log (1+t)<u(z_0)+\epsilon /2.  \] This ball is outside the unit ball for large $R$. Off $F_\epsilon $, its values are at most $\log R+\gamma (u)-\epsilon <u(z_0)-\epsilon /2$. The submean inequality at $z_0$ forces at least half its volume to lie in $F_\epsilon $. Therefore \[  |F_\epsilon \cap B(0,R)|\geq p|B(0,R)|,\qquad p=\tfrac 12(t/(1+t))^{2n}>0  \] for all sufficiently large $R$. If all sufficiently large spheres had fraction less than $p/2$, polar-coordinate integration would contradict this volume estimate. Take $q=p/2$. $\square$

The product-max formula makes its Robin constant the maximum of $\gamma (E_ A)$ and $-\log r$, and its closed-unit-ball extremal supremum the maximum of the corresponding two suprema. The $E_ A$ terms dominate for large $A$, so the same ratio diverges. Every $K_ A$ lies in the unit ball by the choice of $r$. $\square$

Its fibers are finite, since they are compact sets of isolated zeros. Around the finitely many preimages of $w_0$ choose disjoint small closed discs on whose boundaries $F-w_0$ is nonzero. For $w$ close to $w_0$, all its preimages lie in those discs: otherwise properness would give an extra preimage of $w_0$ by taking a convergent subsequence. On each boundary the integral \[   rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int  rac{F'(z)}{F(z)-w}\, dz  \] is a continuous integer, equal to the number of zeros by local factorization and Cauchy's formula. It is therefore constant for nearby $w$. The image of $F$ is open and closed in the disc, using properness for closedness, and hence is the whole disc. This map is injective and has nonzero derivative. Its image $U$ is disjoint from $-U$: opposite values would have equal squares and hence come from the same point, whereas $s$ never vanishes. Then $u=V_ K^*$ is positive and harmonic on $\Omega $, is bounded near its finite boundary, and satisfies \[  \lim _{|z|	o \infty }(u(z)-\log |z|)\in \mathbb R,\qquad \lim _{\Omega 
i z	o \xi }u(z)=0 \quad (\xi \in \partial \Omega \setminus P)  \] for a polar set $P$. It is the least positive harmonic function on $\Omega $ with these growth and quasi-everywhere zero boundary conditions. It is the unique such function bounded near the finite boundary. On every bounded complementary component $V_ K^*=0$. Proof. The logarithmic family and equilibrium-support theorems give $u\in \mathcal L^+$, $u\geq 0$, and maximality off $K$. In one complex variable maximality is harmonicity. Its logarithmic growth makes it nonconstant on $\Omega $, so the minimum principle gives strict positivity there. It is bounded on a neighborhood of the compact $K$ by local boundedness. Outside a large disc, $u-\log |z|$ is bounded and harmonic; inversion gives a bounded harmonic function on a punctured disc. Canonical puncture removability gives the asserted finite limit. The raw envelope is zero on $K$. Its discrepancy from $V_ K^*$ is polar, so $u(\xi )=0$ off a polar subset $P$ of $K$. Upper semicontinuity and nonnegativity give the stated full boundary limit there. If $B$ is a bounded complementary component, every polynomial is bounded on $B$ by its supremum on $\partial B\subset K$. The polynomial extremal formula therefore gives $V_ K=0$ on $B$, and consequently $V_ K^*=0$ on that open component. Let $v$ be any other positive harmonic function on $\Omega $ with the stated logarithmic asymptotic and quasi-everywhere zero boundary limits. The harmonic function $v-u$ is bounded below near $K$, since $v>0$ and $u$ is bounded there, and is bounded near infinity, since the logarithmic terms cancel. Its boundary limits are zero off the union of the two polar exceptional sets. The complement of $\Omega $ contains the nonpolar set $K$, so the canonical Myrberg theorem makes $\Omega $ Greenian. The canonical planar boundary minimum principle with polar exceptions now gives $v-u\geq 0$. Its planar unbounded-domain version needs no extra boundary condition at infinity. If $v$ is bounded near $K$, the same lower-bound argument applies to $u-v$; interchange the functions to get equality. This proves both minimality and bounded-boundary uniqueness. $\square$ Example 3.8.3 . FADCC209A003 Quasi-everywhere zero boundary limits alone do not specify a Green function uniquely. In the unit disc, for every $t>0$ the functions \[  -\log |z|+t\operatorname {Re} rac{1+z}{1-z}  \] are positive harmonic off zero, have the required logarithmic pole, and tend to zero at every boundary point except $1$. In the exterior of the closed unit disc, the corresponding functions \[  \log |z|+t\operatorname {Re} rac{z+1}{z-1}  \] are positive harmonic, have the required finite logarithmic limit at infinity, and again have zero boundary limits except at $1$. The exceptional singleton is polar. The added Poisson term is positive in each indicated domain, diverges at $1$, and is harmonic across the finite pole in the first formula. Thus the weaker boundary condition must be supplemented by minimality, or by the bounded boundary condition above, when it is used as a characterization. For a finite pole on a bounded domain, the canonical Green function is likewise the least function meeting the weaker conditions. If $v$ is another such function, $v-G$ has a removable pole and is bounded below near the boundary, since $v>0$ and $G$ is bounded there. The polar boundary minimum principle gives $v\geq G$. If $v$ is also bounded near the boundary, apply that principle to $G-v$ to get equality. Here boundedness of the canonical $G$ near the boundary follows from $G(z,a)\leq \log (C/|z-a|)$ with $C>\operatorname {diam}D$.

title: Proposition 9.20.1
section: 9.20 Complex geodesics on bounded convex domains
text: Proposition 9.20.1 . 659A580EE96C Let $A$ be the disc algebra. If a finite complex measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb T$ annihilates $A$, then $d\mu =H^*dm$, where $H$ is holomorphic, $H(0)=0$, and $\sup _{r<1}\int |H(r\zeta )|dm<\infty $. For every holomorphic function with this last bound, the radial functions converge in $L^1$ to their almost everywhere boundary values. A nonzero such function has nonzero boundary values almost everywhere. Proof. We give the analytic boundary argument, including the absolute continuity assertion. The positive Fejer kernels are approximate identities, so trigonometric polynomials are dense in $L^2(\mathbb T)$; orthogonality and this density give Parseval on circles. For $H^2$, write the Taylor series. Bounded square means are equivalent to square summability of the coefficients. Their $L^2$ Fourier sum $g^*$ has only nonnegative frequencies; $g(r\zeta )$ is its Poisson integral. The Poisson kernels are approximate identities, so convergence holds in $L^2$ and at every Lebesgue point. The latter assertion follows directly by splitting the integral into dyadic arcs about that point, using $P_ r(\theta )\leq C(1-r)/((1-r)^2+\theta ^2)$. Now let $F\in H^1$, meaning that its integral means of absolute value are bounded. Remove a possible zero at zero. Jensen's formula follows by factoring the finitely many zeros inside a circle, applying the harmonic mean identity to the zero-free factor, and using $\int \log |r\zeta -a|dm=\log \max (r,|a|)$ for each zero. It gives the Blaschke condition for its remaining zeros $a_ j$: $\sum _ j-\log |a_ j|<\infty $. Indeed the means of $\log |F|$ are bounded above by the logarithm of its bounded absolute means. The factors $b_ a(z)=(|a|/a)(a-z)/(1-\bar a z)$ satisfy $|1-b_ a(z)|\leq C_ K(1-|a|)$ on each compact subdisc. Thus their product $B$ converges there, has precisely the prescribed zeros, and has modulus at most one. Moreover $|B^*|=1$ almost everywhere: $B\in H^2$, and Jensen's formula for the factors gives \[  \int -\log |B(r\zeta )|dm =\sum _ j-\log \max (r,|a_ j|)\longrightarrow 0.  \] Dominated convergence for the sum and Fatou's lemma prove the claim. An origin factor contributes only $-k\log r$ and causes no change. For each finite subproduct $B_ N$, $F/B_ N$ is holomorphic and has $H^1$ norm at most that of $F$: let the circle radius tend to one, where $|B_ N|$ tends uniformly to one, and use monotonicity of absolute means. Compact convergence and Fatou give the same bound for $G=F/B$. This function is zero free. Choose a holomorphic square root $g$ of $G$ on the disc. Both $g$ and $h=Bg$ lie in $H^2$, and $F=gh$. Their $L^2$ boundary convergence and Cauchy–Schwarz give $F(r\zeta )\to g^*h^*$ in $L^1$ and almost everywhere. In particular the $H^1$ norm equals the boundary $L^1$ norm, and the Cauchy and Poisson formulas hold with these boundary values. For a nonzero $F$, its boundary values cannot vanish on a set of positive measure. After removing an origin zero, Jensen gives $\int \log |F(r\zeta )|dm\geq \log |F(0)|$, whereas the positive parts of these logarithms have uniformly bounded integrals. Fatou applied to their negative parts would contradict this inequality if the almost everywhere boundary function vanished on such a set. Finally, annihilation of $1,\zeta ,\zeta ^2,\ldots $ says that the Poisson integral of $\mu $ has only strictly positive Fourier frequencies. It is therefore a holomorphic $H$ with $H(0)=0$. Convolution with $P_ r$ bounds its absolute means by $\| \mu \| $. The $H^1$ conclusion just proved gives strong $L^1$ convergence to $H^*$. Poisson convolution also converges weakly to $\mu $ as a measure, so $\mu =H^*dm$. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.20.2
section: 9.20 Complex geodesics on bounded convex domains
text: Proposition 9.20.2 . 415609592B60 Let $D$ be bounded and convex, and let $f:\Delta \to D$ be an extremal disc for two distinct points. Normalize its nodes to $0,t$, where $0<t<1$. There is a nonzero $H\in H^1(\Delta ,\mathbb C^ n)$ such that \[  h(\zeta )=\frac{H(\zeta )}{\zeta -t},\qquad \operatorname {Re}(z-f^*(\zeta ))\cdot h^*(\zeta )\leq 0 \quad (z\in \overline D)  \] almost everywhere on $\mathbb T$. The boundary covector $h^*$ is nonzero almost everywhere. This disc is extremal for every pair of its nodes; in particular $\delta _ D(f(\lambda ),f(\eta ))=q(\lambda ,\eta )$. Proof. Translate the coordinates so that $0\in D$. Let $p$ be its real Minkowski functional; it is sublinear and Lipschitz, and bounded above and below by positive multiples of the Euclidean norm. On $C(\mathbb T,\mathbb C^ n)$ put $P(u)=\max p(u)$, and let $\mathcal L$ consist of the disc-algebra maps with the same values as $f$ at $0,t$. We claim $\inf _{\mathcal L}P=1$. For the upper bound, $f(r\zeta )$ has $P\leq 1$; add $\zeta (f(t)-f(rt))/t$ to restore the second value. The correction tends uniformly to zero. For the lower bound, suppose $g\in \mathcal L$ has $P(g)<1$. Its dilations $g(r\zeta )$ with the same affine correction converge uniformly to $g$, extend past the closed disc, and still have image compactly contained in $D$. A dilation of one of these maps by a factor slightly larger than one retains its image in $D$ and attains the second target at a node smaller than $t$. This contradicts extremality. This argument uses the Lipschitz gauge $p$, without identifying it with a Euclidean norm. Put $d(\zeta )=\zeta (\zeta -t)$ and $Y=dA^ n$; then $\mathcal L=f_0+Y$ for any interpolation polynomial $f_0$. Define $\ell (sf_0+y)=s$ on the real space $\mathbb R f_0+Y$. If $s>0$, the preceding infimum gives $P(sf_0+y)\geq s$; if $s\leq 0$, the inequality follows from $P\geq 0$. Real Hahn–Banach extends $\ell $ with $\ell \leq P$. The complex functional $L(u)=\ell (u)-i\ell (iu)$ is bounded, annihilates $Y$, has $\operatorname {Re}L(f_0)=1$, and satisfies $\operatorname {Re}L(u)\leq P(u)$. Represent its coordinates by finite complex measures $\mu _ j$ on the circle. To reduce this representation to the canonical positive-functional representation, for a bounded real functional $l$ set $l^+(u)=\sup _{0\leq v\leq u}l(v)$ for $u\geq 0$. This is additive on the positive cone: split any $0\leq v\leq u_1+u_2$ as $\min (v,u_1)+(v-\min (v,u_1))$, and use the reverse inequality by adding two admissible functions. Thus $l^+$ extends positively, as does $l^+-l$, and each is represented by a finite positive measure. For a positive functional on $C(\mathbb T)$, apply the canonical representation on $\mathbb R^2$ to restriction of compactly supported functions; the resulting measure is supported on the circle. Apply this to real and imaginary coordinate functionals. Since $d\mu _ j$ annihilates $A$, Proposition 9.20.1 gives $d\mu _ j=\zeta H_ j^*dm$, with $H_ j\in H^1$. Consequently $d\mu =h^*dm$, where $h=H/(\zeta -t)$. For a covector $w$ put $p^*(w)=\max _{z\in \overline D}\operatorname {Re}z\cdot w$. The dual bound implies \[  \int p^*(h^*)dm=1.  \] Here the left side is precisely $\sup _{P(u)\leq 1}\operatorname {Re}\int u\cdot h^*dm$: the upper bound is pointwise; for the lower bound choose maximizers from a countable dense subset of $\overline D$, approximate the resulting finite measurable partition by a continuous partition of unity in $L^1(|h^*|dm)$, and take its convex combination of those points. The reverse inequality $\geq 1$ also follows by applying the functional to an interpolation sequence with $P\downarrow 1$. The bounded holomorphic map $f$ has radial boundary values by the $H^2$ argument. The corrected dilations used above and dominated convergence against $h^*\in L^1$ give $\operatorname {Re}\int f^*\cdot h^*dm=1$. Since $f^*\in \overline D$ almost everywhere, equality of the integrals forces $\operatorname {Re}f^*\cdot h^*=p^*(h^*)$ almost everywhere. One component of $H$ is nonzero, so the boundary nonvanishing part of Proposition 9.20.1 applies. Thus $f^*\in \partial D$ and $h^*$ is a nonzero supporting covector almost everywhere. To change the nodes to distinct $\lambda ,\eta \in \Delta $, multiply $h$ by the meromorphic function whose circle values are \[  \phi (\zeta )= \frac{|\zeta |^2|\zeta -t|^2}{|\zeta -\lambda |^2|\zeta -\eta |^2}>0.  \] Indeed its holomorphic expression is \[  \phi h= \frac{\zeta H(\zeta )(1-t\zeta )}{(\zeta -\lambda )(\zeta -\eta ) (1-\bar\lambda \zeta )(1-\bar\eta \zeta )}.  \] It annihilates all disc-algebra variations vanishing at the two new nodes, by Cauchy's formula. The same holds for bounded holomorphic variations: dilate them and correct their two values by interpolation polynomials, then pass to the integral by bounded convergence. The supporting covector remains nonzero almost everywhere. If a compact-image map $g:\Delta \to D$ interpolated $f$ at those nodes, then for some $\varepsilon >0$ it would satisfy \[  \operatorname {Re}\int g^*\cdot \phi h^*dm \leq (1-\varepsilon )\int p^*(\phi h^*)dm <\operatorname {Re}\int f^*\cdot \phi h^*dm,  \] contradicting annihilation of $f-g$. If a disc achieved the new pair at a strictly smaller disc distance, automorphisms would normalize its nodes to $0,s$, and the new nodes to $0,u$, with $s<u$. Precomposition by $(s/u)\zeta $, followed by the latter automorphism, would give exactly such a compact-image interpolant. This proves the asserted extremality for every pair, and also injectivity of $f$. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.20.3
section: 9.20 Complex geodesics on bounded convex domains
text: Proposition 9.20.3 . 5DE7AB27F999 On a bounded strongly real convex domain with $C^2$ boundary, an extremal disc $f$ extends to a $C^{1/2}$ map on $\overline\Delta $, with $f(\mathbb T)\subset \partial D$. Proof. Compactness and positive real boundary curvature give a fixed interior tangent-ball radius $r_0>0$, a fixed exterior tangent-ball radius $R_0$, and a collar in which the nearest boundary point is unique. For completeness, in local boundary coordinates the real Hessian restricted to the tangent space is bounded above and below by positive constants. Taylor's formula gives both tangent-ball inequalities near the contact point; away from it strict convexity and compactness give a uniform strict supporting-plane gap. Decreasing $r_0$ and increasing $R_0$ extend the inequalities to the entire boundary. The interior centers form a compact subset of $D$. Put $a=f(0)$, and $d(z)=\operatorname {dist}(z,\partial D)$. For $z=\xi -d(z)\nu (\xi )$ in the collar, the interior ball centered at $c=\xi -r_0\nu (\xi )$ gives, using the metric already proved in Theorem 9.18.1 , \[  \delta _ D(a,z)\leq C+ \operatorname {atanh}\frac{r_0-d(z)}{r_0} \leq C'+\tfrac 12\log \frac1{d(z)}.  \] Enlarging $C'$ handles the compact part outside the collar. The preceding proposition gives $\delta _ D(a,f(\zeta ))=\operatorname {atanh}|\zeta |$, so $d(f(\zeta ))\leq C''(1-|\zeta |)$. For the exterior ball tangent at the nearest point, the elementary ball Schwarz estimate gives \[  |f'(\zeta )|(1-|\zeta |^2) \leq \sqrt{R_0^2-|f(\zeta )-c|^2} \leq \sqrt{2R_0d(f(\zeta ))}.  \] To check the first inequality, scale to the unit ball and rotate the image point to $(s,0,\ldots ,0)$. Its automorphism \[  w\longmapsto \left( \frac{s-w_1}{1-sw_1}, \frac{-\sqrt{1-s^2}\, w'}{1-sw_1}\right)  \] sends that point to zero and has differential of length at least $|v|/\sqrt{1-s^2}$. Apply the vector Schwarz lemma after a disc automorphism sends the chosen source point to zero. Thus $|f'(\zeta )|\leq C(1-|\zeta |)^{-1/2}$. Integrating along radii gives boundary limits. For two points at distance $s<1/2$, move each radially to radius at most $1-s$ and join the moved points within that smaller disc. The radial integrals and the joining integral are all at most $C\sqrt{s}$. This proves the claimed closed-disc estimate. The almost everywhere boundary containment proved above and continuity give containment everywhere. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.20.5
section: 9.20 Complex geodesics on bounded convex domains
text: Theorem 9.20.5 . 7264782B9A80 Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be bounded and convex, and $a\neq b$ in $D$. There exist holomorphic maps $f:\Delta \to D$ and $P:D\to \Delta $, and $0<t<1$, such that \[  f(0)=a,\qquad f(t)=b,\qquad P\circ f=\operatorname {id}_\Delta .  \] Consequently \[  c_ D(a,b)=\delta _ D(a,b)=k_ D(a,b)=\sigma _ D(a,b) =\operatorname {atanh}t,\qquad g_ D(b,a)=\log t.  \] Proof. For $C^2$ strongly real convex $D$, take the extremal disc supplied by Theorem 9.18.1 . The preceding three propositions give its continuous positive stationary lift. Proposition 9.18.2 supplies $P$ and all the asserted equalities. We spell out the smooth exhaustion for a general bounded convex $D$. Given a compact $K\subset D$, include $K$ in a compact convex neighborhood $L\subset D$. Supporting half-spaces and compactness give a bounded open convex polytope \[  K\subset L\subset Q=\{ x:\ell _ j(x)<0,\  1\leq j\leq N\} , \qquad \overline Q\subset D.  \] One direct construction separates $L$ from every point of $\partial D$, takes a finite subcover of the compact boundary, and adds a large bounding box. If the resulting polytope met the complement of $D$, a segment from a point of $L$ would meet $\partial D$ inside its closure, contradicting the strict separating inequalities; small inward offsets preserve $L$ and make its closure disjoint from $\partial D$. For small $\varepsilon >0$ and large $M$, the analytic function \[  \rho (x)=M^{-1}\log \sum _{j=1}^ N e^{M\ell _ j(x)} +\varepsilon |x|^2  \] is proper and has positive definite real Hessian. It is negative on $L$, by the uniform negative margin of the $\ell _ j$ there, and its negative sublevel lies in $Q$, since $M^{-1}\log \sum e^{M\ell _ j}\geq \max _ j\ell _ j$. The zero level is regular: a critical point of a strictly convex function is its unique minimum, whose value is negative. Thus the negative sublevel is bounded and strongly real convex with analytic boundary. Iterating the construction with compact exhaustions and the previous closure included in $K$ gives $D_ j\Subset D_{j+1}$ and $\bigcup _ jD_ j=D$. Take the retract discs $f_ j,P_ j$ through $a,b$ in $D_ j$ and their nodes $t_ j$. A fixed compact chain of inner balls joining $a$ to $b$ lies in all sufficiently large $D_ j$. The local affine-disc bounds and the triangle inequality give $\operatorname {atanh}t_ j\leq C$, uniformly. Coordinate Schwarz bounds give $t_ j\geq c>0$. Pass to $t_ j\to t\in (0,1)$ and normal-family limits $f_ j\to f$ and $P_ j\to P$ on their respective domains, using a diagonal sequence for $P_ j$ on the exhaustion. The supporting-hyperplane maximum principle puts $f(\Delta )$ in $D$, because $f(0)=a\in D$. The maximum principle puts $P(D)$ in $\Delta $, because $P(a)=0$. Compact-uniform convergence and $P_ jf_ j=\operatorname {id}$ give $Pf=\operatorname {id}$. Holomorphic contraction and the disc identities now bound all four distances below and above by $q(0,t)$. For the Green function, $\log |P|$ is an admissible negative plurisubharmonic function with a logarithmic pole at $a$, so $g_ D(b,a)\geq \log t$. Pullback to $f$ and the disc pole comparison give the reverse inequality. The case $a=b$ follows with distance zero and Green value $-\infty $. $\square$

title: Example 9.20.6
section: 9.20 Complex geodesics on bounded convex domains
text: Example 9.20.6 . 8E0727128F9C Smooth convex boundary alone does not make every complex geodesic continuous on the closed disc. Choose a smooth convex nondecreasing proper function $\chi :[0,\infty )\to [0,\infty )$ which is zero on $[0,1]$ and has $\chi '>0$ on $(1,\infty )$. For example take \[  \chi (s)=\int _1^ s(s-u)e^{-1/(u-1)}du\quad (s>1), \qquad \chi (s)=0\quad (s\leq 1).  \] The bounded domain $D=\{ |z_1|^2+\chi (|z_2|^2)<1\} $ is convex with smooth boundary; its defining gradient is nonzero on that boundary. The map \[  f(\zeta )=\left(\zeta , \tfrac 12\exp \left(-\frac{1+\zeta }{1-\zeta }\right)\right)  \] has left inverse $P(z)=z_1$ and hence is a complex geodesic. Its second component has no limit at $1$: along a radius it tends to zero, whereas the imaginary part of $(1+\zeta )/(1-\zeta )$ can diverge with bounded positive real part along interior paths. Taking that imaginary part through multiples of $2\pi $ or odd multiples of $\pi $ gives distinct nonzero limiting values.

title: 6.23 Global decreasing smooth approximation
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Theorem 6.23.1 . 49314269C188 Let $n\geq 1$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be pseudoconvex and let $u\in \operatorname {PSH}(\Omega )$. There are finite smooth strictly plurisubharmonic functions $u_ j$ on all of $\Omega $ with $u_ j\downarrow u$ pointwise, including at its pole set. Proof. The smooth-exhaustion construction in Oka's boundary-distance theorem gives a smooth plurisubharmonic $\psi \geq 1$ such that \[  e^{-\psi (z)}<\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega ).  \] More precisely, on a proper domain take $\psi =s+1$, where that construction has $s\geq |z|^2+\max \{ -\log \operatorname {dist}(z,\Omega ^ c),0\} $. On $\mathbb C^ n$ take $\psi =1+|z|^2$, with the distance understood as infinite. Disconnected open sets are treated on their components. Fix a nonnegative smooth radial kernel $\chi $ supported in the unit ball and of integral one. Put $v_ j=\max (u,-j)$ and, for $t<-\psi (z)$, define \[  F_ j(z,t)=\int _{\mathbb C^ n}v_ j(z+e^ t\xi )\chi (\xi )\, dV(\xi ), \qquad J_ j(z,t)=F_ j(z,t)+\frac1j \bigl [-t-\log (-\psi (z)-t)\bigr ].  \] Each $v_ j$ is locally bounded and plurisubharmonic. Rewriting the first integral with the translated/scaled smooth kernel shows that $F_ j$ is smooth in $(z,t)$: on every compact parameter set its derivatives act on a smooth kernel with support in a fixed compact subset of $\Omega $. Regard $t$ as $\operatorname {Re}w$. The same integral equals $\int v_ j(z+e^ w\xi )\chi (\xi )dV(\xi )$, by radial invariance. Each integrand is a plurisubharmonic holomorphic pullback, and local boundedness permits the integral. Thus $F_ j(z,\operatorname {Re}w)$ is jointly plurisubharmonic and independent of $\operatorname {Im}w$. The scalar function $x\mapsto -\log (-x)$ is increasing and convex on $x<0$, so $-\log (-\psi (z)-\operatorname {Re}w)$ is also plurisubharmonic there. The term $-\operatorname {Re}w$ is pluriharmonic. Hence $J_ j$ is jointly plurisubharmonic. For fixed $z$, the function $t\mapsto F_ j(z,t)$ is convex, since its complex Hessian in $w$ is one quarter of its real $t$-Hessian. Moreover \[  (J_ j)_{tt}=(F_ j)_{tt} +\frac{1}{j(-\psi (z)-t)^2}>0.  \] The function $J_ j(z,t)$ tends to $+\infty $ at both ends of the interval $(-\infty ,-\psi (z))$. At the left end use $F_ j\geq -j$; at the right end $F_ j$ remains bounded because the closed ball of radius $e^{-\psi (z)}$ lies strictly inside $\Omega $. There is therefore a unique minimizer $t_ j(z)$ in that interval. The implicit function theorem applied to $(J_ j)_ t=0$ makes $t_ j$ smooth locally; uniqueness makes these local solutions agree. Let $m_ j(z)=J_ j(z,t_ j(z))$. The smooth case of Kiselman's minimum principle gives that $m_ j$ is plurisubharmonic. Explicitly, at the minimizer its Hessian is the Schur complement \[  (m_ j)_{z\bar z}=(J_ j)_{z\bar z} -(J_ j)_{zt}(J_ j)_{tt}^{-1}(J_ j)_{t\bar z}\geq 0,  \] because the joint complex Hessian has blocks $((J_ j)_{z\bar z},(J_ j)_{zt}/2;(J_ j)_{t\bar z}/2,(J_ j)_{tt}/4)$. This uses the checked smooth minimum argument on the actual convex fibers, without requiring a global smoothing theorem as a premise. Write $x=-\psi (z)-t>0$. The penalty is $\psi (z)+x-\log x\geq \psi (z)+1>0$. Since $v_{j+1}\leq v_ j$ and $1/(j+1)<1/j$, we have $J_{j+1}\leq J_ j$ on the same domain, and consequently $m_{j+1}\leq m_ j$. The radial submean inequality gives $F_ j\geq v_ j\geq u$, and the penalty is positive, so $m_ j\geq u$. For every fixed admissible $(z,t)$, local integrability and monotone truncation give $F_ j(z,t)\to F(z,t)$, where $F$ is the convolution of $u$ with the same radius. Indeed $v_ j-u$ decreases to zero and is bounded by the locally integrable $v_1-u$ on the integration ball. Thus \[  \lim _ jm_ j(z)\leq \lim _ jJ_ j(z,t)=F(z,t).  \] As $t\to -\infty $, the canonical decreasing radial regularizations satisfy $F(z,t)\downarrow u(z)$, also when $u(z)=-\infty $. It follows that $m_ j\downarrow u$ everywhere. Finally take $u_ j=m_ j+|z|^2/j$. These functions are smooth and strictly plurisubharmonic, still decrease, and have the same pointwise limit. $\square$

section: 7.23 Unbounded potentials and dependence on regularization
text:
Example 7.23.1 . 20D8C7C9B243 Let $n\geq 2$ and put \[  u(z)=\sum _{k=1}^ n\log |z_ k|^2,\qquad a_ j(z)=\log \left(|z_1\cdots z_ n|^2+j^{-1}\right),\qquad b_ j(z)=\sum _{k=1}^ n\log \left(|z_ k|^2+j^{-1}\right).  \] Both sequences are smooth plurisubharmonic and decrease to $u$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, but with the fixed convention $dd^ c=i\partial \bar\partial /(2\pi )$, \[  (dd^ ca_ j)^ n=0,\qquad (dd^ cb_ j)^ n\longrightarrow n!\, \delta _0.  \] Consequently there is no measure-valued extension on every plurisubharmonic function which agrees with smooth products and commutes with every smooth decreasing approximation. Proof. For a holomorphic scalar function $F$ and $\varepsilon >0$, \[  \partial \bar\partial \log (|F|^2+\varepsilon ) =\frac{\varepsilon }{(|F|^2+\varepsilon )^2} \partial F\wedge \overline{\partial F}.  \] Its complex Hessian is positive semidefinite and has rank at most one, including at critical points of $F$. Thus $a_ j$ is smooth plurisubharmonic and its top product is zero when $n\geq 2$. For a single coordinate define \[  \mu _\varepsilon =dd^ c\log (|z|^2+\varepsilon ) =\frac{\varepsilon }{\pi (|z|^2+\varepsilon )^2}\, dA(z).  \] This is a probability measure on $\mathbb C$, since its mass on the disc of radius $R$ is $R^2/(R^2+\varepsilon )$. It converges weakly to $\delta _0$. The different coordinate forms have square zero, so expansion of the $n$th power gives \[  (dd^ cb_ j)^ n=n!\bigotimes _{k=1}^ n\mu _{1/j}.  \] For any fixed $r>0$ the product measure puts mass tending to one on the polydisc of radius $r$. Its total mass is one. Uniform continuity of a compactly supported test function near zero and the remaining tail bound prove convergence to $\delta _0$. The two limiting measures are therefore distinct. Both sequences decrease to the same $u$, including the value $-\infty $ on the coordinate hyperplanes, which proves the obstruction. In dimension one the two sequences agree and no such obstruction occurs: the positive current $dd^ cu$ is a Radon measure for every plurisubharmonic $u$ by the distributional subharmonic criterion. $\square$ Proposition 7.23.2 . EC436652E435 For $n\geq 2$ there is an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ on which no positive Radon measure-valued $n$-linear map on all plurisubharmonic $n$-tuples extends the locally bounded Bedford–Taylor product. Here multilinearity means additivity and nonnegative homogeneity on the plurisubharmonic cone. Neither locality nor a convergence hypothesis is needed for this obstruction. Proof. Use the canonical infinite-local-mass example in two variables, restricted to $|x|<1/4$, $|y|<e^{-1}$. Put \[  L=-\log |y|,\qquad u(x,y)=(|x|^2-1)\sqrt L\quad (y\ne 0), \qquad u(x,0)=-\infty .  \] It is plurisubharmonic and smooth off $y=0$. The checked Hessian formula is \[  H_ u=\begin{pmatrix}  \sqrt L

& -\bar x/(4\bar y\sqrt L)

\\  -x/(4y\sqrt L)

& (1-|x|^2)/(16|y|^2L^{3/2}) 

\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det H_ u=\frac{1-2|x|^2}{16|y|^2L}.  \] We need an additional gradient bound. Set $B=\operatorname {diag}(\sqrt L,1/(16|y|^2L^{3/2}))$. The diagonal entries of $B^{-1/2}H_ uB^{-1/2}$ are $1,1-|x|^2$, and its off-diagonal entry has modulus $|x|<1/4$. Consequently $H_ u\geq B/2$. The two first derivatives give \[  |u_ x|^2/\sqrt L +16|y|^2L^{3/2}|u_ y|^2 =\bigl (|x|^2+(1-|x|^2)^2\bigr )\sqrt L \leq \frac{17}{16}\sqrt L.  \] Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz therefore gives \[  |\partial u(v)|^2\leq 4(-u)H_ u(v,\bar v) \quad (v\in \mathbb C^2),  \] since $-u\geq 15\sqrt L/16$ and $2(17/16)/(15/16)=34/15<4$. On \[  \Omega =\{ |x|<1/4,\  |y|<e^{-1},\  |z'|<1\}  \subset \mathbb C^2\times \mathbb C^{n-2}  \] put $U=u+|z'|^2-2$; omit the last group when $n=2$. Its Hessian off $y=0$ is $\operatorname {diag}(H_ u,I)$. In the dual Hessian norm the square gradient has length at most $4(-u)+|z'|^2\leq 4(-U)$. Thus \[  |\partial U(v)|^2\leq 4(-U)H_ U(v,\bar v),\qquad U<-1.  \] Its smooth Monge–Ampere measure has infinite mass on any compact product with nonempty $x,z'$ interior and $y$-disc centered at zero: the displayed determinant is bounded below by a positive constant times $1/(|y|^2(-\log |y|))$, whose planar integral diverges. Choose such a compact $K\Subset \Omega $ once and for all. Let $\kappa =1/18$ and, for $s<0$, set \[  f_ j(s)=\frac{\kappa j s}{j-s},\qquad f_ j'(s)=\frac{\kappa j^2}{(j-s)^2},\qquad f_ j''(s)=\frac{2\kappa j^2}{(j-s)^3}.  \] Define $\psi _ j=f_ j(U)$ off $y=0$ and $\psi _ j=-\kappa j$ on that hyperplane. Because $f_ j$ is increasing and convex, $\psi _ j$ is plurisubharmonic off the hyperplane. Its bounded continuous extension is plurisubharmonic by the canonical removable-set theorem, and $-\kappa j\leq \psi _ j<0$ on $\Omega $. The remainder $r_ j=U-\psi _ j$ is also plurisubharmonic. Indeed, off the hyperplane its Hessian satisfies \[  H_{r_ j}\geq \left[1-f_ j'(U)-4(-U)f_ j''(U)\right]H_ U \geq \tfrac 12H_ U.  \] For the last inequality put $q=(-U)/j>0$ and use \[  f_ j'(U)+4(-U)f_ j''(U) =\kappa \left((1+q)^{-2}+8q(1+q)^{-3}\right) \leq 9\kappa =\tfrac 12.  \] Moreover $r_ j<0$ and $r_ j\to -\infty $ on approaching $y=0$, so its upper-limit extension with value $-\infty $ is plurisubharmonic there. This gives the exact cone decomposition $U=\psi _ j+r_ j$ on all of $\Omega $. Suppose the proposed map $T$ existed. Multilinearity and positivity give the measure inequality \[  T(U,\ldots ,U)\geq T(\psi _ j,\ldots ,\psi _ j) =(dd^ c\psi _ j)^ n.  \] On compact subsets off the hyperplane, $f_ j(U)\to \kappa U$ with every derivative, since $f_ j$ and its derivatives converge locally to those of $s\mapsto \kappa s$. Fatou's lemma for the smooth positive densities on $K\setminus \{ y=0\} $ therefore gives \[  \liminf _ j\int _ K(dd^ c\psi _ j)^ n \geq \int _{K\setminus \{ y=0\} }(dd^ c(\kappa U))^ n=+\infty .  \] This contradicts the finite mass of the fixed Radon measure $T(U,\ldots ,U)$ on $K$, proving the assertion. $\square$ Example 7.23.3 . C89C030AFB89 There are positive Radon products for unbounded potentials, and the chosen extension can change the mass carried by the poles. For $u(z)=\log |z|$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, the classical isolated-point extension is $2^{-n}\delta _0$, whereas the locally finite non-pluripolar top product is zero. Proof. The isolated-point construction and its radial mass calculation give $M_ u=2^{-n}\delta _0$. For the non-pluripolar construction, put $u_ k=\max (u,-k)$. The restricted product $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }(dd^ cu_ k)^ n$ vanishes: on this ordinary open set $u_ k=u$ is smooth, and the Hessian of $\log |z|$ has rank $n-1$. Its only other possible mass, on the boundary sphere of the truncation, is discarded by the strict indicator. Thus every restricted product is zero and the non-pluripolar limit is zero, which in particular is locally finite. Both constructions agree with the bounded Bedford–Taylor product on their bounded-input scope; they make different choices at the pole of this unbounded input. This includes $n=1$, where the non-pluripolar degree-one construction discards the atom of the distributional Laplacian. $\square$
