Fatou's lemma for the smooth positive densities on $K\setminus \{ y=0\} $ therefore gives \[  \liminf _ j\int _ K(dd^ c\psi _ j)^ n \geq \int _{K\setminus \{ y=0\} }(dd^ c(\kappa U))^ n=+\infty .  \] This contradicts the finite mass of the fixed Radon measure $T(U,\ldots ,U)$ on $K$, proving the assertion. $\square$

title: Example 7.23.3
section: 7.23 Unbounded potentials and dependence on regularization
text: Example 7.23.3 . C89C030AFB89 There are positive Radon products for unbounded potentials, and the chosen extension can change the mass carried by the poles. For $u(z)=\log |z|$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, the classical isolated-point extension is $2^{-n}\delta _0$, whereas the locally finite non-pluripolar top product is zero. Proof. The isolated-point construction and its radial mass calculation give $M_ u=2^{-n}\delta _0$. For the non-pluripolar construction, put $u_ k=\max (u,-k)$. The restricted product $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }(dd^ cu_ k)^ n$ vanishes: on this ordinary open set $u_ k=u$ is smooth, and the Hessian of $\log |z|$ has rank $n-1$. Its only other possible mass, on the boundary sphere of the truncation, is discarded by the strict indicator. Thus every restricted product is zero and the non-pluripolar limit is zero, which in particular is locally finite. Both constructions agree with the bounded Bedford–Taylor product on their bounded-input scope; they make different choices at the pole of this unbounded input. This includes $n=1$, where the non-pluripolar degree-one construction discards the atom of the distributional Laplacian. $\square$

title: 7.24 Degenerate densities and interior second derivatives

section: 7.24 Degenerate densities and interior second derivatives
text:
The continuous-density ball Dirichlet theorem gives interior $C^{1,1}$ regularity when the $n$th root of the density is $C^2$ on a neighborhood of the closed ball. The same conclusion does not follow from $C^2$ regularity of the density itself. Proposition 7.24.1 . D0960BD969B2 For every $n\ge 3$ there is a nonnegative function $f\in C^2(\mathbb C^ n)$ such that the unique solution \[  u\in \operatorname {PSH}(B)\cap C(\overline B),\qquad (dd^ cu)^ n=f\, dV_{2n},\qquad u|_{\partial B}=0, \qquad B=B(0,1),  \] does not belong to $C^{1,1}$ on any neighborhood of the origin. Here $dd^ c=i\partial  ar\partial /(2\pi )$. Proof. Write $z=(z',w)\in \mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \mathbb C$, and set \[  \alpha =4,\qquad  eta =6n-7,\qquad \eta (t)= egin{cases} \exp (-1/(1-t^2)),& 0\le t<1,\ 0,& t\ge 1.\end{cases}  \] Define $f(z',w)=|z'|^ eta \eta (|w|/|z'|^\alpha )$ for $z'
e 0$, and put $f(0,w)=0$. This is smooth off $\{ z'=0\} $: the function $\eta $ is even at zero and flat at $1$. On its support, $|w|\le |z'|^\alpha $. For a real derivative $D$ of order $j\le 2$, the chain rule gives \[  |Df(z',w)|\le C_ j|z'|^{ eta -j\alpha }\quad (0<|z'|\le 1).  \] Indeed a $w$ derivative costs at most $|z'|^{-\alpha }$ and a $z'$ derivative at most $|z'|^{-1}$; the flat cutoff bounds every remaining factor. All these derivatives tend to zero at the origin since $ eta -2\alpha =6n-15>0$. The function vanishes near every point $(0,w)$ with $w
e 0$. At the origin $f=O(|z|^ eta )$ and its first derivatives are $O(|z|^{ eta -\alpha })$, so their derivatives there also exist and are zero. Thus the zero extensions of the derivatives through order two are continuous and $f\in C^2(\mathbb C^ n)$. The canonical continuous-density Dirichlet theorem supplies $u$ and uniqueness (apply it to the density $\pi ^ nf/n!$ relative to $(dd^ c|z|^2)^ n$). Unitary invariance of the data and uniqueness show that $u$ depends only on $r=|z'|$ and $t=|w|$; write its value as $U(r,t)$. It is increasing in each radius whenever the corresponding product of balls is contained in $B$. To see this, restrict to a complex line through the origin in that variable and apply the subharmonic maximum principle on centered discs. In particular $u(0)$ is the minimum. Also $u<0$ on $B$: it is subharmonic with zero boundary values, and is not constant since $f>0$ on a nonempty open subset. Put $s(t)=U(0,t)$ for $0\le t\le 1$. The function $h(x)=s(e^ x)$ is convex on $(-\infty ,0)$: on an annulus the harmonic function interpolating its constant boundary values is affine in $\log |w|$, and dominates the subharmonic restriction of $u$ to the $w$ axis. Its limit at $-\infty $ is $s(0)$. Set \[  R(t)=\min \{ t^{1/\alpha },\sqrt{1-t^2}\} ,\qquad b(t)=U(R(t),t),\qquad 0<t<1,  \] using the continuous boundary value $0$ when $R(t)^2+t^2=1$. These functions are continuous and $b\ge s$. We first show that $h$ is locally affine wherever $b(t)>s(t)$. Fix such a $t$. On a sufficiently short closed interval $[t_1,t_2]\subset (0,1)$ containing $t$, the affine interpolant $L(x)$ of $h(\log t_1),h(\log t_2)$ satisfies $L(\log 	au )<b(	au )$ for $t_1\le 	au \le t_2$, by continuity and the positive gap. On \[  D=\{ (z',w)\in B:t_1<|w|<t_2,\  |z'|^\alpha <|w|\}   \] the density vanishes. On its two annular ends $u\ge L(\log |w|)$ by radial monotonicity; on its remaining boundary the value is $b$. The comparison principle for the bounded continuous solution with $(dd^ cu)^ n=0$ therefore gives $L(\log |w|)\le u$ throughout $D$; the comparison function is pluriharmonic since $w
e 0$. On the axis convexity gives the reverse inequality. Consequently $h=L$ on $[\log t_1,\log t_2]$, as asserted. Next $s(t)>s(0)$ for every $t>0$. Otherwise let $t_0>0$ be the last radius up to which $s$ equals $s(0)$. It is less than $1$, because $s(0)<0=s(1)$. We have $b(t_0)>s(0)$. This is immediate if $b(t_0)=0$. In the other case, equality would make $u$ constant on \[  \{ |z'|<R(t_0),\  |w|<t_0\} \subset B  \] by radial monotonicity and the global minimum. This contradicts the positive density on an open subset of that product. Thus $b>s$ near $t_0$, and the preceding paragraph makes $h$ affine there. It is constant to the left, hence also to the right, contradicting the choice of $t_0$. There must now be a sequence $\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ with $b(\varepsilon _ k)=s(\varepsilon _ k)$. If $b>s$ on some $(0,\delta )$, the locally affine function $h$ would be affine on $(-\infty ,\log \delta )$. Its finite limit at $-\infty $ forces it to be constant there, contrary to the preceding paragraph. For small $\varepsilon =\varepsilon _ k$, write $\lambda =\varepsilon ^{1/\alpha }$; then $R(\varepsilon )=\lambda $ and \[  u(0)\le u(z',w)\le s(\varepsilon ) \quad 	ext{if } |z'|\le \lambda ,\  |w|\le \varepsilon .  \] The whole closed product lies in $B$ for small $\varepsilon $. Let $d=(\varepsilon \lambda ^{n-1})^{2/n}$ and define on the unit ball \[  v(\zeta ',\zeta _ n) = rac{u(\lambda \zeta ',\varepsilon \zeta _ n)-s(\varepsilon )}{d}.  \] It is bounded, continuous and plurisubharmonic, with $v(0)\le v\le 0$. Biholomorphic covariance and homogeneity give \[  (dd^ cv)^ n =f(\lambda \zeta ',\varepsilon \zeta _ n)\, dV_{2n}(\zeta ).  \] The bounded Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate on the half ball gives \[  \int _{B(0,1/2)}(dd^ cv)^ n\le C_ n(-v(0))^ n.  \] On the fixed set \[  \{ 1/8<|\zeta '|<1/4,\quad |\zeta _ n|<	frac 12\, 8^{-\alpha }\} \subset B(0,1/2),  \] the argument of $\eta $ is at most $1/2$, because $\varepsilon =\lambda ^\alpha $. The density is therefore at least $c_ n\lambda ^ eta $. Combining the positive volume of that set with the preceding upper bound yields \[  s(\varepsilon _ k)-s(0) \ge c_ n\varepsilon _ k^{(2\alpha +2(n-1)+ eta )/(n\alpha )} =c_ n\varepsilon _ k^{\, 2-1/(4n)}.  \] If $u$ were $C^{1,1}$ near the origin, invariance under $w\mapsto -w$ would give zero first derivative on that axis and hence $|s(t)-s(0)|\le Ct^2$. This contradicts the displayed lower bound. $\square$

title: 3.9 Planar boundary distance and convexity
text:
Proposition 3.9.1 . 964B6728E795 Let $D$ be a nonempty proper connected open subset of $\mathbb R^2$, and put $d(x)=\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^2\setminus D)$ for $x\in D$. Then $-d$ is subharmonic on $D$ if and only if $D$ is convex. Proof. Suppose that $D$ is not convex. Choose $x,y\in D$ with $[x,y]
ot\subset D$, and join them by a polygonal path in $D$ having the least possible number of segments. Such paths exist: the set of points reachable from $x$ by polygonal paths is both relatively open and relatively closed in the connected open set $D$. The least number is an integer at least two. If $a,b,c$ are its first three vertices, then $[a,b]\cup [b,c]\subset D$ but $[a,c]
ot\subset D$, since otherwise the path could be shortened by one segment. The three vertices are not collinear, for otherwise their first two segments would already contain $[a,c]$. After a rigid motion, let $[a,c]$ be horizontal and $b$ lie above it. Write $T$ for the closed triangle and $F=\mathbb R^2\setminus D$. The compact set $F\cap T$ is nonempty and avoids the two sides $[a,b],[b,c]$. Let $H$ be its greatest height and choose the rightmost point $p$ of its height-$H$ slice. If $H$ is above the base, $p$ is interior to $T$, so a sufficiently small ball around it lies in $T$. If $H$ is the base height, $F\cap T$ lies on the base and $p$ is interior to that side; on a sufficiently small ball the upper half lies in $T$. In either case, translating $p$ to the origin gives an $r>0$ such that \[  0\in F,\qquad F\cap B(0,r)\subset \{ (x_1,x_2):x_2\le 0\} , \qquad (t,0)
otin F\quad (0<t<r).  \] The last assertion follows from the choice of the rightmost point, with $r$ decreased so that the horizontal points in question stay in $T$. Set $q=(0,r/4)$ and $A=B(q,r/8)\Subset D$. For $z\in A$, every point of $F\cap B(0,r)$ is at distance at least $z_2$ from $z$; every other point of $F$ is at distance at least $r-|z|>5r/8>z_2$. Therefore $d(z)\ge z_2$, while $d(q)=r/4$ because $0\in F$. If also $z_1>0$, equality is impossible: a nearest point exists, and equality would require that point to be $(z_1,0)$, which is absent from $F$. Thus $d(z)>z_2$ on the right half of $A$. Continuity gives \[   rac1{|A|}\int _ A d(z)\, dz > rac1{|A|}\int _ A z_2\, dz= rac r4=d(q).  \] This contradicts the supermean inequality for $d$ if $-d$ is subharmonic. Hence $D$ must be convex. Conversely the distance to the boundary of an open convex set is concave: convex combinations of balls $B(x,s)\subset D$ and $B(y,t)\subset D$ contain the ball with the combined center and radius. Let $s\uparrow d(x)$ and $t\uparrow d(y)$ to obtain the concavity inequality. The negative of this function is convex, and hence subharmonic by convex mollification. $\square$ Proposition 3.9.2 . 59D258340230 Let $F$ be a nonempty proper closed subset of $\mathbb R^2$, and let $G\subset \mathbb R^2$ be a connected open set containing $F$. If $d(x)=\operatorname {dist}(x,F)$ is subharmonic on $G$, then $F$ is convex. Conversely the distance to a nonempty closed convex set is convex, and hence subharmonic, on the whole plane. Proof. We first prove a regularity fact in $\mathbb R^ m$. On a ball $B\Subset G\setminus F$ there is a constant $C$ such that \[  D^2d\le CI  \] in the sense of distributions. Indeed, for every $a\in F$ the Hessian of $x\mapsto |x-a|$ is at most $I/\operatorname {dist}(B,F)$ on $B$. Subtracting $C|x|^2/2$ makes each such function concave; their infimum $d-C|x|^2/2$ is concave as well. Concave mollifications give the distributional assertion. Since $d$ is subharmonic, $\Delta d\ge 0$. Mollify on a smaller ball. The eigenvalues of the smooth Hessian are at most $C$ and their sum is nonnegative, so each is at least $-(m-1)C$. Thus the full mollified Hessians are uniformly bounded. The function $d$ is $1$-Lipschitz. Its mollifications and their gradients are uniformly bounded, and the Hessian bound makes those gradients equi-Lipschitz. Compactness on smaller balls gives a uniformly convergent subsequence of gradients. The segment integral identity identifies its limit with $
abla d$, and the Lipschitz bound passes to the limit. Consequently $d\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(G\setminus F)$, and its distributional Hessian is a locally bounded symmetric matrix $H$. This also follows from the canonical bounded-Hessian regularity theorem. Every $x\in G\setminus F$ has a nearest point $a\in F$, since a minimizing sequence stays bounded and $F$ is closed. The smooth function $|\, \cdot -a|$ dominates $d$ with equality at $x$. Differentiability therefore gives \[  
abla d(x)= rac{x-a}{|x-a|},\qquad |
abla d(x)|=1.  \] In particular the nearest point is unique wherever $d$ is differentiable. Differentiating $|
abla d|^2=1$ weakly gives \[  H
abla d=0\quad 	ext{almost everywhere on }G\setminus F.  \] For clarity this weak product rule needs no additional differentiability theorem: mollify the locally Lipschitz vector $
abla d$, whose weak derivatives are bounded. The vectors converge uniformly on compact sets, the derivatives converge distributionally with common bounds, and the ordinary product rule passes to the limit against test functions. Now take $m=2$. The symmetric matrix $H$ has a zero eigenvalue, because $
abla d$ is a unit vector, and its other eigenvalue is $\operatorname {tr}H=\Delta d\ge 0$. Hence $H\ge 0$ almost everywhere. Mollification on each interior ball and uniform convergence show that $d$ is locally convex on $G\setminus F$. The set $F$ is locally convex, including at its boundary. Fix $p\in F$ and a ball $B(p,r)\subset G$. For $x,y\in F\cap B(p,r)$, restrict $d$ to their segment. If it were positive somewhere, a component interval of its positive set would have two zero endpoints. It is locally convex in that interval, hence convex there by the one-dimensional slope inequalities. Continuity at its endpoints would force it to be at most their zero chord, a contradiction. Thus the whole segment lies in $F\cap B(p,r)$. Define the nearest-point map $P:G	o F$, with $P(x)=x$ on $F$. Off $F$ the preceding formula gives $P(x)=x-d(x)
abla d(x)$, so $P$ is continuous there. At $p\in F$, \[  |P(x)-p|\le |P(x)-x|+|x-p|\le 2|x-p|,  \] so it is continuous on all of $G$. Since $P$ fixes $F$, its image is exactly $F$. Connectedness of $G$ therefore makes $F$ connected. The closed connected local-convexity proposition now makes $F$ convex. Conversely let $F$ be closed and convex. Choose nearest points $a,b$ for $x,y$. For $0\le t\le 1$ the point $(1-t)a+tb$ lies in $F$, and the triangle inequality gives \[  d((1-t)x+ty)\le (1-t)|x-a|+t|y-b| =(1-t)d(x)+td(y).  \] Thus $d$ is convex. Convex mollifications have nonnegative Laplacian, and their locally uniform limit is subharmonic. $\square$ Proposition 3.9.3 . BBEB233BF8A4 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^2$ be nonempty, open and proper, and put $F=\mathbb R^2\setminus \Omega $ and $d(x)=\operatorname {dist}(x,F)$ on the whole plane. If there is a connected open neighborhood $U$ of $\partial \Omega $ on which $d$ is subharmonic, then $F$ is convex. Without connectedness of that neighborhood the conclusion fails, even for a connected $\Omega $ with smooth boundary. Proof. The open set $G=U\cup \operatorname {int}F$ contains $F$, and $d$ is subharmonic there by locality: it is zero on $\operatorname {int}F$. It is connected. In fact every component $V$ of $\operatorname {int}F$ has nonempty boundary, since $F$ is proper, and $\partial V\subset \partial F\subset U$. Thus $V$ meets $U$. The preceding proposition applies to $G$. For the counterexample take two disjoint closed unit discs with centers $a_1=(-3,0)$ and $a_2=(3,0)$, and let $F$ be their union. The complement $\Omega $ is connected: any polygonal path can be modified around the two disjoint discs by circular detours of radius slightly greater than $1$. Its boundary is the union of two smooth circles, while $F$ is not convex, since it contains the centers and not their midpoint. On the disjoint open collars \[  U_ j=\{ x:1/2<|x-a_ j|<3/2\} ,\qquad U=U_1\cup U_2,  \] the global distance to $F$ is $d(x)=\max \{ |x-a_ j|-1,0\} $. Each function is convex and subharmonic on the whole plane, being the maximum of the convex functions $|x-a_ j|-1$ and $0$. Hence $d$ is subharmonic on the open neighborhood $U$ of $\partial \Omega $. This proves the stated failure. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.9.2

Proposition 3.9.2 . 59D258340230 Let $F$ be a nonempty proper closed subset of $\mathbb R^2$, and let $G\subset \mathbb R^2$ be a connected open set containing $F$. If $d(x)=\operatorname {dist}(x,F)$ is subharmonic on $G$, then $F$ is convex. Conversely the distance to a nonempty closed convex set is convex, and hence subharmonic, on the whole plane. Proof. We first prove a regularity fact in $\mathbb R^ m$. On a ball $B\Subset G\setminus F$ there is a constant $C$ such that \[  D^2d\le CI  \] in the sense of distributions. Indeed, for every $a\in F$ the Hessian of $x\mapsto |x-a|$ is at most $I/\operatorname {dist}(B,F)$ on $B$. Subtracting $C|x|^2/2$ makes each such function concave; their infimum $d-C|x|^2/2$ is concave as well. Concave mollifications give the distributional assertion. Since $d$ is subharmonic, $\Delta d\ge 0$. Mollify on a smaller ball. The eigenvalues of the smooth Hessian are at most $C$ and their sum is nonnegative, so each is at least $-(m-1)C$. Thus the full mollified Hessians are uniformly bounded. The function $d$ is $1$-Lipschitz. Its mollifications and their gradients are uniformly bounded, and the Hessian bound makes those gradients equi-Lipschitz. Compactness on smaller balls gives a uniformly convergent subsequence of gradients. The segment integral identity identifies its limit with $
abla d$, and the Lipschitz bound passes to the limit. Consequently $d\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(G\setminus F)$, and its distributional Hessian is a locally bounded symmetric matrix $H$. This also follows from the canonical bounded-Hessian regularity theorem. Every $x\in G\setminus F$ has a nearest point $a\in F$, since a minimizing sequence stays bounded and $F$ is closed. The smooth function $|\, \cdot -a|$ dominates $d$ with equality at $x$. Differentiability therefore gives \[  
abla d(x)= rac{x-a}{|x-a|},\qquad |
abla d(x)|=1.  \] In particular the nearest point is unique wherever $d$ is differentiable. Differentiating $|
abla d|^2=1$ weakly gives \[  H
abla d=0\quad 	ext{almost everywhere on }G\setminus F.  \] For clarity this weak product rule needs no additional differentiability theorem: mollify the locally Lipschitz vector $
abla d$, whose weak derivatives are bounded. The vectors converge uniformly on compact sets, the derivatives converge distributionally with common bounds, and the ordinary product rule passes to the limit against test functions. Now take $m=2$. The symmetric matrix $H$ has a zero eigenvalue, because $
abla d$ is a unit vector, and its other eigenvalue is $\operatorname {tr}H=\Delta d\ge 0$. Hence $H\ge 0$ almost everywhere. Mollification on each interior ball and uniform convergence show that $d$ is locally convex on $G\setminus F$. The set $F$ is locally convex, including at its boundary. Fix $p\in F$ and a ball $B(p,r)\subset G$. For $x,y\in F\cap B(p,r)$, restrict $d$ to their segment. If it were positive somewhere, a component interval of its positive set would have two zero endpoints. It is locally convex in that interval, hence convex there by the one-dimensional slope inequalities. Continuity at its endpoints would force it to be at most their zero chord, a contradiction. Thus the whole segment lies in $F\cap B(p,r)$. Define the nearest-point map $P:G	o F$, with $P(x)=x$ on $F$. Off $F$ the preceding formula gives $P(x)=x-d(x)
abla d(x)$, so $P$ is continuous there. At $p\in F$, \[  |P(x)-p|\le |P(x)-x|+|x-p|\le 2|x-p|,  \] so it is continuous on all of $G$. Since $P$ fixes $F$, its image is exactly $F$. Connectedness of $G$ therefore makes $F$ connected. The closed connected local-convexity proposition now makes $F$ convex. Conversely let $F$ be closed and convex. Choose nearest points $a,b$ for $x,y$. For $0\le t\le 1$ the point $(1-t)a+tb$ lies in $F$, and the triangle inequality gives \[  d((1-t)x+ty)\le (1-t)|x-a|+t|y-b| =(1-t)d(x)+td(y).  \] Thus $d$ is convex. Convex mollifications have nonnegative Laplacian, and their locally uniform limit is subharmonic. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.9.3
text: Proposition 3.9.3 . BBEB233BF8A4 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^2$ be nonempty, open and proper, and put $F=\mathbb R^2\setminus \Omega $ and $d(x)=\operatorname {dist}(x,F)$ on the whole plane. If there is a connected open neighborhood $U$ of $\partial \Omega $ on which $d$ is subharmonic, then $F$ is convex. Without connectedness of that neighborhood the conclusion fails, even for a connected $\Omega $ with smooth boundary. Proof. The open set $G=U\cup \operatorname {int}F$ contains $F$, and $d$ is subharmonic there by locality: it is zero on $\operatorname {int}F$. It is connected. In fact every component $V$ of $\operatorname {int}F$ has nonempty boundary, since $F$ is proper, and $\partial V\subset \partial F\subset U$. Thus $V$ meets $U$. The preceding proposition applies to $G$. For the counterexample take two disjoint closed unit discs with centers $a_1=(-3,0)$ and $a_2=(3,0)$, and let $F$ be their union. The complement $\Omega $ is connected: any polygonal path can be modified around the two disjoint discs by circular detours of radius slightly greater than $1$. Its boundary is the union of two smooth circles, while $F$ is not convex, since it contains the centers and not their midpoint. On the disjoint open collars \[  U_ j=\{ x:1/2<|x-a_ j|<3/2\} ,\qquad U=U_1\cup U_2,  \] the global distance to $F$ is $d(x)=\max \{ |x-a_ j|-1,0\} $. Each function is convex and subharmonic on the whole plane, being the maximum of the convex functions $|x-a_ j|-1$ and $0$. Hence $d$ is subharmonic on the open neighborhood $U$ of $\partial \Omega $. This proves the stated failure. $\square$

title: 16.38 Geometric polynomial approximation and local uniqueness

section: 16.38 Geometric polynomial approximation and local uniqueness
text: Write $V_ K$ for the raw logarithmic extremal and $V_ K^*$ for its upper semicontinuous regularization. For a nonempty compact set $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$, say that $K$ is locally determining if, whenever a connected open set $W$ meets $K$, every holomorphic function on $W$ vanishing on $K\cap W$ is identically zero on $W$. For $f\in C(K)$ put \[  e_ j(f,K)=\inf _{\deg p\le j}\| f-p\| _ K.  \] Theorem 16.38.1 . DE0691E14C0E Let $K$ be nonempty, compact and locally determining. Then the following are equivalent: $V_ K$ is finite and continuous on $\mathbb C^ n$; every $f\in C(K)$ satisfying $\limsup _{j\to \infty } e_ j(f,K)^{1/j}<1$ extends holomorphically to an open neighborhood of $K$. The implication from the first condition to the second does not require local determination. Proof. Assume the first condition and choose $0<q<1$ and polynomials $p_ j$ with $\deg p_ j\le j$ and $\| f-p_ j\| _ K\le Cq^ j$. Such a choice follows directly from the strict limsup inequality, after increasing $C$ to cover finitely many initial indices. The Bernstein–Walsh bound gives, for $0<a<-\log q$ and $U=\{ V_ K<a\} $, \[  \| p_{j+1}-p_ j\| _ U \le 2Cq^ j e^{(j+1)a}.  \] The open set $U$ contains $K$, because the raw extremal vanishes there. Thus $p_ j$ converges uniformly on $U$, and its holomorphic limit restricts to $f$ on $K$. This proves the first implication. For the converse fix $0<q<1$. Let $\mathcal P_ j$ be the polynomials of degree at most $j$, with the norm $\| \cdot \| _ K$. This is a norm: a polynomial vanishing on $K$ vanishes on $\mathbb C^ n$ by local determination. It is a complete finite-dimensional normed space. Explicitly, the point evaluations on $K$ span its dual, so finitely many of them control all coefficients in a polynomial basis. Consider the Banach space \[  X_ q=\left\{ (p_ j)_{j\ge 0}:p_ j\in \mathcal P_ j,\quad \| (p_ j)\| _{X_ q}=\sum _{j\ge 0}q^{-j}\| p_ j\| _ K<\infty \right\} .  \] Completeness follows by taking coordinate limits of a Cauchy sequence, then using the sum bound for the tails. The continuous linear map $T:X_ q\to C(K)$ defined by $T(p_ j)=\sum _ jp_ j|_ K$ satisfies \[  e_ N(T(p_ j),K)\le q^{N+1}\| (p_ j)\| _{X_ q}.  \] Every element of its image therefore extends by hypothesis. Put $U_ m=\{ \operatorname {dist}(z,K)<1/m\} $. For positive integers $m,M$ let $A_{m,M}$ be the set of $x\in X_ q$ for which $Tx$ has a holomorphic extension to $U_ m$ bounded there by $M$. These closed sets cover $X_ q$. The covering follows by compactness of $K$: any holomorphic extension is bounded on the closure of a sufficiently small $U_ m$. To check closedness, take $x_\ell \to x$ and bounded extensions $H_\ell $. Cauchy estimates on relatively compact polydiscs and compactness of equicontinuous families give a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets of $U_ m$. A diagonal exhaustion handles all its components. The limit is holomorphic, bounded by $M$, and restricts to $Tx$ on the compact set $K$. Baire's theorem gives a ball $B(x_0,r)\subset A_{m,M}$ for some $m,M,r>0$. Subtracting extensions for $x_0+x$ and $x_0$, then rescaling, shows that every $Tx$ has an extension to this fixed $U_ m$ bounded by $C_ q\| x\| _{X_ q}$, where $C_ q=4M/r$ is sufficient. For a polynomial $p$ of degree $d$, take the sequence with only its $d$th coordinate nonzero. Its extension agrees with $p$ on every component of $U_ m$: each component meets $K$, and local determination applies to the difference. Consequently \[  \| p\| _{U_ m}\le C_ q q^{-d}\| p\| _ K.  \] Every component meets $K$ since each point of $U_ m$ can be joined to a nearest point of $K$ by a segment in $U_ m$. Since $q<1$ was arbitrary, the canonical neighborhood Bernstein–Walsh criterion now gives finiteness and continuity of the raw extremal $V_ K$. $\square$ Example 16.38.2 . C6B88322442F Global uniqueness on connected neighborhoods of $K$ cannot replace local determination in this characterization. Take $K=\overline\Delta \cup \{ 2\} \subset \mathbb C$. Every holomorphic function on a connected neighborhood of $K$ vanishing on $K$ is zero, by the identity principle on $\Delta $. Nevertheless $V_ K$ is discontinuous at $2$. In fact it is zero on $K$ and equals $\log ^+|z|$ off $K$: the upper bound is the disc extremal, and for $|z|>1$, $z\ne 2$, the polynomials \[  P_ j(z)=\tfrac 13(z-2)z^{j-1},\qquad \| P_ j\| _ K\le 1,  \] give the matching lower bound by taking $j$th roots. Yet every geometrically approximable $f\in C(K)$ has a holomorphic extension to some neighborhood of $K$. Its restriction to the disc extends by the first implication to a slightly larger disc; choose that disc to have radius less than $3/2$. On a disjoint small disc around $2$ use the constant $f(2)$. This gives the required extension. Thus the weaker uniqueness condition does not give the raw-extremal converse. Also $V_ K^*=\log ^+|z|$ is continuous, but the neighborhood Bernstein–Walsh bounds for every $t>1$ fail, by the raw criterion. Example 16.38.3 . 61CD9F3FD5EA Continuity of $V_ K^*$ does not by itself imply the extension property, even when $K$ is a uniqueness set on every connected neighborhood containing it. Let \[  a_ j=2+2^{-j},\qquad K=\overline\Delta \cup \{ 2,a_1,a_2,\ldots \} ,\qquad b_ j=\begin{cases} e^{-j^4},& j\text{ odd},\\ 0,& j\text{ even}. \end{cases}  \] Define $f=0$ on $\overline\Delta \cup \{ 2\} $ and $f(a_ j)=b_ j$. This is continuous. It has no holomorphic extension near $2$: the even subsequence would force that extension to vanish identically there, contradicting its positive values on the odd subsequence. The added countable set is polar, so polar obstacle invariance gives $V_ K^*=V_{\overline\Delta }^*=\log ^+|z|$, a continuous function. The disc again makes $K$ a uniqueness set in the stated global sense. We verify geometric approximation explicitly. For $1\le j\le n$ put \[  L_{j,n}(z)=\frac{z-2}{a_ j-2} \prod _{\substack {1\le k\le n\\ k\ne j}} \frac{z-a_ k}{a_ j-a_ k},\qquad Q_ n(z)=\sum _{j=1}^ n b_ jL_{j,n}(z)(z/a_ j)^{8n^2}.  \] Then $\deg Q_ n\le N_ n=8n^2+n$, $Q_ n(2)=0$, and $Q_ n(a_ j)=b_ j$ for $j\le n$. On the unit disc each numerator in $L_{j,n}$ is at most $4$ in modulus. Also \[  |a_ j-2|=2^{-j},\qquad |a_ j-a_ k|\ge 2^{-\max (j,k)},  \] so $\| L_{j,n}\| _{\overline\Delta }\le 2^{n^2+2n}$. Since $a_ j>2$, \[  \| Q_ n\| _{\overline\Delta }\le n\, 2^{-7n^2+2n}.  \] For $i>n$, separate the product factors with $k<j$ and $k>j$. The positive constant \[  C_0=\prod _{\ell \ge 1}(1-2^{-\ell })^{-1}<\infty  \] is finite because the sum of the corresponding negative logarithms converges. Direct cancellation of the powers of $2$ gives \[  |L_{j,n}(a_ i)| \le C_0^2\, 2^{j-i} 2^{-(n-j)(n-j+1)/2}.  \] Moreover $a_ i\le a_ j$, so the extra power in $Q_ n$ is at most $1$. Splitting the sum at $j=n/2$ therefore gives, uniformly for $i>n$, \[  |Q_ n(a_ i)|\le C\bigl (2^{-n^2/8}+n e^{-n^4/16}\bigr ) \le C'2^{-n^2/8}.  \] The omitted values satisfy $|b_ i|\le e^{-(n+1)^4}$. Combining all parts of $K$ yields \[  \| f-Q_ n\| _ K\le C''2^{-n^2/8}.  \] For $N_ n\le m<N_{n+1}$ use $Q_ n$ as the degree-$m$ approximant. It follows that \[  \limsup _{m\to \infty }e_ m(f,K)^{1/m} \le 2^{-1/64}<1.  \] Thus this $f$ satisfies the geometric approximation condition but has no holomorphic extension to any neighborhood of $K$.

section: 16.39 A continuous foliation by extremal ellipses
text:
Theorem 16.39.1 . DCB9565E6FDC Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ n\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be compact, convex, symmetric about the origin and have nonempty real interior, with $n\ge 1$. Then $\mathbb C^ n\setminus K$ admits a continuous foliation by embedded complex curves on each of which the raw extremal $V_ K$ is harmonic. The leaf space is $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$, and each leaf is biholomorphic to $\{ \zeta \in \mathbb C:|\zeta |>1\} $. Here a continuous foliation means continuous local product charts, whose restrictions to individual leaves are holomorphic coordinates; no differentiability in the transverse parameter is asserted. Proof. Let $p$ be the real norm with unit ball $K$, and let $K^\circ $ be its real polar body. Extend each $\ell \in K^\circ $ complex linearly to $\mathbb C^ n$. The function \[  q(w)=\max _{\ell \in K^\circ }|\ell (w)| =\max _{	heta \in \mathbb R}p(\operatorname {Re}(e^{i	heta }w))  \] is a complex norm. The equality follows by interchanging the two maxima and maximizing $\operatorname {Re}(e^{i	heta }\ell (w))$ over the circle; the norm properties follow from the polar norm formula. In particular $q$ is continuous and is nonzero off the origin. For $q(w)=1$ and $|\zeta |>1$, set \[  F(w,\zeta )=	frac 12(w\zeta + ar w\zeta ^{-1}).  \] The boundary trace $F(w,e^{i	heta })=\operatorname {Re}(e^{i	heta }w)$ lies in $K$. The formula is unchanged by replacing $(w,\zeta )$ with $(e^{i	heta }w,e^{-i	heta }\zeta )$, so descends to the quotient \[  \mathcal X=\{ (w,\zeta ):q(w)=1,\  |\zeta |>1\} /\mathbb S^1.  \] Its base is $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$. On each projective affine chart choose a continuous nonzero representative and divide it by its $q$-norm. This gives a continuous local section of $\{ q=1\} $, and identifies $\mathcal X$ locally with the product of that chart and $\{ |\zeta |>1\} $. On overlaps the fiber coordinate changes by multiplication by a unit scalar, continuously in the base parameter. We prove that the descended $F$ is a homeomorphism onto $\mathbb C^ n\setminus K$. Put \[  A(r)=	frac 12(r+r^{-1}),\qquad B(r)=	frac 12(r-r^{-1}),\qquad r>1.  \] Given $z=x+iy
otin K$, with real $x,y$, define \[  Q_ z(r)=q igl (x/A(r)+iy/B(r) igr ) =\max _{\ell \in K^\circ } \sqrt{\ell (x)^2/A(r)^2+\ell (y)^2/B(r)^2}.  \] Both denominators are strictly increasing. If $r_2>r_1>1$, then \[  Q_ z(r_2)\le \max \{ A(r_1)/A(r_2),B(r_1)/B(r_2)\} \, Q_ z(r_1)<Q_ z(r_1),  \] because $z
e 0$ and the polar separates real vectors. The function tends to zero at infinity. If $y
e 0$ it tends to infinity as $r\downarrow 1$; if $y=0$ its limit is $p(x)>1$. Hence there is a unique $r(z)>1$ with $Q_ z(r(z))=1$. This radius depends continuously on $z
otin K$: for fixed $z_0$, any two radii on either side of its root still bracket the root for all nearby $z$, by continuity of $Q_ z$ and strict monotonicity. Set \[  w(z)=x/A(r(z))+iy/B(r(z)).  \] Then $q(w(z))=1$ and $F(w(z),r(z))=z$, giving a continuous inverse into $\mathcal X$. Conversely, for $\zeta =re^{i	heta }$ put $w'=e^{i	heta }w$. The real and imaginary parts of $F(w,\zeta )$ are $A(r)\operatorname {Re}w'$ and $B(r)\operatorname {Im}w'$. The point is outside $K$: if its imaginary part vanishes, then $w'$ is real with $p(w')=1$, so the real point has norm $A(r)>1$. The root just constructed is exactly $r$, and its normalized vector is $w'$. Thus its inverse quotient class is the original class. This proves bijectivity, continuity and continuity of the inverse, including at real points outside $K$. For fixed $w$, the map $\zeta \mapsto F(w,\zeta )$ is holomorphic and injective with nonzero derivative on the exterior disc. Indeed, zero derivative would give $w\zeta ^2= ar w$, impossible when $|\zeta |>1$; equality at distinct $\zeta ,\eta $ would similarly give $w\zeta \eta = ar w$. It is proper into $\mathbb C^ n\setminus K$: as $|\zeta |	o \infty $ its norm tends to infinity, while approaches to the unit circle have limit points in $K$. It therefore parametrizes an embedded complex curve. The homeomorphism from $\mathcal X$ proves disjointness of the leaves and the required continuous local product structure. Finally \[  V_ K(F(w,\zeta ))=\log |\zeta |.  \] For the upper bound, restrict any competitor $u$ in the logarithmic growth class to this exterior disc. If the restriction is identically minus infinity there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $u(F(w,\zeta ))-\log |\zeta |$ is subharmonic, has boundary upper limits at most zero and is bounded above at infinity. In the coordinate $\eta =1/\zeta $, removability at zero and the disc maximum principle give the upper bound. For the lower bound choose a real polar functional $\ell $ with $|\ell (w)|=1$, which exists by compactness of $K^\circ $. The interval extremal pulled back by $\ell $ is an admissible competitor for $V_ K$. Writing $c=\ell (w)$, its argument is \[  \ell (F(w,\zeta )) =	frac 12(c\zeta +(c\zeta )^{-1}),\qquad |c|=1.  \] The checked Joukowski interval formula gives the value $\log |\zeta |$. Thus equality holds, and it is harmonic in the holomorphic leaf coordinate. $\square$

section: 16.39 A continuous foliation by extremal ellipses
text:
Theorem 16.39.1 . DCB9565E6FDC Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ n\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be compact, convex, symmetric about the origin and have nonempty real interior, with $n\ge 1$. Then $\mathbb C^ n\setminus K$ admits a continuous foliation by embedded complex curves on each of which the raw extremal $V_ K$ is harmonic. The leaf space is $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$, and each leaf is biholomorphic to $\{ \zeta \in \mathbb C:|\zeta |>1\} $. Here a continuous foliation means continuous local product charts, whose restrictions to individual leaves are holomorphic coordinates; no differentiability in the transverse parameter is asserted. Proof. Let $p$ be the real norm with unit ball $K$, and let $K^\circ $ be its real polar body. Extend each $\ell \in K^\circ $ complex linearly to $\mathbb C^ n$. The function \[  q(w)=\max _{\ell \in K^\circ }|\ell (w)| =\max _{	heta \in \mathbb R}p(\operatorname {Re}(e^{i	heta }w))  \] is a complex norm. The equality follows by interchanging the two maxima and maximizing $\operatorname {Re}(e^{i	heta }\ell (w))$ over the circle; the norm properties follow from the polar norm formula. In particular $q$ is continuous and is nonzero off the origin. For $q(w)=1$ and $|\zeta |>1$, set \[  F(w,\zeta )=	frac 12(w\zeta + ar w\zeta ^{-1}).  \] The boundary trace $F(w,e^{i	heta })=\operatorname {Re}(e^{i	heta }w)$ lies in $K$. The formula is unchanged by replacing $(w,\zeta )$ with $(e^{i	heta }w,e^{-i	heta }\zeta )$, so descends to the quotient \[  \mathcal X=\{ (w,\zeta ):q(w)=1,\  |\zeta |>1\} /\mathbb S^1.  \] Its base is $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$. On each projective affine chart choose a continuous nonzero representative and divide it by its $q$-norm. This gives a continuous local section of $\{ q=1\} $, and identifies $\mathcal X$ locally with the product of that chart and $\{ |\zeta |>1\} $. On overlaps the fiber coordinate changes by multiplication by a unit scalar, continuously in the base parameter. We prove that the descended $F$ is a homeomorphism onto $\mathbb C^ n\setminus K$. Put \[  A(r)=	frac 12(r+r^{-1}),\qquad B(r)=	frac 12(r-r^{-1}),\qquad r>1.  \] Given $z=x+iy
otin K$, with real $x,y$, define \[  Q_ z(r)=q igl (x/A(r)+iy/B(r) igr ) =\max _{\ell \in K^\circ } \sqrt{\ell (x)^2/A(r)^2+\ell (y)^2/B(r)^2}.  \] Both denominators are strictly increasing. If $r_2>r_1>1$, then \[  Q_ z(r_2)\le \max \{ A(r_1)/A(r_2),B(r_1)/B(r_2)\} \, Q_ z(r_1)<Q_ z(r_1),  \] because $z
e 0$ and the polar separates real vectors. The function tends to zero at infinity. If $y
e 0$ it tends to infinity as $r\downarrow 1$; if $y=0$ its limit is $p(x)>1$. Hence there is a unique $r(z)>1$ with $Q_ z(r(z))=1$. This radius depends continuously on $z
otin K$: for fixed $z_0$, any two radii on either side of its root still bracket the root for all nearby $z$, by continuity of $Q_ z$ and strict monotonicity. Set \[  w(z)=x/A(r(z))+iy/B(r(z)).  \] Then $q(w(z))=1$ and $F(w(z),r(z))=z$, giving a continuous inverse into $\mathcal X$. Conversely, for $\zeta =re^{i	heta }$ put $w'=e^{i	heta }w$. The real and imaginary parts of $F(w,\zeta )$ are $A(r)\operatorname {Re}w'$ and $B(r)\operatorname {Im}w'$. The point is outside $K$: if its imaginary part vanishes, then $w'$ is real with $p(w')=1$, so the real point has norm $A(r)>1$. The root just constructed is exactly $r$, and its normalized vector is $w'$. Thus its inverse quotient class is the original class. This proves bijectivity, continuity and continuity of the inverse, including at real points outside $K$. For fixed $w$, the map $\zeta \mapsto F(w,\zeta )$ is holomorphic and injective with nonzero derivative on the exterior disc. Indeed, zero derivative would give $w\zeta ^2= ar w$, impossible when $|\zeta |>1$; equality at distinct $\zeta ,\eta $ would similarly give $w\zeta \eta = ar w$. It is proper into $\mathbb C^ n\setminus K$: as $|\zeta |	o \infty $ its norm tends to infinity, while approaches to the unit circle have limit points in $K$. It therefore parametrizes an embedded complex curve. The homeomorphism from $\mathcal X$ proves disjointness of the leaves and the required continuous local product structure. Finally \[  V_ K(F(w,\zeta ))=\log |\zeta |.  \] For the upper bound, restrict any competitor $u$ in the logarithmic growth class to this exterior disc. If the restriction is identically minus infinity there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $u(F(w,\zeta ))-\log |\zeta |$ is subharmonic, has boundary upper limits at most zero and is bounded above at infinity. In the coordinate $\eta =1/\zeta $, removability at zero and the disc maximum principle give the upper bound. For the lower bound choose a real polar functional $\ell $ with $|\ell (w)|=1$, which exists by compactness of $K^\circ $. The interval extremal pulled back by $\ell $ is an admissible competitor for $V_ K$. Writing $c=\ell (w)$, its argument is \[  \ell (F(w,\zeta )) =	frac 12(c\zeta +(c\zeta )^{-1}),\qquad |c|=1.  \] The checked Joukowski interval formula gives the value $\log |\zeta |$. Thus equality holds, and it is harmonic in the holomorphic leaf coordinate. $\square$

title: 7.25 Boundary-zero Green functions and hyperconvexity
text: Proposition 7.25.1 . B63D9FDC459B Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded domain. If $D$ admits a negative plurisubharmonic exhaustion, it admits a continuous negative plurisubharmonic exhaustion. Here exhaustion means that every negative sublevel is relatively compact; the original function may have poles. Proof. Choose concentric balls $K=\overline{B(a,r)}\subset B(a,R)\Subset D$. After multiplying the given exhaustion by a positive constant and taking its maximum with $-1$, obtain $q\in \operatorname {PSH}(D)$ with $-1\leq q<0$, $q=-1$ on $K$, and $q\to 0$ at every boundary point. The multiplication is possible because an upper semicontinuous negative function has a strictly negative maximum on the compact ball $K$. Boundedness of $D$ and the exhaustion property give the stated boundary limit, uniformly in a sufficiently small boundary collar. Set $H=h_{K,D}^*$. The upper-envelope theorem makes $H$ PSH, and $q\leq H\leq 0$. Restricting competitors to $B(a,R)$ and using the explicit relative extremal of concentric balls gives $H=-1$ on $K$, including its boundary. Consequently $H$ itself is a competitor, so $H=h_{K,D}$. In particular $H\to 0$ at $\partial D$. We prove continuity without assuming a continuous exhaustion already exists. Fix $0<\varepsilon <1$. Choose $\eta >0$ such that $K\subset D_\eta =\{ \operatorname {dist}(z,D^ c)>\eta \} $ and $q>-\varepsilon /2$ wherever $\operatorname {dist}(z,D^ c)<2\eta $. On $D_\eta $ let $H_ t$ be the radial smooth convolutions for $0<t<\eta $. They decrease to $H$, are at most zero, and converge uniformly to $-1$ on $K$. The last assertion is Dini's theorem applied on the compact $K$, where the limit is the constant $-1$. Choose $t$ so that $H_ t-\varepsilon \leq -1$ on $K$. Define \[  v_\varepsilon = \begin{cases}  \max \{ q,H_ t-\varepsilon \} ,& D_\eta ,\\  q,& D\setminus D_\eta . \end{cases}  \] Near the new interface $q>-\varepsilon /2$ whereas $H_ t-\varepsilon \leq -\varepsilon $. The pasting theorem therefore makes $v_\varepsilon $ PSH. It is nonpositive and at most $-1$ on $K$, hence $v_\varepsilon \leq H$. We do not assume that $v_\varepsilon $ is continuous. The needed continuous local minorant is instead $H_ t-\varepsilon \leq H$ on $D_\eta $. Since $H_ t\geq H$, for $x\in D_\eta $ this gives \[  \liminf _{y\to x}H(y)\geq H_ t(x)-\varepsilon \geq H(x)-\varepsilon .  \] For any fixed $x\in D$, arbitrarily small $\varepsilon $ permit a choice of $\eta $ with $x\in D_\eta $. Thus $H$ is lower semicontinuous, and its PSH upper semicontinuity proves continuity. The maximum principle and $H|_ K=-1$ give $H<0$ on the connected domain. Finally $q\leq H$ makes every negative sublevel of $H$ relatively compact. Thus $H$ is the required continuous exhaustion. $\square$ Theorem 7.25.2 . 033C98D473B9 For a bounded domain $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ the following are equivalent: $D$ is hyperconvex, with a continuous negative PSH exhaustion; for some $a\in D$, its isolated-pole Green envelope satisfies $g_ D(z,a)\to 0$ as $z\to \xi $ in $D$, for every $\xi \in \partial D$; this boundary limit holds for every $a\in D$. In the second condition no prior pseudoconvexity or continuity of the Green function is assumed. Proof. On a bounded domain the envelope construction and logarithmic ball bounds give a negative PSH Green function with its logarithmic pole. Under the second condition $q=\max \{ g_ D(\cdot ,a),-1\} $ is therefore a bounded negative PSH exhaustion: a sequence in a negative sublevel cannot tend to the boundary, by the assumed limit, and $D$ is bounded. The preceding proposition proves the first condition. For a hyperconvex domain, the shrinking-ball relative-extremal comparison in the existing Green continuity theorem gives boundary zero for every pole. This proves the third condition, which immediately implies the second. $\square$

title: 16.40 Local regularity of analytic polyhedra
text:
We use the analytic principalization input in its real analytic category: for a nonzero real analytic function $F$ on a real analytic manifold $M$, there is a proper surjective analytic modification $\pi :\widetilde M	o M$ such that $F\circ \pi $ is locally a monomial times a nonvanishing analytic function. The spaces have the same dimension. This is the principal-ideal case of the permitted resolution input; its algorithmic proof is external ( Bierstone–Milman , Theorem 2.4, with the real analytic category in (0.1)(2) and Theorem 1.10 ). The exact real category and properness are important here. Lemma 16.40.1 . DD2047D70ACD Let $A$ be an open subset of $\mathbb R^ N$, let $a\in \overline A\setminus A$, and suppose that near $a$ membership in $A$ is a finite Boolean combination of sign conditions on real analytic functions. There is a real analytic map $\gamma $ near $0$ with $\gamma (0)=a$ and $\gamma (t)\in A$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$. Proof. Work in a connected coordinate ball about $a$. Replace identically zero functions in the formula by their constant truth values. All remaining functions $f_1,\ldots ,f_ s$ are nonzero analytic functions. If none remain, membership is locally constant, contrary to the boundary assumption. Their product $F$ is nonzero. Its zero set has empty interior, by the real analytic identity theorem, so there are $x_ j\in A\setminus \{ F=0\} $ tending to $a$. After passing to a subsequence all signs $\operatorname {sgn}f_ i(x_ j)$ are fixed. Principalize $(F)$ on the ball. Surjectivity gives lifts $y_ j\in \pi ^{-1}(x_ j)$. Properness, applied over a compact smaller ball containing the sequence, gives a subsequence tending to $b\in \pi ^{-1}(a)$. Choose analytic coordinates $y$ centered at $b$ in which $F\circ \pi $ is a monomial times a unit. In these coordinates each factor has the form \[  f_ i\circ \pi =c_ i(y)\prod _{\ell =1}^ k y_\ell ^{m_{i\ell }}, \qquad m_{i\ell }\geq 0,\qquad c_ i(0)
e 0.  \] Here is the elementary factorization justification. In the ring of convergent real power series each coordinate is prime, since setting it to zero gives an integral domain. Repeatedly remove the coordinate factors from the product identity. The remaining factors have product a unit and are consequently units themselves. Shrink the chart so that all $c_ i$ keep their signs. Because $F(x_ j)
e 0$, the first $k$ coordinates of $y_ j$ are nonzero. Pass to a subsequence with fixed signs $s_\ell \in \{ -1,1\} $. In the chart take the analytic line \[  y_\ell (t)=s_\ell t\quad (1\leq \ell \leq k),\qquad y_\ell (t)=0\quad (k<\ell \leq N).  \] For small positive $t$, every $f_ i(\pi (y(t)))$ has exactly its sign on the sequence $x_ j$. Thus the entire Boolean formula has the same truth value, including its equality conditions. It follows that $\gamma (t)=\pi (y(t))$ lies in $A$. This map is analytic at zero and equals $a$ there. It cannot be constant, because $a
otin A$. The case $k=0$ cannot occur: all the functions would be nonzero at $a$, making membership locally constant there. $\square$ Theorem 16.40.2 . 8ED77FB38EC4 Let $A\subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, be a bounded nonempty open set which is semianalytic in a neighborhood of every point of its closure. Put $K=\overline A$. For every $a\in K$ and $r>0$, $K\cap \overline B(a,r)$ is L-regular at $a$. In particular $V_ K$ is continuous on $\mathbb C^ n$. Consequently this holds for the closure of every nonempty relatively compact open analytic polyhedron \[  A=\{ z\in U:|f_ j(z)|<1,\  1\leq j\leq m\} \Subset U, \qquad f_ j\in \mathcal O(U),  \] with arbitrary finite $m$; no order-$n$ or finite-fiber hypothesis is required. Proof. Fix $a\in K$ and $r>0$, and set $K_ r=K\cap \overline B(a,r)$. If $a\in A$, the set $K_ r$ contains a ball centered at $a$. The explicit ball profile and obstacle monotonicity give $V_{K_ r}^*(a)=0$ and regularity there. Otherwise use the preceding lemma, identifying $\mathbb C^ n$ with $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Shrink its parameter interval so that $\gamma (t)\in A\cap B(a,r)$ for $0<t\leq \varepsilon $. The convergent real power series of its complex coordinates extend holomorphically near this interval. Every $\gamma (t)$ with $t>0$ is an interior point of $K_ r$, so a contained ball gives $V_{K_ r}^*(\gamma (t))=0$. The compact $K_ r$ contains a ball and is non-pluripolar. Its regularized extremal is therefore finite PSH. Pulling it back by $\gamma $ gives a nonnegative subharmonic function, zero on the punctured real interval. The interval is nonthin at its endpoint, so its value at zero is zero. Thus $V_{K_ r}^*(a)=0$. Since $0\leq V_{K_ r}\leq V_{K_ r}^*$, upper semicontinuity proves raw continuity at $a$. This is precisely the existing analytic accessibility argument, now with its arc constructed. Taking $r$ large enough to contain $K$ proves zero regularized contact at every point of $K$. The existing compact zero-contact criterion then gives $V_ K=V_ K^*$ continuous on the whole space. For the polyhedron, $1-|f_ j|^2$ is real analytic, and relative compactness puts $K$ inside $U$, so its strict inequalities give the required semianalytic description near every point of $K$. $\square$

title: 16.41 Normalized characterization of compact extremals
text: Write $\mathcal L^+$ for the global two-sided growth class \[  \{ u\in \operatorname {PSH}(\mathbb C^ n): |u(z)-\log ^+|z||\leq C_ u\text{ for all }z\} .  \] Its functions are locally bounded; all products below are classical Bedford–Taylor products. Proposition 16.41.1 . 1129B1616DEE Let $n\geq 1$ and let $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be non-pluripolar and compact. Then $V_ K^*$ is the unique $u\in \mathcal L^+$ such that $u=0$ on $K$ outside a pluripolar set and $(dd^ cu)^ n=0$ on $\mathbb C^ n\setminus K$. Proof. The established logarithmic family bound, compact-obstacle maximality and envelope discrepancy theorem show that $v=V_ K^*$ satisfies these conditions. Its lower growth bound comes from the profile of any ball containing $K$. Let $u$ satisfy the same conditions, with exceptional set $P\subset K$. It is a competitor for $V_{K\setminus P}$. The established invariance of regularized bounded-obstacle extremals under polar deletion gives \[  u\leq V_{K\setminus P}\leq V_{K\setminus P}^*=V_ K^*=v.  \] For the converse fix $\varepsilon ,\delta >0$ and put $w=(1+\varepsilon )u+\delta $. Two-sided logarithmic growth gives $w-v\to +\infty $ uniformly as $|z|\to \infty $. Thus on every sufficiently large ball containing $K$ the boundary ordering for the bounded local domination principle holds, strictly. The measure $(dd^ cw)^ n=(1+\varepsilon )^ n(dd^ cu)^ n$ is carried by $K$ and gives no mass to pluripolar sets. Outside the union of the exceptional sets for $u$ and $v$ in $K$ we have $w=\delta >0=v$. Therefore $v\leq w$ almost everywhere for $(dd^ cw)^ n$. Apply the existing local domination principle on the large ball, with $w$ as its measure-bearing potential, to get $v\leq w$ throughout that ball. Every point lies in such a ball, so this holds globally. Let $\delta \downarrow 0$ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. The functions are finite everywhere, and the limit gives $v\leq u$. Together with the first inequality this proves uniqueness. $\square$ The upper-growth condition alone is insufficient. For the closed unit disc in $\mathbb C$, all functions $\alpha \log ^+|z|$ with $0<\alpha \leq 1$ satisfy that upper bound, vanish on the disc and are harmonic outside it. Only $\alpha =1$ belongs to the two-sided class used in the proposition.

section: 7.26 Generalized products and their associated bounded products
text: We first specify an elementary full Colombeau algebra in Euclidean coordinates. In the following definitions test kernels are real valued; generalized functions and distributions may be complex valued. For $q\geq 0$ let $\mathcal A_ q\subset C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d;\mathbb R)$ consist of kernels of integral one with $\int y^\alpha \varphi (y)\, dy=0$ for $1\leq |\alpha |\leq q$. Put $S_\varepsilon \varphi (y)=\varepsilon ^{-d}\varphi (y/\varepsilon )$. These sets are nonempty. Indeed, for any mass-one test kernel $\chi $, choose $c_1,\ldots ,c_{q+1}$ solving the Vandermonde system $\sum c_ j=1$, $\sum c_ jj^ k=0$ for $1\leq k\leq q$. Then $\sum c_ jS_ j\chi \in \mathcal A_ q$. For an open $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ let \[  U(\Omega )=\{ (\varphi ,x):\varphi \in \mathcal A_0, \  x-\operatorname {supp}\varphi \subset \Omega \} .  \] The basic space consists of maps $R:U(\Omega )\to \mathbb C$ smooth in $x$ for each fixed $\varphi $. Write $p_{K,l}(R,\varepsilon ,\varphi ) =\max _{|\alpha |\leq l}\sup _{x\in K} |\partial _ x^\alpha R(S_\varepsilon \varphi ,x)|$. For each fixed $K\Subset \Omega $ and kernel this is defined for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon $. A basic map is moderate if \[  \forall K\Subset \Omega \  \forall l\geq 0\  \exists N\geq 1 \forall \varphi \in \mathcal A_ N: p_{K,l}(R,\varepsilon ,\varphi )=O(\varepsilon ^{-N}),  \] and negligible if \[  \forall K\Subset \Omega \  \forall l,m\geq 0\  \exists q\geq 0 \forall \varphi \in \mathcal A_ q: p_{K,l}(R,\varepsilon ,\varphi )=O(\varepsilon ^ m).  \] The constants and the small-parameter cutoff may depend on the fixed kernel. Let $\mathcal E_ M$ and $\mathcal N$ denote these spaces and put $\mathcal G(\Omega )=\mathcal E_ M/\mathcal N$. The reflection $\varphi (y)\mapsto \varphi (-y)$ converts this convolution convention into the convention with $x+\operatorname {supp}\varphi $. Proposition 7.26.1 . EFE2F92EE4F9 The quotient $\mathcal G(\Omega )$ is a differential algebra. The maps \[  (\iota T)(\varphi ,x)=\langle T,\varphi (x-\cdot )\rangle , \qquad (\sigma f)(\varphi ,x)=f(x)  \] embed distributions linearly and smooth functions as a subalgebra, respectively. They commute with partial derivatives, and $\iota f=\sigma f$ in the quotient for smooth $f$. Proof. Leibniz's formula proves that sums, products and derivatives of moderate maps are moderate: increase the moment order and the exponent to cover the finitely many estimates. The same formula proves that negligible maps form a differential ideal. More explicitly, to multiply a negligible derivative by a moderate derivative of growth $O(\varepsilon ^{-N})$, use negligibility with exponent $m+N$ and moment order at least $N$. Every negligible map is moderate, by its estimate with exponent zero and an increased moment order. Thus the quotient and its derivatives are well defined. On a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, a distribution has finite order $s$, with $|\langle T,\theta \rangle |\leq C\max _{|\alpha |\leq s} \sup |\partial ^\alpha \theta |$ for test functions supported there. Consequently \[  p_{K,l}(\iota T,\varepsilon ,\varphi ) \leq C_\varphi \varepsilon ^{-d-s-l},  \] for small $\varepsilon $, proving moderateness. Distributional differentiation gives $\partial _ j\iota T=\iota (\partial _ jT)$. The corresponding assertions for $\sigma $ follow from ordinary differentiation and multiplication. If $f$ is smooth, Taylor's theorem applied to each derivative of $f(x-\varepsilon y)$ through degree $q$ gives \[  p_{K,l}(\iota f-\sigma f,\varepsilon ,\varphi ) =O(\varepsilon ^{q+1}),\qquad \varphi \in \mathcal A_ q.  \] The moments cancel all positive-degree Taylor terms. This is negligibility for every $l,m$. Its pairing tends to zero, and also to the pairing with $T$. Thus $T=0$, proving injectivity. Lemma 7.26.2 . 8DF858D7EC52 Let $u$ be locally bounded PSH on $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ and let $\rho \geq 0$ be a smooth compactly supported kernel of integral one on $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Positivity of the kernel preserves the PSH submean inequalities. Local boundedness gives the asserted uniform bounds. We prove the capacity claim without assuming radiality or monotonicity in $\varepsilon $. Work in balls $B_1\Subset B_2\Subset \Omega $. title: 5.51 Smooth curves which are not pluripolar
search_title: Smooth curves which are not pluripolar
section: 5.51 Smooth curves which are not pluripolar
text: Theorem 5.51.1 . 283A0A00F1E4 For every $n\geq 2$ there are real functions $f_2,\ldots ,f_ n\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ such that the compact arc \[  K=\{ (x,f_2(x),\ldots ,f_ n(x)):0\leq x\leq 1\} \subset \mathbb C^ n  \] is not pluripolar. In particular its extension with $x\in \mathbb R$ is a closed, properly embedded smooth real curve which is not pluripolar. Proof. We use the planar finite logarithmic energy criterion and Josefson's globalization theorem . We first construct all the sets and functions needed for the slicing argument. Put $Q=2^{n+1}+1$. At each level $k$ choose $n$ bits $(b_ k,a_{2,k},\ldots ,a_{n,k})$ and encode them by the digit \[  d_ k=2\left(2^{n-1}b_ k+\sum _{r=2}^ n2^{r-2}a_{r,k}\right).  \] Thus $d_ k$ ranges over $0,2,\ldots ,Q-3$. Let $D$ consist of all $\sum _{k\geq 1}d_ kQ^{-k}$. It is compact and contained in $[0,1]$. Every prefix of length $k$ gives an interval $I=[s,s+Q^{-k}]$, where $s$ is its finite sum. The starting points of distinct such intervals differ by at least $2Q^{-k}$: after multiplication by $Q^ k$ they are distinct even integers, since $Q$ is odd. The intervals are therefore separated by at least $Q^{-k}$. The tail after level $k$ is at most $(Q-3)Q^{-k}/(Q-1)<Q^{-k}$. If two sequences first differ at level $k$, their encoded points are at distance at least $Q^{-k}$. In particular the encoding is unique. Fix all the bits $a=(a_{r,k})_{2\leq r\leq n,\  k\geq 1}$ and let $C_ a\subset D$ be the compact set obtained by varying just the $b_ k$. Different arrays $a$ give disjoint sets. There is a probability measure $\mu _ a$ on $C_ a$ assigning weight $2^{-k}$ to each of its $k$-prefix cylinders. To see this without assuming a product measure, take the uniform measure on the $2^ m$ points whose first $m$ bits $b_ k$ vary and whose later bits are zero. A weakly convergent subsequence exists on the compact interval. Its limit is supported on $C_ a$. For each fixed level the cylinders lie in finitely many disjoint compact intervals; continuous separating functions show that the limiting weights are $2^{-k}$. Every singleton consequently has measure zero. For a fixed $x\in C_ a$, the points whose code first differs from that of $x$ at level $k$ have measure $2^{-k}$. The separation estimate gives \[  \int _{C_ a}\log \frac1{|x-y|}\, d\mu _ a(y) \leq \log Q\sum _{k\geq 1}k2^{-k}<\infty .  \] There is no contribution from $y=x$. The kernel is nonnegative on $[0,1]$, so Tonelli's theorem also gives finite double logarithmic energy. The planar energy criterion implies that every $C_ a$ is nonpolar. Choose $\beta \in C_ c^\infty ((-1/3,4/3))$, with $0\leq \beta \leq 1$ and $\beta =1$ on $[0,1]$. For $2\leq r\leq n$, let $\psi _{r,k}(x)$ be the sum of $\beta (Q^ k(x-s))$ over the level-$k$ prefixes whose bit $a_{r,k}$ is one. The supports of the summands are disjoint: their lengths are less than $(5/3)Q^{-k}$ and their starting points differ by at least $2Q^{-k}$. Hence, for every integer $\ell \geq 0$, \[  \| \psi _{r,k}^{(\ell )}\| _\infty \leq \| \beta ^{(\ell )}\| _\infty Q^{k\ell }.  \] On $D$, the function $\psi _{r,k}$ equals the encoded bit $a_{r,k}$. Indeed a point lies in its own prefix interval, where the appropriate bump is one, and lies outside every other prefix's bump support. Set \[  c_ k=10^{-k^2},\qquad f_ r(x)=\sum _{k\geq 1}c_ k\psi _{r,k}(x).  \] For every $\ell $ the series of $\ell $th derivatives converges uniformly, because $\sum _ k10^{-k^2}Q^{k\ell }<\infty $. Repeated integration of the uniformly convergent derivative series identifies them as the derivatives of $f_ r$. Thus $f_ r$ is smooth. All the summands have support in a fixed compact subinterval of $(-1,2)$, so $f_ r$ is compactly supported. On $C_ a$ it has the constant value \[  f_ r|_{C_ a}=c(a_ r):=\sum _{k\geq 1}a_{r,k}10^{-k^2}.  \] The common set of possible values $C'=\{ \sum _{k\geq 1}a_ k10^{-k^2}:a_ k\in \{ 0,1\} \} $ is also nonpolar. In fact the tail after the $k$th term is at most $c_ k/9$, since each subsequent ratio is at most $10^{-3}$. Two codes first differing at level $k$ are therefore separated by at least $c_ k/2$. Construct the probability measure with cylinder weights $2^{-k}$ by the same finite-measure limit argument. The prefix compact sets are disjoint, so it has no atoms, and for every $t\in C'$, \[  \int _{C'}\log \frac1{|t-s|}\, d\nu (s) \leq \sum _{k\geq 1}2^{-k}(k^2\log 10+\log 2)<\infty .  \] Again the support has diameter less than one, so this proves finite logarithmic energy and nonpolarity. Suppose now that $K$ were pluripolar. Josefson's theorem supplies $\varphi \in \operatorname {PSH}(\mathbb C^ n)$, not identically $-\infty $, with $\varphi |_ K=-\infty $. Fix any array $a$. The restriction \[  z\longmapsto \varphi (z,c(a_2),\ldots ,c(a_ n))  \] is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. It is $-\infty $ on the nonpolar set $C_ a$, so the second alternative holds. Consequently $\varphi =-\infty $ on $\mathbb C\times (C')^{n-1}$. Restricting to one complex coordinate at a time and using the nonpolarity of $C'$ then proves successively that $\varphi =-\infty $ on $\mathbb C^ j\times (C')^{n-j}$ for $j=2,\ldots ,n$. This contradicts the choice of $\varphi $. The parametrization of the extended graph is injective and an immersion, because its first coordinate is $x$. It is proper, because that coordinate is unbounded as $|x|\to \infty $, and its inverse on the image is the first-coordinate projection. Its image is therefore a closed embedded smooth curve. It contains the nonpluripolar compact arc $K$. $\square$

Suppose now that $K$ were pluripolar. Josefson's theorem supplies $\varphi \in \operatorname {PSH}(\mathbb C^ n)$, not identically $-\infty $, with $\varphi |_ K=-\infty $. Fix any array $a$. The restriction \[  z\longmapsto \varphi (z,c(a_2),\ldots ,c(a_ n))  \] is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. It is $-\infty $ on the nonpolar set $C_ a$, so the second alternative holds. Consequently $\varphi =-\infty $ on $\mathbb C\times (C')^{n-1}$. Restricting to one complex coordinate at a time and using the nonpolarity of $C'$ then proves successively that $\varphi =-\infty $ on $\mathbb C^ j\times (C')^{n-j}$ for $j=2,\ldots ,n$. This contradicts the choice of $\varphi $. The parametrization of the extended graph is injective and an immersion, because its first coordinate is $x$. It is proper, because that coordinate is unbounded as $|x|\to \infty $, and its inverse on the image is the first-coordinate projection. Its image is therefore a closed embedded smooth curve. It contains the nonpluripolar compact arc $K$. $\square$

u (p)$ for its outward unit normal and $x=p-d
