Theorem 16.42.5 . 1E10E926515B Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be a convex body with $C^2$ boundary. Then $\mu _ K$ gives no mass to $\partial K$ and is absolutely continuous on all of $K$. There are constants $0<c\leq C<\infty $ such that \[   rac{c}{\sqrt{\operatorname {dist}(x,\partial K)}} \leq f_ K(x)\leq  rac{C}{\sqrt{\operatorname {dist}(x,\partial K)}} \quad 	ext{for almost every }x\in \operatorname {int}K.  \] No symmetry or positive lower bound for the principal curvatures is assumed. If $K$ is symmetric, its density is the polar-volume formula of proposition 16.42.3 . Proof. First compute the measure of a real ball from the preceding interior formula. For $K=\overline{B_{\mathbb R^ n}(0,R)}$, the image $S_ x(K^\circ )$ is the ellipsoid \[  R^2|\xi |^2-(x\cdot \xi )^2\leq 1.  \] Its volume is $R^{-n}\operatorname {vol}(B_{\mathbb R^ n}(0,1)) (1-|x|^2/R^2)^{-1/2}$. Thus the ball density is this expression multiplied by $n!/(4\pi )^ n$. Its real sphere is contained in the holomorphic hypersurface $\sum z_ j^2=R^2$, hence is pluripolar and receives no mass. Fix a boundary point $p$, write $
u (p)$ for its outward unit normal and $x=p-d
u (p)$ for an interior point sufficiently near it. A ball of fixed radius $r$ centered at $p-r
u (p)$ lies inside $K$. Its distance from $x$ to its boundary is $d$. Since $V_ K\leq V_ B$, contact on the ball interior bounds $f_ K(x)$ above by the ball density, which is at most $C d^{-1/2}$ for $0<d<r$. For the lower bound take an enclosing cube with one face in the supporting hyperplane at $p$, that face centered at $p$, and side length $4\operatorname {diam}K$. It contains $K$. At $x$ the distance to that face is $d$, while the remaining face distances have a fixed positive lower bound. The cube formula and $V_ Q\leq V_ K$ give $f_ K(x)\geq c d^{-1/2}$. The comparisons are justified at every Lebesgue point of $f_ K$ by averaging on a small neighborhood of $x$, where the comparison density is continuous. Interior compact sets are handled by proposition 16.42.2 . This proves the asserted two-sided bounds on the interior, with constants controlled by the diameter, rolling radius and an interior ball. If the boundary is real analytic it is locally contained in a holomorphic hypersurface: complexify its nonzero real-analytic defining function in the real coordinates. A finite covering of the compact boundary shows pluripolarity. The locally bounded product $\mu _ K$ therefore gives it zero mass. For general $C^2$ boundary take the analytic convex approximants $K_ j$ of lemma 16.42.4 . Their interior bounds have common constants, and their boundaries have zero mass. Normal coordinates and the uniform area/Jacobian bounds give \[  \mu _{K_ j}\{ x\in K_ j: \operatorname {dist}(x,\partial K_ j)<s\} \leq C'\sqrt s  \] for all sufficiently small $s$, uniformly in $j$. All these bodies contain a fixed ball. Their radial $C^2$ convergence gives $(1-\delta _ j)K\subset K_ j\subset (1+\delta _ j)K$, with $\delta _ j	o 0$. The continuous real-body extremal and obstacle monotonicity squeeze $V_{K_ j}$ between $V_ K(z/(1+\delta _ j))$ and $V_ K(z/(1-\delta _ j))$. It follows that $V_{K_ j}	o V_ K$ locally uniformly, and hence $\mu _{K_ j}	o \mu _ K$ weakly on compact sets. For the open real-space tube $U_ s=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,\partial K)<s\} $, boundary convergence gives, for large $j$, $K_ j\cap U_ s\subset \{ x\in K_ j:d(x,\partial K_ j)<2s\} $. The measures are supported in one fixed compact subset of $\mathbb R^ n$; their ambient weak convergence is also weak convergence on that real space, by extending real test functions with a cutoff in $y$. The open-set inequality for weak convergence yields \[  \mu _ K(U_ s)\leq \liminf _ j\mu _{K_ j}(U_ s)\leq C'\sqrt{2s}.  \] Let $s\downarrow 0$. This proves $\mu _ K(\partial K)=0$. Together with the interior density and support on $K$, it proves absolute continuity and completes the theorem. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.42.6
section: 16.42 Equilibrium densities and boundaries of real convex bodies
text: Theorem 16.42.6 . 69C6DC7FA336 Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be a convex body symmetric about zero, with nonempty interior. No boundary regularity is assumed. Then \[  \mu _ K(\partial K)=0,\qquad \mu _ K=f_ K\, dx\quad \hbox{on }K,\qquad \int _{\operatorname {int}K}f_ K\, dx=2^{-n},  \] where $f_ K$ is the continuous interior density in proposition 16.42.3 . In fact, writing $M=2^{-n}$, for $0<r<1$ one has \[  \mu _ K\{ x\in K:m_ K(x)\geq r\}  \leq \frac{2(n+1)M\log (1/r)}{\operatorname {arcosh}(1/r)}.  \] Here $m_ K$ denotes the Minkowski functional of $K$, with $m_ K(x)=\inf \{ s>0:x\in sK\} $. Proof. Put $U=V_ K$ and $\gamma (z)=\tfrac 12\log (1+|z|^2)$. The affine/projective dictionary extends $q=U-\gamma $ to a bounded $\omega $-PSH function on $X=\mathbb P^ n$, where $\omega =dd^ c\gamma $ on the affine chart and $\int _ X\omega ^ n=M$. We use the existing bounded-type energy cocycle : \[  E_\omega (b)-E_\omega (a) =\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n\int _ X(b-a) (\omega +dd^ cb)^ j\wedge (\omega +dd^ ca)^{n-j},  \] with $E_\omega (0)=0$. This formula applies to bounded potentials; it does not require differentiating the possibly nonsmooth extremal. Its reference potential is zero, which is a model potential for the Kähler form $\omega $ since the envelope below zero is zero. For $t>1$ let $F_ t[Z_0:Z']=[Z_0:tZ']$ and put \[  a_ t=\frac12\log \frac{|Z_0|^2+t^2|Z'|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z'|^2}, \qquad b_ t=q\circ F_ t+a_ t.  \] Thus $0\leq a_ t\leq \log t$, $\omega +dd^ ca_ t=F_ t^*\omega $, and $\omega +dd^ cb_ t=F_ t^*(\omega +dd^ cq)$. Apply the cocycle to $a_ t,b_ t$ and change variables by the projective automorphism $F_ t$. Each of its $n+1$ mixed integrals becomes the corresponding integral defining $E_\omega (q)$, because $b_ t-a_ t=q\circ F_ t$. Consequently \[  E_\omega (b_ t)-E_\omega (q)=E_\omega (a_ t) \leq M\log t.  \] The inequality follows either from monotonicity and constant shifts of the same cocycle, or from $0\leq a_ t\leq \log t$ and the common mixed mass $M$. Pullback commutes with the bounded products by their local definition. On the affine chart $b_ t-q=U(tz)-U(z)\geq 0$: indeed $U(tz)=V_{t^{-1}K}(z)$ and $t^{-1}K\subset K$. This ordering holds on the hyperplane at infinity as well, since $F_ t$ is its identity and $a_ t=\log t$ there. Apply the cocycle now to $q,b_ t$. All its terms are nonnegative, and retaining its $j=0$ term gives \[  \int _ X(b_ t-q)(\omega +dd^ cq)^ n \leq (n+1)M\log t.  \] The bounded measure gives no mass to the hyperplane at infinity. By proposition 16.34.2 , its affine measure is supported on $K$, where $U=0$. We have therefore proved \[  \int _ K U(tx)\, d\mu _ K(x)\leq (n+1)M\log t.  \] For every $x\in K$ the bipolar identity gives $m_ K(x)=\max _{\eta \in K^\circ }x\cdot \eta $. If $t m_ K(x)>1$, a maximizing functional and theorem 16.33.6 give $U(tx)\geq \operatorname {arcosh}(t m_ K(x))$. Thus for $tr>1$ the last integral bounds $\operatorname {arcosh}(tr)\, \mu _ K\{ m_ K\geq r\} $. Take $t=r^{-2}$ to obtain the displayed layer estimate. Its right side tends to zero as $r\uparrow 1$, since $\log (1/r)/\operatorname {arcosh}(1/r)\to 0$. The decreasing layers have intersection $\partial K$, so finite-measure continuity proves zero boundary mass. The preceding interior-density formula, support on $K$ and total mass $M$ prove the remaining assertions. $\square$

title: 9.21 Hyperconvexity and the space of holomorphic functions
search_title: Hyperconvexity and the space of holomorphic functions
section: 9.21 Hyperconvexity and the space of holomorphic functions
text: Let $\Delta ^ n$ denote the unit polydisc. The space $\mathcal O(D)$ has its compact-open Fréchet topology. Isomorphisms below are continuous complex-linear bijections with continuous inverses; they need not preserve multiplication. Lemma 9.21.1 . EA48C877147E Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be bounded and hyperconvex. Put $H=A^2(D)$, with its usual Lebesgue $L^2$ norm, and let $B_ H$ be its closed unit ball. If $p$ is the $L^2$ norm on any relatively compact open subset of $D$, there are another compact-open continuous norm $q$ and $C>0$ such that, for every $r>0$, \[  \{ f\in \mathcal O(D):q(f)\leq 1\}  \subset CrB_ H+r^{-1}\{ f\in \mathcal O(D):p(f)\leq 1\} .  \] In particular $H$ is dense in $\mathcal O(D)$. Proof. Take a continuous negative PSH exhaustion $\rho $. The function $-\log (-\rho )$ is a PSH exhaustion, so $D$ is pseudoconvex. Choose $a<0$ so that the compact set used for $p$ lies in $\{ \rho <a\} $. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi $, equal to one on $\{ \rho \leq a/2\} $ and supported in $\{ \rho <a/4\} $. These sets are compactly nested, so the ordinary cutoff construction applies. Take a relatively compact open set $D_ m$ containing its support and the compact set for $p$, and set $q(f)=\| f\| _{L^2(D_ m)}$. For $L\geq 0$ put $P_ L=L\max \{ 0,\rho -a\} $. It is PSH, $0\leq P_ L\leq -aL$, vanishes on $\{ \rho \leq a\} $ and is at least $-aL/2$ on $\operatorname {supp}\bar\partial \chi $. Apply the weighted $L^2$ existence theorem with weight $P_ L+|z|^2$ to the closed form $f\bar\partial \chi $. Boundedness of $D$ and the fixed cutoff give a solution $v$ with \[  \bar\partial v=f\bar\partial \chi ,\qquad \int _ D|v|^2e^{-P_ L}\, dV\leq C_0e^{aL/2}q(f)^2.  \] The constant is independent of $L$ and $f$; the smooth part $|z|^2$ has Hessian equal to the identity and its exponential is bounded above and below on $D$. Thus \[  p(v)\leq C_1e^{aL/4}q(f),\qquad \| v\| _{L^2(D)}\leq C_1e^{-aL/4}q(f).  \] The distribution $g=\chi f-v$ is holomorphic on $D$ and belongs to $H$. On the set for $p$ the residual $f-g$ equals $v$. With $R=e^{-aL/4}\geq 1$ this gives $\| g\| _ H\leq C_2Rq(f)$ and $p(f-g)\leq C_1R^{-1}q(f)$. Replace $R$ by a fixed multiple of $r$ to make the second coefficient $r^{-1}$; enlarge the first constant. For the remaining bounded range of $r$, use $g=0$ and $p(f)\leq q(f)$, or the estimate with $R=1$, and enlarge the constant once more. This proves the inclusion for all $r>0$. These $L^2$ norms generate the compact-open topology by local submean estimates. Letting $r\to \infty $ proves density. $\square$ Lemma 9.21.2 . 8BD46FA4016F Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded domain and let $P\Subset D$ be a polydisc, with a concentric larger polydisc still compact in $D$. Let $H=A^2(D)$ and let $H_0$ be the closure of its restrictions in $L^2(P)$. The restriction $R:H\to H_0$ is injective and compact. After a fixed rescaling of the $H_0$ norm it has singular values $0<a_ j<1$ and orthonormal bases $(e_ j)$ of $H$ and $(b_ j)$ of $H_0$ with $Re_ j=a_ jb_ j$. There are constants $c,C>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $j$, \[  c j^{1/n}\leq -\log a_ j\leq C j^{1/n}.  \] Proof. Restriction is bounded and injective by the identity theorem. Local submean and Cauchy estimates give uniform bounds and equicontinuity on compact subsets for the unit ball of $H$. Compactness of restriction follows from finite coverings and the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem. We recall the elementary Hilbert argument which supplies its singular system. The compact positive operator $R^*R$ attains its largest Rayleigh quotient on the unit sphere. Indeed take a maximizing sequence, use weak Hilbert compactness and compactness of the operator to pass to the limit, and normalize the limit if necessary. Variation in directions orthogonal to a maximizing unit vector makes it an eigenvector. Repeat in its orthogonal complement. The positive eigenvalues tend to zero, since the images of an orthonormal sequence under a compact operator cannot stay separated. On the remaining orthogonal complement the operator vanishes; otherwise the same maximization would give another positive eigenvector; its eigenvalue would be bounded above by all the preceding eigenvalues, which tend to zero. Injectivity removes this kernel. Taking square roots of the eigenvalues gives $a_ j$ and $e_ j$; $b_ j=a_ j^{-1}Re_ j$ is orthonormal and complete because $R$ has dense range in $H_0$. Rescale the target norm so that $\| R\| <1$. Let $N_ m=\binom {m+n}{n}$, the dimension of polynomials of total degree at most $m$. Taylor truncation on the concentric polydiscs, with Cauchy estimates on the larger one, gives an operator of rank at most $N_ m$ approximating $R$ with error at most $C_0\theta ^ m$, where $0<\theta <1$. To be explicit, the coefficient bound is $C_1s^{-|\alpha |}\| f\| _ H$ on a larger polydisc of radius $s$; the tail on a smaller radius $t<s$ is bounded by $C_1\sum _{k>m}\binom {k+n-1}{n-1}(t/s)^ k\| f\| _ H$. This is at most $C_0\theta ^ m\| f\| _ H$ after slightly increasing $\theta $. The truncated polynomials lie in $H$, hence in the target closure. The singular system shows $a_{N_ m+1}\leq C_0\theta ^ m$: any rank-$N_ m$ operator has a kernel vector in the span of the first $N_ m+1$ singular vectors. Conversely enclose $D$ in a polydisc of radius $T$. Orthogonality of monomials on $P$ gives, for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $m$, a bound $\| p\| _ H\leq C_2C_3^ m\| p\| _{H_0}$. Indeed the squared norm of $z^\alpha $ on a polydisc of radius $t$ is $\pi ^ n\prod _{k=1}^ nt^{2\alpha _ k+2}/(\alpha _ k+1)$; apply Cauchy–Schwarz to its finite Taylor sum on the enclosing polydisc. The resulting polynomial factors in $m$ are absorbed by increasing $C_3>1$. Translation of the polydiscs and the fixed norm rescaling only change the constants. In the $N_ m$-dimensional polynomial subspace there is a unit vector orthogonal to $e_1,\ldots ,e_{N_ m-1}$. For that vector the singular expansion bounds the restricted norm above by $a_{N_ m}$, so $a_{N_ m}\geq C_2^{-1}C_3^{-m}$. Since $N_ m$ is comparable to $m^ n$, the two bounds prove the claim. In particular $\sum _ ja_ j^ t<\infty $ for every $t>0$. $\square$ Proposition 9.21.3 . 35087713FD64 For a bounded hyperconvex domain $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$, $\mathcal O(D)$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal O(\Delta ^ n)$ as a Fréchet space. It admits a basis which is orthonormal in $A^2(D)$. Proof. Put $E=\mathcal O(D)$ and use the Hilbert spaces and singular system of lemma 9.21.2 . Density from lemma 9.21.1 identifies $H_0$ also as the closure of restrictions of $E$. Its norm $p_0$ is a continuous norm on $E$. Choose increasing relatively compact open sets exhausting $D$, containing $P$, and let $p_ k$ be their $L^2$ norms, scaled if necessary so that $p_ k\geq p_0$. These generate the topology of $E$. First, for every $k$ there are $C_ k>0$ and $0<\lambda _ k<1$ such that, for $f\in H$, \[  p_ k(f)\leq C_ kp_0(f)^{\lambda _ k}\| f\| _ H^{1-\lambda _ k}.  \] Here is the propagation argument. Local submean estimates bound $f$ on a small ball in $P$ by $Cp_0(f)$, and on every fixed larger ball compact in $D$ by $C\| f\| _ H$. On three concentric balls the maximum-modulus bound is logarithmically convex in the logarithm of the radius: restrict to each complex line through the center and apply the subharmonic maximum principle to $\log |f|$ minus the harmonic interpolant in $\log |\zeta |$ on a planar annulus. Connect the initial ball to a finite covering of the compact set for $p_ k$ by finitely many overlapping balls, all with their fixed larger balls in $D$. Repeated three-radius interpolation propagates the initial estimate with an exponent which is a finite product of positive numbers less than one. This proves the inequality; take the smallest of the finitely many exponents, using $p_0\leq \| \cdot \| _ H$. Consequently $p_ k(e_ j)\leq C_ ka_ j^{\lambda _ k}$. Define $\ell _ j\in E'$ by $\ell _ j(f)=a_ j^{-1}\langle f|_ P,b_ j\rangle _{H_0}$. Its dual norm for $p_0$ is $a_ j^{-1}$ and its norm on $H$ is one. For a functional $\ell $ write $p_ k^*(\ell )$ for its supremum on the $p_ k$ unit ball and $p_ H^*(\ell )$ for its supremum on $B_ H$. The splitting lemma and optimization in $r>0$ give, for some $m=m(k)$, \[  p_ m^*(\ell )\leq C_ k' p_ H^*(\ell )^{1/2}p_ k^*(\ell )^{1/2}  \] whenever the quantities on the right are finite. Starting with $p_0$ and iterating gives, for every integer $s\geq 1$, an index $k_ s$ and a constant $A_ s$ independent of $j$ such that $p_{k_ s}^*(\ell _ j)\leq A_ sa_ j^{-2^{-s}}$. Thus, for every $t>0$, choose $s$ with $2^{-s}<t$ to obtain \[  \sum _ j|\ell _ j(f)|a_ j^ t \leq A_ sp_{k_ s}(f)\sum _ ja_ j^{t-2^{-s}}<\infty .  \] Conversely, if a sequence $(c_ j)$ satisfies $\sum _ j|c_ j|a_ j^ t<\infty $ for every $t>0$, then $\sum _ jc_ je_ j$ converges absolutely for every $p_ k$, by the primal interpolation bound. Completeness of $E$ gives its sum in $E$. The functionals satisfy $\ell _ j(e_ i)=\delta _{ij}$. For any $f\in E$, the series with $c_ j=\ell _ j(f)$ equals $f$: it converges in $E$ and in $H_0$, and its $H_0$ sum is precisely the orthonormal expansion in $(b_ j)$. The identity theorem identifies the functions on all of $D$. These estimates in both directions prove the topological isomorphism \[  E\simeq \{ (c_ j):\sum _ j|c_ j|a_ j^ t<\infty \text{ for every }t>0\} .  \] The basis $(e_ j)$ is also an orthonormal basis of $H$. Finally $-\log a_ j$ is comparable to $j^{1/n}$. Ordering the monomials of the unit polydisc by total degree gives the same sequence space: their degrees are comparable to $j^{1/n}$ after finitely many indices, and the Cauchy estimates identify compact-open convergence of Taylor series with $\sum _ j|c_ j|r^{\deg \alpha _ j}<\infty $ for every $r<1$. Changing the positive constants multiplying $j^{1/n}$ just changes the parameter $t>0$. This proves the asserted isomorphism. $\square$ Proposition 9.21.4 . 9028D1B15EA2 Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded domain of holomorphy. If $\mathcal O(D)\simeq \mathcal O(\Delta ^ n)$ as Fréchet spaces, then $D$ has a negative PSH exhaustion and is hyperconvex. Proof. Let $T:\mathcal O(\Delta ^ n)\to \mathcal O(D)$ be the isomorphism and put $f_\alpha =T(z^\alpha )$. For $\alpha \ne 0$ set $v_\alpha =|\alpha |^{-1}\log |f_\alpha |$. On every compact subset $K\Subset D$, continuity of $T$ gives constants $C_ K>0$, $r_ K<1$ such that $\sup _ K|f_\alpha |\leq C_ Kr_ K^{|\alpha |}$. The regularized tail envelopes \[  u_ m=\left(\sup _{|\alpha |\geq m}v_\alpha \right)^*,\qquad \rho =\lim _{m\to \infty }u_ m  \] are PSH and decrease; their limit is PSH or identically $-\infty $. The local uniform bound just obtained gives $\rho <0$ everywhere, and $\rho (z)\geq \limsup _{|\alpha |\to \infty }v_\alpha (z)$. Fix $0<r<1$ and choose $r<r_1<r_2<1$. If $\rho (z)\leq \log r$, there is a finite constant $A_ z$ such that $|f_\alpha (z)|\leq A_ zr_1^{|\alpha |}$ for every multi-index, including $\alpha =0$ after enlarging $A_ z$. For $g\in \mathcal O(D)$, expand $T^{-1}g=\sum c_\alpha z^\alpha $. Cauchy's coefficient estimate on the polydisc of radius $r_2$ gives \[  |g(z)|\leq A_ z\sum _\alpha |c_\alpha |r_1^{|\alpha |} \leq A_ zC_{r_1,r_2}\| T^{-1}g\| _{r_2\overline{\Delta }^ n}.  \] The Taylor expansion may be evaluated after $T$ because it converges in the compact-open topology and $T$ is continuous. Continuity of $T^{-1}$ gives one compact $L\Subset D$ and $C'>0$, depending on $r_2$ but not on $z$ or $g$, such that the last norm is at most $C'\| g\| _ L$. Apply this bound to $g^ k$, where $k$ is an arbitrary positive integer. Taking $k$th roots and letting $k\to \infty $ eliminates the finite constant $A_ zC_{r_1,r_2}C'$ and proves $|g(z)|\leq \| g\| _ L$. Although $T$ need not preserve multiplication, it applies to every $g^ k$ with the same estimate. Hence \[  \{ \rho \leq \log r\} \subset \widehat L_{\mathcal O(D)}\Subset D.  \] The last compactness is holomorphic convexity of a domain of holomorphy. If $\rho $ were identically $-\infty $, this inclusion would put the whole noncompact open domain $D$ in one compact subset of $D$, which is impossible. Thus $\rho $ is a negative PSH exhaustion. Apply proposition 7.25.1 to obtain a continuous negative PSH exhaustion, proving hyperconvexity. $\square$ Theorem 9.21.5 . EA836E82DAC5 For a bounded domain $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ the following are equivalent: $D$ is hyperconvex; $D$ is pseudoconvex and $\mathcal O(D)$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal O(\Delta ^ n)$ as a Fréchet space; for some $a\in D$, $g_ D(z,a)\to 0$ at every point of $\partial D$; the same boundary limit holds for every $a\in D$. Proof. A hyperconvex domain is pseudoconvex, and the Bergman sequence-space proposition proves the required linear isomorphism. Conversely the theorem 9.13.2 makes a pseudoconvex domain a domain of holomorphy, so the preceding proposition proves hyperconvexity. The last two equivalences are theorem 7.25.2 . $\square$

This is at most $C_0\theta ^ m\| f\| _ H$ after slightly increasing $\theta $. The truncated polynomials lie in $H$, hence in the target closure. The singular system shows $a_{N_ m+1}\leq C_0\theta ^ m$: any rank-$N_ m$ operator has a kernel vector in the span of the first $N_ m+1$ singular vectors. Conversely enclose $D$ in a polydisc of radius $T$. Orthogonality of monomials on $P$ gives, for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $m$, a bound $\| p\| _ H\leq C_2C_3^ m\| p\| _{H_0}$. Indeed the squared norm of $z^\alpha $ on a polydisc of radius $t$ is $\pi ^ n\prod _{k=1}^ nt^{2\alpha _ k+2}/(\alpha _ k+1)$; apply Cauchy–Schwarz to its finite Taylor sum on the enclosing polydisc. The resulting polynomial factors in $m$ are absorbed by increasing $C_3>1$. Translation of the polydiscs and the fixed norm rescaling only change the constants. In the $N_ m$-dimensional polynomial subspace there is a unit vector orthogonal to $e_1,\ldots ,e_{N_ m-1}$. For that vector the singular expansion bounds the restricted norm above by $a_{N_ m}$, so $a_{N_ m}\geq C_2^{-1}C_3^{-m}$. Since $N_ m$ is comparable to $m^ n$, the two bounds prove the claim. title: Proposition 9.21.3
section: 9.21 Hyperconvexity and the space of holomorphic functions
text: Proposition 9.21.3 . 35087713FD64 For a bounded hyperconvex domain $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$, $\mathcal O(D)$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal O(\Delta ^ n)$ as a Fréchet space. It admits a basis which is orthonormal in $A^2(D)$. Proof. Put $E=\mathcal O(D)$ and use the Hilbert spaces and singular system of lemma 9.21.2 . Density from lemma 9.21.1 identifies $H_0$ also as the closure of restrictions of $E$. Its norm $p_0$ is a continuous norm on $E$. Choose increasing relatively compact open sets exhausting $D$, containing $P$, and let $p_ k$ be their $L^2$ norms, scaled if necessary so that $p_ k\geq p_0$. These generate the topology of $E$. First, for every $k$ there are $C_ k>0$ and $0<\lambda _ k<1$ such that, for $f\in H$, \[  p_ k(f)\leq C_ kp_0(f)^{\lambda _ k}\| f\| _ H^{1-\lambda _ k}.  \] Here is the propagation argument. Local submean estimates bound $f$ on a small ball in $P$ by $Cp_0(f)$, and on every fixed larger ball compact in $D$ by $C\| f\| _ H$. On three concentric balls the maximum-modulus bound is logarithmically convex in the logarithm of the radius: restrict to each complex line through the center and apply the subharmonic maximum principle to $\log |f|$ minus the harmonic interpolant in $\log |\zeta |$ on a planar annulus. Connect the initial ball to a finite covering of the compact set for $p_ k$ by finitely many overlapping balls, all with their fixed larger balls in $D$. Repeated three-radius interpolation propagates the initial estimate with an exponent which is a finite product of positive numbers less than one. This proves the inequality; take the smallest of the finitely many exponents, using $p_0\leq \| \cdot \| _ H$. Consequently $p_ k(e_ j)\leq C_ ka_ j^{\lambda _ k}$. Define $\ell _ j\in E'$ by $\ell _ j(f)=a_ j^{-1}\langle f|_ P,b_ j\rangle _{H_0}$. Its dual norm for $p_0$ is $a_ j^{-1}$ and its norm on $H$ is one. For a functional $\ell $ write $p_ k^*(\ell )$ for its supremum on the $p_ k$ unit ball and $p_ H^*(\ell )$ for its supremum on $B_ H$. The splitting lemma and optimization in $r>0$ give, for some $m=m(k)$, \[  p_ m^*(\ell )\leq C_ k' p_ H^*(\ell )^{1/2}p_ k^*(\ell )^{1/2}  \] whenever the quantities on the right are finite. Starting with $p_0$ and iterating gives, for every integer $s\geq 1$, an index $k_ s$ and a constant $A_ s$ independent of $j$ such that $p_{k_ s}^*(\ell _ j)\leq A_ sa_ j^{-2^{-s}}$. Thus, for every $t>0$, choose $s$ with $2^{-s}<t$ to obtain \[  \sum _ j|\ell _ j(f)|a_ j^ t \leq A_ sp_{k_ s}(f)\sum _ ja_ j^{t-2^{-s}}<\infty .  \] Conversely, if a sequence $(c_ j)$ satisfies $\sum _ j|c_ j|a_ j^ t<\infty $ for every $t>0$, then $\sum _ jc_ je_ j$ converges absolutely for every $p_ k$, by the primal interpolation bound. Completeness of $E$ gives its sum in $E$. The functionals satisfy $\ell _ j(e_ i)=\delta _{ij}$. For any $f\in E$, the series with $c_ j=\ell _ j(f)$ equals $f$: it converges in $E$ and in $H_0$, and its $H_0$ sum is precisely the orthonormal expansion in $(b_ j)$. The identity theorem identifies the functions on all of $D$. These estimates in both directions prove the topological isomorphism \[  E\simeq \{ (c_ j):\sum _ j|c_ j|a_ j^ t<\infty \text{ for every }t>0\} .  \] The basis $(e_ j)$ is also an orthonormal basis of $H$. Finally $-\log a_ j$ is comparable to $j^{1/n}$. Ordering the monomials of the unit polydisc by total degree gives the same sequence space: their degrees are comparable to $j^{1/n}$ after finitely many indices, and the Cauchy estimates identify compact-open convergence of Taylor series with $\sum _ j|c_ j|r^{\deg \alpha _ j}<\infty $ for every $r<1$. Changing the positive constants multiplying $j^{1/n}$ just changes the parameter $t>0$. This proves the asserted isomorphism. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.21.4
section: 9.21 Hyperconvexity and the space of holomorphic functions
text: Proposition 9.21.4 . 9028D1B15EA2 Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded domain of holomorphy. If $\mathcal O(D)\simeq \mathcal O(\Delta ^ n)$ as Fréchet spaces, then $D$ has a negative PSH exhaustion and is hyperconvex. Proof. Let $T:\mathcal O(\Delta ^ n)\to \mathcal O(D)$ be the isomorphism and put $f_\alpha =T(z^\alpha )$. For $\alpha \ne 0$ set $v_\alpha =|\alpha |^{-1}\log |f_\alpha |$. On every compact subset $K\Subset D$, continuity of $T$ gives constants $C_ K>0$, $r_ K<1$ such that $\sup _ K|f_\alpha |\leq C_ Kr_ K^{|\alpha |}$. The regularized tail envelopes \[  u_ m=\left(\sup _{|\alpha |\geq m}v_\alpha \right)^*,\qquad \rho =\lim _{m\to \infty }u_ m  \] are PSH and decrease; their limit is PSH or identically $-\infty $. The local uniform bound just obtained gives $\rho <0$ everywhere, and $\rho (z)\geq \limsup _{|\alpha |\to \infty }v_\alpha (z)$. Fix $0<r<1$ and choose $r<r_1<r_2<1$. If $\rho (z)\leq \log r$, there is a finite constant $A_ z$ such that $|f_\alpha (z)|\leq A_ zr_1^{|\alpha |}$ for every multi-index, including $\alpha =0$ after enlarging $A_ z$. For $g\in \mathcal O(D)$, expand $T^{-1}g=\sum c_\alpha z^\alpha $. Cauchy's coefficient estimate on the polydisc of radius $r_2$ gives \[  |g(z)|\leq A_ z\sum _\alpha |c_\alpha |r_1^{|\alpha |} \leq A_ zC_{r_1,r_2}\| T^{-1}g\| _{r_2\overline{\Delta }^ n}.  \] The Taylor expansion may be evaluated after $T$ because it converges in the compact-open topology and $T$ is continuous. Continuity of $T^{-1}$ gives one compact $L\Subset D$ and $C'>0$, depending on $r_2$ but not on $z$ or $g$, such that the last norm is at most $C'\| g\| _ L$. Apply this bound to $g^ k$, where $k$ is an arbitrary positive integer. Taking $k$th roots and letting $k\to \infty $ eliminates the finite constant $A_ zC_{r_1,r_2}C'$ and proves $|g(z)|\leq \| g\| _ L$. Although $T$ need not preserve multiplication, it applies to every $g^ k$ with the same estimate. Hence \[  \{ \rho \leq \log r\} \subset \widehat L_{\mathcal O(D)}\Subset D.  \] The last compactness is holomorphic convexity of a domain of holomorphy. If $\rho $ were identically $-\infty $, this inclusion would put the whole noncompact open domain $D$ in one compact subset of $D$, which is impossible. Thus $\rho $ is a negative PSH exhaustion. Apply proposition 7.25.1 to obtain a continuous negative PSH exhaustion, proving hyperconvexity. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.21.5
section: 9.21 Hyperconvexity and the space of holomorphic functions
text: Theorem 9.21.5 . EA836E82DAC5 For a bounded domain $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ the following are equivalent: $D$ is hyperconvex; $D$ is pseudoconvex and $\mathcal O(D)$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal O(\Delta ^ n)$ as a Fréchet space; for some $a\in D$, $g_ D(z,a)\to 0$ at every point of $\partial D$; the same boundary limit holds for every $a\in D$. Proof. A hyperconvex domain is pseudoconvex, and the Bergman sequence-space proposition proves the required linear isomorphism. Conversely the theorem 9.13.2 makes a pseudoconvex domain a domain of holomorphy, so the preceding proposition proves hyperconvexity. The last two equivalences are theorem 7.25.2 . $\square$

title: 9.22 A smooth boundary for a proper biholomorphic image
search_title: A smooth boundary for a proper biholomorphic image
section: 9.22 A smooth boundary for a proper biholomorphic image
text: Lemma 9.22.1 . 9D4AAB621920 Let $(P,Q):\mathbb C^2\to \mathbb C^2$ be a polynomial automorphism and fix $S>1$. Put \[  D_0=\{ |P/S|<1\} ,\qquad D_ N=\{ |Q+T(P/S)^ N|<T\} ,\quad T=\lceil e^{\sqrt N}\rceil .  \] On any fixed ball, $\partial D_ N$ tends to $\partial D_0$ in $C^ m$ for every fixed $m$, with the interior sides agreeing. More precisely, given a ball $B_ R$, an integer $m$ and $\epsilon >0$, for sufficiently large $N$ there is a smooth diffeomorphism $\Phi _ N$ of $\mathbb R^4$, equal to the identity outside $B_{R+2}$, such that \[  \| \Phi _ N-\operatorname {id}\| _{C^ m} +\| \Phi _ N^{-1}-\operatorname {id}\| _{C^ m}<\epsilon , \qquad \Phi _ N(D_0)\cap B_ R=D_ N\cap B_ R.  \] The norms of differences include the zeroth derivative. Proof. Write $p=P/S$, $a=Q/T$ and $\delta _ N=(16\sqrt N)^{-1}$. All derivatives of $P,Q$ on $\overline B_{R+3}$ are fixed before $N$ is chosen. On the band $||p|-1|<2\delta _ N$ we have $|p|^ N\geq e^{-\sqrt N/4}$ for large $N$, so $|a/p^ N|<1/2$. The logarithm given by its power series at one therefore defines the smooth real function \[  r_ N=|p|^2\exp \left(\frac2N\operatorname {Re} \log (1+a/p^ N)\right)-1.  \] Its negative set on this band is exactly $D_ N$. For each fixed derivative order $l$, repeated product and chain differentiation gives \[  \| r_ N-(|p|^2-1)\| _{C^ l} \leq C_ lN^{A_ l}e^{-c\sqrt N}  \] on the band, for constants depending on the fixed polynomials and ball. Indeed derivatives of $p^{-N}$ contribute only powers of $N$ and bounded derivatives of $p$, while its size is at most $e^{\sqrt N/4}$; the factor $T^{-1}$ contributes $e^{-\sqrt N}$. Each term involving the logarithm has at least one such small factor. Its power series and all fixed-order differentiated series converge uniformly when $|a/p^ N|<1/2$. This proves the estimate, with some $c>0$. Outside the narrower band $||p|-1|<\delta _ N$, the two domains agree on the fixed ball: if $|p|\leq 1-\delta _ N$, then $|p^ N+a|\leq e^{-\sqrt N/16}+O(e^{-\sqrt N})<1$; if $|p|\geq 1+\delta _ N$, the reverse triangle inequality gives $|p^ N+a|\geq e^{\sqrt N/32}-O(e^{-\sqrt N})>1$. Choose a cutoff in $|p|$ which is one on the narrower band and zero outside the wider one. Its derivatives have only polynomial growth in $\sqrt N$. Multiplying the difference above by this cutoff and also by a spatial cutoff equal to one on $B_{R+2}$ and supported in $B_{R+3}$, then extending by zero, gives $e_ N$ with arbitrarily small $C^ l$ norm on the whole space. The function $|p|^2-1+e_ N$ defines $D_ N$ on the ball: on the transition band both unmodified defining functions have the same sign, so their convex interpolation preserves that sign. The gradient of $|p|^2-1$ is nonzero near $|p|=1$, since $P$ is a coordinate of an automorphism. It has a positive lower bound on the relevant compact band. The same holds for $r_ t=|p|^2-1+t e_ N$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, when $N$ is large. The vector field \[  X_ t=-e_ N\frac{\nabla r_ t}{|\nabla r_ t|^2}  \] is smooth on the band and zero near its edges. Extend it by zero there, and multiply by a spatial cutoff equal to one on $B_{R+1}$ and supported in $B_{R+2}$. Its time-one flow transports the two defining functions near $B_ R$, since $\frac d{dt}r_ t(\Phi _ t(x))=0$ there. The displacement can be made less than the spatial margin. The differential equations for the flow and its derivatives show that the flow and its inverse tend to the identity in $C^ m$ when $e_ N\to 0$ in $C^{m+1}$: differentiate the flow equation successively and integrate the resulting linear bounds. This proves all assertions. $\square$ Theorem 9.22.2 . CE10A564601F There is a proper domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^2$ with smooth boundary which is biholomorphic to $\mathbb C^2$. Proof. Fix a large integer $T_1>10$, let $F_1$ be the identity, and put $P_1=w$, $P_0=z$. Inductively choose integers $N_ j$ and $T_ j=\lceil e^{\sqrt{N_ j}}\rceil $, and let $H_ j$ add $T_ j(P_{j-1}/T_{j-1})^{N_ j}$ to the other coordinate of $F_{j-1}$. Thus $F_ j=H_ j\circ F_{j-1}$ is an alternating polynomial shear composition, with determinant one, and its newly changed coordinate is \[  P_ j=P_{j-2}+T_ j(P_{j-1}/T_{j-1})^{N_ j}.  \] Set $D_ j=\{ |P_ j|<T_ j\} $. The two coordinates $P_{j-1},P_{j-2}$ of $F_{j-1}$ form a polynomial automorphism, up to their order. Consequently the preceding lemma applies at every step. Take $R_ j=jR_0$, with $R_0>4T_1+10$, and a positive summable sequence $\epsilon _ j$ with $\sum \epsilon _ j<1/10$. Choose $N_ j\geq j^2$ sufficiently large that: $T_ j>2(j+2)$; there is a diffeomorphism $\Phi _ j$ transporting $D_{j-1}$ to $D_ j$ on $B_{R_ j}$, with both $\Phi _ j$ and its inverse within $\epsilon _ j$ of the identity in $C^ j$ on $\mathbb R^4$; $\| F_ j^{-1}-F_{j-1}^{-1}\| _{C^ j(\overline B_ j)}<2^{-j}$. All these conditions can be imposed at the same step. The second is the lemma, with all earlier polynomials fixed. For the third, on $B_{j+1}$ the inverse shear differs from the identity by a monomial with coefficient $T_ j/T_{j-1}^{N_ j}$. Its derivatives of each fixed order tend to zero because $j+1<T_{j-1}/2$ and $\log T_ j=O(\sqrt{N_ j})$. The derivatives of $F_{j-1}^{-1}$ are already fixed, so the chain rule in $F_ j^{-1}=F_{j-1}^{-1}\circ H_ j^{-1}$ proves the claim. Increase $T_1$ or use a smaller first target ball if necessary for the first step; the stated $T_1>10$ already suffices. We describe the local limit of the domains carefully. For fixed $k$, the compositions $\Phi _ j\circ \cdots \circ \Phi _{k+1}$ converge in $C^\infty $, together with their inverses, to a smooth diffeomorphism. To check this, fix a derivative order $m$. After finitely many indices all maps and their inverses are $C^ m$-close to the identity by a summable amount. The chain rule bounds their first derivatives by a convergent product; at each higher order it gives the same product times already bounded lower derivatives and a summable error. Induction gives bounded derivatives and the Cauchy property at every order. The inverse limits are inverses by uniform convergence and the common displacement bound. On $B_{R_ k-2}$ these compositions transport $D_ k$ to $D_ j$: all intermediate points move by less than $1/10$ and remain inside the balls where the transport identities hold. Thus $D_ j$ converges locally, with its interior side, to a smooth open set $D_\infty $. Equivalently, a point is in $D_\infty $ if a neighborhood of it is contained in all sufficiently late $D_ j$. The diffeomorphism description on each smaller ball proves this characterization and its consistency on overlaps. It also proves that the boundary is smooth, that compact interior sets eventually lie in $D_ j$, and that limits of bounded sequences $x_ j\in D_ j$ belong to $\overline{D_\infty }$. Since $D_1=\{ |w|<T_1\} $ and the total displacement is less than $1/10$, the limit contains a neighborhood of zero and excludes a neighborhood of $(0,2T_1)$. Let $\Omega $ be its component containing zero. It is proper and has smooth boundary: locally the interior side of a smooth hypersurface is connected, so a boundary patch of this component is a boundary patch of $D_\infty $. We next prove convergence of the forward maps on $\Omega $. Given a compact $K\Subset \Omega $, choose a connected relatively compact open neighborhood in $\Omega $ containing $K$ and zero. For all sufficiently large $j$ it lies in $D_ j$. The holomorphic functions $P_ j/T_ j$ map this neighborhood to the disc and vanish at zero. Normal-family compactness and the maximum principle give a constant $0<\eta _ K<1$ with $|P_ j/T_ j|\leq 1-\eta _ K$ on $K$ for all late $j$. Otherwise a locally uniform subsequential limit would have modulus one at an interior point and vanish at zero, a contradiction. Hence \[  \| F_{j+1}-F_ j\| _ K \leq T_{j+1}(1-\eta _ K)^{N_{j+1}}.  \] The series converges because $\log T_ j=O(\sqrt{N_ j})$ and $N_ j\geq j^2$. Thus $F_ j\to F$ locally uniformly on $\Omega $, and $\det F'=1$ by convergence of derivatives. By the third inductive condition, $G_ j=F_ j^{-1}$ converges locally uniformly on all of $\mathbb C^2$ to a holomorphic map $G$ with $\det G'=1$ and $G(0)=0$. If $V$ is a bounded target ball, then $G_ j(V)\subset D_ j$ for large $j$, since the active coordinate of $F_ j(G_ j(z))=z$ is bounded by the radius of $V<T_ j$. Local convergence of the domains and maps gives $G(V)\subset \overline{D_\infty }$. The map $G$ is open, so $G(\mathbb C^2)\subset \operatorname {int}\overline{D_\infty } =D_\infty $. Connectedness and $G(0)=0$ place its image in $\Omega $. For $x\in \Omega $, take limits in $G_ j(F_ j(x))=x$, using a fixed compact target neighborhood of $F(x)$, to get $G(F(x))=x$. For $z\in \mathbb C^2$, the points $G_ j(z)$ eventually lie in a fixed compact neighborhood of $G(z)\in \Omega $, so limits in $F_ j(G_ j(z))=z$ give $F(G(z))=z$. These identities prove that $F$ and $G$ are inverse biholomorphisms, completing the construction. $\square$

Thus $F_ j\to F$ locally uniformly on $\Omega $, and $\det F'=1$ by convergence of derivatives. By the third inductive condition, $G_ j=F_ j^{-1}$ converges locally uniformly on all of $\mathbb C^2$ to a holomorphic map $G$ with $\det G'=1$ and $G(0)=0$. If $V$ is a bounded target ball, then $G_ j(V)\subset D_ j$ for large $j$, since the active coordinate of $F_ j(G_ j(z))=z$ is bounded by the radius of $V<T_ j$. Local convergence of the domains and maps gives $G(V)\subset \overline{D_\infty }$. The map $G$ is open, so $G(\mathbb C^2)\subset \operatorname {int}\overline{D_\infty } =D_\infty $. Connectedness and $G(0)=0$ place its image in $\Omega $. For $x\in \Omega $, take limits in $G_ j(F_ j(x))=x$, using a fixed compact target neighborhood of $F(x)$, to get $G(F(x))=x$. For $z\in \mathbb C^2$, the points $G_ j(z)$ eventually lie in a fixed compact neighborhood of $G(z)\in \Omega $, so limits in $F_ j(G_ j(z))=z$ give $F(G(z))=z$. These identities prove that $F$ and $G$ are inverse biholomorphisms, completing the construction. $\square$

section: 16.43 Boundary flux and nonproper mass comparison
text: Proposition 16.43.1 . A9104D666EA7 Suppose that a proper domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is biholomorphic to $\mathbb C^ n$ and has a nonempty smooth boundary patch. Then there are smooth strictly PSH functions $u,v$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ such that \[  0<\tfrac 12\leq u\leq v,\qquad u-v\longrightarrow 0\quad \text{at infinity},\qquad \int _{\mathbb C^ n}(dd^ cu)^ n> \int _{\mathbb C^ n}(dd^ cv)^ n,  \] and both integrals are finite. In particular $u=v+o(v)$ at infinity. The smooth domain constructed above gives such functions in dimension two. Proof. Let $F:\mathbb C^ n\to \Omega $ be a biholomorphism. In a ball $U$ meeting the smooth patch choose a smooth defining function $r$, negative on $\Omega \cap U$, with $dr\ne 0$ on its boundary. Choose $0\leq \chi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$ nonzero at a boundary point and extend $\psi =\chi r$ by zero to $\mathbb C^ n$. Thus $\psi $ is smooth, compactly supported, nonpositive on $\Omega $, and zero on all of $\partial \Omega $. Set $\gamma (w)=\tfrac 12\log (1+|w|^2)$ and $\phi _\epsilon =\gamma +\epsilon \psi $. For sufficiently small $\epsilon >0$, the function $\phi _\epsilon $ is strictly PSH on $\mathbb C^ n$: on the compact support of the perturbation the smallest eigenvalue of $dd^ c\gamma $ has a positive lower bound and $dd^ c\psi $ is bounded. Decrease $\epsilon $ also so that $\epsilon \| \psi \| _\infty <1/2$. Put \[  v=1+\gamma \circ F,\qquad u=1+\phi _\epsilon \circ F.  \] They are smooth and strictly PSH, and $1/2\leq u\leq v$. For $t>0$, the set $\{ w\in \overline\Omega \cap \operatorname {supp}\psi :|\psi (w)|\geq t\} $ is compact and disjoint from $\partial \Omega $, hence compact in $\Omega $. Its inverse image under the homeomorphism $F$ is compact. This proves $\psi \circ F\to 0$ at infinity, uniformly in the usual outside-compact sense. Since $v\geq 1$, it also proves the asserted relative asymptotic equality. At points tending to the finite boundary patch the values of $\gamma $ stay bounded, while their inverse images under $F$ leave every compact set. Thus $v$ is not an exhaustion. Write $\omega =dd^ c\gamma $ and $\omega _\epsilon =dd^ c\phi _\epsilon $. The forms are closed and strictly positive. Stokes' formula, with the boundary oriented outward, gives \[  \int _\Omega (\omega _\epsilon ^ n-\omega ^ n) =\epsilon \int _{\partial \Omega \cap U} d^ c\psi \wedge \sum _{j=0}^{n-1} \omega _\epsilon ^ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1-j}>0.  \] Indeed the difference is the exterior derivative of the compactly supported form on the right. One may apply Stokes in a bounded boundary chart; the integrand vanishes on the artificial outer boundary. On $\partial \Omega $, $d^ c\psi =\chi d^ cr$. The positive oriented-boundary calculation of proposition 16.35.5 shows that wedging this with a strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form gives a nonnegative density, strictly positive where $\chi >0$. This set contains a relatively open piece of the boundary, proving strictness. Both $\gamma $ and $\phi _\epsilon $ equal $\gamma $ outside a compact set and belong to the logarithmic full-growth class. Their full-space top masses are $2^{-n}$ by proposition 13.5.1 ; in particular their masses on $\Omega $ are finite. Biholomorphic change of variables identifies these restricted masses with those of $v$ and $u$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, respectively. The strict Stokes inequality proves the conclusion. $\square$ Corollary 16.43.2 . BD99C3A4D1ED There are positive smooth strictly PSH functions $u,v$ on $\mathbb C^2$ with $u-v\to 0$ at infinity and finite total Monge–Ampère masses, such that $\int (dd^ cu)^2>\int (dd^ cv)^2$. Proof. Apply the proposition to the smooth proper biholomorphic image constructed in theorem 9.22.2 . $\square$
